articles.title: UK economy grows at fastest rate for more than two years
articles.standfirst: ﻿The UK economy grew by 0.7% in the three months to September, according to official figures.
paragraphs: ﻿The UK economy grew at its fastest rate for more than two years in the three months to September.
Between July and September, the economy expanded by 0.7%, accelerating from the three months previously, official figures show.
The robust growth suggests a far more resilient economy than expected over the summer, despite the impact of higher energy prices from the Iran war.

Strong growth in the services sector - the largest part of the economy, which includes non-physical goods such as consultancy services and computer programming as well as hotels and restaurants - helped boost the numbers.
Within services, computer programming registered its fastest growth for the past three years, helped by AI linked spending.
The boost from computer programming and consultancy services has been the biggest driver of growth so far this year.
Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the Office for National Statistics, said it was "possible growth could have been even stronger" if there hadn't been a war in the Middle East.
But he says households may still not feel better off, and that prices might soon start to rise more quickly than wages.
However, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures were "welcome news".
He said: "Despite a year where events around the world have pushed up costs here at home, our economy is growing, bringing hope for the future.
The latest figures put the UK on course to be the second fastest growing economy across the major G7 countries which also includes Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France.
However, Jake Finney, senior economist at consultancy PwC, cautioned that growth was likely to slow over the coming months "unless energy markets stabilise".
A sharp rise in energy bills is forecast for January, which is likely to hit consumer spending and confidence, he said.
Entrepreneur Richard Benc says the UK watch market and exports have been surprisingly resilient
Richard Benc, founder of mechanical watch company Studio Underdog, says sales are better than he expected.
"We've seen more resilience than we had forecast for and expected. We are still projecting growth this year," he says.

The business exports about 80% of its watches. "We've seen a surprising amount of resilience, particularly from our US customers," he adds, although some UK customers are now taking longer to buy watches.
Do you have any views, comments or questions about this story?

articles.title: Gas bills to rise as Middle East turmoil persists
articles.standfirst: Gas bills will increase by about 5% from 1 December, Island Energy announces.
paragraphs: Island Energy said customers can contact its customer team for support
Gas customers in Jersey will see their bills increase by about 5% from 1 December after Island Energy announced a rise in tariffs for households and businesses.
The company said its mains gas, mini bulk tank and cylinder tariffs would increase by 1p per kilowatt hour (kWh) for all domestic and commercial customers from 1 December 2026.
It said the increase reflected higher wholesale gas and liquefied petroleum gas costs amid disruption to exports and shipping routes in the Middle East after the conflict with Iran.
Chief executive Graeme Millar said: "We recognise that any price increase is unwelcome, particularly during winter."
Securing fuel at lower prices in advance had limited the impact of wholesale cost increases on customers, Millar said.
However, the energy boss added: "It cannot fully protect customers from sustained increases in the cost of fuel and bringing it to Jersey."
Island Energy said customers concerned about paying their gas bills could contact its customer team to discuss what support might be available.

articles.title: The UK-EU summit will be a test of the political salience of Brexit
articles.standfirst:
The UK-EU summit will be a test of the political salience of Brexit sam.macrory Thu, 12/11/2026 - 09:00 What are they key issues to look for as Andy Burnham seeks a new EU deal? 5 Comment Jill Rutter Institute for Government Yes Andy Burnham is set to test the politics of Brexit - and the appetite for reopening debate. International relations Economy Foreign affairs Trade Immigration Labour Burnham government
No

Dynamic alignment. Derogations or carve-outs. Transitions. Youth mobility. Preferential university fees. Budget contributions. Commission oversight. ECJ jurisdiction. 

All these terms in the EU lexicon would have been highly contentious and provoked huge debate and division in the first post-Brexit decade. A Labour prime minister would see a pragmatic softening of a deal that made life a nightmare for too many British businesses exporting to Europe. Others would have portrayed such a move as a pathetic betrayal of the 52% who voted Leave by Brexit loyalists.

So the scale and vehemence of opposition to “undoing” Brexit will be the first issue to look out for when Andy Burnham heads to Brussels. There will still be some voices of protest, and the Conservatives have said they will tear up any agreements the PM reaches. But at this year's Conservative conference Kemi Badenoch's biggest argument against reopening the Brexit debate was asking her audience if they could “imagine having to go through that again”. It was hardly the staunchest defence of Brexit. Nigel Farage, meanwhile. proved surprisingly camera shy when Keir Starmer launched these negotiations at the first summit 18 months ago. 

Reaction to whatever is agreed on youth experience will be worth watching

When, in spring 2024, the European Commission first floated the idea of putting youth mobility into any future discussions with the UK, the Guardian managed a headline about the Commission plotting a return of “free movement” (which it certainly was not). Both mainstream parties rushed to denounce it as the general election approached, and then the newly-elected Labour government repeatedly rejected any suggestion that it was prepared to countenance a youth mobility scheme. But even Keir Starmer was forced to come round as he realised this was one of the EU’s few demands, and that it would not budge on other aspects of the reset until he was prepared to look at this issue. It turned out too that the British public was much more relaxed about a limited scheme for under-30s than much of the political class. 

That said, the details of the youth experience scheme have proved hard to agree. There is the problem that the Commission itself cannot guarantee that member states, who have competence on migration from third countries, will let young Brits come to work or study. Then there was the EU’s objection to UK demands for an annual cap – and it will be interesting to see where that number settles. But most difficult of all has been the EU demand, not mentioned in last May’s Common Understanding (the summit communique), that any EU student studying in the UK should only pay home fees. That puts a potentially big price tag on the scheme, with either UK universities losing a chunk of income, or the government footing the bill – a bill that would come on top of the hefty contribution the UK had already agreed to reassociate with the Erasmus programme in 2027, and one that it is likely to increase when/if it reassociates for the next multi-year budget period when the UK’s bill may well go up.

The EU will be unwilling to operationalise the deals on agriculture and emissions until the UK settles the issue on student fees of the new deal. But in any case, although youth mobility is not freedom of movement, it will be interesting to see if the prospect of thousands of young Europeans being able to come here again (and young Brits going in the other direction) provokes more than a shrug. 

Can Andy Burnham secure any comfort on Made in Europe – and at what price? 

Since the initial Common Understanding was agreed, a new problem has emerged for the prime minister – the risk to UK manufacturing supply chains of the EU’s more protectionist Made in Europe stance. This is not aimed at the UK – but it risks being collateral damage unless the prime minister can convince the EU that the UK (and potentially other third country trade partners too) should sneak inside the EU’s protective wall. But that will not be costless. A proposal from German chancellor Friedrich Merz and French president Emmanuel Macron would see the UK exempted from Made in Europe restrictions on cars, provided it agreed to align its external tariff with the EU’s to prevent it being a backdoor route for Chinese EVs into the EU.

More generally it will be interesting to see what, if any, carve-outs from EU regulations the UK has secured as part of its commitment to realign with EU rules on agrifood exports and to join the EU emissions trading scheme – and the extent to which that triggers a row over energy prices. Ditto the scale of the UK contribution towards the administration of these schemes – and how far the UK government can claim there are offsetting domestic savings. Last, but not least, we may learn more about what the famed ambition for “decision-shaping”, designed to sweeten the pill of rule-taking, looks like in practice.

The prime minister has promised a speech setting out future options. Whatever happens next week, it may well be overshadowed by what Andy Burnham says about the destination beyond the summit. That will be the real test of the current state of the politics of Brexit.

 

On 20 November Andy Burnham goes to Brussels for his first formal summit with the European Union. articles.title: The top cities in Central Asia and the South Caucasus in 2026
articles.standfirst: While rarely recognised as such, the major cities of Central Asia and the South Caucasus are among the most dynamic urban economies in the world.
paragraphs: Often overlooked in favour of the rapidly growing cities in China and India, and far from matching the economic might of those in North America and Europe, Central Asia and the South Caucasus rarely feature in discussions of the world’s leading city economies. Yet, a closer look at the region’s major cities in our 2026 Global Cities Index reveals strengths that should not be ignored, including impressive standings across Human Capital and Economics metrics.

While rarely recognised as such, the major cities of Central Asia and the South Caucasus are among the most dynamic urban economies in the world. Over the next 25 years, we forecast real GDP growth across 10 of the region’s largest city economies to average 4.1% per year, well ahead of the 2.7% average across Asia Pacific’s cities. This growth is led by some of the fastest-expanding cities anywhere globally, with Tashkent (Uzbekistan) and Bishkek (Kyrgyzstan) both ranking among the top 10 of the 1,000 cities covered in our 2026 Global Cities Index. By 2050, we forecast the region’s combined city GDP to be more than two and a half times what it is today.

Yet, the region’s cities are far from matching the economic might of megacities in North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific, and have remained outside the upper reaches of our 2026 Global Cities Index, held back by weaker Governance and Environment scores. But with the region taking on a growing role as a key trade route between China and Europe, a closer look reveals strengths that should not be ignored. Robust economic growth is augmented by impressive standings across Human Capital, reflecting a large, growing, and increasingly skilled population that is set to underpin its rise in the decades ahead.

The strongest-performing category for the region’s cities is Human Capital, ranking highest of all five components for eight of the 10 cities we cover. In fact, four of these cities hold places among the top 150 cities for Human Capital globally, including Almaty and Astana in Kazakhstan at 66th and 98th, respectively, Tashkent (Uzbekistan) in 108th, and Ashgabat (Turkmenistan) at 146th.

For many of these cities, this strength rests on a solid educational foundation. Baku’s universities rank 57th globally, closely followed by Almaty’s at 67th, with the Kazakh city home to almost a third of the country’s university students. Kazakhstan has also moved to deepen its talent pool by attracting leading international institutions, with more than 30 foreign university branches now in operation, including Cardiff University’s Astana campus, the only Russell Group campus in Central Asia. Educational attainment is high across the region too, most notably in Tbilisi, which ranks 36th in the world for the mean years of schooling among its adult residents.

Crucially, the region’s highly educated labour force is also growing quickly. Unlike many advanced economies grappling with ageing populations and rapidly declining fertility rates, these cities are home to some of the fastest-growing populations in the world. Astana, Almaty, Dushanbe, and Bishkek all rank among the top 10% of cities globally for population growth, led by Astana in 16th, whose population is set to double by 2050. Over the next 25 years, we project that the region’s major cities will add more than 8 million residents. The pace of growth, however, is stronger in Central Asian cities than it is for those in the South Caucasus: Yerevan (Armenia), for example, is forecast to see its population decline, reflecting its more mature demographic profile.

This growing population is translating into rapidly expanding levels of employment. Employment growth across much of the region ranks among the fastest in the world, with Dushanbe (23rd) and Astana (25th) both in the global top 25. Combined with rising productivity, this trend is set to power the region’s rapid economic growth, increasing income level, and consumer appetite in the decades ahead.

Tashkent offers one of the clearest examples of the region’s best strengths and overall potential, and features in the new Cities to Watch section of our 2026 report. While the Uzbek capital ranks 343rd overall, it posts the region’s highest Economics score (188th), underpinned by its fast economic growth forecast and favourable score for economic stability. We expect its economy to grow on average by 6.2% a year over the next 25 years, the seventh-fastest of any city globally, putting it on course to overtake Almaty as the region’s largest city economy within the next few years, and even to outgrow established European capitals such as Rome and Vienna by 2050.

Much of this momentum stems from Uzbekistan’s programme of economic liberalisation and opening to international markets, with construction- and investment-led expansions taking place across a range of sectors. The city is emerging as a regional leader in technology and finance, anchored by the Tashkent IT Park, while ‘New Tashkent’, a large-scale megaproject to build a modern city district, is fuelling construction activity. Its position along the Middle Corridor trade route connecting Europe and Asia is further cementing its role as a key regional logistics hub.

Tashkent’s skills base is another key attraction, with its universities among the best in the region and a growing pool of skilled labour drawing in businesses. As GDP per capita is still relatively low, the city has considerable room for catch-up growth, with productivity forecast to almost triple by 2050. However, this income gap also raises the risk of talent leaving for wealthier countries. Environmental pressures, particularly water stress (with Uzbekistan relying on external sources for 80% of its water) and high housing costs also weigh on its overall standing. How effectively these challenges are managed will shape whether Tashkent can sustain its momentum and growing regional leadership.

Indeed, sustaining the region’s urban growth momentum and ascent up our overall rankings will depend on addressing several key weaknesses. For most Central Asia and South Caucasus cities, Governance and Environment rank among their weakest categories. All 10 place outside the global top 500 for civil liberties and the global top 600 for temperature anomalies. High emissions intensities and poor air quality also weigh on Environment scores, particularly in Tashkent, Ashgabat, and Dushanbe. Strengthening institutions and addressing these environmental pressures will be key to ensuring the region’s growth translates into lasting prosperity and quality of life for residents.

Overall, the major cities of Central Asia and the South Caucasus are quietly emerging as a new frontier for growth, from the region’s highest-ranked cities Almaty and Astana to the rapid ascent of Tashkent. With a large, growing, and increasingly skilled population, the region is one that business decision makers would do well to watch closely in the years ahead.
To explore the full rankings and see how other cities perform, visit the 2026 Global Cities Index site.

articles.title: Robot vessels take on the dangerous work of mine hunting
articles.standfirst: The conflict in the Gulf is an opportunity for the US to test its autonomous mine-hunting systems.
paragraphs: This South Korean vessel is among the ships damaged in the Strait of Hormuz
Traversing the Strait of Hormuz remains one of the most dangerous trips a vessel can take.
Despite assistance from the US Navy, ships are still being attacked.

"To transit the Strait of Hormuz you need agreement between the captain and the crew to take the risk. You need war risk insurance. And the captain has to make the final decision," says Steve Cameron, a former merchant navy officer and maritime consultant.
Missiles and drones are a threat from the air, but under the surface mines may also be lurking.
"If you're a captain, you'd like to see evidence mines aren't present," Cameron adds.
Modern mines rest on the seabed and detonate when they detect an acoustic or magnetic signal, triggering a pressure wave that will break the keel of a passing vessel.
Others can rise through shallow waters or float, or be powered towards a target.
The technology itself is not difficult or costly, but the mere threat can stop a tanker fleet from sailing.
Ian McFarlane of French defence group Thales is a naval architect who knows mine warfare well. "Mines are a very cheap way of waging a naval war, as the Royal Navy is acutely aware," he says.
Finding sea mines has traditionally been the job of specialist mine-hunting vessels, with crews of around 80 sailors.
To keep humans out of harm's way, an increasing amount of the work is done by systems that are autonomous and monitored from the shore.
They might only need 20 personnel, working in shifts on land. With the recruitment and retention challenges facing Nato navies these highly-portable robot systems are very attractive.
Such tech has been under development for 20 years.
During the 2003 Iraq war the US Navy poked around the seabed looking for mines with a torpedo-shaped robot called the Remus 100.
Pinging around with sonar these little machines operated down to around 100ft depth and spared divers a difficult and dangerous task.
Iran's military published this picture of a US submersible captured in the Gulf
The latest conflict in the Gulf is testing much more capable systems.
The US military is sparing with details about their mine-hunting craft, but we have seen glimpses of them.
Iranian forces hauled an uncrewed US autonomous sub out of the waters of the Strait of Hormuz in early September.

The Pentagon claimed this robot, an Extra Large Uncrewed Underwater Vehicle (XLUUV) from US autonomous defence tech venture Anduril, was a malfunctioning older device with no classified equipment on-board.

Whatever its mission, no sailors were imperilled. That, says William Lupton, a naval analyst with Shephard Group, "was a drop in the ocean compared to having prisoners taken", and part of the point of uncrewed vessels.

What if an uncrewed vessel is captured? Nato navies are reluctant to go into details, but computer drives can be wiped or destroyed remotely by various means. This may have taken place inside the humming circuit boards of the XLUUV seized by Iran.
The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle is packed with sensors
Such autonomous tech is being embraced by forces around the world.
Cooperation between Thales, the Royal Navy, and France's Marine Nationale has produced a robot motor launch.
The Thales Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) is packed with sensors programmed to detect mines via sonar that was developed for the oil and gas industries.

It tows a 5m long rectangular box, similar to a large torpedo, that takes a hi-resolution look at the seabed and creates a 3D picture refined by AI. The latest mines are designed to blend into their surroundings and the software spots anything that looks like a mine.
Autonomous systems are cheaper than conventional minehunters, plus they can be deployed, along with containerised control centres, by air.
Steve Prest, associate fellow at the RUSI defence think tank, introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy and was its first fleet robotics officer, a title he acquired in 2014.
"There is a bunch of ways to look for a mine using robot boats or robot subs, and while you can't prove the negative, that no mines are there, you can reduce the risk."
He says US robot minehunters can either blow up a mine or just mark the spot as somewhere to avoid.
"We'll see more use of autonomy but also the missions and capability will expand. And AI will be analysing data from those vessels on the spot as opposed to data being analysed when a drone returns."

The Royal Navy recently announced its concept of a hybrid navy - mixing drones with conventional warships. But Prest thinks for this vision to succeed the fleet must operate as one distributed force, sharing data in what he terms a cognitive architecture.

The robot only makes a real difference as part of this scheme and it's a mistake to focus on individual uncrewed assets. "Uncrewed or autonomous vessels are not the operating system. They are applications running on it."
Steve Prest introduced uncrewed mine hunting into the Royal Navy
While robots are on the rise, people are what really matter in the Strait.

Neil Roberts speaks for insurers at Lloyd's of London on marine matters and says the psychological impact of the mine threat is inescapable, as is the uncertainty around just how many mines, if any, are out there.
"The US says it has cleared the Omani route and believes the mine threat is being managed, with shipments running at about 75% of pre-conflict levels."
Fear of the unknown is the most potent aspect of the sea mine threat and robots are now the weapon of choice to confront that fear.

articles.title: Burnham’s choices are about political economy, not theories of growth
articles.standfirst:
Andy Burnham declared in his first speech as Prime Minister that he has a theory of growth, something his predecessor was criticised for lacking. But Jo Michell argues that not even economists have coherent theories of growth. Instead, Burnham should make an ideological decision: does he believe the Government should have an active role when … Continued
The post Burnham’s choices are about political economy, not theories of growth first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Andy Burnham declared in his first speech as Prime Minister that he has a theory of growth, something his predecessor was criticised for lacking. But Jo Michell argues that not even economists have coherent theories of growth. Instead, Burnham should make an ideological decision: does he believe the Government should have an active role when it comes to shaping the economy or not.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

In the run up to the Budget, former Bank of England chief economist Andy Haldane laid out a stark choice: 1950s-style big-state socialism with Burnham or 1980s-style small-state capitalism with Badenoch; “the rightward fork is far more likely to succeed”, he concluded. Given this framing, anyone inclined towards the leftward fork was likely disappointed by Healey’s first Budget, which entailed little more than minor fiscal tinkering. The contrast with Burnham’s rhetoric about overturning forty years of neoliberalism was hard to miss.

Healey’s “do no harm” strategy is, in a way, a mirror image of that adopted by Reeves who, despite her cautious technocratic language, substantially increased the size of the state: across her two Budgets, Reeves raised taxes by around £66bn a year and increased spending by around £70bn a year, pushing the tax take towards a post-war high of 38 per cent of GDP.
The choice Burnham faces is not between the right or wrong theory of growth – even economists don’t really have those. Burnham’s choice is an ideological one.

Debates about economic policy are almost invariably (and often unhelpfully) framed in terms of the implications for growth. The Economist, in a pre-budget column which focused mainly on the Chancellor’s lack of hair (the word “bald” appears fifteen times), decried the Chancellor’s apparent lack of a “theory of growth”. This phrase went viral following a post by political scientist Ben Ansell which argued that Starmer and Reeves had adopted an incoherent pick-and-mix approach to growth theory. In an impressive case of academic “impact”, Andy Burnham, in his first speech as prime minister felt compelled to declare, “I have a theory of growth”. While Starmer and Reeves were excoriated for their lack of a theory, Burnham’s critics acknowledge that he has one, but claim that it is inadequate or wrong. But the choice Burnham faces is not between the right or wrong theory of growth – even economists don’t really have those. Burnham’s choice is an ideological one: does he or does he not believe in a stronger role for the state in managing the economy?

The demand that politicians possess a theory of growth is puzzling given that economists, for the most part, do not have one. In the 1950s, the seminal Solow growth model assigned all growth unexplained by increased employment or capital investment to an unexplained residual, “total factor productivity” – “a measure of our ignorance” as Abramovitz memorably put it. Despite decades of intervening effort – and several million statistical analyses – economists have made little progress in coming up with a more complete answer beyond “it’s complicated”.

Given that economists have only a vague idea where growth comes from (I disagree with Giles Wilkes’ assertion that “the attributes … are widely known”), asking politicians to enunciate their theory of it will produce little of interest. They will usually explain why the things they already plan to do will lead to growth. The reality is that growth can occur under a wide range of circumstances for a wide range of reasons. Politicians can therefore either do what they think is best and hope for growth, or they can incoherently pursue growth as an objective in itself – a pursuit which can be actively harmful if adopted on the basis of misguided theory.

One widely held view, for example, is that lower interest rates provide a route to higher growth. This was central to George Osborne’s justification for austerity: lower borrowing would lead to lower interest rates and thus resurgent growth. Echoes of this position could be heard from Reeves: she presented her November 2025 Budget as giving the Bank room to cut rates. Yet there is no mainstream economic theory in which lower interest rates lead to higher long term growth.

There are ultimately two main views on how to manage the economy. These are better described as ideologies than theories. The first, which broadly coincides with the post-war experience in the UK, holds that the government has an important role in managing the composition and level of economic activity, and in determining the distribution of income.

The opposing view is that government is a hindrance to economic progress and should be kept out of the way: deregulation, privatisation, and cuts to government spending will, in Haldane’s view, “unleash animal spirits” (an odd choice of phrase given that it originates with Keynes, who is associated with the former position). But there is little compelling evidence to suggest that the “rightward fork” will lead to better economic outcomes; the policy shift of the 1980s was not followed by sustained higher growth rates.
There are ultimately two main views on how to manage the economy. These are better described as ideologies than theories.

In recent times, no government has cleanly adopted either ideological approach, with policy often reflecting an incoherent mix of the two. A pure small-state or large-state strategy is, of course, impossible: all rich economies combine a significant state footprint with a more or less regulated private sector. Nonetheless, lack of ideological coherence has led recent UK governments to something approaching the worst of both worlds.

One widespread criticism of Burnham conflates his rejection of the post-1980s policy turn with a desire to return to the earlier post-war era. Martin Wolf, chief economics commentator at the Financial Times responded to Burnham’s list of post-1980 policy errors with, “Did the pre-Thatcher UK of the 1970s work well? No”. Burnham’s own invocations of 1945 invite the comparison, but this is a non-sequitur: pointing out the errors of the last four decades is not an argument for a return to the pre-1980 status quo.

Even if a return to the postwar era were desirable, it would not be attainable. Trade unions were strong, global trade was less developed and China was yet to emerge as a manufacturing powerhouse. The post-war UK economy operated in a world of fixed exchange rates, a dollar standard and capital controls. The breakdown of this institutional framework in the 1970s was one of the drivers of the Thatcherite turn.

The mobility of finance, in particular, makes a return to something akin to the post-war social democratic policy framework implausible. The disconnect between Healey’s “do no harm” budget and Burham’s rhetoric makes more sense when looked at in the light of increased financial mobility. Given the determination of Labour’s opponents (and much of the press) to talk up policy-induced bond market instability, Healey’s caution is understandable. If avoiding market ructions was his primary objective, the budget was a success. Perhaps paradoxically, Reeves’ courage on taxation provided Healey the short run cover to do nothing.

But the big decisions must soon be faced. At some point, Burnham and Healey will have to decide if, as their critics claim, they are standard bearers for big government. In the aftermath of the pandemic, with an ageing population and a growing population of the economically inactive, the state is going to be larger not smaller. Creative accounting or adjustments to fiscal rules could enable public corporations to increase their borrowing and raise investment – one of the few things that most economists agree would probably be good for growth. But much of the increase in state capacity will have to be funded out of taxation. Healey and Burnham can only ignore this reality for so long, and no theory of growth will save them from it

Jo Michell is Professor of Economics at UWE Bristol, Chair of the Post-Keynesian Economics Society, and Fellow of the Forum for Macroeconomics and Macroeconomic Policies of the Hans-Böckler Foundation and a member of the Progressive Economy Forum Council. He was a founder of Reteaching Economics.

articles.title: KPMG M&A Outlook 2027: From market resilience to renewed deal activity
articles.standfirst: Despite economic and geopolitical disruption, Germany's M&A market held firm in 2026. Activity is expected to strengthen from 2027, supported by international investment, public spending, and business succession, with deal counts forecast to peak in 2028.
paragraphs: Discover how international investment and AI are shaping Germany’s M&A outlook through 2030.

In collaboration with KPMG Germany, Oxford Economics surveyed over 200 M&A decision-makers from German corporates, private equity funds, and family offices. We combined their insights with transaction data and economic forecasts to examine the forces shaping German dealmaking.

German M&A proved resilient in 2026 despite weak domestic growth, higher borrowing costs, and geopolitical disruption. International interest was particularly strong, led by US investors seeking German industrial and technology assets.

The outlook for 2027 is cautiously positive. Nearly half of respondents expect German M&A activity to increase. Our modelling forecasts deal counts to rise through 2028, supported by SMEs succession, international investment, and the gradual effect of public spending.
AI is also changing how and why deals are pursued. Adoption in M&A processes has doubled, although most firms still rely on general-purpose tools.

Max is based in the London office and supports the Thought Leadership team across business sectors and disciplines. Max graduated from the University of Warwick with a BA in Politics, International Studies and Quantitative Methods and an MSc in Behavioural and Data Science.

Often this is in collaboration with his economist colleagues to blend qualitative and quantitative analysis, and to explore the impact of corporate actions at a business, industry and economy level.

John joined Oxford Economics in 2014, after 25 years as a Financial Controller, financial management consultant and, most recently, a thought leadership expert for IBM’s Institute for Business Value, focused on global public sector issues. Prior to joining Oxford Economics, she was Practice Lead for Trade Analysis with Expeditors, a global logistics company, and Head of Global Economics with FrontierView. Prior to joining Oxford Economics, Alice worked for a technology start-up focused on food sustainability. articles.title: Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough
articles.standfirst:
Discover how AI advancements will reshape global economies, boosting knowledge
sectors while traditional industries face challenges in growth.
paragraphs: Discover how AI advancements will reshape global economies, boosting knowledge sectors while traditional industries face challenges in growth.

Knowledge-intensive service sectors are set to benefit significantly from advancements in AI technology. By 2040, global gross value added (GVA) is projected to rise by approximately 6% higher than our baseline forecast in this scenario, with sectors like information and communications technology (ICT) and financial services seeing GVA around 9% to 10% above baseline.

In contrast, the physical economy, including agriculture, extraction, and construction, is expected to see minimal growth—less than 1% in agriculture and only 3% in both extraction and construction. These sectors face challenges due to their reliance on manual, on-site work, limiting AI’s impact.

The report highlights that the 2030s will be pivotal, with substantial productivity gains anticipated as AI adoption becomes mainstream. Financial and business services are expected to lead this growth, while sectors like manufacturing and agriculture may lag behind, with less than half of their projected gains realised by 2035.

Oxford Economics is dedicated to help you better understand key global sector developments and risks affecting your markets and supply chains, support you in benchmarking global sector performance and quantify market potential. Our services are backed by a global team of economists and sector experts and supported by Oxford Economics proprietary economic and sector forecasting models.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Tariff Regime: Comparative Perspective
articles.standfirst:
Pakistan’s National Tariff Policy 2025–30 (NTP) sets out an ambitious programme to promote export-led growth through reforms of the import tariff structure. 

This is an independent comparative analysis to establish a consistent basis for comparing tariff structures, particularly the treatment of para-tariffs and provides an updated assessment that reflects Pakistan’s tariff reforms introduced in the fiscal year (FY) 2025–26 budget and recent changes in comparator countries, where data are available.

The short analysis covers Pakistan and nine comparator countries as set out in the NTP: India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, Vietnam and Türkiye. It draws on the latest available international data, published research by reputable international institutions and, where necessary, OE calculations using internationally comparable statistics. Together, the analysis tests whether the data support the NTP’s characterisation of Pakistan’s tariff protection relative to the comparator economies.
paragraphs: The National Tariff Policy 2025–30 (NTP) presents Pakistan’s average tariff, including para-tariffs, as higher than those of eight comparator economies: India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Thailand, Cambodia, Indonesia, and Vietnam. This report reassesses the NTP’s international comparisons by examining Pakistan’s customs duties and para-tariffs on a consistent basis alongside those of the nine comparator economies, including Türkiye. The analysis incorporates Pakistan’s recent tariff reforms and available data for the comparator countries.

Pakistan’s average customs duties are in the middle of the study-country range. Its simple-average most-favoured-nation (MFN) tariff is 9.5%, below those of India, Bangladesh and Nepal and equal to Vietnam’s. Its trade-weighted average is 6.7%, also in the middle of the group.

Moving beyond average tariff levels, the analysis of tariff peaks shows that Pakistan’s share of high-duty tariff lines is comparable to the regional level. In 2025, 31.0% of its tariff lines carried duties above 15%, compared with the five-country South Asian average of 30.7%, placing Pakistan fourth among the ten study economies.

Pakistan compares more favourably with its peers when higher thresholds are used to define tariff peaks. A separate sensitivity analysis using common-year 2023 data places Pakistan below the South Asian study-country average at thresholds of 25%, 35% and 50%. This suggests a concentration of moderately high duties rather than an unusually large share of extreme rates compared to regional peers.

Including para-tariffs changes the comparison, but does not make Pakistan uniquely high among the selected economies. Its estimated combined simple average of tariffs and para-tariffs is 17.7%, compared with 28.1% for Bangladesh, 19.3% for Sri Lanka, 17.3% for Türkiye and 16.0% for India. Consistent treatment of these additional charges is therefore essential. Differences in data coverage, reference periods and policy changes mean these estimates remain a best-effort comparison, not a comprehensive measure of all import charges.

Overall, the data do not support the claim that Pakistan has the highest tariff levels among the economies compared. An analysis of simple average tariff rate and export as a share of GDP also show no clear correlation between the two. These findings suggest that Pakistan’s export strategy should rest on how reform would improve export competitiveness rather than on tariff reduction alone. Two broader implications are important going forward. First, tariff reform needs to sit within a broader package that strengthens exporters’ competitiveness, including improvements in energy, logistics, finance and skills. Second, amid rising protectionism, the sequencing of tariff reductions and trade negotiations deserves careful consideration. Preserving scope to offer preferential tariff concessions could help Pakistan negotiate reciprocal access to overseas markets.

Thang Nguyen-Quoc, Ph.D. leads macro consulting practice within the Asia Consulting team in Singapore. In this capacity, he supports clients with carrying out bespoke scenario modelling, offering strategic advice as well as developing thought-leadership reports on trade and green transition. He also brings unique expertise for analysing and quantifying the international trade and investment policies, at country and global level.

Prior to joining OE in 2022, Thang spent a decade delivering flagship economic reports on Asian and African economies at the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) in Paris. He also worked in various roles at the World Bank, National Academy of Social Sciences (US), and Vietnam Commercial Bank. He got a Ph.D. in International Economics from University Paris-Dauphine, M.Sc. from Barcelona School of Economics and B.A. from Ohio Wesleyan University. His doctoral thesis evaluated the impacts of digitalization, protectionism and regionalism on the trade patterns of developing countries, using a range of econometric techniques.

He also bring expertise in fintech and cryptocurrency, both as a former founder and an economic researcher.

articles.title: Claude chatbot maker set for $1.3tn stock market debut despite 'catastrophic' AI warning
articles.standfirst: The AI company behind the Claude chatbot will offer its shares at between $70 and $78, which is lower than what was expected.
paragraphs: Anthropic, the artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the Claude chatbot, could be valued at around $1.3 trillion (£1 trillion) when it lists its shares for sale on New York's Nasdaq stock exchange.
The loss-making company says it will offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each and will raise up to $64bn when it floats this month.
It would value Anthropic at between $1.1tn and $1.3tn which, although large, is below the $2tn some backers of the firm predicted in summer, according to the Financial Times.
The huge valuation comes despite the company warning last month that AI could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity".

It is floating at a volatile time for big tech firms. After last week's US midterm elections, the Nasdaq fell sharply on concerns a Democrat-led Congress could slow development of AI and the buildout of data centres.
There are also wider fears over the billions of dollars being spent on AI and whether it will pay off.
In its most recent results for the six months to the end of June, Anthropic's revenues jumped to $16.2bn from $1.1bn in the same period last year.
However, its pre-tax loss jumped to $80.7bn from $12.9bn.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, said the $64bn Anthropic wants to raise is "fairly bullish" within "the volatility [and] concerns towards AI that we've seen in sort of particularly last week".
She told Reuters: "It's showing that they are still sort of upbeat about the outlook as far as AI is concerned and that obviously that they think that the demand is going to be there."
Anthropic, which will list under the symbol ANT on 19 November, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.
At $1.3tn, Anthropic's possible valuation is below SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and artificial intelligence company, which listed its shares in June and was valued at nearly $1.8tn.
Anthropic is just five years old. It was co-founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei along with five others – all of whom worked at OpenAI, the rival AI giant behind ChatGPT.
It announced its intention to list on the stock market in June and OpenAI followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year.
The listing announcements were followed by a series of incidents involving AI agents, which are bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously, going rogue.
Current and former staff of both companies have warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI.

Anthropic has admitted that advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".
The company has reiterated promises to develop AI to be beneficial to people.
It has warned investors its future success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, and that "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

articles.title: Sales of tinned food and bottled water  jump after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
articles.standfirst: Sales of essential goods such as hand sanitiser soar after the government called on households to be prepared for emergencies.
paragraphs: Sales of essential goods such as bottled water and canned food soared in the 10 days following the launch of the government's "Be Ready" emergency preparedness campaign on 22 October, research indicates.
Hand sanitiser sales were up 83%, sales of bottled water rose 67% and tinned and jarred goods climbed 37%, according to data from retail research firm Worldpanel by Numerator.
The government's public awareness campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.
However, Worldpanel said that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying.
The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.
Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.
After the campaign launch, the equivalent of an extra 400,000 people per day bought tinned meat, Worldpanel said, although the typical amount remained at 500g, which suggests a gradual stocking-up.

"Shoppers clearly took notice of the 'Be Ready' campaign, but this wasn't panic buying, with less than a third of households buying bottled water in October," said Fraser McKevitt, head of retail and consumer insight at Worldpanel by Numerator.

"Growth came from more people adding the recommended items on the government's checklist to their weekly shop, not from shoppers piling their trolleys high, which is very much in line with what the government wanted households to do," he said.
Sales of tinned and jarred goods rose from £58.2m in the 10 days to 2 November 2025 to £79.5m over the same period in 2026.
Bottled water sales jumped from £13.6m to £22.8m compared with a year earlier and hand sanitiser sales climbed from £497,000 to £908,000.
Further evidence of stockpiling came from food firm Princes on Tuesday, which said demand for tinned tuna, meat and vegetables had risen following the government's campaign.
Princes interim chief executive Giuseppe Mastrolia said the jump in demand "further reinforces the relevance of our core categories in providing affordable, nutritious and convenient food solutions".

The "Be Ready" campaign warns that severe weather and cyber attacks could disrupt essential services, and British households need to make sure they have what they need - for example, bottled water, and long-life food that doesn't need to be kept in the fridge such as dried fruit and nuts.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said everyone should have "those supplies in the house to get you through those moments".
Disaster recovery expert Lucy Easthope previously told the BBC that the UK was playing "massive catch up" to other European nations in terms of preparedness.
These include France, Germany Denmark, Sweden, and Norway.

A number of experts have been calling for the UK to put more emphasis on food security, with some arguing that the government itself should take responsibility for food stockpiling, rather than individual households.

In October, a group of more than 180 experts signed an open letter to Burnham and first secretary of state Louise Haigh calling for local authorities to have a duty to prevent and respond to food supply emergencies.
They pointed out that a government survey found that 29% of people in the UK could not afford to keep a few days worth of food in the house.
Have you been stockpiling? If so, what have you been buying?

articles.title: US inflation higher than expected in October - here's what is happening with prices
articles.standfirst: Prices rose by 0.4% over the month, driven by increases in shelter, food and energy costs.
paragraphs: US inflation rose at a faster-than-expected pace in October, according to official figures.
Prices rose by 0.4% in the month, which was lower than the 0.6% increase in September.
However, analysts had expected prices to rise by 0.3%, and the higher-than-expected pace could add to arguments for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December.
The new figures come a week after the midterm elections which were fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
Over the month of October, prices rose by 0.4%, driven by increases in housing, food and energy costs.
However, the pace of energy price rises, at 0.7% in October, was much lower than the 5.2% increase seen in September.
While the Bureau of Labor Statistics would normally provide figures for the 12-month change in prices, it did not collect data in October 2025 so it could not provide that estimate.
For the 12 months to September, inflation was 3.7%.
The US Federal Reserve has a target for keeping annual inflation at 2%.
When inflation is too high the Fed tends to raise interest rates in order to encourage people and businesses to save more and spend less money in the hope this will slow price rises.

While there was no annual figure published for inflation this month, analysts say the fact inflation was higher in October than expected increases the chance of an interest rate rise at the Fed's December meeting.

Federal Reserve governor Chirstopher Waller, who spoke before the latest inflation figures were published, also suggested he was leaning towards a rate increase in December even if October's figures were slower than expected.
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
US President Donald Trump raised tariffs

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
While inflation is currently above where the Federal Reserve would like it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.
The value of social security benefits is changed to largely keep up with inflation, protecting people's ability to purchase their usual goods and services through the cost-of-living adjustment.

Shortly after September's inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.
The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.
The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.

articles.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.standfirst: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?
paragraphs: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.
9 November 2026
Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.
Wind turbines represent homegrown energy, but they come with potential problems
Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.
But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."
"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."
There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"
Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.
Fahnbulleh, centre, at Jackdaw last month. She says the drilling will have minimal impact on energy prices

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".
"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.
Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.
But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.
The debate around Rosebank and Jackdaw has sparked vehement opposition from climate protesters

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.
With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.
The alternative is to build.
Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.
Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.
All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.
And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.
And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.
I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".
Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.
Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.
"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.
Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.
Foreign investment, then - just not from China.

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.
Donald Trump is a big exponent of fossil fuels

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.
And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.
If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

articles.title: Californians reject wealth tax for billionaires
articles.standfirst: Proposition 40 targeted Californian billionaires with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income.
paragraphs: California voters have voted to reject a wealth tax on its billionaires.

The ballot proposal would have levied a one-time tax on the state's mega wealthy to help fund healthcare. It took nearly a week of counting votes after the midterm election to determine a projection on the measure.
There are about 200 billionaires in the state, including Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, reality television star Kim Kardashian and media mogul Oprah Winfrey.

Proposition 40 targeted Californians with a wealth of more than $1.1bn (£800m) with a 5% tax on their total wealth, including assets such as shares as well as income. It failed amid divisions among Democrats and labour unions.
Had it passed, experts believe it would have been the world's first wealth tax targeting billionaires.
The tax would have raised about $100bn to make up for federal funding cuts to healthcare in California as a result of President Donald Trump's sweeping tax and spending bill.
Those who backed the measure had argued it would help ensure that the ultra-wealthy were contributing their fair share and helping backfill gaps in the state's budget.
The wealth tax faced fierce opposition, including from Google co-founder Sergey Brin, as well as California Governor Gavin Newsom and labour unions.
Newsom, whose tenure as governor is coming to an end, had expressed concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

Some billionaire critics of the measure spent millions trying to crush it, with a handful even moving out of the state to evade the possible tax. Brin gave more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the tax, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Dave Regan, head of the union that led the charge for the measure, said on election night that the billionaires' efforts to block the tax created "a lot of confusion and a lot of second-guessing among people who really in their hearts know what the right the thing to do is".
Regan, who is president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, pledged to seek a billionaire tax once more in 2028.
The measure had odds stacked against it, with two other propositions on the ballot that would have effectively reversed it, even if it passed.

California, home to some 23 million registered voters, has the largest economy in the country and boasts the fourth largest global economy. It is home to one of the highest concentrations of billionaires in the world, but also has one of the highest wealth gaps.

articles.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
articles.standfirst: AI safety regulator will also be created after a rogue OpenAI agent hacked government websites.
paragraphs: PM Anthony Albanese says the law needs to catch up with a "fast-changing world"
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.
On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.
AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".
"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.
One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .
This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".
The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.
This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.
In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.
OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.
It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.
Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.
Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

articles.title: Civil servant who secretly held five jobs found guilty of fraud
articles.standfirst: Kashim Chowdhury had secretly held multiple public sector jobs on full-time salaries.
paragraphs: Civil servant Kashim Chowdhury juggled multiple public sector jobs
A civil servant who secretly held multiple public sector jobs on full-time salaries has been found guilty of nine counts of fraud.
Kashim Chowdhury, from east London, had five government jobs that overlapped in the spring of 2023. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.
The prosecution accused the 56-year-old of ''deliberate, intentional dishonesty'' and of ''exploiting the system''.
After seven hours of deliberation, the jury unanimously found Chowdhury guilty of eight counts of fraud by false representation and one count of fraud by a failure to disclose.
The judge said Chowdhury faced a ''very significant custodial sentence''. He added he was refusing bail because of the significance of the crime and for Chowdhury's own wellbeing.
"This was sustained and deliberate dishonesty," said Sarah Melo, specialist prosecutor at the CPS Serious Economic Organised Crime and International Directorate.
"He knew he could not legitimately hold multiple full-time positions at the same time, but continued to conceal what he was doing."
A Defra spokesperson said Chowdury "abused the trust placed in him as a public servant", adding that it would use all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending.
The judge said Chowdhury faced a ''very significant custodial sentence''
Between 2020 and 2023 Chowdhury had eight full-time public sector roles that overlapped and earned him £350,000 in total.

The prosecution told the court that on application forms he provided inaccurate information about his employment status and failed to disclose to government departments that he was already a civil servant. Once he secured the roles he didn't tell his employers he was working elsewhere.

He was allowed to work entirely from home because he told his employers he was caring for his mother, whom he lived with in east London. She had dementia and was diagnosed with terminal cancer in 2023.

But rather than reduce his workload to look after her, he kept taking on new jobs. In the spring of 2023, when his mother was a few months away from death, he had jobs at the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, the Department of Health and Social Care, the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office.
During this period he was contracted to work 183 hours a week - more than the number of hours that exist in seven days.

Chowdhury said he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment in the past. He was made redundant from a job at the Department for Education in 2013 and was given a diagnosis of PTSD.
He said he had not been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".
But the prosecution barrister, Lucy Organ, told the jury: "He's lied to you in evidence, he's lied to you under oath, which demonstrates the level of deceit he has descended to."
A succession of his managers told the court about his poor performance. Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney who managed Chowdhury at Defra.

He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time". McCartney said that during video calls Chowdhury had his camera switched off blaming technical problems. McCartney said this went on for four to five months.
But McCartney said that because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job and remained there for two years.
Chowdhury told the jury he had not worn make-up during a work video call

The prosecution argued that he used sick notes to cope with his impossible schedule. In March 2023, he was on sick leave from four of the organisations he worked for. But he kept working at the Home Office and did not tell them he was ill.

His line manager at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), Aleesha Adams, organised a video call with him in May 2023. By this point he'd been off sick for three months and she wanted to make a plan to get him back to work.
She told the jury that at the start of the call he was coughing a lot and waving tissues up to the camera. She also told the jury that he had been wearing white make-up to try to look ill.
Adams told the court that as the meeting went on the make-up started coming off his forehead. ''He was sweating, it was like rubbing off so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck."
Chowdhury told the jury this was a smear and that he had not been wearing make-up.
After the call, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it he blamed a technical error.
Adams grew suspicious. ''I believed he was lying,'' she told the jury. She escalated her concerns up the chain at the UKHSA. But his fraudulent behaviour went on for several more months.

The government's National Fraud Initiative flagged suspected fraud to Defra in 2023. Following this, the Defra Investigations Team launched an investigation and as a result, Chowdhury was arrested and interviewed under caution in July 2023. He was dismissed by the civil service in September 2023.
Chowdhury has also been accused by his siblings of bullying their mother into increasing his share of the family home days before she died.
In a case at the High Court, Chowdhury's two brothers and sister allege that he put "undue influence" on Faijun Nessa to sign documents that meant he would inherit half of her home.
The four-storey, six-bedroom home in east London has been valued at £2.1m.

His siblings say their mother could not have understood what she was signing because she was "desperately unwell". In January 2023 she was given a terminal diagnosis of stage four metastatic colorectal cancer.

The claimants also allege that Mrs Nessa, who was nearly blind and could not speak English, was unaware of what she was signing because the documents were not translated into her native Bengali at the time they were signed.
Kashim Chowdhury denies the claims. That case is ongoing.
Additional reporting by Ben Sturt.

articles.title: Qantas to outsource 850 local jobs with most roles moving to India
articles.standfirst: The Australian airline said the move was aimed at modernising its IT systems and noted the impact of AI.
paragraphs: Qantas CEO Vanessa Hudson apologised for the "hard news" of 850 job cuts
Qantas will outsource 850 local corporate jobs to consulting giant Accenture with most roles moving to India as the airline fast-tracks AI investment.
In an internal email to staff on Tuesday, the Australian company's CEO Vanessa Hudson said "this is hard news for some and I'm sorry for the uncertainty it brings".

The job cuts will begin mid-2027, she said, and start with finance, procurement, people and marketing roles shifting "mostly" to teams in India and "some in Australia" as the firm seeks to modernise its IT systems.
Hudson said the "scale and speed of change in technology and AI is something none of us has seen in our lifetime", and it was in talks with unions and staff on the plans.
The move comes days after the airline provided a market update, flagging fare increases and flight cuts amid higher fuel costs.
On its new multi-year deal with Accenture, Hudson said it was about "modernising" the airline's IT systems to become "more efficient".
Qantas spends more than AU$1bn (US$691m; £514m) a year on technology, she said, and the company's back-end systems needed to be upgraded.
"Like every airline, we run on technology built up over decades for a different era, including more than 1,000 legacy applications that were never designed to work together," she said.

The deal with Accenture means "we will redesign and simplify parts of how our corporate functions work and reduce duplication", Hudson said, so staff can "spend more time on work that creates value for our customers and the business".
The company said that "in time", the work that Accenture takes over will be "transformed further with automation and AI".
Staff affected by the job cuts will be redeployed "where possible", the firm added, including new roles in Australia.
Qantas - which employs about 28,000 staff in Australia and another 4,000 globally - said thousands of its staff already use AI in their daily work.
The BBC has contacted the Australian Services Union for comment.
