articles.title: Antonia Romeo now needs reforms to match her rhetoric
articles.standfirst:
Antonia Romeo now needs reforms to match her rhetoric sam.macrory Tue, 10/11/2026 - 22:32 The cabinet secretary’s “burning platform” warning must be followed by urgent civil service reform. 4 Comment Hannah Keenan Alex Thomas Institute for Government Yes Antonia Romeo, speaking at the IfG in 2023. Civil service Civil service reform Civil servants Artificial intelligence Cabinet secretary Prime minister Cabinet Office
No

Antonia Romeo used a lecture at the LSE to set the scene for radical change in the civil service, rightly arguing that the confluence of challenges facing the state means incremental change is not enough. It was a compelling argument, but her civil service reform programme has not yet shown that the system is braced for serious change.  

It is right to dial up the rhetoric on state reform

The cabinet secretary correctly describes the civil service as on a “burning platform”. Part of that is the confluence of factors Romeo identified: AI will shift how people interact with the state; complex global threats will demand more of government; the productivity story reflects the inflexible bureaucracy civil servants regularly describe to us – and a state that has failed to adapt to the challenges it faces.  

Her focus on trust being essential for the civil service’s legitimacy was particularly welcome, with recent Institute for Government research highlighting systemic long-term problems with ministerial trust in the civil service. While sketch-writers might raise an eyebrow at the prime minister sitting in the front row during Romeo’s speech, it was a very good sign indeed that Andy Burnham and first secretary of state Lou Haigh were deliberately present; rebuilding that relationship is a team effort.

The “burning platform” is also a good storytelling device. Romeo is the leader of half a million people, who have grown used to reform efforts being promised and failing to take hold. Not surprisingly, inertia prevails – and Romeo is trying to shock the system into changing at the scale and pace now urgently required.

Related content

When trust is lost: Making sense of the damaged relationship between ministers and civil servants

When trust is lost: Making sense of the damaged relationship between ministers and civil servants

Ministers have lost trust in the civil service: that is damaging. We identify five traits of civil service behaviour and skills that are necessary for ministerial trust to be built and sustained today.

Read our report

Romeo’s focus on changing the incentives for civil servants is refreshing

Much of what the cabinet secretary described was in line with the Institute’s recommendations. A promise to shift incentives so that civil servants do not have to move jobs to get a pay rise, or are constrained to a career only inside the service, are some of our longstanding recommendations. These are exactly the type of system-wide fixes needed for the workforce. As is tackling poor performance, another Institute hobby horse.

Some reforms are already in train. The new Office for the Prime Minister and Cabinet (another piece of IfG advice) is welcome – although it now needs to show it that the change is more than a rebranding exercise. Recent changes to senior officials’ pay, linking to performance, is the right step but only a small move towards reforming the mess of civil service pay structures.  

Romeo is rightly cautious in some areas. She was at pains to emphasise repeatedly that civil servants work for ministers and have no agenda other than that of the elected government. She could not get ahead of the publication of the 10-year plan or rewiring the state white paper. She acknowledged the risks around uncritical AI adoption and automation and is treading the right path between innovation and needing to earn and hold public trust.  

But the brakes need to come off the rest of the programme.

Don’t set the platform on fire if you’re not prepared to jump

The frustration of Romeo’s speech was not in what she said, but in what she did not. For example, Romeo rightly promised “decisive action” on poor performance. The same promise previously made by Darren Jones in January, by Pat McFadden six months before that, and by Francis Maude more than a decade previously. And yet the civil service remains in a cycle of losing ministerial trust when the same poor performers bounce around different parts of Whitehall. The public, repeatedly, feel the consequences.

Romeo’s review into the civil service – kicked off in July 2026 – will not report to the prime minister until summer 2027. Even for the most enthusiastic of civil service reform watchers, it is hard to suspend disbelief for quite so long. Romeo knows this. It came up repeatedly in the post-speech Q&A – that this cannot be all talk, and to get the cultural shift the civil service needs requires people to believe that change will come.

Romeo needs some quick, big wins to show that this is real. Compulsory exit rounds for poor performers and performance-related pay to be in place for the next financial year would shift the dial, but there are other routes too.  

If not, belief in the cabinet secretary’s plans for change will fade. Her "burning platform" warning was the right one, but it also leaves Romeo playing with fire. The civil service needs action, not just words, speeches or reports, important as those can be. The trust of her workforce, ministers, and the public depends on it.

articles.title: The top Canadian cities in 2026
articles.standfirst: On average, Canadian cities outscore the US on Human Capital, Governance, and Quality of Life, but lag marginally on Economics and Environment.
paragraphs: Driven by a strong economy and favourable quality of life measures, Canada’s major cities continue to offer significant benefits to the world’s highest-skilled workers. On average, Canadian cities outscore the US on Human Capital, Governance, and Quality of Life, but lag marginally on Economics and Environment where three of the bottom four scores in North America belong to Canadian cities. This partly reflects the country’s seasonal weather fluctuations, which drag on their Environment scores.

The majority of Canadian cities are set to grow at a slower rate than US cities over the next five years, with the exception of oil-rich Edmonton and Calgary. However, the Canadian cities tend to average higher on Quality of Life score, with a more even income distribution, higher life expectancy, and lower crime rates.

In our 2026 Global Cities Index, Toronto is the top-ranking Canadian city overall, placing 20th in the world out of 1,000 cities. As Canada’s premier centre for business, finance, culture, and art, it performs best in the Economics and Human Capital categories. It is an economic powerhouse and continues to boast some of the most robust employment growth rates in the region, with migrants attracted to its buoyant jobs market and high-wage sectors. Lower immigration targets announced by the federal government in 2025 have slowed the pace of growth compared with 2022–2024, but the city is not alone in Canada or the wider Western world in facing demographic challenges.

Canada’s other major cities also score highly in our index, and like Toronto, they tend to have their strongest results in the Economics and Human Capital metrics. Vancouver ranks 24th globally and second in Canada, above US powerhouses such as Miami and San Diego. This is largely due to the city’s tech and business services sectors, which have underpinned Vancouver’s steady economic growth over the past decade and attracted workers and businesses from around the world. In fact, many US tech firms have established offices in Vancouver to more easily recruit talent from overseas. Unlike some other Canadian metros, Vancouver also performs well in the Environment category. It boasts very good air quality, and the city has historically been proactive in implementing well-defined energy transition and climate adaptation plans.

Montreal, Canada’s third-ranked city, places 62nd globally. Its economic outlook is slightly cloudier than Toronto’s and Vancouver’s, but the city still scores in the top decile globally thanks to its large economy, high life expectancy, and skilled workforce. In fact, Montreal is a key hub for education and innovation in the country and globally: it is home to McGill University, a global leader in medical research, and is also a hub for AI research and video game development, attracting skilled professionals from around the world.

In a similar vein, Calgary (fourth in Canada, 69th globally) and Ottawa-Gatineau (fifth in Canada, 104th globally) are regional bright spots with strong Human Capital scores. Ottawa-Gatineau has high levels of educational attainment thanks to its large government and public policy-adjacent sectors, while Calgary is home to many corporate headquarters and leads the country in population growth thanks to high incomes and easy access to national parks.

Calgary’s Albertan neighbour, Edmonton, is a place we have designated as a ‘City to Watch’ in the coming years. While not quite at the same level as Canada’s other major metros, partly due to its dependence on oil refining, Edmonton is a city we believe is primed to move up the rankings at pace, through a process of self-reinforcing economic growth and business development. It is among North America’s fastest-growing urban economies, recording strong gains in GDP, employment, and population. And this robust economic growth will have positive downstream effects: disposable incomes in the city, which are already higher than the national average, are set to rise at one of the fastest rates in Canada, boosting consumer spending.

House prices are still relatively affordable in Edmonton too, which cannot be said for many other Canadian cities. Residents of Toronto and Vancouver in particular typically spend a larger portion of their income on housing than residents in nearly every other city in the world. High housing costs have pulled down the Quality of Life scores for several Canadian cities, and is an enduring challenge for local and provincial governments around the country.

The other key challenge currently facing Canadian cities is the trade war with the US. The volatility around the USMCA renegotiations and broader uncertainty have stymied business investment in the country and harmed the economies of export-producing cities. The oil exporters Edmonton and Calgary have largely been spared as Canadian oil exports have targeted non-US markets with the aid of the Trans Mountain Pipeline and shipping from Vancouver. However, the manufacturing sectors of Toronto, Montreal, and Hamilton have been hit hard, both directly and through the higher cost of input materials. In our index, Hamilton ranks very similarly overall to Detroit and Pittsburgh, two cities with a similar industrial heritage and exposed to the current uncertainty.
To explore the full rankings and see how other cities perform, visit the 2026 Global Cities Index site.

articles.title: Tariff Update: Where Things Stand After the Supreme Court Ruling
articles.standfirst: The US Supreme Court struck down the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) tariffs in February, so why are Americans still paying tariffs?
paragraphs: The Supreme Court struck down the IEEPA tariffs in February, so why are Americans still paying tariffs? The administration replaced them, first with temporary Section 122 tariffs and now with 10 to 12.5 percent Section 301 tariffs on nearly every US trading partner.

Kyle sits down with cohost Erica York to catch up on tariffTariffs are taxes imposed by one country on goods imported from another country. Tariffs are trade barriers that raise prices, reduce available quantities of goods and services for US businesses and consumers, and create an economic burden on foreign exporters. policy. Together, they look at how tariffs may cancel out the investment boost from full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. and discuss the ongoing court cases that could still strike down the new tariffs.

articles.title: Digital Services Taxes in the United Kingdom and Belgium Create Large Economic Harms per Unit of Revenue
articles.standfirst: Evaluations of digital services taxes in the UK and Belgium show tiny annual revenue collections relative to the total treasury revenue raised by the government. Our dynamic modeling shows digital services taxes reduce both labor and capital supply, lowering investment, GDP, and labor compensation.
paragraphs: Digital services taxes (DSTs) are taxes on gross revenues that large companies earn from certain digital activities. Most cover revenue from digital advertising or other intermediation, though designs vary. The most economically significant DSTs are typically levied by European countries and aimed at very large software companies, most of which are based in the United States.

A significant flaw in DSTs is nonneutrality, which creates economic inefficiencies. The nonneutrality comes from discrimination by industry or business model, implicit discrimination through thresholds or carveouts that define the list of in-scope payers, and the gross receipts base.

As a result of these qualities, DSTs are comparatively harmful, relative to other taxes, per unit of revenue raised. This paper will discuss the economic theory undergirding this claim and examine two specific examples.

One of these is Belgium; Tax Foundation Europe most recently made this argument in testimony before the Belgian Finance and Budget Committee on August 31, 2026.[1] The testimony described several drawbacks of the Belgian DST proposal and employed both quantitative and qualitative analyses.

This paper will recap the Belgian analysis and extend its methods to the United Kingdom’s DST as well. Then it will discuss the foundations, methods, and limitations of quantitative modeling in Tax Foundation’s DST work.

Tax Foundation’s quantitative and qualitative analyses are consonant with each other; they come from the same roots in key public finance works studying tax neutrality, and generally support neutrality as a pillar of sound tax policy. However, the quantitative and qualitative analyses serve different roles. In some cases, quantitative work makes effects more understandable and tangible—and in other cases, qualitative analysis might help describe effects for which quantitative modeling methods do not exist.

The results below concern the effects of DSTs on the supply of labor and capital—and ultimately, the gross domestic product—of both Belgium and the UK. The model results are simplifications in many respects, but the simplifications are for practical reasons. More robust or complex modeling of DSTs may even strengthen the case against them.

For Belgium, Tax Foundation Europe’s testimony included modeling of a tax proposal that is not explicitly named as a DST, but mirrors one in intent and economic properties. Though DSTs have typically been assessed as a tax on gross receipts, the Belgian proposal adds an extra step. Rather than taxing gross receipts directly, it calculates an imputed income from a static deemed profitability percentage. This deemed profitability is assumed, not demonstrated via accounting. Then, the policy taxes a percentage of that deemed income. This intermediate step does not, however, change the form of the tax to something notably different from a DST; gross receipts multiplied by two percentages (the deemed profitability, then the tax rate) can reduce mathematically to gross receipts multiplied by one percentage, as the written testimony shows.
The DST proposal is by any measure a very small tax relative to the total size of the Belgian economy, so all the effects described are modest. However, the overall results are not favorable.

The DST is modeled as a proportional tax on gross output, with its corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. deductibility feature partially reducing its burden on capital. The model finds a reduction in GDP and total labor compensation coming from two different sources: roughly, people working slightly less efficiently, and people working slightly less overall.

The DST slightly reduces the overall returns to work, in part by simply reducing the after-tax purchasing power for Belgian consumers, and in part by reducing the overall productivity of Belgian work, including by discouraging investment by Belgian firms. These effects combine to reduce after-tax returns to work, and in turn, the modeled workers are more likely to engage in non-market activities.

The revenue modeling of Belgium’s tax borrows revenue-estimating techniques from the already-existing French DST, while the economic modeling is based on neoclassical production functions, a number of long-established public finance results, and a few critical economic elasticities used consistently throughout Tax Foundation’s work.[2]
The United Kingdom’s digital services tax raised £808 million in tax year 2024/25. As for Belgium, this tax is modelled with similar effects as a proportional output tax.
The DST is deductible from corporate income tax according to British law.[3] A non-deductible DST would have a stronger negative effect on output.

Its less sizable effect on output is largely explained by Britain’s taxing labor more moderately at the margin than Belgium. The DST adds a small wedge to the tax on labor, and labor supply responds to the after-tax wage.

Because additional labor compensation is already taxed at about 35.9 percent in Britain against 65.0 percent in Belgium (or 49 and 84 percent after consumption taxes) for a single worker earning the country’s average wage, the same proportional wedge adds a larger hit to what a Belgian worker keeps, so labor supply and total output contract more strongly.[4]

Digital services taxes present some significant challenges for dynamic policy modeling, including by Tax Foundation. Tax Foundation has often used qualitative critiques of digital services taxes, such as highlighting their complexity, nonneutrality, and pyramiding. However, these properties—those that make DSTs poor tax policy—often are the same properties that make them more challenging to model. The overall result is that our modeling of the harms of DSTs is in many respects conservative or understated, because the data, the elasticities, or the computations required to fully show the harms of DSTs are impractical or unavailable.

Digital services taxes create several different economic deadweight losses. Some are common among tax policies, and others are present only in taxes with particular structural defects. Below, we will discuss the different possible deadweight losses and the challenges they present for modeling.

One common effect of many taxes, no matter how well-structured, is that they raise the relative value of activities outside of formal markets: for example, for leisure and socialization rather than market work used to pay for market consumption.

Non-market activities are still valuable activities, and ones we would expect even in the absence of any tax burden. But these become more attractive relative to the alternative if the alternative is taxed. A tax on market activity encourages people to forgo some of those market activities and instead do non-market activities, a decision that would not have been freely made in the absence of tax.

This is a moderate but well-studied effect, quantifiable through a labor supply elasticity. Tax Foundation Europe’s modeling here uses 0.2 for these purposes, meaning that a 1 percent reduction in real after-tax compensation results in 0.2 percent less work effort.[5]

Importantly, this tax burden holds in general equilibrium regardless of whether one considers the tax “passed on” to the consumer or “passed back” to the worker. In either case, it reduces the value of market activity after a complete closed loop from earning money to spending it on consumption.

Additionally, this tax burden is integrated across different types of taxes. For example, taxes on worker income interact with excise taxes, creating a greater combined impact than the sum of the two impacts calculated independently. The “Harberger triangles” representing deadweight loss vary with the square of the tax rate, so calculating excise or commodity taxes independently of the underlying general tax regime will understate their burden.[6]

Tax Foundation integrates consumption and excise taxes together with labor taxes to form the overall tax burden on market activity; this interaction, which is more severe in Belgium than in the UK, is the primary factor explaining why Belgium’s tax incurs a greater impact per unit of revenue raised.

A uniform tax on consumption distorts only the margin described above, between nonmarket or “leisure” activities and market activities. A nonneutral consumption taxA consumption tax is typically levied on the purchase of goods or services and is paid directly or indirectly by the consumer in the form of retail sales taxes, excise taxes, tariffs, value-added taxes (VAT), or income taxes where all savings are tax-deductible.—one that falls on some goods but not others—adds a second form of distortion. This distortion lies within the realm of market activities, rather than on the market-nonmarket margin. When consumption taxation is nonneutral, people have an incentive to shift consumption from heavily taxed goods or services to lightly taxed goods or services. The incremental amount of change that consumers make only in the presence of the uneven tax regime reduces consumer surplus.

There are some noted exceptions to the optimality of neutral taxation, often concerning internalizing externalities, or approximating a user feeA user fee is a charge imposed by the government for the primary purpose of covering the cost of providing a service, directly raising funds from the people who benefit from the particular public good or service being provided. A user fee is not a tax, though some taxes may be labeled as user fees or closely resemble them. for a government service. However, the benchmark of neutrality shown by Anthony Atkinson and Joseph Stiglitz (1976) remains the default frame of reference.[7]

Unfortunately, adequately representing this inefficiency at scale and in detail exceeds the scope of data availability, researched elasticities, and general model-building capacity, whether at Tax Foundation or elsewhere. It would in principle require a vast catalog of goods and services in the economy, along with elasticities of substitution between each of them. (An elasticity of substitution measures the amount that consumers shift their budget from one activity to another possible alternative as a result of a tax.)

Consumers may, for example, largely shift to close substitutes that roughly resemble the forgone option, but also shift some spending to weaker substitutes and unrelated goods that are substantially different from the forgone option. The complexity of such calculations can expand polynomially with the quantity of potential spending options, as each one has a relationship with the others. Furthermore, the deadweight loss comes in part from lost consumer surplus—the difference between what a consumer paid and what a consumer hypothetically would have been willing to pay for the good received. This quantity is not easily derived; economists can typically only infer that it has been reduced in the tax-motivated consumption change.

A tax on gross receipts, like a DST, with no crediting or deductibility system to avert double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income., further extends the nonneutrality problems of differential consumption taxation, while also producing a few new issues as well.

The problems of gross receipts taxes are especially salient for multi-firm chains where the same value-added ends up an explicit or implicit cost of revenue for several in-scope businesses throughout the chain.

Economists have understood the drawbacks of gross receipts taxation for decades, and advised against taxing intermediate inputs.[8] Unfortunately, the taxation of intermediate inputs is relatively common in DST design, and a specialized chain of diverse software providers can quickly find itself paying a DST multiple times on the same activity, as Tax Foundation has recently shown with stylized examples.[9]

Some of the drawbacks of nonneutrality from pyramiding are virtually the same as those described above, but amplified: there is an even greater range and variety of effective tax rates across different patterns of economic activity. The incentive for buyers to substitute away from multiply taxed goods and services becomes even stronger. Indeed, as deadweight losses tend to vary with the square of tax rates rather than linearly, double taxation is more than doubly distortive.

But there are also a few extra distortions from taxing business inputs that are not quite fully captured in models of nonneutral consumption taxes. Business inputs impact production allocation, not just consumption allocation.

These concepts are related, but not entirely the same. In either case, the economy produces, for tax reasons, something less than what would maximally make consumers happy. In a closed economy that consumes its own output, these are arguably the same effect, and the difference is driven by who makes the tax-motivated decision.

But in an open economy, like the typical European economy, a nonneutral tax on business inputs can artificially change the profitability of different production processes for export industries, introducing a new kind of inefficiency that would not be present in any kind of consumption tax system. Roughly, companies in a DST-levying country may choose to export less valuable services purely to avert the DST on the production inputs of the otherwise more lucrative export.

Difficulties in quantifying these DST drawbacks, of course, are even more substantial. The model of the different consumption options and substitution elasticities between them would have to extend to the intermediate inputs and model different production options for different firms, with changes in decision-making coming from the taxes on intermediate inputs. These inefficiencies are real and relatively simple to show in a stylized example with only a handful of products, where a consumer or producer shifts to a less-desirable or less-profitable product, simply for tax reasons. But these effects are impossible to quantify systematically in a large dynamic economy with many goods and unknown preferences.

Taxes on business inputs may, in some cases, impact investment. The effect that will be described below is arguably an extension of the production efficiency concerns described above. But it deserves special discussion because of the role of capital in typical models of macroeconomic growth, including our own.

An economy’s available productive capacity is often shown as a function of factors including labor and capital; the original form, developed by Paul Douglas and Charles Cobb, is commonly taught in early textbooks.[10] (A production function may include other terms or residuals as well; an efficient or inefficient tax code driving efficient or inefficient production allocation would likely be called a form of “total factor productivity” in a typical production function.)

If a DST contributes to the cost of a capital good, it may have an impact on the cost of capital in business decisions, and ultimately, the time structure of production: not just what or how to produce in any given period, but how much to create capital goods—such as equipment, software, or ideas—that assist in production in future periods. Tax the process that creates capital goods, and one ultimately gets fewer of them.

Tariffs in the US have spurred a high-quality discussion of taxes on business inputs and their impact on investment behavior in the United States. A seminal framework for an after-tax user cost of capital, developed by Robert Hall and Dale Jorgenson, undergirds much of this work.[11] Calculations published by Tax Foundation in July 2026 show that even under a corporate income tax system with full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs.—which eliminates the tax wedgeBroadly speaking, a tax wedge is the difference between the pre-tax price or return and after-tax price or return. For labor income, it is the difference between the total labor costs to the employer and the corresponding net take-home pay of the employee. on marginal investments in the basic Hall-Jorgenson model—a distortive tax on business inputs can still impact the user cost of capital.[12] A more detailed extension of these insights was published by American Enterprise Institute and Tax Policy Center scholars later the same year.[13]

Though this research was aimed at a US audience and US policy, much of this discussion would apply to European DSTs as well. DSTs have some similar properties to tariffs, as discussed explicitly in Tax Foundation research.[14] And they too can constitute an unrebated tax wedge on the creation of a capital good, for example, when software or physical capital are created with goods or labor located through online search or digital marketplaces.

Overall, there is good reason to model gross-receipts taxes generally, and DSTs specifically, as falling in part on the capital production factor, not just the labor factor. This explains the modeling choices made by Tax Foundation for DSTs; they are modeled to fall on gross output, not consumption, but the incidence on capital is reduced in part by corporate income tax deductibility, where applicable.

Overall, our modeling of the economic effects of DSTs may be conservative. Though it captures the extensive margin of economic production versus leisure, and the margin of investment versus consumption, both of which are important, it does not capture the significant substitutions within those categories that come from inefficient differential taxation of production and consumption. In other words, our modeling does not fully capture the insights that key pillars of public finance literature like Diamond-Mirrlees and Atkinson-Stiglitz might have to offer on DSTs.
This modeling conservatism is attributable primarily to the limitations of data, the economic literature, and calculation, not doubt in the overall value of tax neutrality.

Moving beyond pure models of taxes and economic decision-making behavior to capture messy real-world realities would be further outside the scope of Tax Foundation modeling, but it merits some mention: Tax Foundation testimony on the Belgian DST proposal notes legal disputes, relabeling disputes, treaty obligations, and administrative complexity as additional drawbacks of DSTs. These legal, compliance, and enforcement issues are outside of the quantitative modeling tradition from which Tax Foundation operates, but economic insight can be applied to them. Disputes over taxes occupy productive resources, such as skilled professionals, who could better be put to use in more productive parts of the economy.
Overall, even though the modeling results above show significant drawbacks from DSTs, they do not quantify all of the drawbacks. A more complete assessment could be even more negative.

[2] Tax Foundation, “Overview of the Tax Foundation’s General Equilibrium Model,” July 2026, https://www.taxfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ModelMeth26.pdf
[3] HMRC, “Digital Services Tax Manual, DST47100 – UK CT Deductibility of DST,” Jul. 31, 2024, https://gov.uk/hmrc-internal-manuals/digital-services-tax/dst47100.
[4] OECD, “Labour Taxation – OECD Comparative Country Indicators,” OECD Data Explorer, accessed Apr. 22, 2026, https://data-explorer.oecd.org/; author’s calculations.

[5] Tax Foundation, “Overview of the Tax Foundation’s General Equilibrium Model,” July 2026, https://www.taxfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/ModelMeth26.pdf; see also Congressional Budget Office, “How the Supply of Labor Responds to Changes in Fiscal Policy,” Oct. 25, 2012, http://cbo.gov/publication/43674.

[6] Lawrence H. Goulder and Roberton C. Williams III, “The Substantial Bias from Ignoring General Equilibrium Effects in Estimating Excess Burden, and a Practical Solution,” Journal of Political Economy 111:4 (August 2003): 898-927, https://doi.org/10.1086/375378.

[7] Anthony B. Atkinson and Joseph E. Stiglitz, “The Design of Tax Structure: Direct versus Indirect Taxation,” Journal of Public Economics 6:1-2 (July-August 1976): 55-75, https://doi.org/10.1016/0047-2727(76)90041-4.

[8] Peter A. Diamond and James A. Mirrlees, “Optimal Taxation and Public Production I: Production Efficiency,” American Economic Review 61:1 (March 1971): 8-27, https://www.aeaweb.org/aer/top20/61.1.8-27.pdf.

[9] Alan Cole, “Taxing the Matchmakers: How Digital Services Taxes Cascade Through Online Commerce,” Tax Foundation, Jul. 16, 2026, https://www.taxfoundation.org/research/all/global/digital-services-tax-online-commerce/.

[13] Kyle Pomerleau, Thomas Brosy, Robert McClelland, and John Wong, “The Impact of Tariffs on the Cost of Capital in the US,” American Enterprise Institute, Sep. 30, 2026, https://www.aei.org/research-products/report/the-impact-of-tariffs-on-the-cost-of-capital-in-the-us/.

[14] Alan Cole, “Tariffs by Another Name: How Discriminatory Taxes on Cross-Border Services Threaten America’s Export Edge,” Tax Foundation, Apr. 15, 2026, https://www.taxfoundation.org/research/all/global/tariffs-discriminatory-cross-border-services-taxes/.

Alan Cole is a Senior Economist with Tax Foundation’s Center for Global Tax Policy. His areas of focus include business taxes, cross-border taxes, and macroeconomics. In addition to work at Tax Foundation, Alan has served on the Joint Economic Committee and with The Conference Board.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.

Alex Mengden is an Economist at the Tax Foundation, where he focuses on international tax issues and tax policy in Europe. He holds a BA in philosophy and economics from the University of Bayreuth and an MSc in economics from the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich.

articles.title: How a civil servant got away with juggling five jobs for so long
articles.standfirst: Kashim Chowdhury has been convicted of fraud after pocketing £284,000 of taxpayers' money over three years.
paragraphs: Kashim Chowdhury fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money
Aleesha Adams joined a video call with Kashim Chowdhury in May 2023.
He'd been on sick leave from his job at the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for nearly three months and Adams, his line manager, wanted to put a plan in action to ease him back into work.
At the start of the call, Chowdhury was coughing and waving tissues up to the camera in an attempt to show how ill he was. But what really caught Adams' attention was how pale he looked.
She noticed white powder had started separating from his forehead. "He was sweating, it was like rubbing off, so it was darker underneath and darker on the neck," she told his trial.
She claimed he was wearing white make-up to look sick. Something he denied in court.
Little did she know UKHSA was not Chowdhury's only employer.

That month, he was also being paid to work full-time for the Department for the Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), the Department for Business and Trade, the Food Standards Agency and the Home Office. He was contracted to work 183 hours a week – more than the number of hours in seven days. He fraudulently earned more than £284,000 of taxpayers' money.
In total, he had eight overlapping full-time public-sector jobs between 2020 and 2023. During that time, this relatively junior civil servant was paid £350,000.

Soon after her call with Chowdhury, Adams discovered that he had logged into the call using a Defra email address. When she challenged him about it, he blamed it on a technical error. She told the jury at his trial at Southwark Crown Court: "I believed he was lying." She escalated her concerns up the chain.
But his fraudulent behaviour remained undetected. Chowdhury was able to keep working multiple government jobs for several more months.

It was the government's National Fraud Initiative that flagged suspected fraud to Defra. As a result, the Defra Investigations Team launched an investigation and Chowdhury was arrested and interviewed under caution in July 2023. He was dismissed by the civil service in September 2023.
On Monday he was found guilty of nine counts of fraud and told by the judge that he would be facing a "very substantial custodial sentence".
Chowdhury, 56, arrived each day at court alone. He is married, yet there never seemed to be any friends or family there to support him.
He would often make his way down the corridors of the court building carrying two plastic carrier bags, with a bobble hat perched on his head.
He sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box.

Chowdhury, who had a diagnosis of PTSD in 2015, said that he had taken on so many roles because he feared losing his livelihood after experiencing insecure employment. He said he'd been forced out of a job at the Department for Education in 2013.
He said he hadn't been thinking clearly when applying for jobs ''because of my stress, distress and trauma and due to my panic at the time".
But the prosecution argued his behaviour was "deliberate" and "intentional dishonesty" and that he had exploited the system.
Chowdhury sometimes looked bewildered in the witness box
However, the case raises important questions for the Civil Service. How was he able to get away with it for so long?

Part of the explanation is that the Civil Service's human resources system is not centralised. Chowdhury did not declare on government application forms that he was already a civil servant, so the system did not spot the duplication.

Hannah Keenan, who works at the Institute for Government, says the system clearly failed. "Government departments are taking hiring decisions independently of each other and without systems that join up," she said.
"That the model and the culture surrounding it aren't working shouldn't be a surprise though - we've known for a long time about poor performers flying under the radar by shuffling between jobs."

There are more than 550,000 people employed across the Civil Service, many in offices in Whitehall, in central London. They are responsible for carrying out government policy and the daily administration of the country.

Another reason why Chowdhury's fraud went undetected is that he was working entirely from the east London house he shared with his mother. In 2023, she had dementia and terminal cancer, and he told his employers that he needed to be at home to look after her.
But rather than reducing his workload to concentrate on her care, he took on more jobs. He covered up his impossible daily schedule by getting sick notes from his GP.
In April 2023, he was off with what he called "mixed anxiety and depressive disorder" from Defra, the UKHSA, the Department for Business and Trade and the Food Standards Agency.
While the sick notes were shown to the jury, they were not given evidence about what caused the depressive disorder or of a psychiatric assessment having been done during this period.
His sickness did not prevent him from starting yet another job – this time at the Home Office. He did not mention to them he was ill, nor did he tell them he was working elsewhere.
Unsurprisingly, a succession of his line managers told the jury he had not been very good at his jobs.

Especially damning was the evidence given by Dan McCartney, who managed Chowdhury at Defra. He said he had to "effectively tell him what to do the whole time" and that Chowdhury kept his camera off during video calls for four months, claiming technical problems.
But because Chowdhury was not subject to any formal performance measures at Defra, he was given a permanent job. He remained there for two years.
In September 2023, Chowdhury was found to have more than £40,000 in his bank accounts as well as significant investments, including £45,000 in premium bonds.
A recent survey of 1,700 civil servants by the independent think tank Re:State found 76% of respondents thought it did not do a good job of tackling poor performers.
An ex-senior civil servant told the BBC that much of the Civil Service is culturally averse to performance management.
"Whitehall's known for ages it has to be less risk averse. Shrinking the Civil Service and the adoption of artificial intelligence technology make that more vital," they said.

"But don't underestimate the fear factor: fear of drawn-out grievances and fear of being accused of wasting taxpayers' money if the Civil Service was to do what big private sector firms do, which is cut to get rid of poor performers by offering some money and a settlement agreement."

A Defra spokesperson said: "Kashim Chowdhury abused the trust placed in him as a public servant and defrauded taxpayers out of almost £285,000. He will now rightly face the consequences for his actions.

"This conviction is the result of a thorough and painstaking investigation led by the Defra Counter Fraud and Investigations team. It sends a clear message that fraud against the public purse will not be tolerated and those responsible will be held to account."
The spokesperson said Defra would use "all available avenues to recover the proceeds of Chowdhury's offending on behalf of taxpayers".
Chowdhury's case also illustrates a wider issue.

He was engaged in what is being called "polygamous working", where people hold down several jobs secretly. Websites have even been set up offering people advice on how to keep their employers in the dark.
Its rise has been blamed on larger numbers of people working from home.

The government's National Fraud Initiative has identified 23 cases of "polygamous working" across London in its most recent report. It uncovered £500,000 of overpaid salaries over a period of a few months.

Alongside the fraud case, Chowdhury is involved in a legal dispute with his three siblings, who accuse him of ''bullying'' their mother into signing over half of her £2.1m home to him in the final days of her life. He denies it.

At times during his criminal trial, Chowdhury appeared confused by what he was hearing and blamed trauma for the web of lies he had spun. The jury took seven hours to reach their verdict and decided he was motivated by personal gain - stealing tens of thousands of pounds from the taxpayer.
Chowdhury now faces a significant custodial sentence.

articles.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.standfirst: The share price dropped wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the value of Nvidia.
paragraphs: Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.
Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.
However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.
The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.
The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.
"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."
After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.
US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".
However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.
While Nvidia shares fell, the US stock market opened the week on a positive note after last week's turmoil, with Nvidia's rival chipmakers benefiting.

But analysts suggested the hit to the company would be short-lived. Victoria Fernandez, chief market strategist at Crossmark Global Investments said investors would not abandon Nvidia, because the chipmaker was so important to the AI industry.
"Nvidia is the core of this AI trade, and without them, all these other pieces start to fall apart because the financing's not there," she told the BBC.
Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia, which is central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies, with two other engineers in 1993.
Its chips were initially designed for gaming, but he decided to turn its focus on AI development, turning it into the world's second most valuable company.
A key concern for investors going forward is what would happen to Nvidia if Jensen Huang was removed from the company, as Fernandez said there was "no natural successor" to the chief executive.
Jensen Huang, unlike other founders in the tech industry, is vulnerable to any move by Nvidia's board of directors to oust him.
He owns only around 3.5% of the company, and Nvidia operates on a single class voting structure, meaning his stake would not be enough to act as a veto power over any board decision.
By contrast, many tech founders who lead their companies, including Mark Zuckerberg of Meta and Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, hold significant percentages of multiple types of stock in their companies.

Fernandez said she does not believe the board will remove Jensen Huang as chief executive, unless there is glaring evidence of wrongdoing related to national security or intellectual property, "but I bet they start bringing someone up as his number two, to have there for the future."
The modest fall in its shares mean investors believe it is unlikely he will step down or be removed as chief executive, but that the outcome of the investigation will be closely watched.

Even people who do not directly own shares in Nvidia can be affected by rises and falls in its value. Pensions or savings invested in pots which have stakes in the company through index tracking funds can be impacted, for example.
Nvidia chips have been a major focus of the AI race between the US and China and the White House has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.
The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.
But Jensen Huang has been against restricting the sale of Nvidia's chips to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.
In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.
Additional reporter by Samira Hussain, North America business correspondent.

articles.title: State Tax Rates on Long-Term Capital Gains, 2026
articles.standfirst: Savings and investment are essential for individuals’ and families’ financial security and for long-term economic growth. Policymakers should therefore consider reforms that can help mitigate—rather than add to—tax codes’ biases against saving and investment.
paragraphs: When taxpayers sell capital assets like real property or corporate stock, net earnings on those sales (capital gains) are generally subject to taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities., and net losses (capital losses) can generally be deducted when calculating income tax liability.

One major shortcoming of current capital gains taxation is that the tax basis, or the purchase price of an asset, is not indexed for inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin. As a result, capital gains are measured in nominal dollars, with the original purchase price subtracted from the sale price without any adjustment for the value of money over time. This means taxpayers are taxed on a combination of real gains and fictitious income that does not reflect an actual increase in purchasing power (although the tax code provides some accommodations, such as for qualifying sales of owner-occupied homes and properties transferred to heirs). In some cases, this lack of inflation indexingInflation indexing refers to automatic cost-of-living adjustments built into tax provisions to keep pace with inflation. Absent these adjustments, income taxes are subject to “bracket creep” and stealth increases on taxpayers, while excise taxes are vulnerable to erosion as taxes expressed in nominal dollars, rather than rates, slowly lose value. can be significant enough that taxpayers owe taxes on what appears to be a capital gain on paper, but is, in real terms, a net loss.

The federal tax code partially addresses this shortcoming through the preferential treatment of long-term capital gains. Long-term capital gains, defined as net gains on assets held for more than one year, are taxed under a separate rate schedule with lower rates and different brackets. Depending on a taxpayer’s overall taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. , long-term capital gains are taxed at rates of 0 percent, 15 percent, or 20 percent.

At the state level, accommodating the effects of inflation is less commonly seen. Thirty states and the District of Columbia overtax capital gains income simply by subjecting capital gains to the same rate schedule that applies to ordinary income.

Three states—Maryland, Minnesota, and Washington—expose some capital gains to higher rates than those that apply to ordinary income. Specifically, Maryland adds an additional 2 percent capital gains surtaxA surtax is an additional tax levied on top of an already existing business or individual tax and can have a flat or progressive rate structure. Surtaxes are typically enacted to fund a specific program or initiative, whereas revenue from broader-based taxes, like the individual income tax, typically cover a multitude of programs and services. to the state income tax due on income exceeding $350,000; Minnesota taxes most capital gains at ordinary rates but levies an additional 1 percentage point tax on net investment income exceeding $1 million; and Washington imposes a 7 percent rate on capital gains income up to $1 million and an additional 2.9 percent excise taxAn excise tax is a tax imposed on a specific good or activity. Excise taxes are commonly levied on cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, soda, gasoline, insurance premiums, amusement activities, and betting, and typically make up a relatively small and volatile portion of state and local and, to a lesser extent, federal tax collections. on capital gains income over $1 million.

Eight states, like the federal government, apply lower effective individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source rates to long-term gains than to ordinary income, either by applying lower statutory rates or by offering an exclusion for a portion of otherwise taxable capital gains, while Missouri exempts capital gains from its income tax. Eight states avoid this dilemma by forgoing an individual income tax altogether.

It is worth noting that several states provide targeted preferential tax treatment for certain types of capital gains, often providing exemptions for qualifying capital gains from investments in certain industries. For example, Colorado offers a subtraction of up to $100,000 to farmers for capital gains from sales of qualifying agricultural real property, while Maine offers a subtraction to certain housing organizations for a portion of capital gains from the transfer of certain properties to be used for affordable housing. While these types of provisions vary considerably from state to state, their existence indicates that policymakers recognize that taxing capital gains the same as ordinary income can disincentivize investment and create economic distortions. However, these provisions are often very narrowly targeted, offering tax advantages to only a small subset of taxpayers.

At the state level, taxing long-term capital gains at lower rates or excluding a set percentage of capital gains income (for all taxpayers and for all types of capital gains) helps offset the fact that capital gains taxes apply to nominal, not real, capital gains. Therefore, more states should reconsider their treatment of long-term capital gains, either by applying a lower statutory rate to capital gains income or excluding a certain percentage of otherwise taxable capital gains. Additionally, states should also ensure they provide robust and timely deductions for capital losses.

Even when lower rate schedules or exclusions are granted, capital gains taxes represent a form of double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. on investment income. To illustrate this, consider an individual who decides to save for the future by purchasing shares of stock in a company. Unless the shares are purchased through tax-advantaged investment accounts—like a 401(k) or IRA, where invested income is taxed only once, either on the way in (Roth accounts) or on the way out (traditional accounts)—the investment is made using ordinary wage or salary income that has already been taxed under standard federal and state individual income tax rate schedules.

Under favorable circumstances, the value of that investment will grow over time. The growth reflects corporate earnings that have already been subject to corporate income taxes, reducing the amount of income ultimately distributed to investors. Years or decades later, when the investor sells their shares and realizes a capital gain, the same underlying income will be taxed again under the individual income tax.

While preferential rates applied to long-term capital gains reduce this burden, they do not eliminate it. Moreover, the burden can be compounded by the fact that capital gains are measured by nominal rather than inflation-adjusted dollars. Thus, taxpayers may owe tax not only on previously taxed earnings but also on inflationary gains that do not represent a real increase in purchasing power.

When evaluating the tax treatment of investment income, state policymakers should consider all layers of taxes on those earnings, including corporate income taxes, and understand how the failure to inflation-index the tax basis, combined with most states’ failure to adjust rates accordingly, results in the widespread overtaxation of capital gains income in the United States.

Savings and investment are essential for individuals’ and families’ financial security and for long-term economic growth. Policymakers should therefore consider reforms that can help mitigate—rather than add to—tax codes’ biases against saving and investment.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Nicole Fox is a Policy Analyst with the Center for State Tax Policy at the Tax Foundation, where she serves as a resource to policymakers in their efforts to modernize and improve the structure of their state tax codes.
Cole Kellison is a 2026 summer intern with the Tax Foundation’s Center for State Tax Policy.

articles.title: How Worried Is The MPC About The Risk Of ‘Sticky’ Inflation?
articles.standfirst: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate this week for the first time in three years, to 4 per cent. Our view, set out in Thursday’s press notice and will...
paragraphs: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate this week for the first time in three years, to 4 per cent. Our view, set out in Thursday’s press notice and will develop in next week’s Economic Outlook, is that the Monetary Policy Committee is behind the curve given the size of the energy shock and the evidence that inflation expectations are already above levels consistent with the 2 per cent target.

This post asks a narrower question: what can we infer from the November Monetary Policy Report about the MPC’s own view of the risks – particularly the risk that inflation proves to be ‘sticky’, falling back more slowly than hoped – and what that adds to our understanding of how it is setting rates.

The question arises because, under the banner of its “monetary policy transformation”, the Bank now publishes a great deal of information about the distribution of outcomes and what it might mean for policy, but not the one thing that would answer the question directly. Unlike the Riksbank or Norges Bank, it publishes no preferred path for Bank Rate; unlike the Fed, not a ‘dot plot’. Instead, we get a central projection on a path set by the market, two scenarios, model-generated policy paths for each, nine individual paragraphs in the minutes and a survey of market participants.

Some history explains why this is a live issue. Before the financial crisis many central banks became what Lars Svensson christened ‘inflation-forecast targeters’, setting rates so that the modal forecast for inflation returned to target at a horizon fixed by their view of the transmission mechanism.

That approach breaks down when the risk of an extreme outcome should affect policy today even if it leaves the modal forecast unchanged. The obvious example came after the financial crisis, when rates were at the lower bound and a further downside shock could not have been met with lower rates. The one most relevant now is the risk that inflation turns out far higher than expected because of an energy shock, as it did in 2022. Following the Bernanke Review, which recommended scenario analysis as a way of communicating such risks, the Bank is now trying to unpack its full distribution to explain its decisions. That is ambitious, and no other major central bank publishes this much of its risk analysis. But this comes with a risk of, at best, muddying the Committee’s main message; at worst unsettling inflation expectations. Whether the exercise clarifies or confuses depends on whether readers can extract the Committee’s conditional plan from it. We make the attempt.

Start with the central projection. It is conditioned on the path for Bank Rate implied by market prices, which rises to 4.9 per cent by the end of 2027 and is still 4.7 per cent at the end of 2029. On that path, CPI inflation peaks at around 5 per cent next summer, returns rapidly to the 2 per cent target in the second half of 2028 and ends the forecast at 1.8 per cent, with output about 1 per cent below potential throughout (Figure 1).

Taken at face value this is not a bad outcome for an inflation-targeting central bank. Inflation is back at target two years out and drifts only a little below it in year three; one could argue the undershoot is small enough to be splitting hairs. The cost is continued slack: the output gap widens for 18 months and then closes only partially, a judgement that rests on the Bank’s estimate of potential output, which is unobservable and on which members disagree. But, on the Bank’s own numbers, which are admittedly indicative projections “broadly consistent” with the MPC’s central view, the end of the forecast has inflation below target and output below potential at the same time, which argues for easier policy than the curve, at least later on, without any trade-off. The Governor’s remarks at the press conference pointed the same way.

The central projection is not, however, a description of what the Committee expects to do, and the minutes say so. Most members describe a further increase or two as likely or possible and the path thereafter as conditional; Alan Taylor calls the November move “one-for-now” and says the next “could be up, down, or sideways”. The Bank’s survey of market participants says the same from outside: the median respondent expects Bank Rate to peak at 4.25 per cent in February and to be back at 3.5 per cent two years out, against a curve at 4.9 per cent. The Bank attributes the difference to risk premia.

The Report then shows what would happen if policy departed from the market path. For each projection it publishes two illustrative paths from the Bank’s models: an optimal policy projection that minimises a loss function over inflation, the output gap and changes in rates, and a Taylor-type rule that responds to non-energy inflation and the output gap. The Bank calls these illustrative, and comparable to the market curve as overall stances rather than forecasts of Bank Rate. They are nonetheless the closest thing to a preferred path in the published material and will have been debated at length as reasonable positions.

Figure 2 shows them for the central projection, and the Report’s own summary is curious. It says the rule paths are “broadly similar to the market curve in the near term, but somewhat lower further out”. The second half is right: both rules end 2029 at 4.1 to 4.3 per cent against the curve’s 4.7, having cut by around 90 basis points from their peaks where the curve cuts by 20. The first averages two paths that disagree. The Taylor-type rule sits below the curve through 2027; the optimal path is above it from the start, at 4.8 per cent in the first quarter against 4.2 on the curve, and peaks at 5.2 per cent that autumn. And these alternative paths do better on both objectives: inflation at 2.0 to 2.2 per cent at the end of 2029 rather than 1.8, and an output gap of 0.6 to 0.9 per cent rather than 1.1.

The Committee also publishes two scenarios on the same conditioning path. In the adverse inflation scenario, energy prices settle around 30 per cent (oil) and 50 per cent (gas) above the futures curve and second-round effects are stronger; inflation is still 3 per cent at the end of 2028. In the weaker demand scenario, energy follows the curve but demand falters, no second-round effects emerge, and inflation falls to 1.2 per cent by 2029. Each comes with the same two rule paths.
The Bank’s staff paper on policymaking under uncertainty offers two answers to what the scenarios are for.

The first is that they are contingency plans. If energy prices settle well above the curve and second-round effects take hold, the adverse scenario and its policy paths tell us roughly what the Committee would do; if demand falters, the weaker demand scenario does the same. On this reading the scenarios are forward guidance conditional on the state of the world, and the minutes support it: the scenarios “would all require different monetary policy responses if any of them were to materialise”. They also prepare readers for outcomes away from the centre of the distribution.

The second reading turns the scenarios into a test. If the Committee were a risk-neutral policymaker, the probability-weighted forecast would explain its decision. If it is not, we would need to appeal to ‘risk management’: a deliberate tilt away from the average to head off the outcomes it fears most, which is how several members describe their votes. Indeed, Alan Taylor calls the November move a “risk-management ‘one-for-now’ insurance hike”, Swati Dhingra describes it as “insurance against upside risks”, and Catherine Mann argues for 50 basis points “from a risk management and credibility perspective”. The scenarios let us ask whether the mean forecast is enough to explain the decision, or whether something more is needed.

Doing well needs a definition. The remit asks the Committee to return inflation to 2 per cent in the medium term – in practice the two- and three-year horizons – without creating more spare capacity than necessary. A path can therefore be judged on two gaps, inflation from 2 per cent and output from potential. The three projections on the market curve all end the forecast with inflation at or below target and output below potential; the rule paths get closer to both objectives.

The two readings are closer than they look. In a linear model with a quadratic loss, which is what the Bank’s simulations use, the best single path for a committee uncertain about the scenario is the weighted average of the paths that are optimal in each. The weighted average is therefore the benchmark for a risk-neutral policymaker, and anything beyond it is risk management proper.

Read as contingency plans, the paths answer a practical question: given that the scenario will only be revealed over time, where should policy start? The answer barely depends on the scenario. Through the first half of 2027 the optimal paths for the central and weaker demand cases are identical to a tenth of a point, at 4.4 per cent this quarter and 4.8 per cent next, and the adverse case is only 0.2 to 0.4 points higher. The paths separate only from mid-2027, by which time the pay round and the energy data will have revealed which world we are in. The model’s advice is to go to around 4.5 per cent now and 5 per cent by the spring whatever one believes, and then to cut, by more and sooner than the market expects, as Figure 3 shows.

Read as a risk-management problem, the paths need weights. We tried a range, from one that puts half the probability on the central case and most of the rest on weaker demand, to one that puts 45 per cent on the adverse scenario. The result is the same in every case, as Figure 3 suggests it would be: the three paths differ mainly in their peaks, not in their shape. The weighted optimal path peaks between 5.25 and 5.55 per cent in late 2027 and ends 2029 between 4.1 and 4.45 per cent; the Taylor-type path peaks around 5 per cent in 2028 and ends between 3.95 and 4.25. Over every possible combination of weights the optimal path ends below the curve’s 4.7 per cent in 93 per cent of cases, and the Taylor-type path in all of them. Moving from equal weights to a strongly hawkish tilt shifts the end-point by about 0.2 points.

Mean inflation across the scenarios is above the central projection at two years (2.1 to 2.3 per cent against 2.0) but not at three, and both alternative scenarios carry more slack, so the two effects on policy largely offset. The shape of the preferred path, a peak at or above where the market has it and a lower level further out, does not depend on the weights. At the very least, then, the mean forecast gives no reason why the MPC might signal fewer near-term rate rises than the market curve implies, as some members appear to be doing. Where it does point to easier policy is further out, and there the Bank’s models and the market already agree.

The Bank’s own models, then, say higher in the near term than the market and lower further out, and that conclusion needs no appeal to risk aversion: it holds for the central case alone. The Committee has instead moved 25 basis points, and most of its members describe the next step as conditional on evidence of second-round effects. That is the logic of the Bank’s other rule, the Taylor-type path, which responds to non-energy inflation only as it arrives and sits at 3.8 to 4.0 per cent through the same period in every scenario. The two rules the Bank publishes give opposite answers on where to begin, 4 per cent or 5 per cent, and the Committee appears to have chosen the one that delivers a lower level of rates. It is also the one that, on the Bank’s own account, does not return inflation to target within the forecast period.

On the face of it, then, the Committee’s caution is not well explained by its own analysis of the central case, let alone by the risks around it. A risk-neutral policymaker who believed the Bank’s model would be aiming for a peak in Bank Rate that is a percentage point higher than the Committee seems to be signalling now; a risk-averse one, worried that second-round effects switch on above some threshold of inflation, would be higher still. Put another way, the Committee is behaving as though it can afford to wait for evidence of second-round effects before responding and that it is not worried about the risk that inflation turns out to be much more persistent. This seems hard to reconcile with the experience of 2022. Of course, individual MPC members might simply not believe these model-based scenarios – but, if that’s the case, it would be helpful for those members to say why. The point of publishing scenarios and policy paths is to explain decisions. And it’s clear that the Bank is giving us a lot of information to help us do that. On this occasion that material helps to explain the decision the Committee did not take, rather than the one it did.

articles.title: Ignore the rate rise, worry about the forecast
articles.standfirst:
Rate rises can squeeze households. But Thursday’s hike from the Bank of England – its first in more than three years – brings mixed fortunes, compared with the universally grim forecasts published alongside it. Let’s start with the group you’d tend to worry about when rates go up: mortgagors. They’ve already taken a hit In … Continued
The post Ignore the rate rise, worry about the forecast appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: Rate rises can squeeze households. But Thursday’s hike from the Bank of England – its first in more than three years – brings mixed fortunes, compared with the universally grim forecasts published alongside it.
Let’s start with the group you’d tend to worry about when rates go up: mortgagors.

In the end, the Bank took a little more than eight months to raise rates after the outbreak of the Iran war in February – but financial-market traders knew what was coming. They immediately raised their expectations for the level of Bank Rate in the coming years, and it’s these expectations that affect the price of fixed-rate deals that dominate the mortgage market today. As a result, mortgage rates rose by about a percentage point, even as the Bank stood still. For a typical first-time buyer (with a £220,000 mortgage) that rise costs an extra £140 a month relative to deals on offer in February.

While we should spare a thought for the roughly one-in-eight households on variable rates, most mortgagors have been shielded entirely from rising rates by their aforementioned fixes. That means the full pain of higher rates will only be felt slowly as people roll off their fixes onto higher rates. That will be around 1.4 million households over the next year, and their collective repricing will push the nation’s mortgage interest bill to a projected £72 billion in 2027 – £9 billion higher than in our pre-war projections. Granted, that doesn’t sound great, but we already knew it was on the way. Thursday’s announcement itself changed very little.[1]

The bigger story this week wasn’t the rate rise, it was the Bank’s new economic outlook. Inflation is now forecast to peak at 4.9 per cent next spring and not to get back to the 2 per cent target until the third quarter of 2028. That’s a full two years later than the Bank expected back in the halcyon days of February.

And getting inflation down won’t come cheap. In the Bank’s forecast, it hikes interest rates to nearly 5 per cent (although it has been at pains to stress that this is not a guide to future policy). Higher rates mean that growth is now expected to average a feeble 1.1 per cent annual pace over the next two years. More inflation and less growth add up to a nasty outlook for pay. Private-sector earnings are forecast to fall by 0.5 per cent in real terms next year, meaning the average worker in 2027 is set to be paid £390 less in real terms than they were in 2025.

That squeeze won’t only affect mortgagors. Falling earnings will hit social tenants, renters, outright owners – anyone who relies on a pay packet. Next to that, the £100 Council Tax rebates announced in last week’s Budget look pretty small.

Official forecasts have been coming thick and fast over the past month, and each one has brought a gloomier outlook. We started well in October, with the IMF boosting Britain’s near-term growth outlook and giving us a pat on the back for our prudent fiscal plans. But then, just a couple of weeks later, the OBR lowered the tone. As my colleagues pointed out on Budget night, its living standards forecast has the average Briton set to be just £400 better at the end of the 2020s than at the start (each of the previous five decades saw gains of at least £3,400). And this week’s forecast from the Bank is more worrying still, with an inflation peak more than a percentage point higher than the OBR’s. Add that into the mix, and the OBR’s meagre living standards growth could vanish entirely. The rates might be grabbing the headlines, but the forecast is the part I’ll be watching closely.
Simon is on Bluesky. This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.
[1] UK interest rates rose a little on the back of the Bank’s decision and publication of its Monetary Policy Report, but were broadly flat over the day as a whole.
