roll out AI-scribing’, Digital Health, 1 April 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.digitalhealth.net/2026/04/hertfordshire-community-nhs-trust-to-roll-out-ai-scribing  Similarly, in stroke care, AI brain-scan software is now in use across all 107 NHS stroke centres, with impressive preliminary results, though this rollout began under the previous government in 2023.20 NR Times, ‘NHS AI tool will help 50% of stroke patients recover’, 2 September 2025, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://nrtimes.co.uk/nhs-ai-tool-will-help-50-of-stroke-patients-recover-lpc25 ,21 Department of Health and Social Care, The Rt Hon Steve Barclay MP and Chloe Smith, ‘£21 million to roll out artificial intelligence across the NHS’, press release, 23 June 2023, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/21-million-to-roll-out-artificial-intelligence-across-the-nhs  However, more broadly, the speed at which AI has developed, means that we have very little data (including in surveys) about NHS staff’s use of AI before 2024, and it is difficult to assess Labour’s progress in this area. Likewise, it is also hard to distinguish between simple AI ‘adoption’ (where trusts and services have bought services) versus true embrace and regular use of these technologies by NHS staff.

Perhaps most importantly, the piecemeal and often bottom-up adoption of AI in different parts of the NHS, and limited reporting/evaluation of these technologies, makes any assessment of their benefits (beyond specific clinical use cases) challenging. It is also unwise to assume straightforward efficiency gains through AI adoption. There is little existing literature considering how freed-up time, resulting from time-saving technologies, is actually repurposed.22 Moulds A and Horton T, ‘How would clinicians use time freed up by technology?’, The Health Foundation, May 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.health.org.uk/reports-and-analysis/briefings/how-would-clinicians-use-time-freed-up-by-technology  Staff time might be used for more activity, but it also might be used to spend more time with each patient (improving patient experience but not driving up productivity, per se), conducting training (which has knock-on productivity benefits that aren’t immediately clear), or completing administrative tasks that might otherwise be done during work breaks or during overtime. All these are worthwhile uses of time, but they don’t automatically equal greater productivity or more patients treated.

Labour has made consistent progress on the NHS App

Building on the anticipated rollout of the SPR, the Starmer government promised that an improved NHS App will create convenience for patients and save resource for the NHS.23 Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England, ‘Managing healthcare easy as online banking with revamped NHS App’, press release, 3 July 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/managing-healthcare-easy-as-online-banking-with-revamped-nhs-app  The App will be complemented by a raft of other AI-enhanced ‘My X’ services, like the My NHS GP tool (available 24/7, for non-urgent cases), and the My Choices tool.* For service users, the NHS App will be the most visible sign of a digital shift in the way the NHS manages care.

NHS England’s online NHS App roadmap24 NHS England, ‘NHS App roadmap’, 5 November 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://digital.nhs.uk/services/nhs-app/roadmap  tracks completed, current and future projects aimed at improving patient access and experience. Release notes25 NHS England, ‘NHS App release notes’, 25 March 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.nhs.uk/nhs-app/about/nhs-app-release-notes  indicate that there have been small (bug fixes) as well as large improvements (introduction of new services, such as the integration of online consultation and Patient Care Aggregator services) to the NHS App at a near fortnightly rate since Labour took office. Clearly, work is being done.

And, use of the App is growing. There have been over 40 million NHS App account registrations, with app login sessions in June 2026 79.9% higher than in the same period in June 2024.26 NHS England, ‘NHS App management information – June 2026’, 24 July 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/nhs-app-statistics/june-2026  The government set a target for 85% of hospitals to make appointment information available through the app by March 2025. This was met, with 87% of trusts hitting the target in March 2025, up from 68% in July 2024.27 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Major NHS App expansion cuts waiting times’, press release, 28 April 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/major-nhs-app-expansion-cuts-waiting-times

As with many areas of digital innovation, greater uptake of technologies alone does not equal success and focusing solely on uptake or expansion of online services risks obscuring whether these changes are adding value for service users. But patients are broadly positive about the App; a Healthwatch survey, conducted in the summer of 2025, found that 57% of participants agreed that the NHS App helped manage their health.**,***

There remain risks in an ‘App-first’ approach. Those with lower digital literacy skills are most obviously at risk of marginalisation28 Pilot L, Offline and Overlooked: Digital exclusion and its impact on older people, Age UK, 2024, www.ageuk.org.uk/siteassets/documents/reports-and-publications/reports-and-briefings/offline-and-overlooked-report.pdf ,29 Healthwatch Derby, ‘NHS app: awareness and experiences report 2024’, 8 August 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://nds.healthwatch.co.uk/reports-library/nhs-app-awareness-and-experiences-report-2024 ,30 Lloyds Banking Group, 2025 Consumer Digital Index: The generative AI edition, 2025, www.lloydsbankinggroup.com/assets/pdfs/media/consumer-digital-index/2025/2025-consumer-digital-index.pdf ,31 The King’s Fund, ‘Connection lost: people’s experiences of using digital technology in health and care’, 2023, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://features.kingsfund.org.uk/connection-lost/index.html?_ga=2.182180519.1637327810.1727786389-964730683.1724858879  but many beyond this group feel ‘forced’ into using the App and frustrated by imperfect services and inaccurate records, even if they valued the App’s ease of use and convenience, overall.32 Healthwatch Oxfordshire, ‘Digital health care and the NHS App, Voices from Oxfordshire’, 2025, https://nds.healthwatch.co.uk/sites/default/files/reports_library/NHS%20App%20final%20final%20Nov%202025.pdf  Digital change of this kind will also require physical service redesign and standardisation across the country in order to avoid confusion across services, repetition or errors.33 Devereux E, ‘NHS App breaking cancer diagnoses before clinicians’, HSJ, 18 November 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/technology-and-innovation/nhs-app-breaking-cancer-diagnoses-before-clinicians/7040409.article; quoted in Mistry P, ‘Is the NHS ready for the AI-powered patient?’, The King’s Fund, 26 May 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/nhs-ready-for-ai-powered-patient

* Other services promise convenience and personalisation for patients, including greater ability for self-referral, remote consultation, self-management of medication and vaccine regimens as well as managing their own care as well as that of their children.

**Creating a ‘one stop shop’ for care would go some way to improve the digital experience of even those who   are very digitally confident, many of whom use multiple apps, websites and login details to access care. http://kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/the-reality-of-and-potential-for-digitally-enabled-care-in-the-community 

***The most common use of the App in one survey was to order repeat prescriptions (76%), followed by viewing GP health records (70%). Indeed, app users view their GP health record over 35 million times each month, with 12 million views of test results. https://nds.healthwatch.co.uk/sites/default/files/reports_library/NHS%20App%20final%20final%20Nov%202025.pdf;http://digital.nhs.uk/services/nhs-app/roadmap 

Recommendations

For the government to make a success of its digital shift, it first needs to get the basics right, address ongoing funding concerns, fill staff skill gaps, build public trust and implement more systematic approaches to data collection and data sharing. 

It should also prioritise investment in IT basics that would definitely improve productivity before investment in more speculative technologies such as AI, where the benefits are far more uncertain. These are well-established priority areas where trade associations, think tanks and charities have called for improvements for many years.34 Nuffield Trust, written evidence to the House of Commons Health and Social Care Committee inquiry on digital transformation in the NHS (DTN0051), 5 July 2022, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/109146/html ,35 Keck L and Godec S, ‘Trust and confidence in technology-enabled care’, The Health Foundation, November 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.health.org.uk/reports-and-analysis/briefings/trust-and-confidence-in-technology-enabled-care ,36 techUK, ‘Driving digital transformation: techUK’s recommendations for health and social care’, 21 November 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.techuk.org/resource/driving-digital-transformation-techuk-s-recommendations-for-health-social-care.html ,37 The NHS Alliance, ‘Digital transformation in the NHS: a reference guide’, 11 December 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://thenhsalliance.org/resources/digital-transformation-in-the-nhs-a-reference-guide ,38 House of Commons Health and Social Care Committee, Digital Transformation in the NHS: Eighth report of session 2022–23 (HC 223), The Stationery Office, 2023, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5803/cmselect/cmhealth/223/report.html Those enabling factors are vital before ministers get too carried away with the “white heat” of AI, genomics and wearables technology.

The government should also ensure it makes a strong case to the public for the need for change. Previous attempts at digital reform – such as the ‘care.data’ scheme and the General Practice Data for Planning and Research (GPDPR) programme – were slowed or failed due to a lack of public support.

The current approach of ad hoc adoption of AI technologies across the NHS does create a useful laboratory for innovation, reducing risk by keeping technologies localised to small geographies or service areas with the option to scale those that have proven benefits. However, without proper evaluation of these technologies (probably led by central government) and frameworks for adoption, patient trust, safety and efficiency could be undermined. The NHS should build upon the recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare to rapidly build a regulatory framework for AI use in the NHS.39 Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare: Recommendations for a future regulatory framework, 10 September 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-commission-into-the-regulation-of-ai-in-healthcare-recommendations-for-a-future-regulatory-framework  The Commission notes that current frameworks are designed for products that are “more static and easier to reliably assess at a single point in time”. AI-enabled products “may iterate rapidly, perform differently in different settings and depend on the data, workflows, people and organisations around them”.40Ibid. Without greater clarity, the NHS runs the risk that trusts and services within the NHS deploy AI (at significant cost) without clear evaluations, use cases or the proper technical architecture and staff training needed to enable success.*

Following decades of work,41 Robertson A, Bates DW and Sheikh A, ‘The rise and fall of England’s National Programme for IT’, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, 2011, vol. 104, no. 11, pp. 434–35, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3206716/ the NHS has finally achieved near-full coverage of EPRs.42 NHS England, ‘Digitising the frontline’, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/digitaltechnology/digitising-the-frontline  But there are still problems with how the service uses EPRs. Many staff still report issues sharing or accessing data across different parts of the service.43 Moulds A and Horton T, ‘Which technologies offer the biggest opportunities to save time in the NHS?’, The Health Foundation, April 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.health.org.uk/reports-and-analysis/briefings/which-technologies-offer-the-biggest-opportunities-to-save-time-in , 44 NHS England, ‘Interoperability’, 15 May 2023, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/interoperability  It is positive that the government has made it a priority over the course of 2026 to optimise EPR “functionality, efficiency and usability”, conduct digital maturity assessments and provide support (including through a tiger team service) to trusts as they embed EPRs. As part of this, the NHS should implement more consistent approaches to data collection and coding standards which hamper interoperability and formalise data sharing agreements between places to maximise the benefits of EPRs.

There are considerable digital skills gaps across the NHS. The service struggles to hire digital specialist roles because of less competitive pay and work conditions relative to the private sector.45 Dawood S, ‘The NHS’s digital problem: how old infrastructure is slowing down healthcare services’, The New Statesman, 23 August 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.newstatesman.com/spotlight/healthcare/nhs/2024/08/nhs-digital-transformation-infrastructure-technology-patient-records-artificial-intelligence-wa…  There is also a history of high turnover of digital and data workforce, affecting institutional memory and delivery.46 Mistry P, ‘Infrastructure for innovation: getting the NHS and social care ready for AI’, The King’s Fund, 25 June 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/infrastructure-nhs-social-care-ai#%E2%80%8B%E2%80%8Borganisational-and-system-capabilities-  The cutting of non-clinical staff in trusts alongside headcount reductions in NHSE, DHSC and ICBs risks the loss of digital capabilities, institutional memory and programme delivery capacity at a vital time. The government should ensure that it has sufficient data and digital capacity to deliver its digital ambitions.

* Early evidence indicates that this has been the case in many trusts that have adopted Palantir’s Federated Data Platform. https://www.ft.com/content/a3e94197-87a8-4ba5-8a6d-4b7193993af9?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.ft.com/content/cc1f2e28-117f-41bb-96b9-030746cf9530?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.ft.com/content/63bfdeb2-efb1-4e3a-8c89-a884eb5bd618?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.ft.com/content/da888f06-b9bc-4d83-8020-e82f5d5fa609?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v48/n13/peter-geoghegan-and-lucas-amin/this-looks-absolutely-rubbish

paragraphs: In a speech defending his record after the 2026 local elections, Keir Starmer argued that he had “got the big political choices right”, using falling NHS waiting times as evidence.1 Starmer K, ‘Prime Minister and Leader of the Labour Party Keir Starmer’s speech in Central London (11 May)’, 11 May 2026, https://labour.org.uk/updates/stories/prime-minister-and-leader-of-the-labour-party-keir-starmers-speech-in-central-london-today-11-may/ He did have some success managing the NHS. The elective waiting list – people waiting for planned care, such as hip replacements or cataract removals – is slightly lower than it was at the 2024 general election and people are not waiting so long for that care.

There have been other areas of improvement. The NHS has achieved a large increase in the salaried GP workforce and steady improvement in patient satisfaction with general practice. Ambulance response times have dropped considerably since 2024.

That is only a partial picture of Starmer’s record on the NHS however. His government also spent considerable time, energy and political capital on its structural reforms – the abolition of NHS England (NHSE) and reorganisation of integrated care boards (ICBs) – and pursuit of 50% headcount cuts in those organisations. The Starmer government handled those reorganisations very poorly. The Burnham government has been marginally, though not much, better: both are still foundering due to a lack of clear political direction and foresight.

As health secretary, Wes Streeting also stressed the importance of the NHS returning to financial balance, breaking the cycle of financial deficits and emergency funding injections that has characterised its finances for the last few years. The NHS seems to have achieved that goal.2 Harvey-Rich O and Warner M, Is the era of annual NHS top-ups over?, Institute for Fiscal Studies, 28 August 2026, retrieved 14 October 2026, https://ifs.org.uk/articles/era-annual-nhs-top-ups-over But given the relatively modest (by historical standards) funding settlement for the NHS, reaching financial balance has required trusts to slow their activity growth and cut (particularly non-clinical) staff.

Moreover, a focus on elective performance, structural reorganisation and financial balance has prevented the NHS from making progress on other priorities. Away from electives, other areas of NHS performance – A&E waiting times, children’s community care and waiting times for diagnostic tests, among others – have seen little or no improvement.

Similarly, there is little evidence that the NHS is making significant progress on the “three shifts” (from hospitals to the community, from treating sickness to prevention and from analogue to digital) that the Starmer government outlined in its flagship strategy, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England (10YHP hereafter).

The Burnham government’s NHS inheritance is therefore mixed and he faces important decisions. The new prime minister has emphasised his commitment to a more devolved set of public services. But NHS reforms initiated under his predecessor are drawing power towards central government. If he wants to go ahead with those reforms, he needs to explain how they square with the “devolution by default” approach.

This chapter assesses NHS performance against the government’s stated goals for the service. It will first look at performance on elective care – so far the government’s primary focus – followed by other areas of NHS performance. It will then look at how the government has handled structural reorganisations and finally the progress made on each of the three shifts.
It draws on analysis of publicly available data and dozens of semi-structured interviews with policy experts and staff working in government, NHS England, trusts and in general practice.

From the start, the Starmer government made reducing elective waiting times its primary objective for the NHS. One of Starmer’s five ‘missions’ was an NHS mission. To demonstrate progress on that mission, he set a ‘milestone’ (a target) that 92% of patients would be treated within 18 weeks of a referral for elective care by March 2029.1 HM Government, Plan for change: Milestones for mission-led government, Gov.uk, 5 December 2024, p. 6,https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6751af4719e0c816d18d1df3/Plan_for_Change.pdf

This was not a new ambition. The New Labour government introduced the 92% target in the 2000s and it is now part of the NHS constitution, which outlines the right patients have to NHS care.2 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Handbook to the NHS Constitution for England’, guidance, Gov.uk, 24 January 2025, retrieved 17 September 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/supplements-to-the-nhs-constitution-for-england/the-handbook-to-the-nhs-constitution-for-england

Performance against that target has long been poor. After elective performance improved under the 1997–2010 Labour governments, meaning the NHS reached that target, performance declined again under the coalition and then Conservative governments. The last time that the NHS hit the 92% target was in September 2015, when the waiting list stood at 3.5m cases.3 NHS England, ‘Consultant-led Referral to Treatment Waiting Times Data 2026-27’, England.NHS.uk, (no date), retrieved 17 September 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/statistics/statistical-work-areas/rtt-waiting-times/rtt-data-2026-27/ Performance worsened substantially during the pandemic and was only at 58.9% in June 2024, just before Labour took power, with a waiting list of 7.6m cases.
Under Starmer, the Labour government set three targets for 18-week elective performance in this parliament:

Between June 2024 and the end of 2025, the NHS made steady – though not dramatic – improvements in the elective waiting list. That improvement accelerated in the first months of 2026, meaning that in March 2026, there were 7.1 million cases waiting for care, a drop of 515,000 cases, or 6.8%, compared to June 2024. While an improvement, it is still historically very high: 2.5m cases (or 55.4%) higher than in February 2020, the eve of the Covid-19 pandemic.

That reduction in the waiting list led to improved performance on waiting times for elective care. In June 2024, just before the government took power, 58.9% of elective cases were waiting 18 weeks or less for care, far below the constitutional target of 92%. By March 2026, some 65.3% of cases had been waiting 18 weeks or less for care, a 6.4 percentage point increase from June 2024, meeting the first elective target.

Most of that improvement came between January and March 2026. At the end of January, 61.5% of cases had been waiting less than 18 weeks. The subsequent 3.8 percentage point (pp) improvement is the largest two-month gain on record (outside of the pandemic). As discussed in more depth below, trusts largely achieved this by delivering intensive operational activity, rather than more sustainable increases in activity, paid for with short-term, one-off funding.1 Institute for Government interview.

Since March 2026, however, progress has reversed. The waiting list grew by 264,000 cases between March and August 2026 and the proportion of cases waiting less than 18 weeks was marginally worse, at 65.2% in August.

Alongside the national target, the NHS set a target for every trust to improve their elective performance by five percentage points by March 2026 (compared to a November 2024 baseline), with all trusts hitting a minimum of 60%.2 NHS England, ‘2025/26 priorities and operational planning guidance’, England.NHS.uk, 30 January 2025, retrieved 17 September 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/publication/2025-26-priorities-and-operational-planning-guidance/

Of the 133 trusts for which there is consistent data between those two months, 58.6% hit both parts of their target while 6.8% hit neither part of their target. Of the remaining 46 trusts that hit one of the two targets, the vast majority (42) hit the minimum 60% target but not the 5pp increase.

Some trusts had exceptionally large increases in elective performance in that time, including 21 trusts that had a 10pp or greater improvement. The Princess Alexandra trust in Harlow, Essex had the largest increase: 22.4pp from 41.8% to 64.1%, through a combination of rigorous waiting list management, improved data quality from its new electronic patient record system, redesigning patient flow, optimising discharges and taking stronger operational grip on performance.1 Institute for Government interview.

Of those 21 trusts, 13 (61.9%) were in the bottom quartile of performance in November 2024. As a result, the range of performance among acute trusts has narrowed since Labour won the election, with particularly strong improvement among some of the worst performing trusts. In June 2024, there was a 44.7pp gap between the best and worst performing trusts and a 9.5pp gap between the trusts at the 25th and 75th percentiles. In August 2026, this narrowed to 33.3 and 6.8pp respectively.

Alongside the 18-week target, the Labour government also gave the NHS the target to reduce the proportion of cases waiting more than 52 weeks to less than 1% by March 2026. This followed the NHS’s inability to eliminate them by March 2025, initially targeted by the Conservative government.1 Comptroller and Auditor General, Managing NHS backlogs and waiting times in England, Session 2022- 23, HC 799, National Audit Office, 2022, p. 29, www.nao.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/managing-NHSbacklogs-and-waiting-times-in-England-Report.pdf

There was improvement in that metric over the course of 2025/26: the proportion of cases fell from 2.4% in March 2025 to 1.3% in March 2026. This was still 0.3pp above the government’s target. Since then, it has increased slightly and in August 2026 sat at 1.5%.

The elective waiting list shrank from September 2024 onwards because the NHS increased removals from the list by more than additions have increased. In 2025/26, the NHS removed* 21.8m cases from the waiting list (an increase of 3.5% compared to 2024/25), while only 21.5m were added (an increase of 2.6%). That has helped to bring the waiting list down, as described above.

*A removal can be because the NHS started treating that person, or because the NHS took the case off the waiting list for administrative reasons, such as if the person was uncontactable. Most removals are due to people completing treatment: 85.4% in 2026/26.
Interviewees gave three reasons for improved national figures: increased diversion of referrals, a greater focus on waiting list management and sprint funding in the final quarter of 2025/26.

The NHS adds a case to the elective waiting list following a referral from another part of the health system.* Before making a referral, professionals can use a mechanism called ‘specialist advice’ to consult with a specialist doctor in hospital. The specialist can recommend that they do not make the referral. This is known as a ‘diverted referral’.

Diverting referrals helps elective performance by lowering additions to the waiting list. Trusts can use the freed-up appointments to work through the cases already on the waiting list, reducing the time people wait for care.

It can also lead to better outcomes for the patient by providing a quicker route to expert input, rather than waiting months for care. The NHS says that diverted patients receive more appropriate and timely care elsewhere in the service, such as in general practice or community care. However, it is impossible to know if this is the case, as there is no public data that shows the outcomes of those who the NHS diverts.

Specialist advice is not a new tool and its use has grown gradually for years. In 2019, there were just over 600,000 requests for pre-referral specialist advice.** This rose to 2.6 million requests in 2023/24, the last full year the NHS was under Conservative control.

The Labour government rapidly identified this as a vital route to reducing waiting times for elective care. Therefore it further incentivised its use in 2025/26 by including a £20 payment for GPs for every request for advice they make, which the NHS said “will deliver up to 4 million advice requests from GPs in 2025/26”, up from 2.4 million in 2024/25.1 NHS England, ‘Reforming elective care for patients’, England.NHS.uk, 6 January 2025, retrieved 17 September 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/reforming-elective-care-for-patients
The number of requests did rise substantially that year, from 2.9 million to 3.6 million, a 23.7% increase.

* Most referrals come from general practice: roughly 62% in 2025/26. A referral from a secondary care consultant is the second most common source: 18%** Technically, this was for Advice and Guidance, which is a type of pre-referral specialist advice, but for consistency and ease of reading, we will continue to refer to all of these as specialist advice.
That resulted in 1.7m diverted referrals, a 23.1% increase compared to 2024/25 and meant that diversions rose from 6.6% of additions to the waiting list in 2024/25 to 7.9% in 2025/26.

Despite that increase in diverted referrals, interviewees told us that additions to the elective waiting list grew faster than expected in 2025/26, meaning that the waiting list fell by less than hoped, and making it harder for the NHS to meet the target for March 2026. Last year, 2025/26, was a record year for additions, reaching 21.5m, an increase of more than half a million (2.6%) compared to 2024/25. The government expected additions to grow by 2%,2 Institute for Government interview. meaning that there were just under 130,000 more additions than expected. That would have been higher if not for the growth in diverted referrals. If additions had been diverted at the same rate as 2024/25, there would have been 283,000 more additions, resulting in 4.0% growth, rather than 2.6%.*
Interviewees attributed that faster than expected increase at least in part to a rising number of GP appointments, the source of most referrals for the elective waiting list.
* And assuming that all diverted referrals would have resulted in an addition to the waiting list.

The number of GP appointments grew 2.4% between 2024/25 and 2025/26. That is the largest increase in GP appointments since the pandemic and above the average annual increase between 2019/20 and 2024/25 (1.7%). This is likely the result of the government successfully recruiting thousands more salaried GPs into the service (discussed in more depth below). That growth has accelerated further in the first five months of 2026/27. There were 5.6% more GP appointments in that time compared to the same period in 2025/26.

Additions to the waiting list that were the result of a referral from GPs grew even more quickly than the number of GP appointments between 2024/25, by 4.4%, meaning that a greater proportion of GP appointments resulted in an addition to the waiting list, despite more diverted referrals.*
* From publicly available data, it is very difficult to accurately calculate what proportion of GP appointments result in a referral.
There could be hidden costs to increased use of specialist advice

Interviewees expressed mixed views on the expanding use of specialist advice. One GP interviewee said that they have increasingly come to like it and called it a “common sense approach” which allows for better decision making.1 Institute for Government interview. Another interviewee argued that it makes more sense for some specialities – dermatology was the example they gave – than for others, where the condition might be more complex.2 Institute for Government interview.

But there was scepticism about its expanded use. An interviewee said that the NHS’s ambition to divert 25% of referrals by March 20273 Department of Health and Social Care, NHS England, ‘Neighbourhood health framework’, policy paper, Gov.uk, 17 March 2026, retrieved 17 September 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/neighbourhood-health-framework/neighbourhood-health-framework was “overambitious” and that they couldn’t “imagine it would be possible without a lot of additional resources in general practice to manage that [additional demand from patients not progressing to secondary care]”.4 Institute for Government interview.

The same interviewee pointed out that there still has not been a comprehensive evaluation of the effect of widespread use of specialist advice. For example, there is no understanding, or reporting, of what happens to a patient whose referral is diverted. They might return repeatedly to primary care or end up being referred to hospital later, when their condition has worsened.

A recently-published report by the Health Services Safety Investigations Body (HSSIB) redresses some of that evidence gap by providing an assessment of the impact of specialist advice on patient safety. That report found several concerns, including that some requests are delayed by months, that harm to patients had arisen due to delayed or missed diagnoses, and that there is substantial variation across the country in how areas implement specialist advice.5 Health Services Safety Investigations Body, Electronic patient record systems – electronic referrals for ongoing care: advice and guidance, 18 August 2026, www.hssib.org.uk/patient-safety-investigations/electronic-patient-record-systems-electronic-referrals-for-ongoing-care/interim-report/

Specialist advice may also affect hospital doctors’ capacity. While it may reduce demand for outpatient care, it also takes time for clinicians to respond to requests for advice. An interviewee reported that currently this activity is not recognised within workforce planning and job plans.

The second factor which interviewees identified as supporting improved elective performance was the increased levels of validation. Validation is the process when a hospital regularly reviews patients on the waiting list to ensure they still require treatment. It could be that a decision has been made that alternative care is more appropriate, the patient has been treated elsewhere (for example, in the private sector) but has not alerted the NHS, or has died.

There is no data collected or published on the number of cases removed by validation. Many validation removals will show up in NHS data as ‘unreported removals’ from the elective waiting list. But that is still an imperfect proxy. This is because unreported removals also include patients who were removed for other reasons, such as if they received treatment that the NHS failed to report at the time.6 Illman J, ‘Exclusive: NHSE pays three trusts £1m each to remove patients from waiting lists’, HSJ, 9 June 2026, retrieved 17 September 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/quality-and-performance/exclusive-nhse-pays-three-trusts-1meach-to-remove-patients-from-waiting-lists/8023643.article Still, they are the best publicly available proxy about the extent of validation removals.

The government pushed for the NHS to undertake more extensive validation exercises in 2025/26 and paid trusts £33 for each validation removal.7Ibid. This payment was designed to cover the additional staff costs required to validate a higher proportion of the waiting list.
The NHS was successful: unreported removals increased from 2.9m in 2024/25 to 3.2m in 2025/26 (a rise of 7.9%), faster than the growth in completed cases due to treatment (2.3%).

The increase in unreported removals in 2025/26 led some commentators to argue that it is an unusual and illegitimate method of reducing the waiting list.1 Wright O, ‘Labour pays millions to make hospital stats more flattering’, The Times, 1 February 2026, retrieved 17 September 2026, www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/article/labour-nhs-waiting-lists-starmer-streeting-2cfxhm7c8 However, as a proportion of additions to the waiting list, unreported removals in 2025/26 remained below pre-pandemic levels. Unreported removals were 14.8% of additions in 2025/26 compared to 17.0% in 2016/17 (the first year for which there is data).

One interviewee argued that high staff turnover during and after the pandemic had led to a loss of expertise in waiting list management, reducing the quantity and quality of validation.2 Institute for Government interview. Another said that widespread pressure in the service during the pandemic diverted attention away from validation towards operational concerns. As a result, there was a higher number of errors in trusts’ waiting lists, such as duplicated cases, out of date records and patients that had received treatment elsewhere.

Validation is therefore an important component of effective waiting list management that cuts wasted administrative time in trusts and helps patients by reducing the amount of unnecessary contact from their hospital.

The final factor which interviewees identified as driving improved performance was elective ‘sprint’ funding.3 Institute for Government interview. This is a pot of money worth £120m which the NHS gave to trusts between January and March 2026 to hit the 65% interim target.4 Illman J, ‘Exclusive: £120m ‘sprint’ will drive last-ditch attempt to hit elective target’, HSJ, 19 February 2026, retrieved 17 September 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/quality-and-performance/exclusive-120m-sprint-will-drive-last ditch-attempt-to-hit-elective-target/7041147.article

That money was allocated to short-term measures, such as increasing the number of first outpatient appointments (which is the stage at which most elective cases are closed), pushing even further on waiting list validation and targeting cases that had been waiting more than 18 weeks.5 Institute for Government interview.

The result was a record number of removals in March 2026: 2.1 million. The next highest month on record was October 2024 (1.9 million). It was also the highest number of unreported removals in a single month, at 352,000, with the next highest 332,000 in October 2018.

Sprint funding was also used to treat a record proportion of cases that had been waiting for more than 18 weeks in March 2026: 39.0% of all removed cases in that month. In comparison, only 33.2% of all cases treated in April to December 2025 (the 9 months of 2025/26 not covered by ‘sprint’ funding) had been waiting more than 18 weeks. The proportion then dropped back rapidly after March to 35.1% between April and August 2026.

There are questions about the efficacy of this funding. By its nature, trusts have targeted sprint funding at short-term initiatives to meet an immediate target. But that type of spending does nothing to address the structural drivers of demand, capacity constraints or pathway inefficiencies that contribute to waiting list growth.

One manager responsible for elective care in an acute trust told us that elective sprint money “is obviously welcome” but that it would have been better if the government had “spent the funding on care outside the hospital – in primary care and adult social care”1 Institute for Government interview. – as that would reduce demand for elective care in the long run. Instead, they were forced to spend the money on short-term initiatives.

The benefits of sprint funding are time constrained; there will be no real benefit for the service from that funding beyond the window that it was allocated, and indeed completed cases fell back after the funding finished and the waiting list grew again. One interviewee suggested that the more enduring benefit of elective policy in 2025/26 will be improved waiting list management, which will likely continue to lead to higher than otherwise validation removals.

The same interviewee said that building on those improvements will require the NHS to continue to focus on operational discipline and invest in the capability needed to carry out validation. That latter point could be problematic. As discussed in more detail below, financial pressure is leading trusts to cut non-clinical employees, potentially including those who would carry out validation. Additionally, there is probably an upper limit on the extent to which validation can improve elective performance – at a certain point trusts will run out of errors to find.

The ambition to return to the 18-week target by March 2029 is incredibly stretching. It took the last Labour government more than a decade in power to make a large difference to elective waiting times2 Murray R, ‘Lessons from the 2000s: the ambition to reduce waits must be matched with patience and realism’, King’s Fund, 29 July 2021, retrieved 22 September 2026, www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/nhs-waiting-times and it did that alongside record increases in funding. Even then, the NHS only hit the 92% target in January 2012, two years after Labour left government.

At its core, hitting the 92% target requires the NHS to remove many more cases from the waiting list than it adds. But if the trend between April 2024 and April 2026 (removals growing at 3.2% and additions at 2.6% per year) continues until 2029, the NHS will miss its target. Under that central estimate, 78.7% of cases will be waiting less than 18 weeks by the end of March 2029 – more than 13pp lower than the target of 92%.*
* For more details about the modelling we used to calculate this figure, please see the Methodology.

While below the government’s target, this would be a substantial improvement on performance compared to June 2024, though would still be below the level of February 2020, the eve of the pandemic (82.9%).
However, there are a range of possible future trajectories of additions and removals from the waiting list.

Despite expanded use of specialist advice, additions to the waiting list grew at 2.6% per year between April 2024 and April 2026. That is higher than the 2.0% annual growth during the 2010s. If additions fell back to that level, performance would improve but would still be far short of the 92% target, all else being equal, at 82% (this is the “Additions slowdown scenario” in the table above).

Similarly, if the measures that the NHS is implementing to increase activity are successful (discussed below), and removals growth rises to 4.0% per year while additions growth remained constant, then this would lead to performance of roughly 82% in March 2029 (“Removals accelerate” scenario).
Even under our most optimistic scenario – in which additions slow to 2.0% and removals accelerate to 4.0% per year – the NHS would fall just short of the 92% target, at 88%.

Achieving either, let alone both, of those outcomes is extremely unlikely. Indeed, both trends have gone in the wrong direction in 2026/27: growth in removals has slowed while the rate of additions has accelerated. If those trends continue then performance would improve even more slowly, reaching just 72% by March 2029 (“Recent trends” scenario), before eventually falling again beyond the time horizon of this modelling.
The NHS hopes that planned initiatives will further slow referral growth and increase activity. These include:

Views on these initiatives are very mixed. While some GP interviewees were positive about specialist advice, they were far less supportive of mandating its use or having stretching targets that could distort care. Publicly, GP leaders claim that mandatory specialist advice takes away GPs’ right to refer and means they end up “rationing care”.6 Iacobucci G, ‘Patients at risk from new “advice and guidance” referral rules, GP leaders warn ‘, BMJ, 13 March 2026, retrieved 29 October 2026, https://www.bmj.com/content/392/bmj.s492

Specialist hubs, CDCs and use of the private sector have been successful in the past, particularly with certain specialties. But it is unclear how much additional capacity the NHS can wring from those sources.
Switching follow-up appointments has flatly failed in the past to reduce outpatient appointments and there is no explanation for why it will work this time.

The Health Foundation showed that the “crack teams” approach worked mostly by increasing unreported removals, rather than completed pathways, as touted by the NHS.7 Opie-Martin S and Tallack C, ‘Are “crack teams” reducing NHS waiting lists?’, blog, The Health Foundation, 15 April 2025, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.health.org.uk/features-and-opinion/blogs/are-crack-teams-reducing-nhs-waiting-lists As the experience from 2025/26 shows, this can help improve performance, but it is unclear how many additional removals this could create if scaled across the entire NHS.

Overall, there is evidence that some of these approaches improve elective performance. But it is very unclear if they will be sufficient to reach the 92% target by March 2029, particularly as many of these – specialist hubs, PIFU, use of the private sector and specialist advice – are by now relatively mature policies, where the easiest gains have been realised.
Alongside those anticipated tailwinds for elective performance, there are some headwinds over the coming years.

One interviewee pointed out that national performance could improve more slowly as the best performing trusts reach high levels of performance.8 Institute for Government interview. They said that a small handful of trusts that have had elective performance in the region of 80% to 85% have pulled the national average up. But as those trusts approach or exceed the 92% target, the NHS will need worse performing trusts to make larger gains.

Another interviewee also said that performance is likely to become far more dependent on better diagnostic performance nearer the 92% target9 Institute for Government interview. – something the CEO of NHS England, Jim Mackey, has himself acknowledged.10 House of Commons Committee of Public Accounts, ‘Oral evidence: Reducing NHS waiting times for elective care’, HC 820, 11 September 2025, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://committees.parliament.uk/oralevidence/16463/html/ That is a problem as diagnostic performance is currently well below target level and has actually worsened throughout Labour’s time in power. Interviewees have suggested that is because it has been a low priority for trusts while they have been pursuing the elective target. It is welcome, therefore, that the government has prioritised this area with a target in 2027.

If faster growth of GP appointments is driving quicker-than-expected growth of additions to the waiting list, then the government faces somewhat of a tension between its ambition to expand access to primary care and its 18-week performance target. It has successfully increased the number of salaried GPs working in primary care, from 10,826 in June 2024 to 14,355 in August 2026, a 32.6% increase (though the number of GP partners continues to fall). The NHS hopes to accelerate the expansion of GP capacity in 2026/27.11 Opie-Martin S and Tallack C, ‘Are ‘crack teams’ reducing NHS waiting lists?’, The Health Foundation, 15 April 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.health.org.uk/features-and-opinion/blogs/are-crack-teams-reducing-nhs-waiting-lists That seems to be bearing fruit: as already shown, GP appointments are growing much faster than in previous years. That is likely to mean that additions to the waiting list also grow more quickly than in recent years.

Finally, there could be further financial headwinds for the NHS. Since settlements were decided at the 2025 spending review, the inflation forecast has worsened, reducing the real terms generosity of the NHS’s allocation over the rest of this parliament. That situation could further worsen if Trump’s war with Iran results in yet more inflation.

As part of the 10YHP, the government also outlined its intention to shift funding away from acute hospitals. There is little evidence this has happened so far (as discussed further below), but if it does come to pass, then hospitals will struggle to increase activity.

Following a UK government agreement with the US government, the NHS will pay up to 25% more for branded pharmaceuticals in the future.1 Gainsbury S and Lomas J, ‘US-UK medicines partnership: the impact assessment of the costs and benefits must be published’, Nuffield Trust, 13 May 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.nuffieldtrust.org.uk/news-item/us-uk-medicines-partnership-the-impact-assessment-of-its-costs-and-benefits-must-be-published Analysis published in the British Medical Journal estimates that this will cost the NHS an additional £866m, £1.3bn, and £2.0bn in 2027, 2028, and 2029 respectively.2 Cross S, Claxton K and Hill A, ‘Health costs of the UK-US trade deal on pharmaceuticals’, BMJ, 1 July 2026, retrieved 29 October 2026, www.bmj.com/content/394/bmj-2026-340588?__cf_chl_f_ tk=KaCMbKw11ZC_u_1HqDMPElQBp8o6GN5.iwP9JVi6u3g-1783359340-1.0.1.1-IjKwiPVmOoFKwumtyTCZy8a vhFIni2sB2yKtn.1itHg The government has not provided the NHS with further funding to cover that additional cost meaning that it will have to come from existing budgets.
With limited additional funding, the NHS may have to slow the growth in elective activity, putting its elective target further out of reach.
Elective care is only one area where the government sets the NHS targets. There are many other metrics on which we should judge the government’s performance since 2024.

In 2025/26, the NHS missed hospital targets for cancer performance (receiving a diagnosis within 28 days of an urgent referral and starting treatment within 62 days of a referral), on ambulance response times (though this was a very near miss and followed substantial improvement) and on the proportion of people who wait more than 4 hours for care in accident and emergency (A&E) departments, though again this was a near miss, less than one percentage point below target.

The other major target that the NHS hit was on long waits (12 hours or more) for care in A&E. But that was largely due to the target being incredibly unambitious, merely to improve on the previous year. Therefore, the NHS hit the target by reducing the proportion of people waiting 12 hours or more from 10.6% in 2024/25 to 10.0% in 2025/26.

Despite hitting the target, NHS performance is far from impressive on long waits. One in 10 attendees waited more than 12 hours for care in 2025/26. January 2026 was the second highest month for 12-hour waits on record, with 13.1% of attendees waiting more than 12 hours. The only month which was worse was December 2022, during the worst NHS winter crisis on record.

Waits of that long were virtually unheard of at the start of last decade. In 2011/12 (the first year for which there is data) only 0.6% of people attending A&E waited more than 12 hours. More people waited 12 hours or longer for care in 2025/26 than between April 2011 and August 2019.

The normalisation of 12-hour waits is worrying given their relationship with higher mortality rates.1 Jones S, Moulton C and others, ‘Association between delays to patient admission from the emergency department and all-cause 30 day mortality’, Emerg Med J, 2022, vol. 39, pp. 168–173, http://emj.bmj.com/content/emermed/39/3/168.full.pdf The Office for National Statistics (ONS) estimates that patients* who wait 12 hours in A&E were more than twice as likely to die in the following 30 days as those who waited two hours. The government and the NHS should not allow this extent of 12-hour waits to become normalised.2 ONS, ‘Association between time spent in emergency care and 30-day post-discharge mortality, England: March 2021 to April 2022’, ons.gov.uk, 17 January 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthcaresystem/bulletins/associationbetweentimespentinemergencycareand30daypostdisc…
Away from acute hospitals, there are other areas where the NHS is not performing well.

The NHS has a target that 80% of cases waiting for community care – a wide range of support that the NHS provides to people outside of acute hospitals and primary care settings3 NHS England, ‘What are community health services?’, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.england.nhs.uk/community-health-services/what-are-community-health-services/ – should be seen within 18 weeks of a referral. It aims to hit that target in 2028/29, with an interim target of 78% by March 2027.
Since the general election, the NHS’s performance for all cases on the community waiting list has worsened slightly, from 76.0% in June 2024 to 75.8% in August 2026.

But there is a stark difference between children’s and adults’ services. Some 85.3% of adult cases were waiting less than 18 weeks in August 2026, up from 83.7% in June 2024, and already meeting the NHS’s target.
But performance on children’s services worsened considerably, falling from the already-poor 54.9% in June 2024 to 46.9% in August 2026, an eight-percentage point decline.

The story is worse still when looking at waits of more than 52 weeks. In January 2023, roughly one in 17 (5.9%) children on the list had waited more than a year. By August 2026, it was more than one in four (27.0%). That is a trend that started before Labour won the election, but the government has not been able to halt it since then.

One interviewee argued that the increase in long waits is due to higher demand from the special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) sector. They thought that higher demand for assessments for education, health and care plans (EHCPs), which is the most acute tier of provision, was putting more pressure on the community waiting list.1 Institute for Government interview. This would tally with the rising number of EHCPs that we describe in the schools chapter of this report.

In comparison to the acute hospital sector, the NHS sets primary care relatively few targets in the Medium-Term Planning Framework (MTPF). There are two targets for the sector. The first is that 90% of “clinically urgent appointments” happen on the same day they are booked. The NHS has set this target for every year between 2026/27 and 2028/29. The second is that patient experience of access to general practice improves year on year throughout that time.2 NHS England, ‘Medium Term Planning Framework – delivering change together 2026/27 to 2028/29’, (no date), p. 31, https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/medium-term-planning-framework-delivering-change-together-2026-27-to-2028-29.pdf

Unlike the metrics used for the acute hospital sector, both measures are relatively new. The NHS has never explicitly tracked or held general practice to account for the former. The latter comes from the Office for National Statistics’ (ONS’s) ‘Health Insight Survey’,3 ONS, ‘Health Insight Survey’, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.ons.gov.uk/surveys/informationforhouseholdsandindividuals/householdandindividualsurveys/healthinsightsurvey a dataset which the ONS has collected since only mid-2024.

The MTPF does not offer a definition for an “urgent” appointment. In subsequent guidance, the NHS says that “It is for the GP practice to determine which patients are clinically urgent, in the same way they do now…based on the patient’s presenting complaint”.4 NHS England, ‘Recording same day appointments for all clinically urgent patients’, 16 March 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/recording-same-day-appointments-for-all-clinically urgent-patients

This metric changed little over the nearly first four years of available data. There was only a 1.3 percentage point increase (to 73.1%) from the year before the 2024 election to 2025/26, leaving the metric roughly 17 percentage points beneath the NHS’s target.*

Since the introduction of the target in April 2026, there may be some evidence, however, of a shift. The proportion of urgent appointments seen on the same day in August 2026 was 77.8% – 4.5 percentage points above the March 2026 level. This indicates that the NHS’s decision to track this from April 2026 has led to a rapid change in behaviour.
Forcing practice to prioritise urgent appointments may backfire

GP leaders have raised concerns about this target. The British Medical Association (BMA, the union that represents most doctors in England), argues that it puts more pressure on an already-overburdened general practice.1 Triggle N, ‘GPs told to guarantee same-day appointments for urgent cases’, BBC News, 24 February 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, http://bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm28vp0pkzro

One interviewee who works in general practice argued that the NHS’s decision to give practices discretion over what constitutes an urgent appointment was leading to “absolutely wild variation” in designating patients as urgent.2 Institute for Government interview. This makes sense. If the government is holding practices to account for this metric, then there is a strong incentive for practices to only record the appointments they can see that day as urgent. If that is happening, then it severely undermines this metric’s usefulness.* There is an issue with comparability here. This data shows the proportion of appointments in general practice that are recorded as “general consultation acute” that happen on the same day. This is the category of appointment that the NHS wants practices to use to record “urgent” appointments, starting from April 2026. That means the data recorded in practice systems between October 2022 and March 2026 may be different to the data recorded from April 2026 onwards, as practices change what they consider to be a “generalconsultation acute” appointment. Still, this is the best approximation that is available against which to compare current performance.

The NHS is targeting ‘year on year’ improvement in the ONS’s metric of patient experience of general practice. So far, the ONS has only collected two years’ worth of data from this survey. When comparing the two years, the NHS has achieved its target, but only just, with the number of patients reporting a good experience of general practice,* rising from 72.5% to 73.1%.

A recent editorial in the British Journal of General Practice identified some limitations of the Health Insight Survey (HIS). These include the representativeness of the ONS surveys, smaller sample sizes at ICB level, and falling response rates over time.1 Routledge J, Opie-Martin S and Pettigrew L, ‘ONS Health Insight Survey in general practice: insight, not oversight’, British Journal of General Practice, 2026, vol. 76, no. 767, pp. 248–249, https://bjgp.org/content/76/767/248

The authors argue this makes it difficult to interpret change over time and raise concerns about the NHS’s ambition to use this to performance manage ICBs. It is also difficult to understand variation between practices, as the sample size is too small to draw conclusions about individual practices.2Ibid.

Instead, the authors urge the NHS to use this alongside the longer-standing annual General Practice Patient Survey (GPPS), which uses a larger sample size and allows for better comparison between practices and over time.3Ibid.
* The Health Insight Survey asks patients the question “Overall, how would you describe your experience of your GP practice?”

The results of the 2026 GPPS show continued gradual improvements in the proportion of patients satisfied with general practice: rising from 75.4% in 2025 to 76.7% in 2026. It is not possible to compare 2026 performance with any result before 2024, but given the large drop in performance between 2018 and 2023, it is likely that satisfaction has not recovered to pre-pandemic levels.
Alongside the measures described in the electives section above, interviewees claimed that there were other factors which made it harder than expected for the NHS to improve performance.

After resolving their dispute with the government soon after the 2024 general election, resident doctors* returned to picket lines in the summer of 2025. Throughout 2025/26, resident doctors walked out on three occasions: in July, November and December 2025 for a total of 15 days. That resulted in 127,036 cancelled or rescheduled elective appointments or operations.1 NHS England, ‘Data on the impact of the industrial action by resident doctors from the British Medical Association (BMA)’, 14 May 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, http://england.nhs.uk/publication/preparedness for-potential-industrial-action-in-the-nhs/#heading-3

Not all those appointments would have resulted in a case leaving the elective waiting list. One interviewee told us that each round of strike action resulted in approximately 20,000 fewer removals from the waiting list.2 Institute for Government interview. If so, that means the waiting list was 60,000 cases (0.8%) higher by March 2026 than it would have been in the absence of industrial action.

In June 2026, the government and the BMA reached an agreement that brought the latest round of resident doctor strike action to a conclusion.3 Roberts M, ‘Resident doctors in England accept pay deal and end strikes’, BBC News, 29 June 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwy01n5z48qo However, the NHS cannot rest easy. Consultants voted in favour of strike action in July 2026, and are due to walk out for 48 hours between 25 and 27 of November 2026.4 Tonkin T, ‘Consultants announce strike action ’, British Medical Association, 26 October 2026, retrieved 4 November 2026, www.bma.org.uk/news-and-opinion/consultants-announce-strike-action

The 10YHP claims that the NHS “has developed an addiction to deficits” and that the government will “restore financial discipline”.5 Department of Health and Social Care, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England, CP 1350, The Stationery Office, p.133, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6888a0b1a11f859994409147/fit-for-the-future-10-year-health-plan-for-england.pdf NHS trusts ran deficits in every year between 2013/14 and 2024/25, except for 2020/21 and 2021/22 when there was additional funding to meet Covid pressures.6 The King’s Fund, ‘NHS funding deficits’, 12 March 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/data-and-charts/nhs-trusts-deficit

The government made financial balance a strong focus of its agenda for the NHS in 2025/26. That seems to have worked. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) shows that the NHS largely stuck to its budget for 2025/26.7 Harvey-Rich O and Warner M, ‘Is the era of annual NHS top-ups over?’, IFS, 28 August 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://ifs.org.uk/articles/era-annual-nhs-top-ups-over

Financial discipline comes at a cost, however: there is a direct trade-off between financial constraint and NHS activity.8 The NHS Alliance, ‘Targets and trade-offs: NHS finance and performance ambitions in 2026/27’, 18 May 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://thenhsalliance.org/resources/targets-and-trade-offs-cost-of-nhs-finance-and-performance-ambitions For example, interviewees told us that trusts did not undertake additional elective activity that would help reduce the elective waiting list, as doing so would incur further costs.9 Institute for Government interview. At the Institute for Government conference in January 2026, then-health and social care secretary Wes Streeting acknowledged that aiming for financial balance was leading to lower elective activity: “some parts of the service… have over-steered and are therefore under-delivering on elective activity”.10 Tidman Z, ‘Streeting accuses trusts and ICBs of seeking to cut deficits too sharply’, HSJ, 13 January 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.hsj.co.uk/finance-and-efficiency/streeting-accuses-trusts-and-icbs of-seeking-to-cut-deficits-too-sharply/7040794.article * Previously known as junior doctors.

Some of the effect of the cost cutting drive is visible in staffing data. Between April 2019 and June 2024, the number of clinical and non-clinical staff* working in NHS trusts grew in lockstep, by 23%. Since then, growth rates have diverged. Between March 2025 and July 2026, clinical staff grew by 1.7% while non-clinical staff shrank by 1.6%. Interviewees working in trusts said that cutting non-clinical staff was one of their organisation’s first responses to tight financial pressure.

As our previous work has shown, cutting management, admin and back-office staff is often a false economy, resulting in worse productivity as vital work is shifted to clinical staff and effective decision-making capacity across systems is reduced.
* This includes managers, support staff for doctors, nurses and ambulance staff and those working in central functions such as HR.

Similarly, there was a slowdown in the growth of NHS activity in 2025/26. The rate at which diagnostic tests, outpatient appointments, and urgent cancer appointments grew was lower compared to the previous year and was the slowest growth since 2023/24. In the case of admitted elective cases, there was a decline in activity. Growth in all those areas was well below pre-pandemic average annual growth rates.*

This general slowdown is almost certainly the result of tighter financial control, as trusts slowed activity to remain within their budgets. The exception is completed non-admitted elective cases, where the growth rate ticked up in 2025/26 compared to 2024/25 and was above pre-pandemic levels.

That pattern seems to have worsened in the first five months of 2026/27, with growth further slowing in elective care, outpatient and urgent cancer care. The exception is GP appointments, where activity has accelerated.

By choosing elective performance as the ‘milestone’ for the NHS mission, the government drove the NHS to focus more attention and resources on that area of care in 2025/26. When combined with tight financial control, the result is slow performance improvements in other parts of the system – A&E and diagnostic test waiting times, among others.
The early indication from the first few months of 2026/27 is that this pattern has continued, though even elective care no longer seems immune, with activity growth slowly considerably there too.
* The exception to this is general practice, where there is no comparable pre-pandemic data.

As shown, the current target to treat 92% of elective cases within 18 weeks of a referral by March 2029 is almost certainly unachievable. That focus on electives also comes at the expense of other important areas of NHS performance and, as we show beneath, is making it harder for the government to achieve its wider goals for the system, such as moving care into the community.
There is little point, therefore, in pushing the service to hit an unachievable target while sacrificing other goals.

Cooper and Burnham should adjust the elective target. They should aim to return performance to 83%, the performance level on the eve of the pandemic. This lower level has a few benefits. It is stretching but achievable, as our analysis above shows, which is important to avoid demoralising staff. It will also allow for more flexibility of focus across systems, avoiding the distorting features of the current target. Finally, it still provides the government with a strong political story. Burnham and Cooper could legitimately argue that they had cleared the pandemic backlog.

They should also reassess their commitment to other NHS targets. The lesson from using electives as the milestone for the NHS mission is that the system responds strongly to political prioritisation. Cooper and Burnham should ensure that the targets the NHS is pursuing support their wider priorities. Where they do not, they should either pare them back or drop them entirely. This will require a wider assessment of whether they want to stick to the same priorities as Starmer and Streeting, particularly around the 10YHP.

In March 2025, the Starmer government first announced the abolition of NHS England – the arm’s length body tasked with running the day-to-day operations of the NHS since 2013 – and its intention to bring some of its functions and staff into DHSC. It then announced a major cost cutting exercise in NHS integrated care boards (ICBs), the organisations established in 2022 to better integrate health and care services in a local area.

We have argued repeatedly that the government botched its March 2025 announcement of the abolition of NHSE. Chaotic early days do not necessarily condemn the rest of the process to failure. The government could have run the abolition and merger with DHSC more effectively. But that has not been the case.

There has been progress since the announcement. Some teams – such as the strategy teams – merged very quickly after the announcement. Other teams, such as policy, have followed. In January 2026, the Starmer government announced the ‘indicative timeline’ for the abolition to staff, which laid out milestones such as the publication of a ‘target operating model’ by the end of May 2026, and confirmation that the merger will be finalised by April 2027 (though headcount reduction may continue after that).1 Kituno N, ‘DHSC-NHSE merger timetable revealed’, HSJ, 27 January 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, http://hsj.co.uk/workforce/dhsc-nhse-merger-timetable-revealed/7040985.article There has been slippage against that timeline: as of November 2026, the government still has not published the target operating model.

The government has also introduced the Health Bill to parliament which will abolish NHS England, alongside other changes, such as the introduction of the single patient record and the abolition of Healthwatch England. That bill is currently passing through parliament. Following uncertainty during Cooper’s first months in her role,2 Anderson H, ‘NHSE abolition on the cusp of being delayed’, HSJ, 15 October 2026, retrieved 23 October 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/policy-and-regulation/nhse-abolition-on-the-cusp-of-being-delayed/8124580.article she announced that the government will establish “a transitional Special Health Authority to host the NHS regions that is accountable to the Secretary of State through the NHS Group within the Department”.3 Cooper Y, Letter to Layla Moran, chair of the Health and Social Care select committee, ‘An update on DHSC NHSE transformation’, 4 November 2026, https://committees.parliament.uk/publications/55696/standard/pdf That brings slightly more clarity to the future structure, though still leaves key questions unanswered.

One of the most drastic parts of the March 2025 announcement was the ambition to cut 50% of staff working in DHSC and NHSE. At that point, there were 18,236 full-time equivalent (FTE) employees working across both organisations. A 50% reduction in staffing therefore implies a cut of 9,118 FTE staff.
In August 2026, there were 15,560 staff working in both organisations, a fall of 2,676 or 14.7% since March 2025.

Headcount reduction has so far been shared equally across NHSE and DHSC. The former has reduced its workforce by 14.6% and the latter by 14.9%. The government still needs to make extensive cuts to reach its target, a further 6,442 FTE staff.

The extent of the planned cut to the workforce is extreme. The government is right that there is some duplication of roles between DHSC and NHSE. But it is unlikely that half of staff across NHSE and DHSC are simply not needed, particularly as the government is also cutting staff in ICBs, as discussed below. Previous IfG and Nuffield Trust work showed that roughly 45% of staff working in NHSE and DHSC are operational staff, meaning that to achieve headcount cuts of 50% while protecting operational roles would require 9 in 10 policy roles to be cut.

Interviewees and Streeting himself clarified that the final headcount might differ from the 50% (by a few percentage points in either direction) following a more thorough assessment of the needs of the future department.1 Health and Social Care Committee, ‘Oral evidence: The work of NHS England’, House of Commons, HC 563, 8 April 2025, Q.214, https://committees.parliament.uk/oralevidence/15740/pdf But even with that flexibility, the commitment to deliver such extensive cuts may end up distorting final decisions about size and structure of the department, potentially leading to inefficiencies from an under-resourced centre.

There is also a risk that the government achieves its target headcount number, but then immediately starts growing the department again, to reach a sufficient level of staffing. That would be highly inefficient, and would result in many experienced staff leaving, only to be replaced by less experienced recruits.
While there has been some progress on integrating the two organisations, interviews reveal the process has not been smooth.
Some staff described problems of having a manager from the other organisation, making it hard to see them frequently. These issues will likely abate as the merger progresses.

More concerning are reports of a ‘culture clash’ between the two organisations. Some interviewees reported that NHSE staff tend to be more inward looking and defensive than DHSC colleagues. Others said that DHSC staff tend to be less expert in some policy areas than NHSE counterparts, particularly in operational areas.

Maybe more than anything else, pay has emerged as a sticking point. NHSE staff are on (often far) higher salaries than counterparts in DHSC. For example, the Health Services Journal (HSJ) reports that a grade 6 (the last civil service grade before the senior civil service) in DHSC is paid between £70,730 and £78,721, while equivalent staff in NHSE are paid between £79,504 and £108,814.2 Kituno N, ‘On call: the big NHSE-DHSC pay divide’, HSJ, 5 March 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/expert-briefings/on-call-the-big-nhse-dhsc-pay-divide/7041160.article However, civil servants receive better pension benefits than NHSE staff.

The government currently plans to keep NHSE staff on the same salaries when they enter the department. It has not yet clarified what will happen when staff subsequently move roles, leaving open the possibility that staff will then move onto the civil service pay scale, effectively taking a pay cut at that point. If this comes to pass, it could disincentivise staff from moving into new roles and brings a real risk that staff with operational expertise – many of whom currently work in NHS regions – will leave the service rather than accept civil service pay and conditions.

As a result of this uncertainty, interviewees and public reports3 Collins A and West D, ‘NHSE staff could be kept out of DHSC’, HSJ, 3 September 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, http://hsj.co.uk/policy-and-regulation/nhse-staff-could-be-kept-out-of-dhsc/8124229.article indicated that the government may create a new organisation outside of the department to house certain functions and staff to reduce the risk that they leave. These reports seem to have been proved right with the government’s announcement about the establishment of the Special Health Authority (SHA) to host the NHS regions. This may allow the NHS to pay staff more than they would receive in DHSC, thus retaining them when they may otherwise leave.

Another option that one interviewee suggested was to give NHSE staff who move into DHSC an additional specialist pay allowance on top of their base pay. The civil service already uses this uplift to recruit and retain staff with specialist skills, for example in digital and data.4 Government Digital Service, ‘What we do at GDS’, Civil Service Careers, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.civil-service-careers.gov.uk/gds-what-we-do-at-gds Another interviewee with experience of another departmental merger said that departments can end up classifying many staff as specialists due to lack of clear definition.

Interviewees report that the root cause of much of this uncertainty – over the target operating model, the status of NHSE staff and even whether there will be an organisation that replaces NHSE outside the department – stems from Streeting’s failure to provide sufficient political direction for the process.

In the absence of political direction, senior leaders in DHSC and NHSE have been left to fight for their own versions of a future NHS. Unsurprisingly, NHSE leaders want to maintain some kind of operational independence from government, to avoid what they see as undue political interference, while DHSC wants to bring more power into the department. The stories emerging in the press are a symptom of this, with each side briefing journalists about their preferred outcome.

That has created immense uncertainty for staff. Many do not know if they will have jobs – or even what organisation they will be working in – come April 2027. One interviewee described the process as “utter chaos”.5 Institute for Government interview. Other interviewees expressed similar intense unhappiness with the communication and progress of the merger.

That sentiment is supported by data. Of all the departments in Whitehall, DHSC had the largest drop in its civil service ‘engagement score’* in 2025 compared to 2024: 5.7 percentage points (albeit after a 5-percentage point increase in 2024 compared to 2023).

When asked whether they believe that their organisation’s senior leaders have a clear vision for the future of the department, the change was even more dramatic: an 18.8 percentage point drop in 2025 compared to 2024. The next largest decline was 9.5 percentage points, in the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT).

While those survey results are a snapshot of sentiment in DHSC in September and October 2025,1 Intellectual Property Office, ‘People survey results’, Gov.uk, 27 February 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/people-survey-results-2025 interviewees conveyed similar sentiments in the summer and autumn of 2026.

The reorganisation has wider implications for performance in the NHS. Embroiled in the unresolved debate about the future of DHSC, interviewees tell us that leaders in both organisations have less time to spend working out how to implement the 10 Year Health Plan for England, or drive performance improvement.

The new secretary of state needs to quickly provide the political direction her predecessor did not. It should not have taken more than 18 months since the abolition announcement for the decision on the SHA to be made, but it makes sense for the future of NHS regions to be decided as part of wider discussions on how to ‘rewire the state’ and for there to be a transitional arrangement in the meantime.

She should further clarify the future organisational structure of the department and the NHS, including whether the SHA is intended to be a permanent organisation or only temporary, and which functions or teams she expects will sit within NHS regions. That should include considerations over how to retain sufficient NHSE staff with the expertise needed to run the future organisation.

Cooper should ignore the arbitrary headcount target set by her predecessor. She should assess the capacity and capability that the future structure needs and staff it accordingly. If she deems that the 50% cut would result in poor performance and inefficiencies, then she should abandon it. Any reduction in savings from smaller cuts will be more than offset by more effective running of the largest public service in the country.

In March 2025, the government also announced that ICBs would need to cut their operating costs by 50% by October of that year.2 Digital Health, ‘Model Integrated Care Board – Blueprint v1.0’, (no date), p. 18, https://www.digitalhealth.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Model-Integrated-Care-Board-%E2%80%93-Blueprint-v1.0.pdf As a result, many ICBs started the process of merging or clustering with neighbours.

The government has handled the ICB reorganisation abysmally. The announcement came out of the blue, catching leaders unaware, and was the second time that ICBs had been forced to reorganise since their establishment in only 2022. The government then repeatedly set unrealistic timelines for the reorganisation, before having to push them back. The initial October 2025 deadline for cost cutting was pushed back to December 2025.
