That too proved impossible, when it transpired that ICBs did not have sufficient funding to pay for mandated redundancies,3 Campbell D and Bawden A, ‘Labour’s NHS job cuts plan in chaos amid row over £1bn costs’, The Guardian, 20 September 2025, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.theguardian.com/society/2025/sep/20/nhs-integrated care-boards-england-job-cuts-row triggering a months-long negotiation between DHSC and the Treasury.4 Lovell T, ‘Wes Streeting gives the go ahead for ICB and NHS job cuts’, Digital Health, 12 November 2025, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://www.digitalhealth.net/2025/11/wes-streeting-gives-the-go-ahead-for-icb-and-nhs-job-cuts/

In interviews with the Health Foundation, one ICB leader described the decision-making process as more “on the hoof” than previous reorganisations.5 Arnold-Forster A, Dunn P and others, ‘Integrated care systems in England: where next?’, health.org.uk, 2026, p. 28, www.health.org.uk/sites/default/files/upload/publications/2026/ICS%20report_Final.pdf Other leaders were less polite, calling the process “disgraceful”, “unprofessional”, and “an absolute shitshow”.6Ibid. That is echoed by our own interviews. One interviewee described the government’s handling of the process as “a shambles”.7 Institute for Government interview.

To add further to the uncertainty of this reorganisation, the Burnham government announced that ICBs would now be required to align their boundaries with strategic authority (SA) boundaries.8 Cabinet Office, ‘Rewiring the State – Cabinet Statement’, policy paper, gov.uk, 31 July 2026, retrieved 17 July 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement/rewiring-the-state-cabinet-statement-html This is in contrast to the approach taken under Streeting when the NHS was allowed to design ICB boundaries in line with its own priorities.9 Anderson H, ‘ICBs told to redraw boundaries again’, HSJ, 31 July 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.hsj.co.uk/policy-and-regulation/icbs-told-to-redraw-boundaries-again/8123939.article

That will mean a further round of reorganisation, including for ICBs that have just finished their restructure. In October 2026, the government confirmed that it has paused the reorganisation of 20 ICBs that were due to merge in April 2027 until “at least 2028” while it considers how to fulfil the prime minister’s goal of aligning services’ boundaries.10 Launder M, ‘ICB mergers suspended due to ‘devolution discussions’’, HSJ, 7 October 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/policy-and-regulation/icb-mergers-suspended-due-to-devolution discussions/8124509.article

That decision will extend uncertainty for staff and further slow delivery of the government’s goals, an incredibly frustrating outcome for the staff working in ICBs. The 2025 NHS staff survey showed that all 20 of the ICBs that had results in both 2024 and 2025 reported declines in morale and staff engagement. All but one reported a decline in staff motivation (the one ICB that improved did so by only 0.01 out of 10). Nineteen out of the 20 had a decline in morale that was larger than the NHS-wide result. The average decline in morale among ICB staff was 0.44 (on a scale from 1 to 10) compared to 0.06 across the entire NHS.

That low morale holds back the government’s reform agenda, much of which relies on ICB staff to implement strategy. Launching another reorganisation likely means that low morale will continue throughout this parliament.

Despite that, the government is right to ensure that ICB boundaries align with SA boundaries. Aligned boundaries support better integration of services and, in a world where mayors set more of the NHS’s priorities, allow for greater accountability of local NHS leaders, as we’ve argued before.
To support Burnham’s devolution agenda, the government should therefore align ICB and SA boundaries on a one-to-one basis, so that a single mayor can hold local NHS leaders to account.

Given that some Mayoral Strategic Authority (MSA) footprints are smaller than current ICB footprints, some argue that it should be possible for a single ICB to contain multiple MSAs. We argue that having multiple MSAs within a single ICB hugely dilutes that vital accountability by making it impossible for ICB leaders to choose between the priorities of mayors that may come from different parties or simply have different objectives.

Constant disruption to ICBs is undoubtedly poor for morale and for the government’s wider objectives for the NHS. But aligned boundaries are a necessary bedrock of any government’s desire to further devolve responsibility for services. Ideally, the Starmer government would have taken more time to consider the entire landscape of services’ boundaries before launching ICBs into a disruptive reorganisation, and his government rather than Burnham’s deserves blame for ongoing disruption. The goal now should be to create a coherent set of organisations across all public services and then refrain from further reorganisations.

The government has provided multiple rationales for the reorganisation. When Jim Mackey first briefed system leaders about the cuts, he framed them as part of the NHS’s attempt to erase its deficit.1 West D, Anderson H and Kituno N, ‘ICBs ordered to cut costs by 50%’, HSJ, 12 March 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/policy-and-regulation/icbs-ordered-to-cut-costs-by-50/7038846.article

Subsequently, the government has pushed the idea of ICBs as “strategic commissioners”, in other words pursuing improved population health outcomes through effective purchasing of services.2 Integrated Care Systems Network, ‘Strategic commissioning’, NHS Alliance, 2025, https://nhs-alliance.uksouth01.umbraco.io/media/xvvjqrny/pioneers-of-reform-summary.pdf That is a worthy, if not novel, aim.3 Smith S, ‘Same cycle – different bike?’, The King’s Fund, 22 July 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/blogs/same-cycle-different-bike-strategic-commissioning-population-health To achieve that, the government is giving ICBs more power over commissioning, including over primary care services, which currently sits in NHSE.4 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Health Bill: ICBs as strategic commissioners – fact sheet’, Gov.uk, 9 September 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/health-bill-icbs-as-strategic-commissioners-fact-sheet/health-bill-icbs-as-strategic-commissioners-fact-sh… Crucially, though, being able to effectively fulfil the role of strategic commissioning requires slimming down ICBs’ other responsibilities.5 Gault B, ‘Strategic commissioning: how it will shift the role of ICBs’, Healthcare Leader News, 29 July 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://healthcareleadernews.com/integrated-care-boards/strategic-commissioning-how-it-will-shift-the-role-of-icbs/ Following the publication of the “model ICB blueprint”, it looked like the government was going to follow through on that goal by substantially cutting the functions that ICBs are responsible for. Since then, however, the government has flip-flopped. One interviewee reported that of the 18 functions or activities that the NHS initially classed as under “review for transfer” out of ICBs,6 Digital Health, ‘Model Integrated Care Board – Blueprint v1.0’, (no date), p. 13, https://www.digitalhealth.net/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/Model-Integrated-Care-Board-%E2%80%93-Blueprint-v1.0.pdf it has decided to keep 14 within ICBs, raising questions about how effectively ICB staff will be able to focus on strategic commissioning, especially following cuts of 50%.
Worse, having been told they would no longer have responsibility for those 14 functions, many ICBs made the staff delivering them redundant.7 Institute for Government interview.
The combination of deep cuts, an unclear vision for the system and a pressing timeline will make it very difficult for DHSC and ICBs to retain key staff.

For example, previous IfG work shows that confusion over whether ICBs would be responsible for special educational needs and disability (SEND) services led to ICBs heavily cutting those staff, despite DHSC eventually deciding that they would continue to fulfil that function.

Another example is medicines optimisation in ICBs.*,8 NHS England, ‘Regional arrangements for medicines optimisation in the NHS in England’, 31 July 2023, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/regional-arrangements-for-medicines-optimisation-in-the-nhs-in-england Interviewees spoke positively about the cost savings that arose from effectively staffing that function but said that it was an area that had been subjected to heavy cuts, as ICBs no longer have a statutory duty to fulfil this function.9 Institute for Government interview.

Interviewees also said that ICBs face a trade-off over whether to invest in strategic commissioning skills and the staff needed to deliver the statutory functions which remain the responsibility of ICBs.

The same story holds in the centre of the NHS. So far, exits from DHSC have been managed mostly through voluntary exit or voluntary redundancy schemes. The IfG has argued previously that these schemes are generally poor ways of retaining high performing staff. As pressure mounts on the department to hit its headcount target, it may fall back on cutting staff based on ease rather than on an assessment of their necessity to the future DHSC operating model. The NHS itself sees this as a risk: in its June 2026 board meetings, NHSE updated its operational risk register to include “Loss of workforce talent and critical capability during pre-integration with DHSC”.10 NHS England, ‘Agenda and papers for the NHS England Board meeting – 4 June 2026’, 3 June 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/publication/agenda-papers-nhs-england-board-meeting-4-june-2026

From a broader perspective, the 50% headcount cuts in NHSE, DHSC and ICBs, as well as the reduction of non-clinical staff working in trusts and partners working in general practice, is a substantial loss of management capacity across the NHS. That is capacity the service can ill afford to lose. As previous IfG work has repeatedly shown, the NHS is undermanaged, with persistently low productivity since the pandemic at least partly the result of too little management capacity, rather than a surfeit.
* Medicines optimisation is a function which ensures that patients receive the correct medicines at the correct time, and reduces wasteful spending.
At the heart of the 10YHP are three shifts that it wants the NHS to achieve. These are shifts from:
We have written in support of all three. Achieving any would represent a significant step-change in the way the NHS operates.

Unlike the performance metrics described above, however, it is much harder to assess the NHS’s performance against these shifts.* In what follows, we have set out what we consider to be the most appropriate metrics by which to judge whether the NHS is progressing towards these shifts.

These shifts come from the Starmer government’s 10 Year Health Plan for England. Since coming to office, Burnham and Cooper have not explicitly endorsed the Plan. In her speech to the Labour conference, Cooper made one short reference to the 10YHP and spent more time explaining her priorities on maternity care, Sure Start and reducing violence against women and girls.11 Cooper Y, ‘Read Health Secretary Yvette Cooper’s conference speech in full’, Labour List, 30 September 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://labourlist.org/2026/09/yvette-cooper-labour-party-conference-2026 Despite the lack of clarity over this government’s commitment to them, it is worth assessing the progress of the three shifts which underpinned Starmer’s and Streeting’s approach to the NHS as the current administration has said that the 10YHP still stands and systems are still using it as a framework for their work.

* Where there are clearer ambitions – for example around improving air quality – there are still no specific targets for how the government intends to measure progress, or what it would deem to be a success after 10 years

The NHS (much like health systems in other countries) has been attempting to shift care into the community for more than 50 years.12 Baird B, Fenney D and others, ‘Making care closer to home a reality’, The King’s Fund, 2024, p. 6, https://assets.kingsfund.org.uk/f/256914/x/ab65341d7a/making_care_closer_home_reality_report_2024.pdf There are three broad aims of this shift:

At the core of this shift is the government’s proposed transition towards “neighbourhood health”, partly through the establishment of the neighbourhood health service (referred to here as NbH). To support the NbH, the government plans to build 250 neighbourhood health centres,13 NHS England, ‘Neighbourhood health centre guidance for regions and integrated care boards’, 16 April 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/neighbourhood-health-centre-guidance-for regions-and-integrated-care-boards “colocat[ing] NHS, local authority and voluntary sector services, to help create an offer that meets population need holistically”.14 Department of Health and Social Care, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England, CP 1350, The Stationery Office, p. 36, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6888a0b1a11f859994409147/fit-for-the-future-10-year-health-plan-for-england.pdf

Key to any proposed transition to a neighbourhood health model is how the NHS chooses to allocate funding between different parts of the health system. To support its vision of shifting care away from hospitals, the 10YHP says that:

“Over the course of this Plan, the share of expenditure on hospital care will fall, with proportionally greater investment in out of hospital care. This is not just a long-term ambition. We will also deliver this shift in investment over the next 3 to 4 years.”
We will, therefore, use this as a yardstick of the government’s progress on the community shift.

The NHS spends far more on the acute hospital sector than on any other area of health and care. In 2022/23,* spending on acute trusts was £109.5bn (in 2026/27 prices). That is more than six times higher than spending on general practice and 23 times higher than spending on community trusts.
* The most recent year for which there is outturn data across all these sectors.
The most comprehensive stocktake of the Labour government’s progress on public services since the 2024 general election.

Rebalancing that funding is vital to shifting resources into the community. Therefore, we should look at how spending on various sectors has changed over time as an indicator of whether the government is committed to transitioning care into the community.

Between 2016/17* and 2024/25, the Conservative government set NHS funding allocations. In that time, the NHS increased spending on acute, ambulance and specialist NHS trusts at a greater rate than for general practice and community trusts. Between 2016/17 and 2024/25, spending on acute trusts rose by 36.8% in real terms, while spending on general practice and community trusts rose by 26.4% and 14.8% respectively,** further growing the proportion of spending going on acute trusts in that time.

In the first year that the Labour government had complete discretion over NHS funding allocations, 2025/26, there was a mixed picture on the balance of spending increases. Spending on acute trusts grew by 1.6% in real terms compared to 2024/25. Positively for the community shift, funding for general practice grew by 3.7% in real terms, the largest increase across all the sectors that we look at here. However, spending on community trusts fell in 2025/26, by 6.3% in real terms.

The scale of that spending cut on community trusts means that, when taken together, spending on community and general practice grew by the same amount in real terms (1.6%) as spending on acute trusts. This hardly signals a large shift in funding towards the community.

* And likely earlier, though there is no data before that year.** For general practice, this is an estimate in the final two years, as there is no outturn data for general practice spending after 2022/23. The projection uses the percentage increases outlined in the GP contract. See the Methodology for more details.
The government has not created financial mechanisms to divert funding

One interviewee argued that, in the absence of a plan to move funding into the community, they would want to see the government implement a mechanism which automatically diverted funding towards primary care and community care, echoing a recommendation made by Dr Ara Darzi in his 2024 review of the NHS.1 Institute for Government interview. ,2 Lord Darzi, Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Summary letter from Lord Darzi to the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care’, 15 May 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/independent-investigation-of-the-nhs-in-england/summary-letter-from-lord-darzi-to-the-secretary-of-state-f… This could be something like the Mental Health Investment Standard (which required ICBs to increase spending on mental health services by at least in line with the growth in their overall budget3 Centre for Mental Health, ‘Mental health at risk of missing out on funding after government changes’, 26 November 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.centreformentalhealth.org.uk/news/item/mental-health-at-risk-of-missing-out-on-funding-after-government-changes/ ) or an annual ratchet in the proportion of spending on primary and community care. But the NHS has not outlined any mechanisms for that to happen.

The NHS might argue that integrated health organisations (IHOs) will deliver this shift. IHOs are intended to have control over the entire population health budget in a local area, “creat[ing] incentives to invest in community-based preventative care”, as the IHO will benefit from supposed subsequent savings.4 NHS England, ‘Fit for the future: towards population health delivery models’, 17 March 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/fit-for-the-future-towards-population-health-delivery-models That is certainly a possibility. But it would represent a real departure from the usual NHS practice of diverting money towards the highly visible and vocal acute sector and would likely require making wider changes to NHS funding arrangements, for example shifting away from payment by activity for elective care, which incentivises spending more in hospitals. In any case, the government still seems to be a long way from establishing IHOs.
Another indicator of whether the NHS is shifting resources into the community would be if the NHS is hiring more staff to work in those settings.
The above chart shows the relative change in various staff groups, indexed to June 2024, the month before Labour won the 2024 general election.

Since June 2024, the longstanding trend of rising numbers of clinical staff (hospital nurses, doctors and ambulance staff) working in the acute hospital sector has continued, though the growth rate of nurses has slowed considerably compared to pre-2024 levels.
In primary care, the government has done nothing to arrest the long-term decline in GP partners (5.9% lower in August 2026 than in June 2024) and the number of GP nurses remains relatively flat.

The trend has shifted for direct patient care staff (DPC) – including physiotherapists, pharmacists and care co-ordinators – as well as salaried GPs. The former has seen a relative flattening out in numbers, after a dramatic increase between 2019 and 2024. The opposite is true for salaried GPs, where the number working in primary care has rapidly accelerated since June 2024.

These phenomena are related. The Labour government loosened restrictions on a funding pot that was previously ringfenced for hiring DPC staff,* to allow practices to use it to hire salaried GPs. That has proved very effective at expanding the numbers of salaried GPs working in the service, but is a direct trade-off with other staff working in primary care.

In the community sector, there was a 7.3% decline in district nurses between June 2024 and August 2026, meaning there are now fewer district nurses than at any point since records began. The Labour government has done nothing to increase the number of health visitors, which has remained largely flat since 2024. The number of other community nurses has continued to grow, albeit at a slower rate than before the general election.
* This is the additional roles reimbursement scheme (ARRS), which the Conservative government introduced in 2019.

Looking at the absolute change in the number of staff is also important when identifying shifts in capacity across the entire NHS. On that basis, hospitals have again won out: there were 25,546 more doctors, nurses and ambulance staff working in hospitals in August 2026 compared to June 2024. In comparison, there were 6,168 more clinical primary care staff and 1,516 more nurses and health visitors working in the community sector.

As a result, two years into Labour’s parliamentary term, there has been no shift in clinical capacity towards community settings. If anything, there has been the opposite. In June 2024, 75.5% of clinical staff were working in the hospital sector. In June 2026, the proportion was the 75.7%. The government intends to publish an updated workforce plan during the autumn of 2026. Cooper should ensure that that document outlines how the NHS will make the shift of staff into the community to support its ambitions on that shift.
While the government has not yet shifted resources away from secondary care towards primary care, the government is, arguably, doing a better job allocating funding within primary care.

As previously argued, the expansion of the salaried GP workforce has been funded through reduced funding for DPC staff. If the government’s goal is to increase access and patient satisfaction with the service, that makes sense. Previous IfG work shows that an additional salaried GP is associated with a statistically significant increase in patient satisfaction, while an additional DPC staff member is not. An additional salaried GP is also associated with more appointments than DPC staff, though this is likely because not all DPC staff activity is captured by appointment data.
The government has done nothing to address the crisis in the partnership model

Despite its progress on salaried GPs, the NHS has done nothing to stop the decline in the GP partner workforce. That is a major concern. GP partners hold contracts with the NHS to provide general practice services in their local area. Without them fulfilling that function, the current partnership model of general practice would not work. Given that the NHS’s neighbourhood framework says that “general practice is the bedrock of neighbourhood health”,1 Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England, ‘Neighbourhood health framework’, 17 March 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/neighbourhood-health-framework/neighbourhood-health-framework it looks like GP partners will be a key component of the government’s future neighbourhood health service. Partners are also the staff that are associated with the largest increases in patient satisfaction with the service and a greater number of additional appointments compared to other GPs.

Despite that, the government has not made it clear how it intends to address the continued crisis of falling GP partner numbers. In the 10YHP, the NHS says that it wants to “create an alternative for GPs” and will “encourage GPs to work over larger geographies by leading new neighbourhood providers”.2 Department of Health and Social Care, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England, CP 1350, The Stationery Office, 2025, p. 30, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6888a0b1a11f859994409147/fit-for-the-future-10-year-health-plan-for-england.pdf What that means for existing partners, or for the future of the partnership model, is very unclear.
Underpinning the community shift is the government’s Neighbourhood Health Service (NbH). The government has four aims for the NbH:

In practice, the government envisages shifting responsibility and accountability for those goals to a more local level through the creation of two new contracts: the single- and multi-neighbourhood provider (SNP and MNP) contracts. These will create organisations to co-ordinate primary and community care activity across populations of 50,000 and 250,000 people, respectively.

There is a precedent for these contracts. In 2019, the Conservative government created primary care networks (PCNs). These are GP-led organisations which co-ordinate primary, community, mental health, pharmacy and other services across population sizes of roughly 50,000 (the same as SNPs).4 NHS England, ‘Primary care networks’, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/primary-care/primary-care-networks

So far, the NHS has established very few of these new organisations. Since September 2025, the NHS has supported 43 sites as part of the National Neighbourhood Health Implementation Programme.5 Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England, ‘Millions of people to benefit from healthcare on their doorstep’, press release, 9 September 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/millions-of-people-to-benefit-from-healthcare-on-their-doorstep A group of GP practices in Kent have also agreed a change in their contracts to deliver some neighbourhood services.6 Kent and Medway NHS Integrated Care Board, ‘Investing in neighbourhoods - Kent and Medway launches new PCN DES Local Variation contract offer to deliver Neighbourhood Health’, press release, 4 June 2026, retrieved 26 October 2026, https://www.kentandmedway.icb.nhs.uk/news/investing-in-neighbourhoods-kent-and-medway-launches-new-pcn-des-local-variation-contract-offer-to-deliver-… But there is still no clear timeline for when the NHS intends to implement these models across all of England.

Interviewees working in primary care expressed concern that the SNP, in particular, will merely reinvent the existing primary care network (PCN) model that the Conservative government created in 2019, albeit it with a different name and potentially different people or organisations holding the contract. This would be a mistake. PCNs have spent years building relationships, new pathways and developing staff. The experience and relationships they have accumulated are valuable. Tearing those up to establish organisations that seem nearly identical, but with politically preferable branding, would reset all that progress. The government should aim for evolution of the PCN model rather than undertake what would essentially be a structural reorganisation to create almost identical organisations.

The government aims to build 120 neighbourhood health centres (NHCs) by 2030 and a total of 250 by 2035, through a combination of new builds and “upgrades” to existing buildings.7 NHS England, ‘Neighbourhood health centre guidance for regions and integrated care boards’, 16 April 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/neighbourhood-health-centre-guidance-for-regions-and-integrated-care-boards It will use those buildings to co-locate general practice, community, social care and local authority staff in one place, to make it easier for patients to access a range of services.8Ibid.The NHS has launched the first wave of investment, with an ambition to open the first 27 NHCs in 2027.9 Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England, ‘Communities to benefit from health centres on their doorstep’, press release, 26 March 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/communities-to-benefit-from-health-centres-on-their-doorstep

As with so much of the Plan, NHCs are not new. They are very similar to the “polyclinics” that Dr Ara Darzi proposed in 2007.10 Darzi A, Healthcare for London: A framework for action, 2nd edition, Nuffield Trust, 2007, p. 90, www.nuffieldtrust.org.uk/sites/default/files/2019-11/1575037889_darzilondon.pdf A contemporary review of the evidence found that co-locating staff was not sufficient for realising benefits and that it required changes in commissioning behaviour and strong leadership to make the most of the investment.From a practical perspective, it is wise to look to the existing public sector estate as a source of buildings for NHCs. It is not uncommon for the public estate to be underused.

But the scale of the ambition seems small. Compared to the 8,911 premises in general practice,*,11Ibid., p. 3.250 centres is a relatively small number. Given the inadequacy of the current general practice estate, it is unclear that a change of this size would make a real difference to the primary care estate.

First, Cooper should clarify her priorities for the neighbourhood shift. Slow progress on establishing the NbH and the wider community shift may be because the NHS is still unclear what it is trying to achieve. The four priorities outlined above are incredibly broad and could point the NHS towards different policy prescriptions. For example, if the primary goal is to provide more proactive, preventative care aimed at improving health outcomes then the NHS may want to target an increase in continuity of care in general practice. But if the goal is to shift care out of hospitals, policy makers may instead want to expand diagnostic capacity in the community, or grow virtual ward beds. These policy aims are not mutually exclusive. But within a limited funding envelope, it will be hard for the NHS to achieve everything.

The government needs a more considered plan for how to make the shift towards the community. As this section has shown, there has been no clear shift in resources – in terms of either spending or staffing – since 2024. The NHS should use the upcoming workforce plan to lay out how the government intends to expand capacity in the primary and community sectors. The government should also clarify how it will fund that shift in resources. The government should break away from the current cycle of single-year contracts for general practice and set a multi-year settlement which shows a real shift in resources towards the sector and provides the financial certainty necessary for planning a longer-term shift. Finally, it should set clearer long-term funding plans for the community sector. There is currently no publicly-available funding projection for that sector, making it impossible to see how the NHS intends to shift funding.

Given the importance of that workforce, the government should make it clear what future it envisages for GP partners. It should either explain how it intends to reverse the long-term trend of declining numbers or else – if it is willing to accept the continued shrinkage of that workforce – its alternative model for providing general practice services.
To make a success of its neighbourhood health service, the NHS should evolve the PCNs into SNPs, rather than tearing up a system that is increasingly working well.

Without additional funding for the entire NHS, there will likely also be a trade-off between faster increases for primary and community care and the acute hospital sector. If Cooper wants to make the community shift a reality, she should clarify which priorities in the acute hospital sector she is willing to deprioritise.

The 10YHP recognises that services are often delivered too late, waiting until someone has reached an acute health crisis before providing support. Instead, the document lays out a vision where the NHS aims to intervene earlier, to prevent ill health from arising at all. As with the community shift, many governments have aimed to make the NHS more preventative. Largely that has failed, with the proportion of NHS spending that goes on the acute hospital sector increasing, while spending on other preventative services outside the NHS – adult social care, housing, early years services such as Sure Start – fell during the first half of the 2010s as local authorities worked out how to deal with lower, austerity-era budgets.

The 10YHP says that “Prevention will be how we restore the means to lead a healthy life in places – like Blackpool – where it has become most difficult” and outlines an ambition to “halve the gap in healthy life expectancy between the richest and poorest regions, while increasing it for everyone, and to raise the healthiest generation of children ever”. 12 Department of Health and Social Care, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England, CP 1350, The Stationery Office, p.58, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6888a0b1a11f859994409147/fit-for-the-future-10-year-health-plan-for-england.pdf
To do this, the 10YHP lays out a few high-level ambitions/areas of focus:

Away from that incredibly high-level goal (halving the gap in healthy life expectancy), other measurable targets are scarcer. For example, there is no target level for obesity, or around alcohol consumption that would give an indication of what the government thinks is necessary to narrow the healthy life expectancy gap and which would make it possible to assess whether the government is on track to deliver that long-term, high-level outcome. The 10YHP commits to working with the Office for National Statistics “and other experts” to “develop a new suite of delivery indicators”.14Ibid., p. 63.From publicly available information, the NHS does not seem to have made any progress towards those indicators.

There are overlaps with the community shift. The NHS intends the NbH to deliver more preventative care, for example the 10YHP says the NHS “will test new delivery models for secondary prevention through the Neighbourhood Health Service” in relation to diabetes and cardiovascular care.15Ibid., p. 72.Similarly, a general practice service that has more time to spend with patients would be able to take a more preventative approach to healthcare.16 Ellenby R, Mandla A, Stewart M and Tzortziou Brown V, ‘Prevention: The general practice role in evidence based and equitable prevention’, Royal College of General Practitioners, September 2026, https://www.rcgp.org.uk/representing-you/policy-areas/prevention-report

The community shift section above has already assessed the extent to which funding is likely to flow towards primary and community care over the course of this parliament – both important sectors if the NHS is serious about shifting towards more preventative care. Spending on public health is another area which would demonstrate intent on this front.

Public health services, commissioned by local authorities, are intended to reduce the likelihood of disease, improve the population’s health and redress health inequalities – all aims that fall squarely within the prevention shift.17 Faculty of Public Health, ‘What is public health?’, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.fph.org.uk/what-is-public-health They include services such as children’s 0-5 public health services, alcohol and drug misuse services, and smoking cessation services.
The government’s primary method of funding public health services is the public health grant, a ringfenced pot of money that it provides to local authorities.
As shown above, the government spends relatively little on public health compared to the acute hospital sector: almost 25 times less in 2022/23.

The public health grant will be 12.9% higher in real terms in 2028/29 than in 2024/25. However, all of the increase comes in the first two years and is due, at least in part, to the new inclusion of drug and alcohol, and smoking cessation funding in the grant from 2026/27 onwards. It is not possible to tell from published data how much the core public health grant increased over this period.18 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Public health ring-fenced grant financial year 2026 to 2027: local authority circular’, 9 February 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/public-health-grants-to-local-authorities-2026-to-2027/public-health-ring-fenced-grant-financial-year-2026… A fairer comparison may therefore be 2026/27 to 2028/29, when funding is due to fall by 0.5% in real terms.

Even with the additional funding, the value of the grant in 2028/29 will still be more than a tenth (11.2%) lower in real terms than it was in 2015/16. Considered alongside the lack of shift in funding towards primary and community care, the slow growth in the public health grant makes it difficult to argue that the government has significantly prioritised funding for preventative health services.
The introduction of PDEL could help drive focus and resources towards preventative spending

At the 2026 autumn budget the chancellor, John Healey, announced that the government would “introduce a new category of ringfenced spending at the spending review in 2027” which it would call ‘preventative DEL (PDEL)’.19 HM Treasury, Budget 2026, HC 726, The Stationery Office, October 2026, p. 34, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6ae20b85460c1346f7be784e/E03668986_HMT_Budget_2026_ELAY__2_.pdf

This is a welcome step and one that the IfG has argued for since 2024. Identifying and protecting preventative spending should create an incentive for services to better protect that spending and will impose a political cost on any politician or service that raids those budgets to fund more acute pressures.
It is still unclear how this will work in practice or what it will mean for services, but this is a welcome step towards a greater focus on prevention in services.

Legislation and taxation are also important public health levers, and the Tobacco and Vapes Act represents a major preventative intervention. The process towards this legislation started under the Sunak government in 202420 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Smokefree generation one step closer as bill introduced’, press release, 20 March 2024, retrieved 26 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/smokefree-generation-one-step-closer-as-bill-introduced and the Starmer government finished the process in 2026.21 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Tobacco and Vapes Bill becomes law’, press release, 29 April 2026, retrieved 26 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/tobacco-and-vapes-bill-becomes-law It aims to create a smoke-free generation, in turn reducing future incidence of cancer, cardiovascular and respiratory disease, tackling health inequalities and reducing NHS pressures.

The government’s own analysis attributes 1 in 4 cancer deaths in the UK to smoking and suggests that one person every minute in England is admitted to hospital because of smoking.22 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Tobacco and vapes: evidence to support legislation’, call for evidence, 8 October 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/calls-for-evidence/tobacco-and-vapes-evidence-to-support-legislation/tobacco-and-vapes-evidence-to-support-legislation This represents a significant time and financial cost to the NHS (£1.8bn a year) and to the wider economy (£18.6bn in productivity losses).23 Action on Smoking and Health, ‘ASH Ready Reckoner’, May 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://ash.org.uk/resources/view/ash-ready-reckoner

Much like the 2006 ban on smoking in enclosed public spaces – a clear policy success, which “has stuck, is widely complied with and now largely accepted with no real risk of reversal” – the 2026 Act will likely reduce smoking-related hospital admissions and illness. The government’s impact assessment estimates that the Act will reduce smoking prevalence for those aged 14 and over from 11.3% in 2023 to 1.5% in 2056.24 Department of Health and Social Care, Tobacco and Vapes Bill: Impact assessment, 2024, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6985eeb7cfe7ccf77efbc74e/tobacco-and-vapes-bill-impact-assessment.pdf

As a bonus, regulation of this kind is low-cost to deliver for the government, with lost future revenues for the exchequer from cigarette and vape duties far less than the estimated combined cost to the NHS and economy (duties were £8.8bn in 2023/24),25 Woolnough S, ‘The Tobacco and Vapes Act – a landmark win for health’, blog, The King’s Fund, 22 April 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/blogs/tobacco-and-vapes-act-landmark-win-health and is also popular with the public.26 Action on Smoking and Health, ‘Majority of public support smokefree generation as new polling shows overwhelming public backing for tougher action on tobacco’, press release, 30 May 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://ash.org.uk/media-centre/news/press-releases/majority-of-public-support-smokefree-generation-as-new-polling-shows-overwhelming-public-backing-…

The 10YHP also claims it wants to “end the obesity epidemic”.27 Department of Health and Social Care, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England, CP 1350, The Stationery Office, 2025, p.61, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6888a0b1a11f859994409147/fit-for-the-future-10-year-health-plan-for-england.pdf Obesity prevalence in England has risen from 22.6% in 2015/16 to 26.6% in 2024/25.28 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Fingertips public health profiles: Obesity prevalence in adults, (using adjusted self-reported height and weight) (18+ yrs)’, [no date], retrieved 12 October 2026, https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/obesity-physical-activity-nutrition#gid/1938133368/ati/6 This costs the NHS an estimated £9.3bn (around 5% of NHS England’s budget in 2025/2629 HM Treasury, Spending Review 2025, CP 1336, The Stationery Office, 2025, p. 122, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/686270a608bf2f53761219fc/E03349913_HMT_Spending_Review_June_2025_TEXT_PRINT_CS.pdf ) and society as a whole £107bn per year.30 Frontier Economics, The Economic and Productivity Costs of Obesity and Overweight in the UK, Nesta, 2025, https://media.nesta.org.uk/documents/The_economic_and_productivity_costs_of_obesity_and_overweight_in_the_UK_.pdf
The group of drugs known as GLP-1s, or weight loss jabs, which include brand names such as Wegovy, and Mounjaro, are a key tool to reduce obesity.

The NHS has taken a staggered approach to rolling out GLP-1s, targeting patients with the greatest clinical need first, before expanding eligibility over the remainder of this parliament.31 NHS England, ‘Interim commissioning guidance: implementation of the NICE technology appraisal TA1026 and the NICE funding variation for tirzepatide (Mounjaro) for the management of obesity’, 2 April 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/interim-commissioning-guidance-nice-ta1026-tirzepatide

That has resulted in a sustained and rapid expansion in the number of jabs that the NHS prescribes. In August 2026, the NHS prescribed 487,000 tirzepatide (brand name Mounjaro) and semaglutide (brand name Ozempic/Wegovy) jabs to patients, up from 172,872 in June 2024 (a 182% increase), though this covers drug usage for both diabetes treatment and management of obesity.

Despite that rise, private use of GLP-1s dwarfs NHS prescribing rates. In July 2025, there were 2.4m private prescriptions of these jabs in the UK, compared to just under 380,000 prescribed by the NHS (though NHS figures are just for England, not the entire UK).1 IQVIA, written evidence to the House of Commons Health and Social Care Committee inquiry on food and weight management (FWM0029), 19 November 2025, https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/146947/pdf/#:~:text=Meanwhile%2C%20IQVIA%20data%20suggests%20that,Figure%20 1

NHS spending on these drugs is rising rapidly. The NHS’s prescribing cost for Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) roughly doubled on 1 September 2025 when the manufacturer, Eli Lilly, increased prices from £90 to £180 for 5mg and £122 to £330 for 15mg pens.1 OpenPrescribing.net, ‘Tirzepatide (BNF code 0601023AZ)’, Bennett Institute for Applied Data Science, University of Oxford, 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://openprescribing.net/ analyse/#org=CCG&numIds=0601023AZ&denom=nothing&selectedTab=chart Greater demand plus higher prices mean that NHS England spends around £80m a month (before discounts are applied) on GLP-1 prescribing costs.*

It is still too early to tell the effect this rapid increase in prescribing will have on obesity rates. The most recent data is still for 2024/25, before more widespread uptake of these drugs. In theory, increased GLP-1 usage could have a rapid effect. One meta-review of academic literature of GLP-1s found that users had an average weight loss of 17.3% after 68 weeks.2 Shah MY, Mohammad A, Samejo RBA and others, ‘Weight Loss That Lasts: Reviewing the Long-Term Impact of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists’, Cureus, 2025, vol. 17 no. 7, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12361690/ That implies that higher prescription rates could reduce obesity rates within this parliament.

Multiple studies have shown, though, that ceasing treatment often results in users regaining lost weight.3Ibid.,4 West S, Scragg J, Aveyard P and others, ‘Weight regain after cessation of medication for weight management: systematic review and meta-analysis’, BMJ, 2026, vol. 392, www.bmj.com/content/392/bmj-2025-085304 That implies that the NHS will have to continue to prescribe these drugs to maintain the benefit.

High vaccination uptake is one of the most effective preventative interventions a government can implement.5 NHS England, ‘NHS England Vaccination Strategy’, ENGLAND.NHS.UK, [no date], retrieved 5 November 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/south/wp-content/uploads/sites/6/2023/12/20231207-NHSE-Vaccination-Strategy-Explainer-v1.0.pdf Despite that, vaccination coverage for most major types of vaccine have declined in recent years, some dramatically, and starting under the Conservative government. In 2024/25, only 71.7% of girls aged 12 or 13 had received the human papillomavirus (HPV, a virus which increases the risk of a range of cancers, particularly cervical cancer) vaccine compared to 91.1% in 2013/14 (the earliest year for which there is data), compared to a target of 90% coverage.

Labour has not stopped that trend. For all the vaccines that have data, coverage was lower in 2025/26 than it was in 2023/24, though in some cases (MenB first dose and Rotavirus) the decline was minimal.*
* For HPV (where the most recent year is 2024/25) coverage was also lower than in 2023/24, though Labour are less responsible for this performance as they took power after the year had started.

Declining rates are related to a range of issues. The Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health (RCPCH) stress that while vaccine hesitancy has likely increased since the pandemic, in their view parents’ inability to access vaccination services far outweighs that uptick.1 Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, Vaccination in the UK: Access, uptake and equity, 2025, p. 17, https://www.rcpch.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2025-06/Vaccination-in-UK-access-uptake-equity_policy-report-2025.pdf

Access problems can be caused by a lack of staff, difficulties booking appointments with providers, or inadequate travel routes for parents to take children to receive vaccinations.2 Royal College of Paediatrics and Child Health, Vaccination in the UK: Access, uptake and equity, 2025, www.rcpch.ac.uk/sites/default/files/2025-06/Vaccination-in-UK-access-uptake-equity_policy-report-2025.pdf

Health visitors are among the first agents of the state to interact with children and their families. Their unique access to the home environment and ability to track the early indicators of development means they have a powerful role to play in a preventative shift among children.

In England, the health visiting service conducted 85.5% of New Birth Visits within 14 days of a child’s birth in 2025/26.3 Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, ‘Health visitor service delivery: data for 2024 to 2025’, 21 January 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/health-visitor-service-delivery-data-for-2024-to-2025 That has remained relatively stable over time, with 87.7% of new health visits completed within 14 days in 2017/18.4 Office for Health Improvement and Disparities, ‘Child and Maternal Health: Proportion of New Birth Visits (NBVs) completed within 14 days’, Fingertips, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/profile/child-health-profiles/data#page/4/gid/1938133223/pat/159/par/K02000001/ati/15/are/ E92000001/iid/93469/age/284/sex/4/cat/-1/ctp/-1/yrr/1/cid/4/tbm/1

Despite relatively consistent visiting rates, the health visiting workforce is operating under enormous pressure. Health visiting numbers have declined by 45% since September 2015 and there is low morale across the workforce.*,1 Institute of Health Visiting, ‘Health visitor survey finds that more babies and young children are missing out on the government’s promise of the “best start in life”’, press release, 18 January 2023, https://ihv.org.uk/news-and-views/news/health-visitor-survey-finds-that-more-babies-and-young-children-are-missing-out-on-the-governments-promise-of-…; Survey results, p. 5, https://ihv.org.uk/media/h3wfffh3/71119_health_visiting_in_england_vision_final_version.pdf As such, while health visiting rates have been broadly stable in the last ten years (excluding the pandemic period), these rates have been maintained with a smaller headcount. Thus, even though the number of children requiring a health visit fell by 14.8% between 2017/18 and 2025/26, the workload on each health visitor increased by more than a quarter (29.2%).2 UCL, ‘Number of health visitors in England falls by a fifth over five years’, 26 March 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.ucl.ac.uk/news/2026/mar/number-health-visitors-england-falls-fifth-over-five-years

Consequently, only 37% of health visitors in England now feel they provide “a good or outstanding service that can adequately safeguard children”.3 Institute of Health Visiting, State of Health Visiting, UK Survey Report: A vital safety net under pressure, 2023, p.6, https://ihv.org.uk/media/h3wfffh3/71119_health_visiting_in_england_vision_final_version.pdf
As previously discussed, Labour has not made a meaningful improvement to the health visitor workforce, with numbers hovering around the same level as when Labour won the election.

* Indeed, at the end of 2024, some 40% of health visitors surveyed by iHV said they intended to leave the profession in the next five years. https://www.nursinginpractice.com/clinical/paediatrics/health-visiting-workforce-cut-beyond-the-bone-in-too-many-areas/

Alongside the shift in resources to the community and primary care sectors, the government should make it clear how it intends to shift funding towards public health services delivered by local authorities. This should be part of a wider government effort to shift resources towards prevention.

There are insufficient clear targets in the 10YHP that would demonstrate progress towards its prevention goal. The government should publish the “delivery indicators” described in the 10YHP. Where those are very long-term, it should provide interim targets that demonstrate progress.

Vaccination is one of the most important preventative health interventions, but coverage has declined in recent years. That trend has continued under Labour. The government should ensure that improving vaccination uptake is a key part of any future preventative agenda.
“We [will] create the most digitally accessible health system in the world” - 10 Year Health Plan

The government has set great store in a digital transformation of the NHS, arguing that moving from “bricks to clicks” is an existential necessity for the service. In doing so, it aims to improve access and convenience for patients; free up capacity to respond to complex need in physical services; and provide financial savings to guarantee its future financial sustainability.
There are three clear “retail” policies that, if successfully rolled out, will change patients’ experience of the NHS most visibly:

There are other programmes which are designed to sit alongside those technologies. The Federated Data Platform (FDP), a product that technology company Palantir is currently contracted to deliver, is the highest profile. It is also the most controversial because of public concerns around the use of personal data and whether it is delivering the improvements the programme set out to, given the level of investment and the NHS’ scale of ambition.4 Booth R, ‘More than 44,000 file legal objections to Palantir NHS platform handling their data’, The Guardian, 30 September 2026, retrieved 26 October 2026, www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/30/legal-objections-palantir-nhs-platform-handling-data ,5 Medact, Briefing: Concerns regarding Palantir Technologies and NHS data systems, 12 March 2026, www.medact.org/2026/resources/briefings/briefing-palantir-fdp ,6 Health and Social Care Committee, ‘Drop Palantir’s Federated Data Platform and look for alternative, MPs tell Health Minister’, UK Parliament, 9 July 2026, retrieved 26 October 2026, https://committees.parliament.uk/ committee/81/health-and-social-care-committee/news/214760/drop-palantirs-federated-data-platform-and-look-for-alternative-mps-tell-health-minister/ ,7 Borrett A and Hughes L, ‘UK raises cost projections for Palantir’s NHS data platform’, Financial Times, 10 August 2026, retrieved 26 October 2026, www.ft.com/content/da888f06-b9bc-4d83-8020-e82f5d5fa609 The 10YHP also sets out bold ambitions on the use of wearables across the NHS. The goal to increase patients’ usage of wearables would undoubtedly change user experience. However, there is little indication that there has been tangible progress (or even aims set) in this area.

As with previous digital health plans, there is still little detail on the ‘plumbing’ that will turn ideas in the 10YHP into reality. As one interviewee put it, across governments “there has been consistent direction-setting, but delivery has long been a challenge”.

Progress is even harder to assess in this shift than the others. There are no good proxy metrics – such as spending or staffing data – for progress. There is also no data about the rate at which different parts of the NHS are adopting tools or, more importantly, how they are using them and to what effect.

The Single Patient Record (SPR) is the centrepiece of the Labour government’s digital strategy. Currently, a combination of electronic records (held by trusts) and some shared patient records8 Steere A, ‘Long read: The Single Patient Record: what the legislation does – and what it will take to deliver it’, Understanding Patient Data, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.understandingpatientdata.org.uk/long-read-single-patient-record-what-legislation-does-and-what-it-will-take-deliver-it (across small geographies and built on ad hoc data sharing arrangements) capture patient data. There is, however, no consistent, unified system for sharing information across the country or across different services.

An SPR would resolve many issues around data fragmentation and, if complemented by extensions to the NHS App, provide patients with easy access to all their health information. It would also allow staff working across primary, secondary, community and social care in every ICB to access the same up-to-date patient records.9 Purbrick-Thompson K, ‘The single patient record explained: what could it mean for patients and the health and care system’, The King’s Fund, 4 August 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/the-single-patient-record-explained-what-could-it-mean-for-patients-and-the-health-and-c…

DHSC has committed to improving clinician access to data by 2027 by improving connections between existing shared care records and aims to give all patients access to their core health data through the NHS App from 2028, with full access by 2030.10 NHS England, ‘Single Patient Record – your health at your fingertips’, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/digitaltechnology/the-single-patient-record

The government has made slow progress in bringing an SPR to life. Since the then-secretary of state Wes Streeting announced plans for an SPR in October 2024, the NHS has launched public deliberations and engagement with stakeholders.

Over the next few years, DHSC plans to work with NHS staff, the public and suppliers to “develop and test prototypes for real-life scenarios in priority areas such as maternity care”, through a phased approach.11Ibid.
DHSC has also introduced the 2026 Health Bill which, if passed, will mandate that data flows across all health and social care providers and IT system providers.

However, suppliers are still uncertain what the NHS will require of them. For example, the Bill compels IT suppliers to share data in a timely manner and says that there will be financial penalties for non-compliance. But the bill does not define “timeliness”, which information standards will be enforced, or a mechanism for penalisation.

Further, with the merger of NHSE into DHSC, alongside cuts to ICB headcounts, it is difficult to discern who will ‘hold the ring’ and ensure delivery on data standards, accountability and liability and how data will flow from different NHS organisations in and out of the SPR. It is even less clear how this data might then be utilised to improve population health management and predictive care.
Increased use of artificial intelligence underpins many of the government’s anticipated productivity improvements for the NHS
The 10YHP also sets out how Artificial Intelligence (AI) might be used to free up staff time, contributing to improved NHS productivity. Key commitments include:

The 10YHP also pledged to develop and implement an “NHS AI strategic roadmap”, providing ethical and governance frameworks, alongside AI upskilling programmes and the use of validated AI diagnostic and administrative tools.13 Department of Health and Social Care, Fit for the Future: 10 Year Health Plan for England, CP 1350, The Stationery Office, 2025, p.118, https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6888a0b1a11f859994409147/fit-for-the-future-10-year-health-plan-for-england.pdf The 10YHP also promises to better harness data for new clinical, decision-support and admin-reduction tools through the new Health Data Research Service.

However, while AI use in the NHS has undoubtedly grown since the 2024 election, it is unclear by how much. There has been mass-adoption of Ambient Voice Technology, with many areas now procuring the technology at scale, though some concern has been raised about the pace of change.14 HTN Health Tech News, ‘Investigation launches into use of ambient voice technology in hospitals’, 6 August 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://htn.co.uk/2026/08/06/investigation-launches-into-use-of-ambient-voice-technology-in-hospitals/ ,15 Concordance, ‘Digital scribes: the first AI tool the NHS actually adopted’, 14 March 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, http://concordance.uk/insights/nhs-digital-scribes ,16 Burns C, ‘NHS urges sector to take advantage of AI scribes’, The Pharmaceutical Journal, 16 January 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://pharmaceutical-journal.com/article/news/nhs-urges-sector-to-take-advantage-of-ai-scribes ,17 NHS England, ‘Midlands leads the way on ambient voice technology’, 15 July 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/midlands/2026/07/15/midlands-leads-the-way-on-ambient-voice-technology ,18 Lovell T, ‘London NHS trusts to roll out AI scribing to 20,000 clinicians’, Digital Health, 8 April 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.digitalhealth.net/2026/04/london-nhs-trusts-to-roll-out-ai-scribing-to-20000-clinicians ,19 Lovell T, ‘Hertfordshire Community NHS Trust to roll out AI-scribing’, Digital Health, 1 April 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.digitalhealth.net/2026/04/hertfordshire-community-nhs-trust-to-roll-out-ai-scribing Similarly, in stroke care, AI brain-scan software is now in use across all 107 NHS stroke centres, with impressive preliminary results, though this rollout began under the previous government in 2023.20 NR Times, ‘NHS AI tool will help 50% of stroke patients recover’, 2 September 2025, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://nrtimes.co.uk/nhs-ai-tool-will-help-50-of-stroke-patients-recover-lpc25 ,21 Department of Health and Social Care, The Rt Hon Steve Barclay MP and Chloe Smith, ‘£21 million to roll out artificial intelligence across the NHS’, press release, 23 June 2023, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/21-million-to-roll-out-artificial-intelligence-across-the-nhs However, more broadly, the speed at which AI has developed, means that we have very little data (including in surveys) about NHS staff’s use of AI before 2024, and it is difficult to assess Labour’s progress in this area. Likewise, it is also hard to distinguish between simple AI ‘adoption’ (where trusts and services have bought services) versus true embrace and regular use of these technologies by NHS staff.

Perhaps most importantly, the piecemeal and often bottom-up adoption of AI in different parts of the NHS, and limited reporting/evaluation of these technologies, makes any assessment of their benefits (beyond specific clinical use cases) challenging. It is also unwise to assume straightforward efficiency gains through AI adoption. There is little existing literature considering how freed-up time, resulting from time-saving technologies, is actually repurposed.22 Moulds A and Horton T, ‘How would clinicians use time freed up by technology?’, The Health Foundation, May 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.health.org.uk/reports-and-analysis/briefings/how-would-clinicians-use-time-freed-up-by-technology Staff time might be used for more activity, but it also might be used to spend more time with each patient (improving patient experience but not driving up productivity, per se), conducting training (which has knock-on productivity benefits that aren’t immediately clear), or completing administrative tasks that might otherwise be done during work breaks or during overtime. All these are worthwhile uses of time, but they don’t automatically equal greater productivity or more patients treated.

Building on the anticipated rollout of the SPR, the Starmer government promised that an improved NHS App will create convenience for patients and save resource for the NHS.23 Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England, ‘Managing healthcare easy as online banking with revamped NHS App’, press release, 3 July 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/managing-healthcare-easy-as-online-banking-with-revamped-nhs-app The App will be complemented by a raft of other AI-enhanced ‘My X’ services, like the My NHS GP tool (available 24/7, for non-urgent cases), and the My Choices tool.* For service users, the NHS App will be the most visible sign of a digital shift in the way the NHS manages care.

NHS England’s online NHS App roadmap24 NHS England, ‘NHS App roadmap’, 5 November 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, https://digital.nhs.uk/services/nhs-app/roadmap tracks completed, current and future projects aimed at improving patient access and experience. Release notes25 NHS England, ‘NHS App release notes’, 25 March 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.nhs.uk/nhs-app/about/nhs-app-release-notes indicate that there have been small (bug fixes) as well as large improvements (introduction of new services, such as the integration of online consultation and Patient Care Aggregator services) to the NHS App at a near fortnightly rate since Labour took office. Clearly, work is being done.

And, use of the App is growing. There have been over 40 million NHS App account registrations, with app login sessions in June 2026 79.9% higher than in the same period in June 2024.26 NHS England, ‘NHS App management information – June 2026’, 24 July 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://digital.nhs.uk/data-and-information/publications/statistical/nhs-app-statistics/june-2026 The government set a target for 85% of hospitals to make appointment information available through the app by March 2025. This was met, with 87% of trusts hitting the target in March 2025, up from 68% in July 2024.27 Department of Health and Social Care, ‘Major NHS App expansion cuts waiting times’, press release, 28 April 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.gov.uk/government/news/major-nhs-app-expansion-cuts-waiting-times

As with many areas of digital innovation, greater uptake of technologies alone does not equal success and focusing solely on uptake or expansion of online services risks obscuring whether these changes are adding value for service users. But patients are broadly positive about the App; a Healthwatch survey, conducted in the summer of 2025, found that 57% of participants agreed that the NHS App helped manage their health.**,***

There remain risks in an ‘App-first’ approach. Those with lower digital literacy skills are most obviously at risk of marginalisation28 Pilot L, Offline and Overlooked: Digital exclusion and its impact on older people, Age UK, 2024, www.ageuk.org.uk/siteassets/documents/reports-and-publications/reports-and-briefings/offline-and-overlooked-report.pdf ,29 Healthwatch Derby, ‘NHS app: awareness and experiences report 2024’, 8 August 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://nds.healthwatch.co.uk/reports-library/nhs-app-awareness-and-experiences-report-2024 ,30 Lloyds Banking Group, 2025 Consumer Digital Index: The generative AI edition, 2025, www.lloydsbankinggroup.com/assets/pdfs/media/consumer-digital-index/2025/2025-consumer-digital-index.pdf ,31 The King’s Fund, ‘Connection lost: people’s experiences of using digital technology in health and care’, 2023, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://features.kingsfund.org.uk/connection-lost/index.html?_ga=2.182180519.1637327810.1727786389-964730683.1724858879 but many beyond this group feel ‘forced’ into using the App and frustrated by imperfect services and inaccurate records, even if they valued the App’s ease of use and convenience, overall.32 Healthwatch Oxfordshire, ‘Digital health care and the NHS App, Voices from Oxfordshire’, 2025, https://nds.healthwatch.co.uk/sites/default/files/reports_library/NHS%20App%20final%20final%20Nov%202025.pdf Digital change of this kind will also require physical service redesign and standardisation across the country in order to avoid confusion across services, repetition or errors.33 Devereux E, ‘NHS App breaking cancer diagnoses before clinicians’, HSJ, 18 November 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.hsj.co.uk/technology-and-innovation/nhs-app-breaking-cancer-diagnoses-before-clinicians/7040409.article; quoted in Mistry P, ‘Is the NHS ready for the AI-powered patient?’, The King’s Fund, 26 May 2026, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/nhs-ready-for-ai-powered-patient

* Other services promise convenience and personalisation for patients, including greater ability for self-referral, remote consultation, self-management of medication and vaccine regimens as well as managing their own care as well as that of their children.

**Creating a ‘one stop shop’ for care would go some way to improve the digital experience of even those who are very digitally confident, many of whom use multiple apps, websites and login details to access care. http://kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/the-reality-of-and-potential-for-digitally-enabled-care-in-the-community

***The most common use of the App in one survey was to order repeat prescriptions (76%), followed by viewing GP health records (70%). Indeed, app users view their GP health record over 35 million times each month, with 12 million views of test results. https://nds.healthwatch.co.uk/sites/default/files/reports_library/NHS%20App%20final%20final%20Nov%202025.pdf;http://digital.nhs.uk/services/nhs-app/roadmap

For the government to make a success of its digital shift, it first needs to get the basics right, address ongoing funding concerns, fill staff skill gaps, build public trust and implement more systematic approaches to data collection and data sharing.

It should also prioritise investment in IT basics that would definitely improve productivity before investment in more speculative technologies such as AI, where the benefits are far more uncertain. These are well-established priority areas where trade associations, think tanks and charities have called for improvements for many years.34 Nuffield Trust, written evidence to the House of Commons Health and Social Care Committee inquiry on digital transformation in the NHS (DTN0051), 5 July 2022, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://committees.parliament.uk/writtenevidence/109146/html ,35 Keck L and Godec S, ‘Trust and confidence in technology-enabled care’, The Health Foundation, November 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.health.org.uk/reports-and-analysis/briefings/trust-and-confidence-in-technology-enabled-care ,36 techUK, ‘Driving digital transformation: techUK’s recommendations for health and social care’, 21 November 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.techuk.org/resource/driving-digital-transformation-techuk-s-recommendations-for-health-social-care.html ,37 The NHS Alliance, ‘Digital transformation in the NHS: a reference guide’, 11 December 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://thenhsalliance.org/resources/digital-transformation-in-the-nhs-a-reference-guide ,38 House of Commons Health and Social Care Committee, Digital Transformation in the NHS: Eighth report of session 2022–23 (HC 223), The Stationery Office, 2023, retrieved 12 October 2026, https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5803/cmselect/cmhealth/223/report.html Those enabling factors are vital before ministers get too carried away with the “white heat” of AI, genomics and wearables technology.

The government should also ensure it makes a strong case to the public for the need for change. Previous attempts at digital reform – such as the ‘care.data’ scheme and the General Practice Data for Planning and Research (GPDPR) programme – were slowed or failed due to a lack of public support.

The current approach of ad hoc adoption of AI technologies across the NHS does create a useful laboratory for innovation, reducing risk by keeping technologies localised to small geographies or service areas with the option to scale those that have proven benefits. However, without proper evaluation of these technologies (probably led by central government) and frameworks for adoption, patient trust, safety and efficiency could be undermined. The NHS should build upon the recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare to rapidly build a regulatory framework for AI use in the NHS.39 Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency, National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare: Recommendations for a future regulatory framework, 10 September 2026, retrieved 9 November 2026, www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-commission-into-the-regulation-of-ai-in-healthcare-recommendations-for-a-future-regulatory-framework The Commission notes that current frameworks are designed for products that are “more static and easier to reliably assess at a single point in time”. AI-enabled products “may iterate rapidly, perform differently in different settings and depend on the data, workflows, people and organisations around them”.40Ibid. Without greater clarity, the NHS runs the risk that trusts and services within the NHS deploy AI (at significant cost) without clear evaluations, use cases or the proper technical architecture and staff training needed to enable success.*

Following decades of work,41 Robertson A, Bates DW and Sheikh A, ‘The rise and fall of England’s National Programme for IT’, Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine, 2011, vol. 104, no. 11, pp. 434–35, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3206716/ the NHS has finally achieved near-full coverage of EPRs.42 NHS England, ‘Digitising the frontline’, (no date), retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/digitaltechnology/digitising-the-frontline But there are still problems with how the service uses EPRs. Many staff still report issues sharing or accessing data across different parts of the service.43 Moulds A and Horton T, ‘Which technologies offer the biggest opportunities to save time in the NHS?’, The Health Foundation, April 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.health.org.uk/reports-and-analysis/briefings/which-technologies-offer-the-biggest-opportunities-to-save-time-in , 44 NHS England, ‘Interoperability’, 15 May 2023, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.england.nhs.uk/long-read/interoperability It is positive that the government has made it a priority over the course of 2026 to optimise EPR “functionality, efficiency and usability”, conduct digital maturity assessments and provide support (including through a tiger team service) to trusts as they embed EPRs. As part of this, the NHS should implement more consistent approaches to data collection and coding standards which hamper interoperability and formalise data sharing agreements between places to maximise the benefits of EPRs.

There are considerable digital skills gaps across the NHS. The service struggles to hire digital specialist roles because of less competitive pay and work conditions relative to the private sector.45 Dawood S, ‘The NHS’s digital problem: how old infrastructure is slowing down healthcare services’, The New Statesman, 23 August 2024, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.newstatesman.com/spotlight/healthcare/nhs/2024/08/nhs-digital-transformation-infrastructure-technology-patient-records-artificial-intelligence-wa… There is also a history of high turnover of digital and data workforce, affecting institutional memory and delivery.46 Mistry P, ‘Infrastructure for innovation: getting the NHS and social care ready for AI’, The King’s Fund, 25 June 2025, retrieved 12 October 2026, www.kingsfund.org.uk/insight-and-analysis/long-reads/infrastructure-nhs-social-care-ai#%E2%80%8B%E2%80%8Borganisational-and-system-capabilities- The cutting of non-clinical staff in trusts alongside headcount reductions in NHSE, DHSC and ICBs risks the loss of digital capabilities, institutional memory and programme delivery capacity at a vital time. The government should ensure that it has sufficient data and digital capacity to deliver its digital ambitions.

* Early evidence indicates that this has been the case in many trusts that have adopted Palantir’s Federated Data Platform. https://www.ft.com/content/a3e94197-87a8-4ba5-8a6d-4b7193993af9?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.ft.com/content/cc1f2e28-117f-41bb-96b9-030746cf9530?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.ft.com/content/63bfdeb2-efb1-4e3a-8c89-a884eb5bd618?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.ft.com/content/da888f06-b9bc-4d83-8020-e82f5d5fa609?syn-25a6b1a6=1; https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v48/n13/peter-geoghegan-and-lucas-amin/this-looks-absolutely-rubbish
An expert panel presented the key findings of the IfG’s annual Public Services Performance Tracker.
Despite progress in some areas, Starmer's reform agenda did not live up to expectations and leaves Burnham with difficult choices.
The most comprehensive stocktake of the Labour government’s progress on public services since the 2024 general election.
