articles.title: 2027 Tax Brackets
articles.standfirst: Explore the IRS inflation-adjusted 2027 tax brackets, for which taxpayers will file tax returns in early 2028.
paragraphs: On a yearly basis, the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) adjusts more than 60 tax provisions for inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin to prevent what is called “bracket creepBracket creep occurs when inflation, or real income growth, pushes taxpayers into higher income tax brackets. Bracket creep results in an increase in income taxes without an increase in real income. Many tax provisions—both at the federal and state levels—are adjusted for inflation. Over time, bracket creep can increase how much income tax people owe as their income grows, either due to inflat.” Bracket creep occurs when inflation, rather than real increases in income, pushes people into higher income tax bracketsA tax bracket is the range of incomes taxed at given rates, which typically differ depending on filing status. In a progressive individual or corporate income tax system, rates rise as income increases. There are seven federal individual income tax brackets; the federal corporate income tax system is flat. or reduces the value they receive from credits and deductions.

The IRS previously used the Consumer Price Index (CPI) as a measure of inflation prior to 2018. However, with the TaxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA), the IRS now uses the Chained Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U) to adjust income thresholds, deduction amounts, and credit values accordingly.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), passed in July 2025, made permanent most of the TCJA individual tax provisions scheduled for expiration at the end of 2025 and made other changes to individual taxes that will impact tax parameters for the 2027 tax year.
The new inflation adjustments are for tax year 2027, for which taxpayers will file tax returns in early 2028.
On average, tax parameters that are adjusted for inflation will increase by about 3.2 percent.

In 2027, the income limits for all tax brackets and all filers will be adjusted for inflation and can be found in Table 1. The federal income tax has seven tax rates in 2027: 10 percent, 12 percent, 22 percent, 24 percent, 32 percent, 35 percent, and 37 percent. The top marginal income tax rate of 37 percent will hit taxpayers with taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. above $661,375 for single filers and above $793,650 for married couples filing jointly.
The standard deduction will increase by $500 for single filers and by $1,000 for joint filers compared to the 2026 tax year (Table 2).

Seniors at or over age 65 may claim an additional standard deduction of $2,100 for single filers and $1,700 for joint filers. On top of this, taxpayers aged 65 and older who either itemize or claim the standard deduction may claim a new $6,000 deduction per qualifying taxpayer, phasing out at a six percent rate for those earning over $75,000 (single) and $150,000 (joint) as part of the separate senior deduction under the OBBBA. This new deduction is not indexed for inflation and is scheduled to expire at the end of 2028.
The personal exemption for 2027 remains at $0 (eliminating the personal exemption was part of the TCJA, and the $0 amount was made permanent as part of the OBBBA).

The alternative minimum tax (AMT) was created in the 1960s to prevent high-income taxpayers from avoiding the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source. This parallel income tax system requires high-income taxpayers to calculate their tax bill twice: once under the ordinary income tax system and again under the AMT. The taxpayer then needs to pay the higher of the two.

The AMT uses an alternative definition of taxable income called alternative minimum taxable income (AMTI). To prevent low- and middle-income taxpayers from being subject to the AMT, taxpayers are allowed to exempt a significant amount of their income from AMTI. However, the exemption phases out for high-income taxpayers. The AMT is levied at two rates: 26 percent and 28 percent.

The AMT exemption amount for 2027 is $93,000 for singles and $144,700 for married couples filing jointly (Table 3), a continuation of the TCJA design adjusted for inflation after the structure was made permanent in the OBBBA.
In 2027, the 28 percent AMT rate applies to AMT excess taxable income above $252,500 for all taxpayers ($126,250 for married couples filing separate returns).

AMT exemptions phase out at 50 cents for every dollar of AMTI exceeding $515,950 for single filers and $1,031,900 for married taxpayers filing jointly (Table 4). The OBBBA’s changes to the AMT returned the phaseout thresholds to 2018 levels and accelerated the phaseout rate from 25 percent previously.

The maximum earned income tax credit (EITC) in 2027 for single and joint filers is $685 if the filer has no children (Table 5). The maximum credit is $4,573 for one child, $7,552 for two children, and $8,496 for three or more children.
The maximum child tax credit (CTC) in 2027 is $2,300 per qualifying child, an increase of $100 compared to the previous year. The OBBBA indexed the CTC to inflation.
The refundable portion of the child tax credit is adjusted for inflation and will be $1,800 for 2027.
Long-term capital gains face different brackets and rates than ordinary income (Table 6).
The TCJA included a 20 percent deduction for pass-through businesses, and the OBBBA made this deduction permanent.

Limits on the deduction begin phasing in for taxpayers with income above $208,300 (or $416,600 for joint filers) in 2027 (Table 7). The OBBBA expanded the income range over which the deduction limitations phase in from $50,000 to $75,000 for single filers and from $100,000 to $150,000 for taxpayers married filing jointly.
In 2027, the gift tax exclusion will increase to $20,000 per recipient, up from $19,000 in both 2025 and 2026.
The exclusion is increased to $201,000 from $194,000 for gifts to spouses who are not citizens of the United States.

The estate taxAn estate tax is imposed on the net value of an individual’s taxable estate, after any exclusions or credits, at the time of death. The tax is paid by the estate itself before assets are distributed to heirs. exemption is adjusted for inflation and will be $15,480,000 in 2027.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Alex Durante is a Senior Economist at the Tax Foundation, working on federal tax policy and model development. Alex worked as a research assistant at the Federal Reserve Board and served as a staff economist on the Council of Economic Advisers.

articles.title: EU Tax Omnibus Proposal: Suggestions for Improving Its Legal Design and Increasing Its Political Viability
articles.standfirst: Tax Foundation Europe's input to the European Commission’s public consultations on the Tax Omnibus proposal reviews selected issues that have an impact on growth and competitiveness.
paragraphs: Tax Foundation Europe’s mission is to develop research and educate policymakers on tax matters that impact the growth and competitiveness of the European Union’s economy. Accordingly, our input to the European Commission’s public consultations on the Tax Omnibus proposal (the “Proposal”) is not comprehensive but a review of selected issues that have an impact on growth and competitiveness. We hope to contribute meaningfully to the discussions currently happening at the Council.

The first issue we address is the elimination of the holding requirement from the Parent-Subsidiary (PSD) and Interest and Royalty (IRD) directives to benefit from the exemption from withholdingWithholding is the income an employer takes out of an employee’s paycheck and remits to the federal, state, and/or local government. It is calculated based on the amount of income earned, the taxpayer’s filing status, the number of allowances claimed, and any additional amount the employee requests. taxes on dividend, interest, and royalty payments. The second is the nature of the Anti-Tax Avoidance Directive (ATAD) as a minimum standard of protection of Member States’ tax bases or minimum harmonization.

The PSD and IRD have slightly different requirements for the equity, debt, and intellectual property (IP) rights holder to benefit from the exemption from withholding tax on the dividend, interest, and royalty payment. Among other requirements, the PSD requires the parent company to hold at least 10 percent of the shares of the subsidiary (directly or indirectly), whereas the IRD requires that associated companies be connected by at least 25 percent of shareholding directly or via a common parent. Below these thresholds and subject to the EU Treaties, Member States remain free to levy a withholding tax on the relevant cross-border payment. The Proposal would abolish those thresholds, meaning that Member States would no longer be free to levy withholding taxes on cross-border payments to so-called portfolio investments (i.e., below 10 percent and 25 percent).

Member States have argued that the amendment would shift the PSD and IRD from facilitating the grouping of companies within the EU toward reallocating taxing rights among Member States. Because that reallocation would affect national tax revenues differently, the Proposal could have asymmetrical fiscal effects across Member States.

We first examine the changing nature of the PSD and IRD and whether the avoidance of double taxationDouble taxation is when taxes are paid twice on the same dollar of income, regardless of whether that’s corporate or individual income. is equally justified for controlling and portfolio investments. We then assess the Proposal’s potential impact on Member States’ tax revenues and suggest alternatives that could address budgetary concerns while preserving the Proposal’s competitiveness objective.

As mentioned in the previous section, for the shareholdings not covered by the directives, Member States remain free to levy a withholding tax on outbound payments of dividends, interest, and royalties.

For dividend income, this might cause triple taxation. First, the distributing company’s profits are taxed with a corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. in its state of residence. Second, the receiving company is taxed by the state of the distributing company on the amount of dividends distributed. Third, the receiving company is again taxed in its state of residence, as the dividends received enter its tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. for corporate income tax purposes.

For interest and royalty income, there might be double taxation. First, the interest and royalties received by the receiving company are taxed via withholding tax by the paying company’s state. Second, the interest and royalties received by the receiving company are taxed in its state of residence as the interest and royalties enter its tax base for corporate income purposes.
EU law sets a limit to this power, as it requires Member States to treat resident and non-resident taxpayers in the same way when they are in a comparable situation.

Broadly, for dividends, this means that Member States cannot levy a withholding tax on all dividend payments (within and outside their territory) and grant an exemption or credit to their recipient only when a resident.[1] In the simplest scenario possible, a Member State that exempts all dividends received by domestic companies from their domestic subsidiaries from corporate income tax cannot simultaneously levy a withholding tax on dividends paid abroad.[2]

For interest and royalties, granting national treatment to non-residents mostly means that source Member States levying a withholding tax may have to take into account the expenses connected to that income in the source state—as it would do for its own residents[3]—and tax that item of income on a net basis.[4] On the other end of the payment, a Member State would typically subject any received interest and royalty payment to tax, regardless of their source being domestic or not, meaning that equal treatment would not help solve the juridical double taxation outcome.[5]

This summary shows that EU fundamental freedoms constrain outbound withholding taxes more strictly for dividends than for interest and royalties. For dividends, Member States’ room for manoeuvre is narrower; for interest and royalties, it is broader. The distinction arises because dividends are distributions of after-tax profits, usually exempted upon receipt, whereas interest and royalty payments are generally deductible expenses for the paying company and income for the recipient.[6]

The double tax conventions (DTCs) entered into by the Member States among each other also limit the Member States’ power to levy withholding taxes on outbound payments. Typically, these DTCs (i) limit the rate of withholding tax that the state of the paying company can levy,[7] and (ii) oblige the state of residence of the receiving company to grant credit for the withholding tax paid abroad.[8]

However, despite the constraints imposed by EU law and DTCs on Member States, there can be instances of definitive double taxation within the internal market. To the extent that source states treat resident and non-resident taxpayers the same, Member States can levy EU law-compliant withholding taxes on dividend, interest, and royalty payments. Double tax treaties may not come to the rescue.[9] In fact, there are instances that DTCs cannot solve, such as triangular or multi-country cases,[10] as well as divergent interpretations of treaty terms by treaty partners. This may lead to instances of definitive double taxation within the Union.

For portfolio investments, there is no clear empirical evidence that the existence of (definitive) withholding taxes per se influences the investment location decision. However, as domestic, EU law or DTC-based exemptions from withholding taxes come with administrative requirements, often Member States levy their (higher) statutory withholding tax instead of the lower (treaty) rate, pending the verification of these requirements. Refunds of the difference come with a time lag. Administrative costs and time lags have been proven to be negatively correlated with investment decisions.[11] In other words, the higher the recovery costs of (over)withheld taxes,[12] the lower the investments in a given jurisdiction, potentially affecting the functioning of the internal market.

The exemption from the application of withholding taxes on outbound payments is currently limited to so-called “direct shareholdings,” i.e., above 10 percent in the PSD and 25 percent in the IRD. Originally, before dropping to 10 percent, the PSD also had a 25 percent shareholding requirement.[13] Scholars have explained that if 25 percent could loosely mimic substantial minority rights under the corporate laws of several Member States, 10 percent looks like an arbitrary threshold to benefit from the avoidance of double taxation.[14]

Besides, the more beneficial treatment of direct holdings compared to portfolio holdings does not seem convincing enough. The OECD Commentary to Article 10 of the OECD Model Convention, which also grants more beneficial treatment to direct holdings (above 25 percent), explains that the reason behind such different treatment is to avoid recurrent taxation and facilitate international investment. However, this may well apply to both direct and portfolio investments.[15] A dividend or an interest payment is taxed twice, once by the paying company’s state via withholding tax and once by the receiving company’s state via corporate income tax, regardless of the percentage of investment.[16]

A more convincing argument concerns neutrality between establishing a subsidiary and operating through a permanent establishment (PE) abroad. Because a permanent establishment is part of the same legal entity as its head office, transfers between them do not constitute dividend distributions and are therefore not subject to dividend withholding tax. If dividends distributed by a subsidiary were subject to withholding tax, businesses could have a tax incentive to choose a permanent establishment instead. Exempting direct holdings from withholding tax therefore helps preserve neutrality between the two legal forms.[17]

However, granting exemption to portfolio investments as well would not defeat that goal.[18] By exempting all dividend payments from withholding taxes, PEs and subsidiaries would still be treated equally, and portfolio investors would not be subject to a double layer of taxation.

The Proposal’s fiscal impact would differ across Member States according to whether, and on which categories of income, they impose statutory withholding taxes on dividends, interest, and royalties. Those statutory rules, however, provide only a partial picture of the Proposal’s effect on Member States’ tax revenues.

As seen in section 1.1. above, EU law and DTCs constrain the source Member States’ ability to levy withholding taxes, in toto or in terms of rate. Furthermore, EU law or DTCs can require residence Member States to credit the withholding taxes levied at source. This means that capital-exporting countries generally provide credit for the taxes withheld at source. Capital-importing countries instead keep the revenues from the taxes withheld at source. The elimination of withholding taxes on outbound payments has positive revenue impacts for the former and negative revenue impacts for the latter.

Eurostat’s balance of payments statistics show that net exporters of portfolio investments are Germany, Italy, Sweden, Denmark, Belgium, Greece, Portugal, Cyprus, Malta, Croatia, Bulgaria, Estonia, Lithuania, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Latvia; while net importers of portfolio investments are Luxembourg, France, the Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, Poland, Romania, Hungary, Austria, Finland, and Czechia.[19]

Bearing in mind the important caveat that these figures combine assets and liabilities held within and outside of the EU, this picture shows that the Proposal might have a negative revenue impact only on those capital-importing countries that currently levy withholding taxes on dividends, interest, and royalties of portfolio investors. To the contrary, it might have positive revenue impacts on portfolio capital-exporting countries, such as Italy or Germany, currently providing credit for those withholding taxes levied abroad.

The asymmetrical revenue impact has been brought forward as a concern by multiple Member States. The claim is that by allowing all flows to go untaxed in the country of source, the directives (especially the IRD) would become instruments that re-allocate taxing powers on these income categories exclusively to the residence Member States.[20]

While (re)allocating taxing powers does not have any impact on economic growth per se, complying with an ineffective allocation does. It has been shown in the sections above that EU law and DTCs leave situations of definitive double taxation to persist within the Union, and that lengthy refunds for over-withheld taxes discourage cross-border investment. As a result, (re)allocating taxing rights in a simpler way by establishing that source countries need not burden outbound payments with taxes does advance the internal market.

However, making cross-border payments flow untaxed does not need to entail an asymmetrical revenue cost. The now-repealed Savings Directive, which transitionally required certain source Member States to tax savings income through a withholding tax, foresaw a revenue sharing mechanism according to which source Member States would retain 25 percent of the withholding tax revenues and residence Member States the remaining 75 percent. Inspired by this solution, it is proposed here that the Council insert a revenue-sharing clause in the directives under which capital-exporting countries that would gain from the Proposal transfer all or part of that gain to capital-importing countries that would lose revenue from its adoption.

In practical terms, the objective would be to preserve the Proposal’s removal of withholding taxes while compensating for its uneven fiscal effects. Member States that gain because they no longer need to credit foreign withholding taxes would contribute toward offsetting the revenue lost by Member States that can no longer collect those taxes at source.

Because tracing individual dividend, interest, and royalty flows would be complex, the revenue-sharing clause could instead use a statistical formula. The formula would first approximate the annual returns on aggregate equity and debt assets held in other Member States. It would then apply separate rates to the (assumed) dividend, interest, and IP rights returns to calculate the amount that capital-exporting countries would transfer to capital-importing countries.[21]

For dividends, it is suggested that a rate of 2.34 percent be applied to the assumed return on equity. The rate is intended to approximate the average maximum withholding tax that a Member State could impose on an outbound dividend consistently with CJEU case-law.

As explained in section 1.1.1, when resident and non-resident corporate shareholders are in comparable situations, the source Member State may not tax an outbound dividend more heavily than an equivalent domestic dividend. The relevant benchmark is therefore the domestic tax burden borne by a resident company receiving a dividend, rather than the statutory withholding tax rate virtually applicable to the outbound payment.[22]

The calculation translates that benchmark into an EU average in two steps. First, it determines the average share of domestic dividends that remains taxable in the hands of resident corporate recipients after applying domestic exemptions or partial inclusions across all EU Member States.[23] Second, it multiplies that average taxable share by the average EU corporate income tax rate, including applicable surcharges and regional taxes.[24] Expressed schematically: average EU CIT rate × average taxable share of domestic dividends = 2.34 percent.

For interest and royalties instead, it is suggested to apply a rate of 6 percent on (assumed) interest and IP rights yields.[25] This common rate is based on average DTC-based withholding tax rates on interest and royalty income in DTCs among EU Member States.

The formula could be updated annually in two respects: each Member State’s classification as a capital importer or exporter and the applicable rates, to reflect changes in domestic CIT rates and DTC withholding tax rates.

An alternative with a clearer EU-wide distributional rationale would be to treat these amounts as EU own resources. Rather than benefiting a single Member State, the revenue forgone would finance common EU expenditures. Only capital-exporting countries would transfer amounts to the EU budget because, absent such a transfer, they would benefit from the Proposal by no longer having to credit foreign withholding taxes. The amounts transferred would roughly correspond to the foreign tax credits they currently grant, making the operation broadly revenue-neutral for those countries compared with the status quo.

The position of capital-importing countries is different. Compared with the status quo, they would lose the revenue they currently collect from outbound withholding taxes and would not receive a direct fiscal transfer in return. They would nevertheless benefit collectively from the fact that capital-exporting countries would continue to forgo an equivalent amount of revenue, now to finance common EU expenditures rather than foreign tax credits.[26] As a result, there is equity in the distributional key of the own resource.

Article 3 of the ATAD provides that the Directive is only a minimum standard of protection of Member States’ tax bases. This means that, subject to compliance with the EU Treaties, Member States can go beyond the measures contained in the ATAD. The Proposal puts this in question in several of the proposed provisions.

As noted already in our June 2026 blog post,[27] the controlled foreign company (CFC) provision and the interest limitation rule in the Proposal contain wording that might limit Member States’ ability to go beyond the “minimum standard” set by the Directive. However, it does so in a manner that remains unclear.

Whereas the new exclusions from the CFC seem to be mandatory, it is not clear whether the same holds true for Model A or the one-third of passive income exclusion, as there is no explicit prohibition on the Member States adopting rules that differ from them, and yet the Proposal uses the wording “the Member States shall.”

Member States and taxpayers therefore face three potentially conflicting signals: (i) Article 3 states the general rule that Member States may adopt measures that go beyond ATAD’s minimum standard; (ii) the proposed CFC rule expressly prohibits divergence from only certain provisions; and (iii) other provisions outside that express prohibition use the mandatory formulation “Member States shall.” It is therefore unclear whether those other provisions establish exhaustive requirements or remain subject to Article 3’s minimum-standard approach.

This lack of clarity gravely undermines the harmonization effort that justifies the adoption of a directive under Article 115 TFEU, as Member States might interpret those provisions in a constellation of different ways. This has repercussions for the competitiveness of the EU’s tax system at large, and legal certainty for businesses operating within it.

Directives may combine different forms of harmonization,[28] and the Proposal appears to move ATAD in that direction. ATAD Article 3 should therefore be amended to state that the Directive establishes a minimum standard of protection “unless otherwise provided.” Under this approach, the minimum-standard rule would continue to apply by default, while provisions using “Member States shall” or other explicit language of exhaustiveness would operate as maximum harmonization.

In parallel, the CFC provision should follow one of two approaches. The first would delete the new paragraph eight—the express prohibition—and use “shall” for mandatory provisions and “may” for optional provisions. The second would retain paragraph eight but extend its express prohibition to paragraphs two and three, making clear that all of those provisions are mandatory.

In a similar fashion, the Proposal clarifies that the newly introduced R&D full expensing provision is a minimum harmonization provision, meaning that Member States can maintain or introduce alternative domestic measures if they consider those domestic measures to provide a more favorable treatment than the one granted by the Proposal. Member States are rightfully concerned about how to assess that equivalence.[29]
The R&D full expensing provision requires Member States to allow the taxpayer to deduct qualifying R&D capital expenditure from their taxable base in the year of acquisition, or within four years.

Subject to compatibility with the state aid prohibition, Member States could grant full expensing to a broader set of asset classes, or extend the period in which the application could be made. However, as there is a variety of R&D incentives in place, Member States are doubtful as to whether their own existing incentive is more favorable than the Proposal’s.

DepreciationDepreciation is a measurement of the “useful life” of a business asset, such as machinery or a factory, to determine the multiyear period over which the cost of that asset can be deducted from taxable income. Instead of allowing businesses to deduct the cost of investments immediately (i.e., full expensing), depreciation requires deductions to be taken over time, reducing their value and disco schedules require businesses to deduct investment costs from their taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. over multiple years, typically reflecting an asset’s expected lifespan. However, since deductions arrive only gradually, inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin and the time value of money erode their value in real terms, raising the cost of capital. The longer the depreciation schedule, the smaller the share of investment costs businesses can recover. Full expensing fixes this by allowing deduction of the entire amount of capital expenditure in the year of acquisition, making the amount of nominal deduction coincide with the real value of the expense.[30]

As a result, one criterion to determine equivalence between a domestic R&D incentive and the Proposal’s full expensing might be the net present value of deductions allowed. In other words, if the domestic rule allows the taxpayer to recover at least the real value of its capital investment, the rule is equivalent. Neutral cost recoveryCost recovery refers to how the tax system permits businesses to recover the cost of investments through depreciation or amortization. Depreciation and amortization deductions affect taxable income, effective tax rates, and investment decisions. rules would be an example, as they adjust depreciation allowances for inflation and a notional return on capital.[31] In certain cases, a super deduction might also give the same economic result.

However, the variety of options potentially emerging from the Proposal only establishing a minimum floor puts into question whether the provision would realize its harmonization goal. This might be problematic from the perspective of the legal basis used for the directive’s adoption—Article 115 TFEU—as the Court of Justice requires that a directive genuinely aims at removing obstacles to the internal market. If the obstacle that the Proposal is aiming at removing is different R&D incentive rules across Member States, having a variety of (economically equivalent) incentives might not deliver on the objective. If the obstacle is facing different tax liabilities for businesses engaged in R&D activities across EU Member States, the provision does not fix that, as it does not establish a common corporate tax base and rate. Hence, it is suggested to clarify the scope of the R&D full expensing provision and the alternative regimes that would be equivalent to it.

Tax Foundation Europe considers the Proposal broadly favorable to the functioning of the internal market and focuses on two legal issues with implications for EU economic growth. First, eliminating the holding thresholds for withholding tax exemptions could strengthen the internal market, particularly if accompanied by simpler requirements for obtaining relief. Although the IRD amendments would shift taxing rights toward residence Member States, their uneven fiscal effects could be addressed through a statistical revenue sharing mechanism or by treating the corresponding amounts as an EU own resource. Second, the ATAD amendments blur the directive’s character as a minimum standard. Article 3 and the CFC provision should therefore distinguish expressly between mandatory and optional rules. The Proposal should also define which domestic R&D regimes are equivalent to full expensing by reference to a clear criterion, such as the real value of the deductions they provide.

[1] That is, unless it has a double tax treaty with the state of the recipient company that would fully offset the higher liability incurred by that receiving company in the state of the distributing company (Joined Cases C-10/14, C-14/14 and C-17/14, Miljoen). However, this requires the creditable amount to coincide with the tax levied in the source state, and the taxpayer not to be in a loss position. See Ivan Lazarov, “Case Law Trend: Withholding Taxation Under the Fundamental Freedom,” Intertax 51:6 (2023).

[2] Correspondingly, a Member State that applies a method to eliminate double taxation of dividends received by a resident company by a domestic subsidiary must allow the same when the dividends are received by subsidiaries in other EU Member States. Case C-319/02, Manninen. For an overview of the case-law, see, for instance, European Parliament, Directorate-General for Internal Policies, “The impact of the rulings of the European Court of Justice in the area of direct taxation 2010,” (2011), https://www.europarl.europa.eu/document/activities/cont/201203/20120313ATT40640/20120313ATT40640EN.pdf.
[3] This also applies to outbound dividend withholding taxes. See Joined Cases C-10/14, C-14/14 and C-17/14, Miljoen.

[5] Case C-513/04, Kerckhaert and Morres. In the literature, Georg Kofler and Ruth Mason, “Double Taxation: A European ‘Switch In Time?’” Columbia Journal of European Law (2007), https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=979750.

[6] This differentiation assumes that there is a clear difference between dividends and interest. However, real-world cases are much more complex, as there are dividends with interest-like features and interest with dividend-like features. See Wolfgang Schön, “International Tax Coordination for a Second-Best World (Part II),” World Tax Journal, IBFD (2010).

[7] As per the OECD Model Convention, source states can levy a withholding tax on dividend income from portfolio investment at the rate of 15 percent and interest at 10 percent, while they would have to exempt royalties altogether. However, Member States can and do deviate from such model rules in their concrete treaty practice.

[8] Double tax conventions do not oblige the state of residence of the receiving company to grant a credit or an exemption for the corporate income tax paid by the distributing company on its profits, before distribution.

[9] As explained above, for dividend payments, the extent to which double taxation can remain within the EU is much smaller, as the Member State of the receiving company would have to relieve the recipient company in the same way that a company receiving domestic dividends is (Manninen).

[10] Triangular situations occur, for instance, if a company is a dual resident and receives income from sources in a third state, or if a company resident in one state receives income from another state that is attributable to a permanent establishment (PE) in a third state. The key issue arising from these situations is that the PE state is not required to apply the conditions of the treaty it has in force with the source state, as the PE is not entitled to treaty benefits in the PE state. See Emily Fett, Triangular Cases: The Application of Bilateral Income Tax Treaties in Multilateral Situations, IBFD, Doctoral Series (2014).

[11] Serena Fatica, Jonathan Pycroft, Andrzej Stasio, and Daniel Stöhlker, “Economic Effects of Simplified Procedures for Claiming Cross-Border Tax Reliefs,” Nordic Tax Journal (2024), https://doi.org/10.2478/ntaxj-2024-0007.

[12] It should also be noted that the amount of withholding tax levied above the permitted double tax treaty rate is not typically creditable under the laws of the residence state, as the double tax convention obliges the residence state to provide a credit only for the taxes levied by the other contracting state “in accordance with the convention.” Articles 23A and 23B of the OECD Model Convention.

[13] According to the case law of the Court of Justice, a 25 percent holding requirement would certainly qualify as a piece of legislation aiming at benefiting situations of definite influence, falling within the scope of the freedom of establishment. See Case C-382/16, Hornbach.
[14] Wolfgang Schön, “International Tax Coordination for a Second-Best World (Part II).”
[16] Unless the receiving company’s State grants indirect credit or exemption for the dividend income.
[17] Wolfgang Schön, “International Tax Coordination for a Second-Best World (Part II).”

[19] Eurostat, Balance of Payment Statistics 2026, https://ec.europa.eu/eurostat/statistics-explained/index.php?title=Balance_of_payments_statistics_-_quarterly_data#Geographical_breakdown_of_current_account_transactions.
[20] Council of the European Union, Interinstitutional files: 2026/0163 (CNS), WK 11001/2026 INIT, 27 July 2026.

For royalties, the European Commission looks directly at Eurostat’s Balance of Payments’ international royalty flows.

[22] This number takes the source state perspective only. It does not take into account whether the less favorable treatment could be mitigated by a double tax convention because the number of potential bilateral combinations would make it very difficult to come to a single number.

[23] Author’s calculations based on data from a survey of the methods used by EU Member States to avoid double taxation of corporate shareholders on domestic dividend distributions, gathered mostly through PwC’s tax summaries.
[24] Cristina Enache, “Corporate Income Tax Rates in Europe, 2026,” Tax Foundation Europe, January 2026.

[25] Author’s calculations of the EU withholding tax treaty average rates on interest and royalty income based on OECD Data Explorer, “Treaty based withholding tax rates – Corporate tax statistics 2026.”
[26] Besides, the ceiling being equal, the new own resource would lower Member States’ GNI-based own resource quota.
[27] Martha Caziero, “Is the European Commission’s Tax Omnibus Proposal a Step in the Right Direction?” Tax Foundation Europe, June 2026.

[28] The Audiovisual Media Services Directive—Directive 2010/13/EU—is an example of a directive that contains clauses of partial, optional, and minimum harmonization, making it difficult to attribute to it an overall harmonization model. See Amedeo Arena, “The Doctrine of Union Preemption in the EU Single Market: Between Sein and Sollen,” Jean Monnet Working Paper 03/10, NYU School of Law.
[29] Council of the European Union, Interinstitutional files: 2026/0163 (CNS), WK 11001/2026 INIT, 27 July 2026.
[30] Lisa Hogreve and Daniel Bunn, “Capital Cost Recovery across the OECD, 2022,” Tax Foundation Europe, April 2022.
[31] Martha Caziero, Alexander Mengden, Sean Bray, Julius Graack, “Does the EU Tax Omnibus’ R&D Expensing Proposal Make the EU More Competitive?” Tax Foundation Europe, July 2026.

Martha Caziero is Head of Policy at Tax Foundation Europe, where she researches European tax policy matters. She holds a PhD in tax law from the Vienna University of Economics and Business, a master’s degree in law from the University of Bologna, and an LLM in International Business Tax Law from Tilburg University. She has authored several academic papers and a book, The Taxing Powers of the European Union: A Legal Analysis of the Levying of EU Taxes, published by IBFD.

articles.title: The 2020s: a horror film in four charts
articles.standfirst:
Last week’s Budget contained one truly terrifying statistic – the 2020s are set to be the worst decade for living standards on record, enjoying a tenth of the growth of the disappointing 2010s. Some things are important enough to dig deep. This blog is for those who don’t just want to watch the horror movie … Continued
The post The 2020s: a horror film in four charts appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: Last week’s Budget contained one truly terrifying statistic – the 2020s are set to be the worst decade for living standards on record, enjoying a tenth of the growth of the disappointing 2010s. Some things are important enough to dig deep. This blog is for those who don’t just want to watch the horror movie but who, like me, enjoy figuring out what’s really going on.

TL;DR it’s bad however you cut it. The typical family looks set to do even worse than the headline, as housing costs and taxes rise. But! There’s a twist in the final act that offers a glimmer of hope…

You first need to know two main characters: RHDI and HBAI. These are the two main measures of living standards, or the incomes of households over time. RHDI (Real Household Disposable Income) is derived from the national accounts – the macro data on the size of the economy and how much of that is going to households, divided by the number of people – and is forecast by the OBR. HBAI (Households Below Average Income) is a survey-based measure of what households’ incomes actually are; we produce our own projections of it and, throughout this blog, use the after-housing-costs version and focus on non-pensioner households. Crucially, HBAI lets us look at what is happening to households of different incomes and characteristics.

These characters are frenemies. RHDI is the big-budget blockbuster shown on Budget day – complete with special effects, like counting the rent homeowners notionally pay themselves as “income”. HBAI is the indie film about real people, released two years late. Both with their strengths and their drawbacks. We tend to avoid putting them on screen together because it gets a bit complicated when they get together – but it can be instructive to compare and contrast.

First, let’s check how these two measures (mean per-person RHDI, and median non-pensioner household income measured after housing costs) compare over different decades. They measure different things but the conclusion is the same: the 2020s are set to be the worst on record for living standards.

The gruesome detail is that typical non-pensioner household incomes are set to fall over the 2020s. I was particularly keen to dig into why we expect typical incomes to fall 3 per cent (a drop of over £1,000) over the next two years while the OBR is forecasting slowly growing RHDI. The chart below breaks down some of the differences between RHDI and HBAI in steps to try and get to the bottom of this.

Two differences stand out. First, housing costs (the difference between the red and green lines), which are deducted from HBAI, rise significantly over the next two years as mortgagors keep refixing at higher rates. The OBR expects the average effective mortgage rate to climb from around 4 per cent in 2026 to 4½ per cent in 2028. Second, a big chunk of the remaining difference (the gap between red and purple) is not explained by the obvious definitional differences. The most likely culprit is that on our reading of the OBR figures almost all of the RHDI growth over the next two years (around 0.9 of 1.1 percentage points) comes from non-labour income. Some of this isn’t cash in anyone’s pocket (homeowners’ imputed rent and pension fund returns), while the part that is – interest and dividends – is poorly captured in survey data and goes disproportionately to richer and older households.
2. The victims are spread across the landscape (of the income distribution…)

It’s all very well talking in averages, or about Mr and Mrs Median, but these can hide families with vastly different experiences. And this time what’s striking is how widely the pain is shared: as the chart below shows, living standards fall right across the income distribution, with no simple rich-versus-poor gradient.

The biggest falls are at the top, but the bottom is hit hard too – and a fall of this size bites far harder for a family with no savings to fall back on. Data can be less reliable for the very poorest households, but the data we do have suggests an extraordinarily difficult 8 per cent fall in living standards for the second-poorest twentieth of the population (we exclude the even-less-reliable bottom 5 per cent). The richest twentieth see the biggest drop. That owes something to tax changes falling especially at the top (and may be overstated if there is non-labour income growth that we are not capturing in our projections).

We showed in our TOTC Budget special that the gap in living standards (RHDI) between the 2020s and the rest of the post financial crisis period was not explained by disappointing growth – GDP per person grows at a similarly sluggish pace, between 0.6 and 0.7 per cent a year, in both periods. The main culprit is net taxes and benefits, which boosted household incomes after the financial crisis but drags on them through the 2020s. We’ve now learnt that the rise in housing costs is also crucial for typical non-pensioner households .

But there’s one more mystery. On the OBR’s forecast (combined with outturns), real average earnings are set to grow by just 1 per cent over the decade, while GDP per worker grows by around 6 per cent. But why? Did I miss a decoupling of earnings and growth?

Well, no – or rather, this decoupling is a feature of the OBR forecast, but not (yet) of the UK as it stands (see our final chart). Up to 2025-26, pay, GDP per worker and GDP per person moved roughly together (even if not by much!). But the OBR judges that, going forward, the labour share will fall back as firms rebuild their margins, and this, alongside consumer prices continuing to rise faster than the prices of what the UK produces, leads to the growing gap.

So, as we look away from Halloween and towards Christmas, here’s a glimmer of hope: if the OBR is wrong about this, then the 2020s could at least get better from here. If incomes grew over the last three years of the decade at the (hardly stellar) pace of the 2010s, RHDI growth this decade would be nearly three times what is now forecast. Still the worst decade on record – but more B-movie than horror show.

articles.title: Is Burnham right about joining the EU single market without a referendum?
articles.standfirst:
Andy Burnham’s Labour could make a case for offering a single market agreement without a referendum, but the Tories and Reform could pledge to reverse it on the same basis, writes Derrick Wyatt. The EU will be looking for stronger signs of UK commitment than this. Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a … Continued
The post Is Burnham right about joining the EU single market without a referendum? first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: Andy Burnham’s Labour could make a case for offering a single market agreement without a referendum, but the Tories and Reform could pledge to reverse it on the same basis, writes Derrick Wyatt. The EU will be looking for stronger signs of UK commitment than this.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

Andy Burnham has said recently that options for future UK links with the EU include a return to the free movement of persons, joining the single market or a customs union, or joining the EU. Burnham has said that a new referendum would be needed to join the EU, but not necessarily to join the single market.

Burnham is right that it would be inconceivable for the UK to rejoin the EU without the backing of a referendum. EU membership involves such far-reaching legal and economic consequences, and would be so difficult and time-consuming to reverse, that simply winning a general election would fail to legitimise joining in the eyes of political parties and voters opposed to the move.

But he is wrong on the second point. If the UK made a single market agreement with the EU, along the lines of the EU/EFTA Agreement, under which Norway and Iceland participate in the single market, a referendum would still be necessary. Under such an agreement, whereby the UK signed up to free movement and the rest of the single market package, including agreeing to apply EU law as interpreted by the Court of Justice of the EU, and making financial contributions to EU projects, the effects for the UK would be analogous to those of full EU membership. A general election result alone would no more politically legitimise single market membership than re-joining the EU itself.

A single market agreement along the above lines would require the UK to apply new EU laws without having a say in their content. Single market rules cannot simply be dismissed as technical trade rules nobody cares about. Some regulate subject matter of political as well as economic importance, such as take-overs and mergers, the regulation of banks and insurance companies, and the rights of patients to go to other EU countries to receive health care at the expense of their home country funding bodies.

Under such an agreement, the EU rules on financial services which would apply to the UK could adversely affect London’s worldwide competitiveness as a financial centre, which could in turn affect the significant tax revenues received by the government from financial and related professional services. By virtue of the UK participating in the single market without being a full EU member, the governments of the EU countries which are home to London’s major competitors in finance -Paris and Frankfurt – would have a large say in the making of such rules, but the UK would have none.
That said, more Brits seem willing to accept the trade-off between perceived economic advantage, and the loss of democratic control implicit in rejoining the single market, than are opposed.
Polls in 2023 and 2024 showed absolute majorities for the UK joining the single market, accepting that that involves the free movement of persons.

According to the 2024 poll, even those intending to vote for Reform UK split 44 /45 per cent when asked if they would accept the free movement of persons if the UK could regain special access to the European market.
In a recent Messina poll, support was down from these earlier highs, but 45 per cent supported joining the single market, either strongly or somewhat, with 23 per cent opposed.

The democratic objections to joining the single market might be overcome if all EU rules applied in the UK had been approved by the UK Parliament, and if the UK was guaranteed a speedy exit if the EU insisted on the UK applying new rules the UK found impossible to accept.
Such an agreement could enter into force for the UK under an Act of Parliament, and suspend most of the current UK/EU Trade and Cooperation Agreement (TCA).

On this hypothesis, the UK Parliament would periodically consider new single market rules introduced by the EU, and vote on incorporating them into UK law. If Parliament accepted the new EU rules, they would be applied in the UK. If Parliament rejected a new piece of single market legislation, or overturned existing EU rules, the EU would be entitled to give notice to terminate the UK’s single market access in, say, one year, and the provisions of the TCA suspended by the single market agreement would be revived. In practice there could be wiggle room if the UK rejected EU legislation which mattered less to the EU than keeping the UK in the single market.
The UK and the EU could terminate the single market agreement anyway if they gave one year’s notice – which is the position in the EU/EFTA Agreement.

Terms of withdrawal, such as residence rights of migrants, and payment of outstanding financial contributions, could be agreed in advance. This would avoid termination of the single marker agreement leading to lengthy negotiations similar to the UK’s withdrawal from the EU and facilitate a smooth and speedy transition back to the TCA.

If these safeguards were adopted, one could argue that a referendum wouldn’t be necessary, because the UK Parliament’s role would not be undermined by EU law, and a speedy exit from the single market could always be ensured.
If the model discussed above were taken forward, no popular vote beyond that involved in the next general election would be needed to legitimise the initiative in democratic terms

But that approach might not prove attractive to the EU, and would suffer from an obvious political weakness. If Labour could take the UK into a single market agreement in the next Parliament without a referendum, the Tories or Reform could simply pledge to reverse the process in the Parliament after that.

The vulnerability of such an agreement to reversal by a hostile future UK government would be off-putting to the EU. Member States and EU institutions would be reluctant to expend time and energy negotiating the UK’s re-entry into the single market with the Labour government only to find that the Conservatives and Reform UK promised to overturn the agreement were they to come to power.

A YouGov poll in June this year showed 55 per cent supporting a return to the EU, with this support falling to 35 per cent if the UK had to re-join without its prior opt-outs. Burnham’s comments indicate he would want opt-outs from the euro and the border-check-free Schengen Area before he would back EU membership for the UK. This could receive a mixed reception across the Channel, but the forecast of two anonymous EU officials reported in Politico was that the EU would be flexible about this.

Burnham has ruled out an election in the next 12 months, but his airing of ambitious options for future EU links might only bring political advantage for as long as a European feel-good factor overshadowed too much argument over details such as the scale of UK financial contributions to the EU if the UK joined a single market agreement or the EU, and in the latter case the tricky question of opt-outs.

paragraphs: The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate by 25bps to 4% on Thursday. December’s meeting now looks like a coin flip, with the path of oil and natural gas prices set to be the decisive factor

The committee’s messaging was more hawkish than before. Higher energy futures prices and more evidence of domestic resilience both increase the risk of second-round effects emerging. The degree of inflationary pressure already in the system means another hike is likely, in December or February.

The majority gave the impression that once Bank Rate reaches 4.25%, subsequent decisions will be a closer call. We continue to think that second-round effects on pay and margins will prove limited, so we maintain our forecast that Bank Rate will peak at 4.25%, but the risks are skewed to the upside.

articles.title: Japan sees limited AI-driven productivity gains in the near term
articles.standfirst: Generative AI should offer some support to Japan’s potential growth by boosting its total factor productivity, but less than in most other advanced economies in the near term. Slow adoption is likely to limit the gains.
paragraphs: Generative AI should offer some support to Japan’s potential growth by boosting its total factor productivity, but less than in most other advanced economies in the near term. Slow adoption is likely to limit the gains.

We think Japan has significant potential to benefit from generative AI, given its relatively high exposure to and preparedness for AI technology. The recent acceleration in corporates’ software investment in response to Japan’s severe labour shortages appears to have laid some of the groundwork for AI utilisation, while the country’s ICT capital stock still lags far behind that of the US.

However, in practice, adoption of new tech is likely to be slow. Japan has lagged behind on digitalisation for many years. The shortage of IT personnel is a key bottleneck, particularly in small and medium-sized enterprises. Its adoption rate is beginning to fall behind those of other advanced economies and China.

There’s high uncertainty around AI’s impact on productivity. Our optimistic ‘AI breakthrough’ scenario features faster adoption and stronger productivity gains than in our baseline, pushing GDP 7ppts above our forecast by 2035. But this still wouldn’t fully offset the drag from the labour supply’s decline on potential growth.

On the downside, there’s considerable risk that the AI boost to workplace efficiency won’t translate into higher productivity at the macro level, given Japan’s rigid corporate structures and labour market practices, particularly among permanent employees. In a scenario of lower pass-through of efficiency gains from workers to the economy, together with slower adoption of the tech, Japan’s potential growth rate would turn negative by the mid-2030s.

articles.title: The State Tax Competitiveness Index Is Your Guide to Economic “Wins Above Replacement”
articles.standfirst: Taxes are an important part of the mix, and modernizing a state’s tax structure helps position it for growth. States that rank better on the Index have better-structured tax codes, and states with better-structured tax codes get Wins Above Replacement.
paragraphs: This week, we published our annual State Tax Competitiveness Index, an extremely valuable diagnostic tool comparing states’ taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. structures across more than 150 variables. Unlike most studies of state taxes, it is focused on the how more than the how much, in recognition of the fact that there are better and worse ways to raise revenue. Inevitably, though, the publication of the Index raises some questions, like: if Wyoming and South Dakota lead in the rankings, why aren’t more companies heading for the Black Hills?

Tax competition is a little like WAR—not conflict, but Wins Above Replacement. The term comes from baseball, where it is intended as a sabermetric statistic to measure how many more wins a team can claim due to a specific player above the amount that would be generated by a replacement-level player. It’s much the same in public finance: a well-structured tax code won’t make the Wyoming Basin a metropolis, nor will poor tax structure make Manhattan a ghost town. But tax structure does play a role in a state’s economic successes or failures, and often a substantial one. Every state can benefit from a simple, neutral, transparent, pro-growth tax structure.

The Index scores states across five sub-indices, each representing a major component of state tax codes: corporate taxes, individual income taxes, sales and excise taxes, property and wealth taxes, and unemployment insurance taxes. Rather than weighting each sub-index equally, their weight is determined according to the variance across states in each category, which has the effect of assigning more weight to areas where states have more room to compete.

Of course, it’s hard to introduce any structural flaws to the design of a tax one does not impose, so some states, by forgoing a tax altogether (the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source, the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax., or the sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. ), score perfectly on a sub-index or some portion of one. This is why states like Wyoming and South Dakota, which both forgo income taxes, do so well on the Index. States that can avoid imposing one or more of the major taxes either have to lean very heavily on the other major tax types (which can mean lower rankings on those components), choose to operate on leaner budgets, take advantage of natural resources like oil and gas, or have demographics (like Florida) where other taxes can generate a surprising amount of revenue.
In other words, the Wyoming model may not be possible in some states—but the Missouri, Utah, North Carolina, North Dakota, Idaho, Indiana, and Oklahoma models are.

Those states ranked 9th through 15th in this year’s Index. They also impose each of the major taxes, but at moderate rates and with comparatively well-designed tax structures. Many of these states have substantially modernized their tax codes over the past two decades: Utah beginning in 2006, Indiana starting in 2011, North Carolina with a string of reforms that began in 2013, Idaho beginning in 2022, North Dakota in 2023, and Missouri with a series of rate cuts and reforms in recent years, including capital gains taxA capital gains tax is levied on the profit made from selling an asset and is often in addition to corporate income taxes, frequently resulting in double taxation. These taxes create a bias against saving, leading to a lower level of national income by encouraging present consumption over investment. repeal in 2025. Oklahoma, too, has adopted tax reforms in recent years, including eliminating its marriage penaltyA marriage penalty is when a household’s overall tax bill increases due to a couple marrying and filing taxes jointly. A marriage penalty typically occurs when two individuals with similar incomes marry; this is true for both high- and low-income couples. and capital stock tax in 2024 and reducing its individual income tax rates and consolidating brackets effective in 2026.

For taxpayers, the Index is a good starting point for understanding how their state compares to its peers. But for policymakers and others interested in how to improve the structure of their state’s tax code, it’s more than that: it’s a valuable diagnostic tool, with tables that allow readers to compare their state to its peers on everything from throwback rules and the treatment of net operating losses to whether the individual income tax’s brackets are indexed and the state authorizes split-roll property taxation.

If you saddled South Dakota with New York’s tax code, the state would struggle. People are clearly willing to pay a premium to live in New York—on real estate, on consumer purchases, and yes, on taxes. But there are limits, to say nothing of the fact that a system that is bearable in Manhattan may be considerably more burdensome in Syracuse. And, as the former governor of New York noted repeatedly, even in states like New York, tax burdens and tax structures matter. New York actually dramatically improved in the corporate component of the Index several years ago due to meaningful corporate tax reforms adopted on a bipartisan basis.

So yes, we’ve heard your questions about whether we are really saying that businesses would rather be in Mitchell, South Dakota, than Manhattan, or Sioux Falls than San Francisco, and there’s clearly a lot more that goes into location decisions than just taxes—rates or structure. But taxes are something within policymakers’ control, and even within a given revenue target, there are better and worse ways to raise that revenue.

The Index measures tax structure, not all the other things businesses care about, like an educated workforce, quality of life, proximity to relevant markets, or even the weather—and some of these things involve trade-offs. Taxes, however, are an important part of the mix, and modernizing a state’s tax structure helps position it for growth. States that rank better on the Index have better-structured tax codes, and states with better-structured tax codes get Wins Above Replacement.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Janelle Fritts is a Senior Policy Analyst with the Tax Foundation’s Center for State Tax Policy. She is the lead researcher on the annual State Tax Competitiveness Index and serves as a resource to policymakers in their efforts to modernize and improve the structures of their state tax codes. Her work has been cited in The New York Times, the Associated Press, Bloomberg, and numerous state media outlets across the country.

articles.title: 2027 State Tax Competitiveness Index
articles.standfirst: The State Tax Competitiveness Index enables policymakers, taxpayers, and business leaders to gauge how their states’ tax systems compare. While there are many ways to show how much state governments collect in taxes, the Index evaluates how well states structure their tax systems and provides a road map for improvement.
paragraphs: The study before you, which has been published as the State Business Tax Climate Index since 2003, was rebranded as the State Tax Competitiveness Index for the 2025 edition to better reflect what it assesses: states’ overall tax competitiveness, not just the business tax climate. This wasn’t just an exercise in slapping a new title on the cover and calling it a day. Rather, we reworked the Index from the ground up to make it a better product.

For more than two decades, the Index has helped policymakers evaluate their tax codes, serving as a road map for reform. Each year, the study underwent methodological refinements—which we always outlined—to capture changing elements of the tax code, like the introduction of global intangible low-taxed income, which has since been changed to net CFC tested income, or the design of remote seller taxes following the Supreme Court’s Wayfair decision. But the pace of change has accelerated in recent years, with the adoption of the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, the Supreme Court’s Wayfair decision, the rise of remote work and other outgrowths of the global pandemic (including a roiling of unemployment insurance tax regimes), the adoption of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the adoption of the nation’s first digital advertising taxes, and an emerging interest in new or expanded taxes on wealth, unrealized gains, data, digital products, and more.

We saw a need to address these more comprehensively, and to provide additional granularity in our evaluation of tax provisions already encompassed by the Index. The old Index did its job well. Indeed, independent evaluations demonstrated a strong correlation between Index ranks and state economic outcomes. But we wanted to expand and refresh the publication before it got stale, to stay ahead of new developments in tax. A refresh also gave us a chance to better systematize and rebalance the treatment of a few outlier state tax provisions that had to be shoehorned into the methodology of prior editions.

With the 2025 refresh, we did more than update the methodology and adopt a new name. We also rethought the presentation of the Index’s treasure trove of tax policy information. The Index’s 150+ variables are no longer hidden away in appendix tables, and the online publication, formerly just an interactive map accompanied by a lengthy PDF, was reimagined for a digital environment.

Now, each state receives its own summary, highlighting several of the most notable features of its tax code and explaining why it ranks as it does on the Index—along with some state-specific reforms that would improve its tax competitiveness. And users now have access to interactive, sortable, filterable datasets, in addition to some new visuals and historical rate tools. We invite you to explore. See your state’s policy choices on every variable in the Index. Add another state or two and compare them. Or drill down to a single variable or set of variables and see how all states perform on them.

This is the third year under the new methodology, but if you’re comparing our rankings this year to old editions from 2024 or before, you might notice that some ranks have shifted a bit more than we usually see from year to year. Some of that, of course, is simply because states have been incredibly busy recently, adopting significant changes to their tax codes. But some of it is due to our methodological changes.

To ensure an apples-to-apples comparison, and in the interest of transparency, we have backcast states’ rankings under the new methodology going back seven years prior to this current edition. These are the controlling rankings, and are the ones that should be cited to show actual movement by states in recent years. This is nothing new: we’ve always backcast to account for methodological revisions. What’s different in the new edition is the scope of the change, as we’ve added more variables and made more adjustments than in prior years.

Readers interested in the details of what has changed are invited to read on to learn about our revised methodology, and for explanations of our variables. Most readers, however, will likely wish to jump ahead to the overall rankings, their state’s page, or the newly interactive datasets.

For all readers, we hope that the 2027 State Tax Competitiveness Index will serve as a useful guide for navigating state tax policy. It ranks, both overall and across five subindices—corporate taxes, individual income taxes, sales and excise taxes, property and wealth taxes, and unemployment insurance taxes—how states compete, and where each has room to improve. And for would-be reformers, our datasets (now much more accessible!) are an invaluable guide to how states structure their tax codes, and where they diverge—for good and for ill—from their peers.

Even a good road map, however, is not always a sufficient substitute for a guide. That’s why the Tax Foundation has a team of state tax experts whose primary purpose is to help educate policymakers and the public. As always, we invite you to reach out with your questions. That’s why we’re here. Katherine Loughead Vice President of State Policy, Tax Foundation

The Tax Foundation’s State Tax Competitiveness Index enables policymakers, taxpayers, and business leaders to gauge how their states’ tax systems compare. While there are many ways to show how much state governments collect in taxes, the Index evaluates how well states structure their tax systems and provides a road map for improvement.[1]

The absence of a major tax is a common factor among many of the top 10 states. Property taxes and unemployment insurance taxes are levied in every state, but there are several states that do without one or more of the major taxes: the corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax., the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source, or the sales tax. South Dakota and Wyoming have no corporate or individual income tax; Alaska and New Hampshire have no individual income or state-level sales tax; Florida, Tennessee, and Texas have no individual income tax; and Montana has no sales tax.

This does not mean, however, that a state cannot rank well while still levying all the major taxes. Missouri and Utah, for example, levy all the major tax types, as do all the other states that rank 11th to 16th: North Carolina, North Dakota, Idaho, Indiana, Oklahoma, and Nebraska.
The 10 lowest-ranked, or worst, states in this year’s Index are:

The states in the bottom 10 tend to have a number of issues in common: complex, nonneutral taxes with comparatively high rates. New Jersey, for example, is hampered by some of the highest property tax burdens in the country, has the highest-rate corporate income tax in the country, and has one of the highest-rate individual income taxes. Additionally, the state levies an inheritance taxAn inheritance tax is levied upon the value of inherited assets received by a beneficiary after a decedent’s death. Not to be confused with estate taxes, which are paid by the decedent’s estate based on the size of the total estate before assets are distributed, inheritance taxes are paid by the recipient or heir based on the value of the bequest received. and maintains some of the nation’s worst-structured individual income taxes.

Tax competition is a little like WAR—not conflict, but Wins Above Replacement. The term comes from baseball, where it is intended as a sabermetric statistic to measure how many more wins a team can claim due to a specific player above the amount that would be generated by a replacement-level player. It’s much the same way in public finance: a well-structured tax code won’t make the Wyoming Basin a metropolis, nor will poor tax structure make Manhattan a ghost town. But tax structure does play a role in a state’s economic successes or failures, and often a substantial one. Every state can benefit from a simple, neutral, transparent, pro-growth tax structure.

The Index scores states across five subindices, each representing a major component of state tax codes: corporate taxes, individual income taxes, sales and excise taxes, property and wealth taxes, and unemployment insurance taxes. Rather than weighting each subindex equally, their weight is determined according to the variance across states in each category, which has the effect of assigning more weight to areas where states have more opportunities in which to compete.

Of course, it is difficult to introduce any structural flaws to the design of a tax one does not impose, so some states, by forgoing a tax altogether (the individual income tax, the corporate income tax, or the sales tax) score perfectly on a subindex or some portion of one. This is why states like Wyoming and South Dakota, which both forgo income taxes, do so well on the Index. States that can avoid imposing one or more of the major taxes either have to lean very heavily on the other major tax types (which can mean lower rankings on those components), choose to operate on leaner budgets, take advantage of natural resources like oil and gas, or have demographics (like Florida) where other taxes can generate a surprising amount of revenue.

In other words, the Wyoming model may not be possible in some states—but the Missouri, Utah, and North Carolina models are. These states all rank in the top 11 on the Index while imposing all of the major taxes, but at moderate rates with comparatively well-designed tax structures.

For taxpayers, the Index is a good starting point for understanding how their state compares to its peers. But for policymakers and others interested in how to improve the structure of their state’s tax code, it’s more than that: it’s a valuable diagnostic tool, with tables that allow readers to compare their state to its peers on a wide range of factors—tax rates, yes, but also throwback rules, the treatment of net operating losses, recapture provisions, indexation, spit roll taxation, convenience rules, expensing, and much more.

If you saddled South Dakota with New York’s tax code, the state would struggle. People are clearly willing to pay a premium to live in New York—on real estate, on consumer purchases, and yes, on taxes. But there are limits, to say nothing of the fact that a system that is bearable in Manhattan may be considerably more burdensome in Syracuse. And even in states like New York tax burdens, and tax structures, matter.
Taxes are not everything, but they do matter, and they are within the control of policymakers. Even within a given revenue target, there are better and worse ways to raise revenue.

The Index measures tax structure, not all the other things businesses care about, like an educated workforce, quality of life, proximity to relevant markets, or even the weather—and some of these things involve trade-offs. Taxes, however, are an important part of the mix, and modernizing a state’s tax structure helps position it for growth. States that rank better on the Index have better-structured tax codes, and states with better-structured tax codes get Wins Above Replacement.

Arizona fell three places overall, from 14th to 17th. The state’s tangible personal property (TPP) tax exemptionA tax exemption excludes certain income, revenue, or even taxpayers from tax altogether. Idaho’s ranking fell four places overall (from 9th to 13th), including falling eight places on the individual income tax component, primarily due to the state’s decision to conform to the OBBBA’s temporary individual deductions for tips and overtime. Indiana fell three spots, to 14th overall. Iowa fell just slightly on this year’s Index, from 17th to 18th overall. One major variable change was its individual income tax ranking, falling eight places to 18th. Because Iowa uses federal taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. as the starting point for state income tax liability, newer federal provisions such as no tax on tips, overtime, and auto loans narrow the state’s individual income tax base. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. and decoupling from the taxation of net CFC tested income. Kansas’ ranking improved four places overall (from 23rd to 19th), including seven places on the corporate tax component and five places on the individual income tax component. As part of the final phase-in of the 2024 tax reform package, Louisiana saw a 17-place improvement in its property tax rank due to the elimination of the state’s capital stock tax, a damaging tax that taxes businesses regardless of profit. Maine slid seven places, from 33rd to 40th, with the adoption of a 2 percent “high-income surcharge” that brings the state’s top individual income tax rate to 9.15 percent on incomes over $1 million. Taxation is inevitable, but the specifics of a state’s tax structure matter greatly.
