articles.title: Graduates are managing AI - but are they learning much else?
articles.standfirst: Graduates are spending more time managing AI, but are they missing out on other work experience?
paragraphs: Managing AI agents is a big part of Lotte Underwood's job
Recent university graduate Lotte Underwood is a public relations executive with a twist - she spends more time using AI than actually doing PR.
Underwood, 25, joined London-based PR agency Fight or Flight in November last year, in the new role of "AI associate" after completing a degree and then a masters in marketing.

She's part of a recently established, dedicated AI team that has built around 30 AI agents. Specific tasks include industry research, client reporting, media interview preparation, helping clients create clearer briefs, and image generation.
A big part of Underwood's job is to manage those agents, check their outputs and feed those to the team members who are dealing directly with clients and the media.
Another key responsibility of hers is to monitor how clients appear in the responses from AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and others.
"A huge part is being in client meetings and calls to work out what is actually going to be most helpful from these agents," says Underwood.
What is an AI agent?
AI is seen as one of the main factors behind graduate job cuts, but companies are also creating dedicated AI-specific graduate roles like Underwood's.

Dillan Patel, for example, joined engineering software company Stride 18 months ago as an intern. A business management graduate, he was put to work developing an internal chatbot designed to capture the knowledge of a senior staff member transitioning into retirement.

Patel, 24, is now an AI automation analyst, tasked with developing further internal agents to provide specific information to individual teams, while also identifying which manual or repetitive tasks across the company could be done by AI.
"My role focuses on finding practical ways to use technology, automation, data and AI to improve how we operate," says Coventry-based Patel.
Debra Maxwell is looking for "AI disruptors"
Such AI savvy graduates are also in demand from companies like ArvatoConnect, an outsourced contact centre company.
CEO Debra Maxwell says the company's usual graduate intake is on hold this year, but she plans to resume it next year with a bigger focus on AI.

"We would be looking for more AI-disruptor type roles, where you can challenge us as an organisation to think more holistically about where AI can be applied and where we could grow our business from," says London-based Maxwell.
"We see our graduates as not filling administrative roles, but actually adding value to the organisation in a different way."

Maxwell adds: "For example, one of our recent graduates is using AI to do deep dives on specific markets, and provide more information for when we're bidding [for new contracts]. It's basically giving him a more rounded role."

If AI can make a graduate job bigger and more integral to the organisation, Maxwell argues that companies can create a more loyal, engaged workforce that is able to contribute more meaningfully, much earlier.
Research from consultancy PwC found that some graduate roles are assuming more responsibilities because of AI, as it allows companies to demand more senior abilities from junior hires.

For the consultancy's 2026 AI Jobs Barometer, it analysed 2.4 million entry-level jobs in the US. It found that the entry-level roles most influenced by AI are now seven times more likely to require traditionally senior-level skills. These include motivational leadership, strategic decision making and team building.
Those entry-level roles with higher expectations have in fact grown 35% since 2019, PwC found, while other entry-level roles actually shrank by 10%.
Cian Clinton uses around ten AI agents for work tasks

Cian Clinton, who joined consultancy Valliance last September after graduating from a Bachelor of Science in 2024, says the incorporation of AI into his role makes him feel less like a graduate, and more like an equal team member. He uses around 10 AI agents daily for different tasks.

"Your ideas and your creativity are a lot more valued because you actually get to implement those firsthand, and the responsibility you take on is a lot greater because of that," says London-based Clinton, 23.
"I am now taking on responsibilities which would usually take me four or five years to get to."
His career progression, he believes, will now be faster as a result.
"AI is killing the 'pyramid' approach…progression is no longer based on your knowledge bank. Now it's more based on your critical thinking and understanding of the processes," says Clinton.
There's no doubt Underwood, Patel and Clinton are developing valuable AI knowledge which can help them across their careers.
But with their time at work so focused on AI, does it matter how much - or how little - time they're spending learning about the professional field they're supposed to be operating in?
Underwood says she'd like to still pick up the traditional PR skills her role isn't currently focused on, but is confident of her future in the agency's growing AI team.
"There's certain things that I haven't had the chance to do yet, like directly pitching to the media. I absolutely plan to do this," she says.

Graduates becoming too AI-centric is an issue for Simon Pratt, chief operating officer at Portman Finance Group. He says being able to use AI effectively is important, but the company's two-year graduate programme is fully centred on "learning the trade".
"Our graduates rotate across four areas at six-month intervals, working directly alongside senior relationship managers to learn their trade," Northampton-based Pratt explains.

"They'll learn all of our financial products, how to draft credit papers for submission to lenders, and how to build meaningful relationships with our customers. They'll progress to running transactions from start to finish."
Claire Reid, PwC UK's chief technology and innovation officer, believes graduate roles that are too AI heavy won't necessarily provide graduates long-term career progression.
"There will be no graduate job now that doesn't require a baseline of AI literacy," says Glasgow-based Reid.
"But AI skills on their own are not going to help you in your career. You've got to couple that with that sector knowledge of what that client actually wants."
Back in Coventry, Dillan Patel is confident his AI work will continue to be valuable, and he wants to keep building on it.

"I don't think I'd want to explore different positions within the business. Through my involvement in AI-related projects, I already work closely with different areas of the business and I'm gaining valuable knowledge and experience along the way," he says.

articles.title: Could London’s fragmented councils offer lessons for Westminster?
articles.standfirst:
Could London’s fragmented councils offer lessons for Westminster? ellie.slee.lamb Wed, 04/11/2026 - 16:57 A hung parliament is a real possibility after the next general election.  5 Comment Megan Isaac Institute for Government Yes Devolution Local government Labour Burnham government Greater London
No

Recent polling has raised the prospect of the next general election resulting in a hung parliament, prompting renewed interest in previous minority and coalition governments – in particular the 2010 coalition agreement between the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats and the 2017 confidence-and-supply agreement between the Conservatives and the DUP.

But Westminster can also draw lessons from local government. Throughout England, where governing without a majority is increasingly common, a range of models of multi-party governance are proliferating across local government.

These arrangements are potentially fragile, as demonstrated by this week’s collapse of Labour-Green power-sharing arrangements in 11 councils, but the UK parliament’s comparative lack of experience with minority government means looking local could be vital preparation ahead of the next general election. 

No overall control is increasingly common in local government 

Held against the backdrop of an increasingly fragmented political landscape, the May 2026 local elections saw more councils in England fall to no overall control (NOC) than were won outright by individual parties, pushing the share of councils across England without a majority to over 50%.1 BBC News, ‘England local election results 2026’, https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/election/2026/england/results  

This pattern also emerged in London, where a record nine of the capital’s 32 councils fell to NOC. Political fragmentation also increased, with the proportion of London’s council seats won by Labour and the Conservatives falling by almost 25 percentage points from 2022 to a low of 60%. The remaining 40% are split between the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Reform UK, other parties and independents. 

There is no single model for governing without a majority 

London illustrates that there are a wide range of ways to govern without a majority and that a hung parliament in Westminster would not necessarily lead to a coalition.

The nine NOC councils in London have adopted a range of models, from formal coalitions and confidence-and-supply agreements to minority administrations that rely on building support on an issue-by-issue basis. The options available depend not only on the arithmetic of the council chamber and the relationships between parties, but also on the council’s executive arrangements, which determine where political power sits and what parties can negotiate over.

Seven of the nine councils have formed minority administrations. In most cases, the largest party has formed the administration, relying on opposition parties to support or at least not block its key decisions.

Elsewhere, councils have agreed more formal cross-party arrangements. In Southwark, the Greens and Liberal Democrats have formed a coalition, ending 16 years of consecutive Labour control.1 Southwark Council, ‘Southward Green Party and Southwark Liberal Democrats form joint administration’, 28 May 2026, https://www.southwark.gov.uk/news/2026/southwark-green-party-and-southwark-liberal-democrats-form-joint-administration   In Wandsworth, the Conservatives and Labour were separated by just one seat, with an independent councillor holding the balance of power and agreeing a confidence-and-supply arrangement with the Conservatives.2 Wandsworth Council, ‘Wandsworth Council leader-elect sets out first steps’, 18 May 2026, https://www.wandsworth.gov.uk/news/news-may-2026/wandsworth-council-leader-elect-sets-out-first-steps/  

The largest party need not lead the administration 

When no party wins a majority, the largest party is not the only one that can lead the administration. This is a rare occurrence in Westminster politics – occurring just once in the past century – but it is much more common in local government.  

Two of London’s NOC councils are not led by the largest party. In Croydon, Labour is the largest party but the directly elected Conservative mayor leads the council and exercises significant executive power due to the requirement of a two-thirds majority to amend or overturn the mayor’s budget and policy framework.3 Croydon Council, ‘The elected mayor of Croydon’, https://www.croydon.gov.uk/council-and-elections/mayors-croydon/elected-mayor-croydon/role-elected-mayor-0   In Southwark, Labour is again the largest party but the council is run by a Green-Liberal Democrat coalition. 

Leadership is not the only thing up for negotiation 

In NOC councils, several sources of influence are ‘tradeable’ in the negotiations to form an administration. Parties can seek commitments on policy, institutional influence and, in some cases, changes to the rules under which the council operates.  

In Barnet, where Labour and the Conservatives won 31 seats each and the Green party won one seat, the Conservatives allowed Labour to form a minority administration in exchange for increased scrutiny, including the Conservative opposition leader attending cabinet as a non-executive member.4 Barnet Council, ‘Local elections 2026: Labour retains control of Barnet Council’, 19 May 2026, https://www.barnet.gov.uk/news/local-elections-2026-labour-retain-control-barnet-council  

Chairs of key committees and the role of civic mayor – who chairs council meetings and has a casting vote when council votes are tied – can also be prized positions in negotiations. In Haringey, the Greens are the largest party and formed a minority administration, but Labour and the Liberal Democrats worked together to distribute the civic mayoralty and most committee chairs between themselves.

Polarisation can make power-sharing fragile 

Power-sharing requires enough common ground on policy red lines for parties to govern together. Fragmentation can increase the number of potential governing combinations, but polarisation can make it harder to construct a majority that is both viable and stable, particularly if some parties are viewed as unacceptable partners.

There are several examples of this outside of London. In Birmingham, Reform UK is the largest party on the council but could not form an administration due to the unwillingness of other parties to work with them. Meanwhile in Oldham, the council has failed to form an administration following four failed attempts to elect a leader. Officers are exercising executive powers under emergency measures, and the council is currently unrepresented on the Greater Manchester Combined Authority board.

Arrangements can also be fragile once in place. Labour’s recent decision to end power-sharing with Green councillors that failed to reject the party’s ‘Zionism is racism’ motion has led to the collapse of 11 NOC administrations in England. This decision also closes off a straightforward Labour-Green alliance in any future hung parliament, and highlights the pressure on parties – which will intensify if fragmentation continues – to set out the policy red lines they are, and are not, willing to compromise on. 

Fragmented politics may require institutions to adapt 

More fragmented politics may require institutions to adapt as well as politicians. In Brent, the new political balance prompted a review of constitutional arrangements, including how questions and motions are allocated between political groups.5 Brent Council, ‘Annual council meeting’, 20 October 2026, https://democracy.brent.gov.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=180&MId=8374&Ver=4   Meanwhile, Lambeth has agreed to introduce a hybrid committee model following the formation of a Green minority administration, aiming to increase scrutiny and cross-party working.6 Lambeth Council, ‘Adjourned meeting (AGM 27 May), council’, 1 June 2026, https://moderngov.lambeth.gov.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=142&MId=18974  

Westminster may need to adapt too. Parliamentary procedures and structures are designed around an adversarial two-party system that no longer reflects the reality of British politics and sits uneasily with an increasingly fragmented political landscape.

With recent British political history offering just a handful of lessons for how minority governments can function, and with Westminster yet to adjust to the reality of a multi-party parliament, it would be wise to pay close to attention to the range of models currently on display across local government.

articles.title: Concrete’s enabling role in building a sustainable and resilient future
articles.standfirst: New Oxford Economics research for the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA) explores how global megatrends are reshaping infrastructure demand and highlights the critical role of cement and concrete in supporting economic development, improving living standards and building a more sustainable and resilient future.
paragraphs: The megatrends that will drive global concrete demand to 2050

Oxford Economics’ latest research for the Global Cement and Concrete Association (GCCA) examines how five major global megatrends—population growth and urbanisation, infrastructure and housing deficits, climate transition and resilience, geopolitical uncertainty, and digitalisation—are reshaping global construction demand.

With global construction activity forecast to increase by more than 70% to US$16.6 trillion annually by 2050, the report highlights the critical role of cement and concrete in delivering essential infrastructure, supporting economic development, improving living standards and strengthening community resilience.

The report also explores the strategic challenges of meeting rising infrastructure demand while reducing carbon emissions, improving productivity, managing costs and ensuring long-term sustainability. It highlights the importance of innovation, resilient supply chains and evidence-based infrastructure planning in delivering greater economic and social value from concrete.

Thomas is a Lead Economist with the Construction and Infrastructure team at Oxford Economics Australia. After joining the company in 2019, he has managed or heavily contributed to a wide range of private consulting and advisory work across Oxford Economics Australia clients, with a heavy focus on market capacity, industry analysis, cost escalation, economic impact and workforce capability.
Head of Construction & Infrastructure Consulting, OE Australia

Adrian has over 23 years of economic analysis and consulting experience with Oxford Economics Australia, focusing on the infrastructure, building, maintenance and mining industries. Adrian has undertaken a wide range of consultancy projects for the public and private sector based on his detailed understanding of construction, mining and maintenance markets, their drivers and outlooks, the range of organisations operating in this space and the issues they face.

This work includes deeper industry liaison, contractor and competitive analysis, pipeline analysis, demand and cost escalation forecasting, and industry capacity and capability projects for the public and private sector. He is the lead author of major reports but also undertakes briefings and workshops for senior management, board members and industry associations, leads in-depth stakeholder consultation, and facilitates and chairs roundtables between government and industry.

Ryan is an Economist currently responsible for supporting the production of the Asian Construction Service. He has experience in econometric modelling and consulting and holds a Bachelor's degree in Commerce and Economics (Honours), majoring in econometrics and finance.

articles.title: What a Democratic Congress Means for Federal Tax Policy in 2027
articles.standfirst: With Democrats retaking control of the US House of Representatives and US Senate, several new federal tax issues are on the table for 2027.
paragraphs: Early results from the US midterm elections are in, and Democrats have retaken control of the US House of Representatives and US Senate. This change in power will shift which federal taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. issues are discussed in Washington over the next two years, as well as the proposals that may receive votes in Congress. New tax cuts are on the table, as are tax increases.

Several parts of the Democratic agenda for the 120th Congress, which begins January 3, 2027, would require major changes in tax policy. Democrats want to restore larger tax credits for the purchase of health insurance, as well as a larger child tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly. (CTC) and earned income tax credit (EITC). They also want to raise taxes on high-income individuals and businesses to pay for these credits and other new spending.

Democrats will have limited maneuvering room in 2027 given Republican control of the White House, but proposals made in 2027 will shape the direction of policy in the future. Democrats have aggressive proposals to raise significant sums of tax revenue, but they must confront trade-offs. Our current spending commitments and associated debt limit the ambitions of new spending programs or tax cuts, and the proposed tax increases will dampen long-term US economic growth.

Democrats in Congress will place a high priority on proposals to raise tax revenue from corporations and very high earners. While their ambitions to raise taxes will be limited by President Trump’s veto, these proposals will serve as messaging and discussion vehicles over the next two years on the direction of the tax code.One top priority will center on proposals to raise the corporate rate from 21 percent. Questions may include how high to raise the rate, whether the rate should be graduated, and what corporate base changes should accompany a rate hike. International tax rules for corporations may also be revisited, including changing tax rules for foreign earnings, calculating liability on a country-by-country basis, and raising guardrails on profit shiftingProfit shifting is when multinational companies reduce their tax burden by moving the location of their profits from high-tax countries to low-tax jurisdictions and tax havens..

The tax treatment of data center and AI investment will be top of mind for some congressional Democrats. In 2026, we’ve seen several proposals to disallow data center bonus depreciationBonus depreciation allows firms to deduct a larger portion of certain “short-lived” investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings in the first year. Allowing businesses to write off more investments partially alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. conditionally or in its entirety, enact a new tax on bits, and impose a new excise taxAn excise tax is a tax imposed on a specific good or activity. Excise taxes are commonly levied on cigarettes, alcoholic beverages, soda, gasoline, insurance premiums, amusement activities, and betting, and typically make up a relatively small and volatile portion of state and local and, to a lesser extent, federal tax collections. on data center electricity use.

Additionally, Democrats in both chambers of Congress have proposed income surtaxes on millionaires, including Sen. Chris Van Hollen’s (D-MD) proposed surtax on taxpayers earning over $1 million at a top rate of 12 percent.

Capital gains taxes will also be an area of focus, following the path of proposals to raise capital gains tax rates, end the step-up in basisThe step-up in basis provision adjusts the value, or “cost basis,” of an inherited asset (stocks, bonds, real estate, etc.) when it is passed on, after death. This eliminates the capital gains tax owed by the recipient, reducing the heir’s tax liability. The cost basis receives a “step-up” to its fair market value, or the price at which the good would be sold or purchased in a fair marke at death for inherited assets, and tax unrealized capital gains annually for very-high-net-worth individuals. Some would go further by levying a wealth tax on billionaire assets each year.

These proposals will spark continued debate among Democrats about whether tax revenue should be raised by adjusting the levers on the existing tax code or by enacting novel and untested tax ideas that have administrative, legal, and economic risks. Either way, most of the proposed tax increases would come with steep economic trade-offs as they discourage saving and investment.

At the top of Democrats’ list for tax cuts may be restoring expanded premium tax credits (PTCs) that expired at the end of 2025. PTCs subsidize the purchase of health insurance on Affordable Care Act exchanges. Democrats enacted temporary and large expansions of these subsidies from 2021 through 2025.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY)—the likely next speaker of the House—has made restoring more generous PTCs a priority. He will encounter difficulties with Republicans in Washington, but next year’s debt limit debate may serve as one opportunity for Democratic leverage. The Congressional Budget Office (CBO) previously estimated that extending the PTC expansion would cost $350 billion over a decade.

The New York Times reported in October 2026 that Jeffries is also prioritizing expansions of the CTC and EITC. Democrats enacted one-year expansions to these credits in 2021 and then tried but failed to extend the expansions in 2022. The CTC expansion could increase the size of the per-child credit from $2,200 in 2026 to $3,000 or more in 2027. The EITC expansion could focus on expanding the credit for childless adult workers.

Restoring the 2021 childless EITC could cost between $60 billion and $120 billion over the next decade, depending on the parameters Democrats choose, while restoring the 2021 CTC could cost more than $500 billion.

Housing tax policy could also be on Democrats’ agenda in 2027, including expansions to the low-income housing tax credit (LIHTC). Republicans expanded the LIHTC in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). It’s unclear what additional changes Democrats would seek to the LIHTC. We recently estimated that repealing the LIHTC and the new markets tax credit would raise $202.7 billion over 10 years. Some Democrats have supported legislation to extend full expensingFull expensing allows businesses to immediately deduct the full cost of certain investments in new or improved technology, equipment, or buildings. It alleviates a bias in the tax code and incentivizes companies to invest more, which, in the long run, raises worker productivity, boosts wages, and creates more jobs. to multifamily residential housing construction, which would lower the after-tax cost of building this type of housing.

Members of Congress and President Trump will also face at least one critical tax deadline in the 120th Congress: the expiration of several tax cuts enacted in the OBBBA on December 31, 2028. On that day, the tips, overtime, auto loan interest, and enhanced senior deduction will expire. The provision that lets manufacturers immediately deduct the full cost of new factory buildings will also expire.

It’s unclear how Democrats would approach the expiring provisions of OBBBA. Some Democratic lawmakers support extending and expanding the tips and overtime deductions. We previously estimated that extending the tips, overtime, auto loan interest, and enhanced senior deductions beyond 2028 would cost $577.3 billion over 10 years.

Some Democratic policymakers have opposed the Trump administration’s imposition of hundreds of billions of dollars in tariffs, and have pledged to vote to roll them back. The issue doesn’t split neatly along party lines, though.

Many Democrats oppose the way President Trump imposed tariffs—unilaterally, on wide swaths of goods, and on economic adversaries and allies alike, with rapid, chaotic changes. However, some support tariffs on specific goods, such as aluminum and steel. Even if Democrats muster the votes to roll back some or all of Trump’s tariffs, it’s unlikely Congress could assemble a veto-proof majority on the issue in the next two years.

The broader US budgetary outlook may also have direct implications for federal tax policy. Federal debt is more than $32 trillion and recently surpassed 100 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). CBO projects large budget deficits in perpetuity, and in the most recent fiscal year, the government spent $2 trillion more than it took in.

Government borrowing costs are rising. The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield has been hovering around five percent in recent weeks. Consumer borrowing costs have risen in tandem, on everything from mortgages to auto loans. Lawmakers may feel pressure from households, businesses, and investors to reduce the gap between spending and revenue in the years ahead.

Even if lawmakers don’t improve the fiscal trajectory in the coming years, a much larger issue looms. The Social Security Trustees currently project the Social Security trust fund will be fully depleted in 2032. Absent congressional action, Social Security would no longer be able to pay out benefits in full. The crop of US senators elected this fall will face this issue in their current six-year term.

In our recent publication, Options for Reforming America’s Tax Code 3.0: A Policymaker’s Guide to Tax Reform Trade-Offs, we outlined a few ways lawmakers could bring additional revenue into the trust fund. Any bipartisan and enduring package for Social Security reform will require a blend of benefit reductions and additional revenue.

The shifting balance of power in Washington should produce a busy session for the 120th Congress starting in January. Even if gridlock means Congress passes few bills next year, the proposals each party makes on tax and trade policy will offer important signals for an even more consequential few years ahead.

From the 2028 presidential election to the expiration of OBBBA tax cuts on December 31, 2028, to persistent budgetary issues in Washington, there is no shortage of ways in which federal tax policy might once again take center stage. Democrats have many tax cuts and tax increases they may try to enact in the new Congress. They will need to balance these priorities with the veto pen of a Republican president and several challenging national trends, including rising budget deficits and an uncertain economic outlook.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

articles.title: How Tax Policy Fared on the Ballot in 2026
articles.standfirst: In red and blue states alike, voters showed wariness toward novel changes to the tax code, with two notable exceptions.
paragraphs: On a night in which voters gave Republicans a drubbing, they mostly rejected sweeping taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. changes, locked in recent reforms, and sent a message that the affordability agenda runs, at least in part, through the tax code. In red and blue states alike, voters showed wariness toward novel changes to the tax code, with two notable exceptions.

The ratification of Florida Amendment 3—a $250,000 homestead exemption for non-school property taxes—clearly demonstrates Floridians’ discontent with high property taxes, but also leaves local governments in the lurch and incentivizes them to raise rates on property still in the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates. or to generate more revenue from less economically efficient taxes. High effective rates on newer homeowners, the result of a prior effort at property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. relief (the Save Our Homes Amendment), may have led voters to adopt yet another temporary patch that will only create more problems down the road.

And in Colorado, voters appear to have narrowly approved a measure that would implement a graduated-rate income tax with a top rate of 8.4 percent, replacing the state’s current 4.4 percent single-rate income tax. (As of this writing, the race has not yet been called, and the outcome could still change.) The state’s constitution currently requires a flat taxAn income tax is referred to as a “flat tax” when all taxable income is subject to the same tax rate, regardless of income level or assets.; Amendment 87, which leads by about one percentage point with 75 percent of votes in, would amend the state constitution to permit a graduated-rate income tax and also implement an initiated statute to establish new rates.
Those are important exceptions, but they are still exceptions.

Outside Florida, voters were more wary of eviscerating the property tax. In North Carolina, voters approved a much more responsible approach to property tax relief by requiring the legislature to implement levy (revenue) limits, capping the annual growth of property tax collections from all existing property in aggregate. Oklahoma voters rejected a measure that would have tightened existing assessment limits, which distort property markets and create highly non-neutral tax burdens. And Wyoming voters rejected an irresponsibly large exemption for house values.

Voters in Iowa and North Carolina adopted new tax limits that restrict the ability of elected officials to raise taxes. Iowans approved a two-thirds supermajority requirement for the legislature to raise income taxes, and North Carolina voters capped the income tax rate at 3.5 percent, just above the 3.49 percent rate planned for 2027. However, voters in both Utah and California rejected measures that would make it more difficult for the voters themselves to approve tax increases through future ballot questions.

And in the night’s star attraction, California voters appear to have rejected the wealth tax, a result with far-reaching economic and political ramifications. California’s failure to pass a first-in-the-nation wealth taxA wealth tax is imposed on an individual’s net wealth, or the market value of their total owned assets minus liabilities. A wealth tax can be narrowly or widely defined, and depending on the definition of wealth, the base for a wealth tax can vary. may dampen enthusiasm for similar measures in Oregon, Minnesota, Hawaii, and Washington. (Nevertheless, supporters of the California measure have already signaled interest in trying again in 2028.) And while some detractors, like Gov. Gavin Newsom, opposed a California wealth tax while supporting a federal wealth tax, members of Congress will likely take note of this result from one of the nation’s most progressive states as well.

The 2026 midterms demonstrated that voters are deeply unsatisfied with the status quo, while also revealing that most voters are wary of far-reaching tax changes from either side of the political spectrum. The results on tax-related ballot measures lack the strong narrative of congressional results, but perhaps that is itself the takeaway: voters’ views on specific tax policies don’t seem to have changed much in recent years, even against a backdrop of significant partisan churn.

Jared Walczak is a Senior Fellow at the Tax Foundation, where he spent five years as Vice President of State Projects, and president of Walczak Policy Consulting.

articles.title: UK Autumn Budget Prioritizes Short-Term Relief over Long-Term Growth
articles.standfirst: The UK’s 2026 Autumn Budget largely favors short-term relief over growth, highlighting the need for pro-growth reforms such as replacing the Stamp Duty Land Tax with annual property or land taxes.
paragraphs: On 28 October 2026, the British Chancellor John Healey announced the Labour government’s Autumn Budget. While most of the measures are technical or incremental in nature, the increase in taxes on banks coupled with the reduction in capital allowances reinforces a broader trend towards prioritizing short-term revenue generation over policies that encourage investment and support long-term growth.
Perhaps the most economically significant changes in the budget concern business taxation and investment incentives.

The budget reshapes capital allowances by reducing the main writing-down allowance from 14 percent to 12 percent, partially offset by an increase in the first-year allowance from 40 percent to 50 percent.

Last year’s budget already reduced the writing-down allowance (WDA) main rate to 14 percent from 18 percent, reducing the real value of deductions for assets in the main rate pool to 70 percent from 75.9 percent of investment costs.

For leased assets in the main rate pool that receive the first-year allowance, the change would raise the real value of deductions from 79.1 to 80.8 percent of investment costs. In contrast, for main rate pool assets without the first-year allowance—such as assets bought second-hand, leased overseas, or main pool cars—the real value of deductions will decline more significantly, from 70 to 62.2 percent. The overall effect is dominated by the latter, projected to raise an annual average of £871 million in revenue until 2031-32.

Generally, improving capital allowances is one of the most cost-effective taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. policy tools to encourage capital investment, as it directly reduces the cost of new capital investment simply by pulling deductions forward in time without giving up tax revenue from the returns on past investment.

In contrast, reducing capital allowances gives up capital investment and economic growth in the medium to long term for immediate revenue retention expected for the next three years. The Chancellor should therefore stay patient and consider reverting course, strengthening capital allowances for sustainable economic growth instead of reducing them for short-term fiscal gain.

Another notable measure is the temporary increase in the bank surcharge from 3 percent to 6 percent, increasing the combined corporation tax and bank surcharge rate from 28 percent to 31 percent between January 2027 and March 2028.

While expected to generate around £1 billion of additional revenue, the measure will further increase the tax burden on a sector that already contributes over £12.3 billion annually through the corporation tax, bank surcharge, and bank levy. Higher taxes on banks may provide a short-term boost to public finances, but they also risk reducing the sector’s capacity to support lending, investment, and economic activity, while potentially undermining the UK’s competitiveness as a financial center.

Ideally, the financial sector should face the same rate of corporation tax as other sectors of the economy, allowing Britain to excel in its comparative advantages rather than steering economic activity elsewhere.

From April 2027, mayors will retain a share of local business rates revenues and permanently keep 20 percent of future business rates growth in their areas. In return, part of their funding from central government grants will be reduced.

Devolving property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. revenues to local governments gives them a fiscal incentive to implement pro-growth policies that improve the local business climate. It also gives local governments an automatic mechanism to fund valuable public investments in local infrastructure that capitalize into higher business property values. Retaining a share of local income taxes lets governments compete for local residents.

The budget also foresees a reduced 10 percent Capital Gains Tax (CGT) rate for qualifying disposals by founders or early investors of high-growth, innovative companies, subject to a lifetime limit of £10 million. To qualify, individuals must hold at least 25 percent of the company and meet a complex set of turnover, employment, growth, and innovation thresholds. While low CGT rates can encourage entrepreneurship and venture capital investment, a narrow scope defined by highly specific rules may reduce its effectiveness by creating legal uncertainty and increasing compliance costs.

One notable change is the increase in the Electricity Generator Levy from 45 percent to 55 percent, which will remain in place until March 2028. The levy applies to revenues earned by electricity generators above a specified benchmark price, after accounting for eligible exclusions, exceptional costs, and annual allowances.

While the measure is expected to raise additional revenue from energy producers, it sits somewhat uneasily alongside the government’s temporary reduction in value-added tax (VAT) on domestic electricity bills from 5 percent to 0 percent between October 2026 and July 2027. On the one hand, policymakers are seeking to lower energy costs for households; on the other, they are increasing the tax burden on electricity generation, which may send mixed signals to investors in the energy sector.

The Autumn Budget includes several measures that will directly affect household consumption. One such change is the increase in the Machine Games Duty on higher-stake gaming machines from 20 percent to 25 percent, representing a targeted rise in the taxation of gambling activity and increasing the tax burden on households that participate in this form of leisure spending. By contrast, the budget reduces the overall tax burden on alcohol by expanding the small-producer alcohol duty relief and reducing the alcohol duty for beverages with low alcohol content, incentivizing the industry to shift to lower-strength products and small-scale production.

Alongside these tax changes, the government has announced a one-off £100 council tax rebate for more than 20 million households in council tax bands A to D in 2027. At an estimated fiscal cost of over £2.6 billion, this is one of the largest measures in the budget by expenditure. While the rebate provides short-term support to households facing cost-of-living pressures, it does not address the underlying shortcomings of the council tax system, which remains based on property valuations dating back to 1991. As a result, the measure only offers temporary relief rather than tackling longer-term concerns about the fairness and efficiency of local property taxation.

The budget contains a mixture of positive and negative changes for savers. Most notably, the budget reverses the previously announced reduction in the Cash ISA annual allowance. Instead of reducing the limit from £20,000 to £12,000 for individuals under 65 from April 2027, the government maintains the £20,000 allowance. Additionally, the withdrawal penalty for Lifetime ISA holders purchasing properties above the £450,000 threshold will be reduced from 25 percent to 20 percent starting in October 2026.
However, these positive developments are accompanied by tax increases. From April 2027, tax rates on savings and property income will rise by a further two percentage points across all bands.

From 6 April 2027 to 5 April 2030, a new pension tax allowance removes income tax for pensioners whose total income does not exceed the full new State Pension, at an annual cost of £50 million from 2027-28. It is worth 20 percent of the gap between the State Pension and the personal allowance and is withdrawn at £1 for every £3 of income above the State Pension, weakening work incentives for pensioners.

One of the more encouraging aspects of the budget is its treatment of international trade. The budget suspends tariffs on 72 products from August 2026 and extends suspensions for 361 products through 2027-28. Additional tariffTariffs are taxes imposed by one country on goods imported from another country. Tariffs are trade barriers that raise prices, reduce available quantities of goods and services for US businesses and consumers, and create an economic burden on foreign exporters. relief applies to food products, fertilizer, kerosene used for heating oil, and various business inputs.
The import tariff suspensions are projected to relieve consumers by a volume of £60 million and businesses by a volume of £145 million in tariff burdens annually until 2028-29.

However, the government also plans to remove the £135 customs duty relief threshold for commercial transactions and introduce new customs arrangements from October 2028, expected to raise only £215 million in the fiscal year 2028-29, with prospective revenues turning slightly negative by 2030.

The 2026 Autumn Budget prioritizes fiscal consolidation largely through tax increases while simultaneously offering a range of temporary household support measures. Although some policies, like extending tariff suspensions and increasing fiscal devolution, move in a positive direction, they are outweighed by measures that raise the cost of investment and capital formation. This budget avoids addressing several longstanding structural weaknesses in the UK’s tax system. Rather than relying primarily on higher taxes and temporary rebates, the government should focus on spending restraints and pro-growth tax reform. Priorities should include improving capital allowances for buildings and structures, broadening the VAT base while lowering rates where possible. A future budget should also return to the Prime Minister’s own pro-growth ideas, such as replacing the Stamp Duty Land Tax with annual property or land taxes.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Cristina Enache writes on the economics of tax policy and is the author of the Spanish Regional Tax Competitiveness Index. She was formerly the Director of Research at Civismo, an economic research organization based in Spain. She also served as head of research at Institución Futuro, a regional think tank based in Navarra in northern Spain. She is also currently Secretary-General at the World Taxpayers Associations and General Manager of the Spanish Taxpayers Union, which she joined in 2016.

Alex Mengden is an Economist at the Tax Foundation, where he focuses on international tax issues and tax policy in Europe. He holds a BA in philosophy and economics from the University of Bayreuth and an MSc in economics from the Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich.

articles.title: Europe’s strained social model
paragraphs: Through the rest of 2026 and in 2027, two-thirds of the European Union population will go to the polls in a series of national and regional elections1. A common feature in many EU countries is the rise of populist and nationalist forces. Why? We argue that the roots of this phenomenon lie in a systemic crisis of the European social model which, for over half a century, has defined Europe’s socioeconomic identity.

While varying across countries (Sapir, 2006, 2025), European social models all embed social cohesion into the architecture of economic governance by balancing market dynamics with universal healthcare, state pensions, education, labour-market regulations and collective bargaining. The European social model has thus enabled the coexistence of capitalism and democratic stability based on a broad intellectual consensus – including among leading political parties – robust organised labour, a dense network of intermediary institutions and favourable demographic conditions.

But these pillars underpinning post-war European stability have eroded. European societies are increasingly fractured economically and socially (poor versus rich, urban versus rural)2, culturally (traditional versus ‘modern’ values) and generationally (young versus old). The historical conditions that gave rise to Europe’s welfare regimes during the Trente Glorieuses (1945-1975) no longer exist. Post-war reconstruction rested on an explicit Beveridge-Keynes consensus, supported by dominant democratic coalitions that regularly commanded two-thirds of the electorate. Today, political fragmentation has shattered these alignments, pushing their combined vote well below 50 percent in many EU countries. To prevent these fractures from becoming a permanent rupture, Europe must forge a renewed social contract.
Three main underlying pressures are particularly visible (Table 1):
Table 1: A fragmented EU social landscape (pre-2004 EU members excluding the UK)

Source: Bruegel based on Eurostat, AMECO (European Commission), OECD, IMF, World Bank and CITD data. Notes: EU14 (EU15 excluding the UK): weighted averages of country data; top income tax rate: simple average. Latest year: 2023 for divorces; 2024 for life expectancy, fertility and expenditure items; 2025 otherwise. *1975, OECD (only nine EU14 countries). **1987 (only 11 EU14 countries, excluding Austria, Finland and Sweden). *** Buti et al (1998). † Own computation using OECD and CITD (Genovese et al, 2016); 11 EU14 countries. ‡ Retirement: IMF (2011), including disability pensions, for 1970 and 2000; Eurostat for the latest year. Health: OECD; only 10 EU14 countries in 1970. § World Bank for 1970 (only 10 EU14 countries) and 2000 (13 EU14 countries); Eurostat for the latest year.

The European social model remains one of Europe’s greatest achievements but its survival cannot be taken for granted. Traditional political parties often frame social policy choices around belt-tightening. Nationalist parties have seized on this fiscal anxiety by promising to preserve traditional social benefits while restricting them to native citizens under a banner of national preference. Where mainstream politics offers fiscal retrenchment, populism offers defensive protectionism. Both are misguided and hence bound to fail.

To construct a new political consensus, mainstream political forces must offer an ambitious vision of a European social market economy that combines economic dynamism with tangible social protection. The political credibility of these mainstream forces will depend on their ability to translate this vision into policies that address citizens’ insecurities, rather than simply denouncing populist rhetoric.

Proposing a blueprint for reform goes well beyond the scope of this analysis. Our goal is simply to outline issues that need to be tackled to rebuild a social compact able to deliver economic dynamism and social protection in the new environment described in the previous section.
Three main issues require urgent political debate and, ultimately, solutions.

While national governments must rebuild their welfare systems, the EU can play a vital role. The EU has a collective interest in well-functioning social models in its member countries for geopolitical reasons. The attractiveness of Europe to third countries and regions that do not want to be squeezed between the United States and China rests on building hard power but also, and equally importantly, on showing that a viable balance between efficiency and equity exists and is sustainable economically, politically and socially.

Currently, EU citizens often view the EU primarily as an enforcer of fiscal constraints, state-aid limitations, trade agreements and market competition, while looking exclusively to national institutions for healthcare, education and social protection. Nationalist movements exploit this asymmetry, portraying the EU as a distant elite project that wants to erode national sovereignty and social protection. Reforming social models could help redress this misperception in three ways. The EU can:
In pursuing these goals, the EU should use its three main instruments – budget, regulation and coordination – in synergy (Buti et al, 2026).

The EU as facilitator boils down to providing incentives to help member countries overcome domestic resistance to change. For this task, two instruments are well suited: the EU budget and coordination through the European Semester economic surveillance and coordination exercise3.

In terms of using EU social programmes to complement market liberalisation, it is useful to recall the experience of the Delors Commission in the late 1980s. To avoid a social backlash, the creation of the single market was coupled with the setup of cohesion policies via the Delors Packages4, alongside the promotion of social dialogue. This approach combined efficiency and equity, market discipline and cohesion policy. A similar approach must be pursued today: the EU must broaden its competitiveness strategy focusing on growth (Draghi, 2024; Letta, 2024) to include a social cohesion strategy, just as in the 1980s it added a social dimension to its single market strategy. Growth and social cohesion are complementary: growth helps finance social-cohesion programmes, and well-designed social cohesion fosters growth.

Finally, the EU should care about social convergence, which is a core part of cohesion. Protecting high social standards and preventing regulatory races to the bottom should become common priorities. With technological developments, especially AI, a sizeable education programme financed by the EU budget would send a clear and forward-looking message5.

Ultimately, the challenge is to demonstrate the EU’s added value rather than resorting to political posturing, or overpromising and failing to deliver. The ongoing battle over the EU’s 2028–2034 budget illustrates just how difficult it will be to reconcile ambitious common priorities with short-term national budgetary objectives (Darvas, 2026)6.

Overcoming the ‘fragmentation trap’ is essential if Europe is to resist the appeal of demagogues of different political colours and preserve the social and democratic foundations on which its integration project rests. Europeans do not want a low-welfare, high-inequality social system. The good news is that there is no need for this.
The authors thank Pedro Lomo for research assistance and, without implicating them, Anton Hemerijck, Mario Nava and Bruegel fellows for helpful comments on an earlier draft.

To find new innovation trajectories in an uncertain world, the EU should play to its strengths, especially its social model
Including national parliamentary elections in Finland, Greece, Italy, Poland and Spain, and France’s April 2027 presidential election.

Already in 1995, then French presidential candidate Jacques Chirac famously denounced “la fracture sociale”, but did little to address it in office. See Kévin Boucaud-Victoire, ‘“Fracture sociale” : mais d'où vient cette expression si Chirac ne l'a pas inventée ?’ Marianne, 24 July 2022, https://www.marianne.net/politique/fracture-sociale-mais-dou-vient-cette-expression-si-chirac-ne-la-pas-inventee.
See Council of the EU explainer, ‘The European Semester explained’, https://www.consilium.europa.eu/en/policies/european-semester/.

The Delors Packages reformed the then European Community budget. Package I (1988-92) set up the first multiannual plan (five-year) for the EU budget and significantly increased the size of funds deployed to poorer regions to accompany the single market and the southern enlargement (Greece, Portugal, Spain). Package II (1993-99) extended budgetary planning to a seven-year framework and provided additional funding to social and cohesion policy, partly related to the creation of the euro. articles.title: The Stern Review on climate change, 20 years on
articles.standfirst:
20 years ago the Stern Review on the economics of climate change argued that cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions made economic sense. David Miliband and Nicholas Stern offer five lessons from the last 20 years on the political blockages and other challenges that prevent governments from acting on the insight that tackling climate change … Continued
The post The Stern Review on climate change, 20 years on first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: 20 years ago the Stern Review on the economics of climate change argued that cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions made economic sense. David Miliband and Nicholas Stern offer five lessons from the last 20 years on the political blockages and other challenges that prevent governments from acting on the insight that tackling climate change is good for the economy.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

It is 20 years since we both stood with Tony Blair and Gordon Brown, then UK Prime Minister and Chancellor respectively, at the Royal Society in London to launch the Stern Review on the Economics of Climate Change. Its central conclusion was that cutting greenhouse gas emissions would be far less expensive than living with rising emissions. Two decades of evidence have only strengthened this finding.

Since 2006, clean technology has advanced remarkably, with great gains in battery capacity, and remarkable falls in the price of solar and wind power. The International Energy Agency reports that nuclear and renewables met 60 per cent of the rise in global energy demand in 2025. Solar and onshore wind now provide the cheapest new source of electricity in many parts of the world, and renewables are set to overtake coal-fired power generation in 2026. Meanwhile the costs of global warming are rising – impacting life and livelihood on every continent.

Yet with rising energy demand, fossil fuel use has kept growing (coal is making something of a comeback in Asia), and so have emissions. Fossil fuels still provide around 80 per cent of global energy supply, spurred in part by enormous subsidies: the IMF puts explicit subsidies at US$725 billion every year, and when implicit subsidies are included (where taxes on fossil fuels are lower than the costs they cause to society), the figure is US$6.7 trillion per year.
Fossil fuels still provide around 80 per cent of global energy supply, spurred in part by enormous subsidies.

The net result is that temperatures (and extreme weather events) keep rising. The target of limiting the rise in global average temperatures to 1.5-degrees Centigrade above pre-industrial levels will not be met. We are already at 1.4 degrees. In fact, every IPCC Assessment Report looks more worrying. Temperature is rising faster than anticipated, at 0.3 degrees Celsius per decade, and so are the risks of crossing major thresholds, such as destabilisation of Greenland and West Antarctica ice sheets or the collapse of the Amazon forest system.

Ironically, many politicians most concerned about migration ignore climate change’s potential to drive even greater numbers of desperate people fleeing more extreme weather, sea level rise, and circumstances that destroy their lives and livelihoods. Of the IRC’s list of countries facing greatest humanitarian risk, three quarters are in the top quartile for climate vulnerability.

Despite the growing evidence of changing climate and its impact, the science and politics are in tension. The physics says that we will only stop temperatures rising and the impacts of climate change increasing when we stabilise concentrations of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, in other words, reach net zero globally. The earlier we get there, the lower the temperature at which we stabilise.

However, climate action faces new barriers. The US Administration has renewed its assault on the science. Financial pressures have fuelled a backlash against the perceived costs of climate action in the West, even where action constitutes sound investment that saves resources in the medium term. China’s lead in electrification and its dominance of critical mineral supplies create further friction around a transition to low carbon. With the science clear, politics that is contested, and technology more positive, there are lessons from the last two decades for the next two. It is vital they are learnt.

First, twenty years ago, investing in adaptation and resilience sounded like giving up on mitigation. But as risks have grown, adaptation has become an imperative. It should no longer be the poor cousin in climate action. According to the Global Commission on Adaptation, every $1 invested in adaptation can generate up to $10 in net economic benefits.

Second, energy security has become more urgent. Chokepoints, from Russian gas pipelines to the Strait of Hormuz, are a new focus of geopolitics. The weaponisation of fossil-fuel supply is a strong long-term reason for decarbonization.

Third, China’s remarkable technical progress could and should be a great boon in the drive for low-carbon growth, but China’s industrial dominance in these technologies creates real problems, as concentrated industrial capacity can create dependency, difficulties of resilience in supply chains, and reduce competition. Building capacity for low-carbon technologies such as solar panels and batteries elsewhere, and rapidly, should be a global priority. And trade and industrial policy will be a crucial element of that task.

Fourth, for European countries, which lack the energy independence of the US, a new imperative is greater cross-border energy system interconnectedness alongside a faster shift away from fossil fuels. Mario Draghi has argued persuasively that this is also key to their competitiveness in world markets.

Fifth, AI was only a gleam in the eye twenty years ago. Today, while it is a rising source of energy demand, it promises more efficient grids, better functioning cities, emissions monitoring, materials discovery, and better climate forecasting to support adaptation. Into the 2030s, AI can make the transition faster, smarter, and cheaper.
Twenty years ago, investing in adaptation and resilience sounded like giving up on mitigation. But as risks have grown, adaptation has become an imperative.

The politics of 2026 are very different from those of 2006, and the next two decades will be turbulent. As Jason Bordoff and Meghan O’Sullivan have written: “Moving to a net-zero global economy will require an unprecedented level of global cooperation but will also lead to conflict along the way and ultimately produce winners and losers.”

The difficulty of the politics is no excuse to abandon the rigour, idealism and imagination of the earlier period; we need more of each. In a world that is interconnected but fragmented, and short of unifying leadership, the countries that want to act should support international action more strongly and build new coalitions of the willing, for example, to expand IFI support for the investment that is sorely needed and to build dependable supply chains for processing critical minerals.
Climate action can drive a new growth story. This is the essential insight of the Stern Review that needs to be revived. Green growth is not a contradiction in terms. It is a necessity.

articles.title: Economic Education Includes Addressing Tax Confusion
articles.standfirst: Economics isn’t just a course with supply and demand graphs and a quirky usage of “guns and butter.” It’s a discipline focused on incentives and responses, and we can see its impact all around us, shaping our world and our choices.
paragraphs: Economics isn’t just a course with supply and demand graphs and a quirky usage of “guns and butter.” It’s a discipline focused on incentives and responses, and we can see its impact all around us, shaping our world and our choices. This morning, you may have asked yourself, “should I stop for a coffee on my way to work?” while a lawmaker might have wondered, “should we modify the tax treatment of business income?” Both were economic decisions with broader implications.

Taxes are a cog in that economic machine, influencing small and large forces in the world around us. Increase taxes, for example, and you must reckon with the new incentive structure for hiring, investing, producing, consuming, and more. All these, in turn, have their own micro- and macroeconomic effects.

No matter the tax, people or businesses will respond. While most research demonstrates that if you tax something, you will get less of it, there are ways to minimize negative economic consequences from taxation.

Taxes on the most mobile factors in the economy, such as capital (machinery and investments), are more distortive and have the most negative impact on long-term growth. The inverse is also true, as taxes on factors that can’t easily be moved, like land, are more stable and less distortive. Understanding this can help us see past the ill feelings toward taxes and identify which ones are better than others.

Even the design of a tax can change its economic impact. Tax rates tend to receive the most attention, but the tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.—what is taxed—can be just as important. Narrow tax bases can cause people and businesses to make decisions for tax reasons that they might not make otherwise, like saving less money or hiring fewer workers, and require higher rates to raise the same amount of government revenue. For example, a state with a narrow sales taxA sales tax is levied on retail sales of goods and services and, ideally, should apply to all final consumption with few exemptions. Many governments exempt goods like groceries; base broadening, such as including groceries, could keep rates lower. A sales tax should exempt business-to-business transactions which, when taxed, cause tax pyramiding. base that has exemptions (like groceries) and sales tax holidays will rely on higher tax rates on taxable goods to generate the same amount of revenue. The resulting price increase can distort consumer decisions on what, or how much, to buy.

Another underappreciated factor that affects the economy is tax illiteracy. If a raise moves you from the 12 percent income tax bracket to the 22 percent and you believe your entire income will be taxed at the higher rate (it will not!), you may forgo a promotion or extra work hours. That decision will impact your spending, saving, and investment decisions too.

Economic and tax education is critical to interacting with our global economy, and you might expect to see educational priorities reflect the weight of the subject matter. Despite a growing number of states mandating financial literacy graduation requirements, some states have repealed requirements for economic education in recent years. But economic literacy and financial literacy go hand in hand.

If more than half of US taxpayers over 18 do not understand basic tax concepts, walking back economic education is quite a puzzling move. Understanding taxation, and economics broadly, helps prepare students for the mundane daily decisions like grabbing a “sweet treat,” inevitable tax questions, and what they can expect from decisions being made at the national level. And those who end up in elected office someday will need to design sound tax policies that generate revenue with minimal economic distortions.

articles.title: What Is the US Debt Limit and Why Does It Matter?
articles.standfirst: The debt limit is one of Congress’s few chances to debate unsustainable borrowing, and reforms should create more room for bipartisan deficit reduction, not less.
paragraphs: With total US government debt recently surpassing $40 trillion, the nation’s debt limit is back in the news. Congress most recently increased the debt limit in July 2025, from $36.1 trillion to $41.1 trillion, under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

While the US government has faced several close calls on its debt payments over its 250-year history, a major default would be unprecedented. Congress has raised or suspended the debt limit dozens of times over the past century. But recent fights over when and how to do so have brought the US to the brink of default.

Default should not be an option for policymakers. The economic consequences of the US failing to meet its debt obligations should be too great for lawmakers to even approach the brink. However, the limit remains one of the only brakes on runaway debt and deficits. Any reforms to the process should maintain or increase opportunities for Congress to debate and improve the fiscal health of the nation.

The debt limit is a legal ceiling on how much the US Treasury Department can issue in outstanding obligations. To put it another way, it sets a maximum amount for government borrowing. Importantly, the debt limit does not commit Congress to new spending; it allows the US government to pay the bills it has already incurred. Table 1 below describes in brief some fiscal terms that will be used throughout this piece.

While simple in concept, the mechanics of the debt limit are complicated. The current limit is $41.1 trillion, but the government won’t simply default when it appears as if total public debt outstanding is about to hit that mark.

Instead, the Treasury Department can use several so-called “extraordinary measures” that enable it to delay the day the government actually hits the debt limit. The measures include pausing investments and reinvestments in federal employee retirement funds the government manages and suspending the issuance of new debt. The most common extraordinary measures are described in Table 2 below.

Exactly when the US government will next reach the debt limit remains highly uncertain, but one often cited estimate from the Bipartisan Policy Center (BPC) puts that date—the so-called “X Date”—at sometime in 2027. BPC’s estimate incorporates Treasury’s use of extraordinary measures.

The debt limit in its modern form has been around since 1939, though policymakers have acted to limit the government’s borrowing through various ways and means since before the nation was a nation. The 1939 law consolidated a number of different limits into one, combined public debt limit of $45 billion (approximately $1.1 trillion in 2026 dollars). The limit ballooned to $300 billion in 1945 to accommodate World War II debt ($5.7 trillion in 2026 dollars). Since then, Congress has increased, suspended, or modified the limit 118 times.

The debt limit has taken on new importance in the 21st century, as US government debt and deficits ascend to levels never before seen in peacetime. At the turn of the century, the debt limit was just shy of $6.0 trillion ($12.0 trillion in 2026 dollars).

Since then, debt held by the public has increased almost tenfold in dollar terms, and from 34 percent to more than 100 percent as a share of the nation’s economy (gross domestic product or GDP). During that time, Congress has had several protracted debates over the debt limit—in 2011, 2013, 2015, 2019, and 2023, for example—that have raised questions over whether the US would default. While the US did not default during those episodes, two of them contributed to credit rating agencies downgrading US government debt from its previous gold-standard AAA rating—S&P in 2011 and Fitch in 2023.

The debt limit is a flawed instrument for improving the US fiscal trajectory. It is also one of the only ones left. In the 1990s, bipartisan budget agreements and a roaring economy lent the US budget surpluses and declining debt. Since then, decades of deficit-financed spending increases and taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. cuts have produced an increasingly unsustainable budget situation.

The nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) projects that the gap between government spending and revenue will continue to grow in the years ahead. CBO estimates that annual deficits regularly surpass $2 trillion per year, and that debt held by the public will increase from $32 trillion in 2026 to $168 trillion in 2056 (and from 100 percent of GDP to 175 percent over the same period).

While CBO’s forecast does not include any legislative efforts to reduce debt and deficits, it also does not include any major, negative shocks to the nation or its economy (e.g., wars, recessions, pandemics, or other crises). In some sense, then, this outlook actually underscores the potential budgetary and economic peril if Congress fails to act.
Some policymakers have proposed repealing it. Doing so without broader fiscal reforms would be a mistake.

Other policymakers have hinted at potentially letting the US default. Default would be an even greater mistake than repealing the debt limit. A default could lead to a permanent increase in US borrowing costs. Higher borrowing costs would further widen the gap between spending and revenue, and increase the likelihood that economically damaging tax increases are needed to close the gap. A default could also delay Social Security and military payments and rattle global markets that treat Treasury bonds as a risk-free asset.

A middle path might be bipartisan debt limit reform that takes the worst of the brinksmanship off the table while establishing more regular intervals for Congress to debate and enact fiscal reforms. Reps. Bill Huizenga (R-MI) and Scott Peters (D-CA) have proposed one such reform, the Responsible Budgeting Act.
Policymakers could apply Tax Foundation’s four principles of sound tax policy to the debt limit debate:

A $40 trillion total government debt—and rising—guarantees that Congress will soon be discussing the debt limit again. At its worst, the debt limit symbolizes a dysfunctional Washington that has yet to rein in an unsustainable budget trajectory. At its best, it represents one of the last, best brakes on runaway debt and spending. Debt limit reform should be simple, transparent, and neutral on policy direction, and it should create more opportunities to stabilize the fiscal outlook.

articles.title: Congress Has a Chance to Improve the Taxpayer Experience in 2026
articles.standfirst: The Senate recently passed the Taxpayer Assistance and Service Act, which contains 65 provisions to improve tax administration and the IRS.
paragraphs: “Simple” and “transparent” are not terms typically associated with filing taxes. On the contrary, the annual taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. filing process fills most with anxiety and confusion, costing Americans $536 billion annually. To make this experience a little less stressful, the Senate recently passed the Taxpayer Assistance and Service (TAS) Act, which would ease some burdens for taxpayers and provide valuable data on where complexity arises in the tax code.

The last major congressional effort to address tax administration was the InflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin Reduction Act, which provided $80 billion to the IRS mostly for enforcement and operations support. However, Congress provided little direction to the IRS on how to use the funding, nor did the law directly streamline IRS functions or processes.
After the experience of the COVID-era IRS issues, Congress, the Taxpayer Advocate Service, and taxpayer organizations proposed reforms to improve tax administration, many of which are in the TAS Act.

The Senate-passed TAS Act contains 65 reforms across 10 titles related to IRS modernization, taxpayers’ rights, tax return preparers, and other tax administration topics. While some provisions address specific taxpayer issues, many will improve the experience for the more than 150 million Americans who file taxes every year, while establishing and strengthening important taxpayer protections.

Since 1998, Congress has required the IRS to produce a report on the source of tax complexity, but the IRS has only rarely released it. While data exists on how costly tax compliance is for taxpayers, no data or report exists on which forms or provisions are causing complexity. The TAS Act clarifies congressional intent for the IRS to produce this report and another on the status of the Act’s implementation.

Paper is the enemy of the IRS. Paper returns take more time and resources for the IRS to process than electronic ones, delaying refunds and diverting staff. The TAS Act requires the IRS to accept digital returns and amended returns and then process them electronically. The bill also requires the IRS to create an online dashboard of call wait times and pushes the agency to expand the availability of callback technology. Further, the “Where’s My Refund?” and “Where’s My Amended Return?” tools are expanded and enhanced.

Most, if not all, financial institutions allow customers to create an online account to access their data. The IRS offers online accounts for taxpayers, but they have limited functionality, hindering their effectiveness. The bill improves online accounts at the IRS by expanding the types of tax documents that are viewable and enhancing tax practitioners’ ability to access their clients’ accounts (with client permission).

Taxpayers and tax preparers often face a fundamental imbalance when addressing an issue with the IRS. The agency has a multibillion-dollar budget, sweeping legal powers, and thousands of employees. Taxpayers, on the other hand, juggle busy schedules and face a complex tax code that wasn’t written for them. Tax preparers may have more knowledge of the tax code than their clients, but they also must balance tight deadlines, multiple clients, and a well-resourced IRS.
The TAS Act would strengthen many taxpayer protections Congress has already written into law and enshrine new ones. Among the pro-taxpayer provisions are:

Even the part of the TAS Act that has generated the most discussion in recent weeks—its new requirements for tax preparers—may enhance taxpayer protections, cut down on preparer fraud, and make it easier for taxpayers to identify good preparers from bad.

The TAS Act contains dozens of bipartisan reforms that could simplify tax filing, enhance transparency for taxpayers in dealing with the IRS, and provide more stability in the year-to-year filing process that fills many Americans with dread. The bill won’t solve every problem at the agency, and it’s no substitute for congressional efforts to reform and simplify the code, but it’s a step in the right direction for a better IRS.
