articles.title: Pillar Two Implementation in Europe, 2026
articles.standfirst: 22 of the 27 EU Member States have implemented both the income inclusion rule and the qualified domestic minimum top-up tax in 2026.
paragraphs: In recent years, countries have debated significant changes to international tax rules affecting multinational companies. In October 2021, after negotiations at the Organisation for Economic Co-Operation and Development (OECD), more than 130 member jurisdictions agreed to an outline for new taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. rules. Pillar Two introduces the global minimum tax with an effective tax rate of 15 percent, increasing tax revenues by an estimated $91 to $155 billion globally, or 6.5 to 8.1 percent of global corporate income taxA corporate income tax (CIT) is levied by federal and state governments on business profits. Many companies are not subject to the CIT because they are taxed as pass-through businesses, with income reportable under the individual income tax. revenue.

Pillar Two includes three main rules that establish the global minimum tax. The first is a qualified domestic minimum top-up tax (QDMTT), which countries could use to claim the first right to tax profits currently being taxed below the minimum effective rate of 15 percent. The second is an income inclusion rule (IIR), which determines when the foreign income of a company should be included in the taxable incomeTaxable income is the amount of income subject to tax, after deductions and exemptions. Taxable income differs from—and is less than—gross income. of the parent company. When a company’s effective tax rate falls below 15 percent, additional taxes would be owed in its home jurisdiction. The third rule in Pillar Two is the undertaxed profits rule (UTPR), which allows a country to increase taxes on a company if another related entity in a different jurisdiction was being taxed below the 15 percent effective rate. If multiple countries apply a similar top-up tax, the taxable profit would be divided based on the location of tangible assets and employees.

Together, the domestic minimum tax, income inclusion rule, and undertaxed profits rule create a minimum tax both on companies investing abroad and foreign companies investing domestically. They are all tied to the minimum effective rate of at least 15 percent and would apply to each jurisdiction in which a company operates.

The EU Directive on Pillar Two obliges Member States with more than 12 in-scope multinational groups to implement the IIR starting 31 December 2023, and the UTPR starting 31 December 2024. Member States with no more than 12 in-scope multinational groups can elect to defer implementing both rules for six years under Article 50 of the Directive.
Twenty-two of the 27 Member States of the European Union have implemented both the QDMTT, the IIR, and the UTPR by 2026, while five have not.

Five EU Member States can opt for a six-year deferral of Pillar Two implementation, and all of them have done so, with Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, and Malta deferring all rules until 2029, while Slovakia selectively implemented only a domestic top-up tax in 2024.

By the year 2030, implementation of the Pillar Two Directive would compromise key design features of the distribution-based corporate tax systems in Estonia and Latvia by obliging in-scope companies to distribute sufficient earnings to meet the 15 percent minimum effective tax rate.

Four EU Member States—Cyprus, Poland, Portugal, and Spain—have implemented Pillar Two rules with delay, despite obligations under the EU Directive. In these countries, the rules apply retroactively for 2024.

Among eight major European countries outside of the European Union, only Norway, Turkey, and the United Kingdom have implemented a QDMTT, an IIR, and a UTPR by 2025. Switzerland implemented a QDMTT in 2024 and an IIR in 2025, but has not set forward any plans to implement a UTPR. Iceland is undergoing public consultation to implement a QDMTT and an IIR in 2026, with no statements regarding a UTPR. Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine, the latest candidates for EU accession, have not publicly announced intentions to implement any Pillar Two rules.

In contrast to many European countries, the US has chosen not to implement changes in line with the global tax deal. In June 2025, the G7 announced a political agreement on a global minimum tax “side-by-side” solution that would exclude US-parented groups from Pillar Two’s IIR and UTPR.

Instead, the US has continued to develop its own cross-border tax framework. Recent changes to US international tax rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) produce an outcome similar to Pillar Two, despite the rules themselves being distinct. The newly introduced net CFC tested income (NCTI) acts as a minimum tax of between 12.6 and 14 percent on all foreign income of US companies, using a blended formula instead of country-by-country. Due to less generous foreign tax crediting, the removal of the substance exclusion, lack of loss carryovers, and interest deductibility rules, the US system may be more stringent than Pillar Two.

articles.title: More flexible European Union spending needs stronger parliamentary scrutiny
paragraphs: The Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU) gives the European Parliament significant powers in relation to the European Union’s budget. The EU’s overall seven-year budget – the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) – cannot pass without the parliament’s consent, while the parliament acts as co-legislator alongside the Council of the EU in the annual budgetary procedure1. Together with the Council, the parliament thus has the authority to determine how EU funds are allocated.

However, the European Commission’s proposal for the 2028-2034 MFF foresees a new architecture for the EU budget, which would exclude the European Parliament from significant allocation decisions and limit its scrutiny powers during implementation2. This is problematic not only from a treaty perspective, but also because the parliament, as the EU’s democratically elected institution, should help ensure that EU spending serves EU priorities.

The Commission’s proposals would give national governments a greater role in allocating EU funds across priorities. Governments may be tempted to use these funds to pursue domestic objectives, which might not necessarily coincide with European priorities. Given that the EU budget accounts for little more than one percent of GDP, compared with public expenditure of around 45 percent of GDP at national level, it is essential that EU spending remains focused on common European priorities.

In Darvas et al (2026), we concluded that the European Parliament should not be excluded from major decisions on the allocation of EU funds. Here, we explore options for involving the European Parliament in the proposed new EU budget architecture, while respecting the Treaty-based roles of the parliament, the Council and the Commission. In particular, a reasonable balance should be struck between ensuring meaningful European Parliament involvement and avoiding unnecessary delays in the budgetary process. While implementing the full set of options proposed in this analysis would be desirable, the objective is to ensure meaningful European Parliament involvement at the various stages of the budgeting and monitoring process.
The European Parliament’s limited role in the proposed MFF architecture

In July 2025, the European Commission proposed a major overhaul for the 2028-2034 MFF: reducing the number of budgetary headings and programmes, harmonising EU budget rules, extending flexibility and strengthening performance assessments. The largest amount of spending would be organised under National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPPs); cohesion, agriculture, fisheries, social, migration, border and internal security spending would be integrated into a single framework, within nationally pre-allocated envelopes (European Commission, 2025).

For the purposes of NRPPs, specific amounts would be earmarked for certain cohesion, agricultural and migration and border management spending. However, almost one-third of total spending via NRPPs would be allocated by EU countries without European Parliament involvement. Moreover, a 25 percent flexibility amount would be left for reprogramming in case of emergency or in the mid-term review, also without European Parliament involvement. Consequently, many substantive allocation decisions that under previous MFFs were more tightly constrained into separate programmes and budgetary structures would shift to the programming and implementation stages, in which the parliament’s role is much more limited.

The NRPPs would be subject to performance-based budgeting, under which disbursements would be conditional on the achievement of specified milestones and targets, rather than on the actual costs incurred. In principle, this approach has considerable advantages (Darvas et al, 2023), but experience with national plans under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) – the main part of the EU’s post-pandemic economic recovery programme – showed significant shortcomings in putting performance-based financing into practice (Darvas et al, 2023; ECA, 2023, 2025; Leino-Sandberg, 2026). While the Commission’s proposed performance framework for 2028-2034 would improve on the RRF framework, its methodology for setting milestones and targets remains insufficiently developed.

Under the proposals for 2028-2034, the European Parliament would have no role in approving or amending individual NRPPs, even though these plans would shape how EU funding is ultimately prioritised and spent. Nor would it have a role in the financial decisions setting out milestones, targets and payout values. Potentially, this would not adequately safeguard the European Parliament’s budgetary prerogatives under the Treaties.

One possible, albeit far-reaching, solution would be to make the European Parliament a co-adopter, together with the Council, of the EU acts that must be adopted to approve each national plan, with these acts also incorporating the relevant financial decisions. This could involve either approval of each plan individually or a joint approval process covering all plans. Major revisions to plans could be subject to similar scrutiny.

However, the European Parliament is not an implementing authority under the EU Treaties and lacks the administrative capacity to scrutinise every national plan in detail. Alternative mechanisms should therefore be considered to safeguard the parliament’s budgetary prerogatives. Instead, we recommend a combination of stronger ex-ante parliamentary influence over major choices concerning spending priorities and financial allocations, scrutiny of major plan amendments, better information access and independent evaluation.
Strengthening the European Parliament’s role before NRPP adoption

Under the Commission’s proposals for 2028-2034, EU countries would have considerable discretion in allocating funding across priorities. Discussions and negotiations between each country and the Commission could significantly influence how EU funding is allocated across EU priorities, while the European Parliament would be excluded from these decisions. This could be addressed by:

This aggregate assessment should take place sufficiently early to allow the findings to be taken into account in final NRPPs. For example, EU countries could be required to submit draft plans at least six months before the deadline for final plans. The Commission would then have one month to assess the aggregate allocations, followed by one month for the European Parliament to express its views. This would leave EU countries and the Commission four months to discuss and incorporate possible revisions before the final plans are submitted. The parliament’s opinion might not be binding, but the Commission should be required to explain how the parliament’s observations were taken into account in the finalisation of NRPPs4.

Under the Commission’s 2028-2034 MFF proposals, the Commission would assess the (final) NRPPs and propose Council sign-off decisions (‘implementing decisions’ in EU jargon), with no option for the European Parliament to intervene at any procedural stage. This process could be strengthened by:

In scrutinising NRPPs, the European Parliament would also benefit from independent assessments of the NRRPs, the Commission’s assessments of NRRPs and the results achieved (Darvas et al, 2026). The Commission’s close involvement in the design and implementation of NRPPs could compromise its ability to provide fully objective assessments, as was the case with the RRF (Darvas et al, 2025). Independent scrutiny could be provided by an Independent NRPP Evaluation Panel, selected through a competitive process and insulated from both national managing authorities and the Commission services responsible for NRPP implementation. The panel would complement, rather than duplicate, the work of the European Court of Auditors (ECA), by providing systematic assessments of NRPP design, implementation and results, while ECA would retain its independent external audit and evaluation functions. We therefore recommend:
The Council may reject a draft NRPP approval proposed by the Commission. This should trigger the same procedure as for the initial plan:
Strengthening the European Parliament’s role during NRPP implementation

The Commission’s proposal would allow the European Parliament only a very limited role during implementation of the NRPPs. The parliament would be able to object to Commission decisions on revising six articles and five annexes of the NRPP regulation (European Commission, 2025), or to revoke the Commission’s power to adopt such decisions. The Commission would also be required to communicate information on irregularities to the parliament. However, the parliament would have no role in other implementation-related dialogues, or in the programming of the 25 percent flexibility amount. Moreover, there would be no regular implementation dialogue between the Commission and the parliament, though a comparable mechanism – the ‘recovery and resilience dialogue’ – is in place for the RRF5. At the time of writing, 23 such RRF dialogues have been held (Loi et al, 2026). These shortcomings in monitoring of implementation could be addressed by:

The NRPP framework as proposed by the European Commission would shift important decisions on EU spending from the legislative stage to the programming and implementation stages, in which the European Parliament would have only a limited role. Combined with the lack of clarity around the proposed performance-based budgeting framework, this shift could undermine the European Parliament’s budgetary prerogatives under the Treaties.

Making the parliament a co-adopter of every NRPP would, however, be difficult to reconcile with the respective institutional roles of the EU institutions and would impose substantial administrative demands on the parliament. A more workable approach would therefore be to strengthen parliamentary influence and scrutiny at several critical points without turning the parliament into an implementing authority. Prior scrutiny of aggregate and national allocations, systematic access to Commission and national documentation, independent evaluation, a regular NRPP dialogue, scrutiny of major plan amendments, integration into the annual budget and discharge procedures and parliamentary approval of material reprogramming through the annual budget would together provide a stronger accountability framework.

articles.title: Your October Round-up
articles.standfirst:
Welcome to October’s round-up! This month, we’re putting the spotlight on workplace mental health tools, a significant topic that we’re seeing a lot of in our pipeline, and asking what it takes for workers to actually use them. With the Budget landing earlier this week, we’ve also pulled out the highlights for founders and investors, … Continued
The post Your October Round-up appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This month, we’re putting the spotlight on workplace mental health tools, a significant topic that we’re seeing a lot of in our pipeline, and asking what it takes for workers to actually use them.
With the Budget landing earlier this week, we’ve also pulled out the highlights for founders and investors, alongside the Resolution Foundation’s overnight analysis.
And as ever, we’ve rounded up the most exciting updates from the WorkerTech world, from demo days to new market reports.
Mind the trust gap: Workplace mental health provision and worker attitudes
An increasing number of employees in the UK are offered mental health support at work. Only a small number use it.
Two new surveys, results of which were released earlier this month give insights into why.

In August and September of this year, Kara Connect, a UK-based wellbeing provider surveyed 2,010 UK employees, and found that while 91% of those employees have access, only 37% would turn to a mental health support tool via their employer. Around a third (32%) worried it would affect their career.

Also released this month was AXA Global Healthcare’s Mind Health Report, which surveyed 19,000 people across 18 countries. It found that while some of the concerns found among UK employees (in Kara Connect’s report) were also present across the world, access was limited. While 84% of those surveyed said they would probably or definitely use at least one form of workplace support if it were available. Only 41% say they have access. 33% of the people surveyed reported concerns that talking about mental health at work would affect job security.
This tells us that there is a design problem at the centre of workplace mental health tools and platforms: trust.

Another piece of evidence that supports our conclusion is found in the Keep Britain Working Review (see section: Culture of Fear), led by Sir Charlie Mayfield, asks employers to share responsibility for health at work. Mayfield has highlighted that a barrier to keeping in work is a widespread culture of fear – employees dealing with early-stage mental health struggles fear that disclosing the same will lead to stigma, discrimination or negative consequences for their career prospects. On the other side, line managers reported being wary of doing the wrong thing in response to such disclosures, and exposure to tribunal action.

Therefore, when it comes to evaluating workplace mental health solutions in our pipeline, we look closely at what workers are being asked to disclose, what the technology is tracking and, crucially, what employers can see.

We also want to see responsible pathways for workplace mental health management; this means just as much of an emphasis on the course of action post disclosure or a flag of worsening mental health as is put on the data collection and evaluation.

As the guidance from Sir Mayfield’s Review starts becoming practice, we expect to see renewed demand for workplace mental health provision tools. Take-up and participation rates will be key to employers assessing a return on investment in such tools, as will the availability of tools and guidance that help line managers support employees that are experiencing mental health strains.

The consequences of ignoring mental health at the workplace may be an early exit, or worklessness. This is especially true for young people, as was discussed in 2024 in research published by the Resolution Foundation, funded by the Health Foundation. The research found that the number of young people workless due to ill health has more than doubled over the past decade, from 93,000 to 190,000, and that people in their early twenties are now more likely to be economically inactive due to mental ill health than people in their forties. Workplace mental health tools that are focused on outcomes in terms of engagement and effective management are poised to succeed in helping solve this issue.

The Chancellor delivered his first Budget on the 28th of October, and as usual the Resolution Foundation’s research team was hard at work producing an in-depth overnight analysis of the measures announced in the budget and what they mean for household incomes for the rest of this Parliament. More on that in the next section.
The Ventures team was on the lookout for announcements or changes affecting founders and startups. Here are a few highlights for the WorkerTech community:

Our overnight analysis of the Budget finds that higher debt interest costs leave the Government with just £14.5 billion of headroom, around three-fifths of its March level. The £4.4 billion cost of living package that was announced is thinly spread and poorly targeted: on average, it is worth less than £15 a year more to households in the poorest half of the income distribution than to those in the richest half.

Typical non-pensioner incomes are set to fall by 3 per cent (£1,050) between 2026-27 and 2028-29. Lastly, the extension of the Local Housing Allowance freeze into 2027-28 means over a million private renting families lose out, with 91 per cent of them in the bottom half of income distribution.

The headline recommendations following the analysis are that future Government cost of living support should be better targeted at lower-income households with high energy needs (rather than thinly spread across the income distribution) and that upcoming reviews of departmental spending and benefits spending will need to be more ambitious if the new Prime Minister and administration’s vision is to be realised.

The real Living Wage (a voluntary hourly pay rate based on what families need to get by) for 2026-27 is £14.10 across the UK and £15.45 in London. Calculated by the Resolution Foundation and overseen by the Living Wage Commission, this year’s rates use a new blended methodology, averaging Minimum Income Standard and relative poverty calculations.

Baltic Ventures’ Demo Day is back Baltic Ventures has welcomed eight new companies onto its accelerator programme, and after 3 months on the programme, they are ready to take to the pitching stage. Baltic Ventures’ mission is to identify and back ambitious and innovative founders outside of London’s startup ecosystem, and this demo day will bring together founders, angels, VCs and ecosystem leaders from across Liverpool City Region and the UK. It’s taking place on November 26th and you can register here.

Ufi Ventures and Tyton Partners release their Q3 2026 VocTech Market Report This latest quarterly report explores how vocational learning and workforce development are changing across the UK, Europe and North America, from evolving skills policy and diverging forecasts of AI’s impact on jobs to where investment is landing. Read the key learnings here. Apply for direct investment from Resolution Ventures We accept applications from WorkerTech ventures on a rolling basis. You can book a slot in our office hours for an initial conversation.

articles.title: How Is The UK’s Deficit Reduction Plan (Actually) Likely To Proceed?
articles.standfirst: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt...
paragraphs: This week’s Budget, like its predecessors, assumes a sizeable fiscal squeeze in the years ahead. On the OBR’s numbers, the primary balance (tax receipts minus spending on everything except debt interest) is forecast to improve by 3 per cent of GDP over the next 5 years, from a deficit of 1.5 per cent in 2025-26 to a surplus of the same size by 2030-31. The IMF singled the UK out this month as one of the few advanced economies where action on the deficit has been taken decisively.

The trouble is that few people outside the Fund expect this squeeze to be delivered. Most of the tightening is scheduled for 2029-30, which could well be the run-up to the next election. This is the familiar pattern of promising fiscal prudence tomorrow, what Charlie Bean once called the “Augustinian approach” to fiscal policy.

None of this is a criticism of the OBR. Its remit requires it to forecast on the basis of the government’s stated policy, so what it publishes is a forecast conditional on the plan being implemented. That is a useful thing, but it’s also not a best guess of what is likely to happen because the stated policies are themselves unlikely to be unbiased.

In this week’s blog, I set out what I think is a credible path for the UK’s public finances. I use the historical record of borrowing forecasts against outturns to discipline how the fiscal plans are likely to be revised in the years ahead. On this path, the primary balance improves but stays in deficit over the next five years. The current budget is in deficit by around £30 billion in 2029-30, so the fiscal rules are missed by a significant margin. The debt ratio rises throughout the forecast, reaching 101 per cent of GDP by 2031-32. My guess is that this is closer to the market’s expectation than the official forecast, and it may help resolve the puzzle of why the UK’s borrowing costs remain the highest in the G7 despite the IMF’s praise.

Figure 1 explains why. It reconstructs one the OBR published in its 2025 Fiscal Risks and Sustainability Report, comparing the OBR’s forecasts for the debt ratio since 2010 with what actually happened. The forecasts are hump-shaped: on average, they show the debt ratio deteriorating for two years and then improving over the later years of the forecast. The outturns are linear: the debt ratio just keeps rising with the forecast horizon. The improvement that every forecast has pencilled in for years three to five has never arrived.
Public sector net debt (as % of GDP), OBR forecasts compared to outturns, 2010-present

What explains this? I can think of three candidate explanations. The first is bad luck: the economy has been hit by a series of adverse shocks over this period. The second is a planning fallacy: planners tend to be overly optimistic about their ability to deliver. The third is that the plans are built to satisfy the fiscal rules and were never meant to be delivered.

To tell these apart, we follow the approach of Beetsma, Giuliodori and Wierts, in a 2009 paper they provocatively titled “Planning to cheat: EU fiscal policy in real time”. The idea in a nutshell is to take the OBR’s forecast errors for borrowing and split them into a part due to government decisions on taxes and spending and a part due to everything else, above all macroeconomic news. Helpfully, the OBR’s own publications make this possible in a way that would be more difficult in most other countries. We use two of its datasets: every official forecast, so we know what was planned each year; and every revision between one forecast and the next, which the OBR itself splits into the effect of policy decisions announced in the interval, classification changes, and underlying changes to the economy and debt interest. The policy estimates include both the direct cost of measures and their indirect effects on the forecast through the economy, such as higher receipts when spending raises GDP.

For each forecast and each year of its horizon, we add up the policy revisions made in every later forecast for that year. Since each forecast reports its revisions relative to the one before, the sum is the total effect on that year’s borrowing of all the decisions taken after the plan was published. An example hopefully helps fix the intuition. Take the March 2021 forecast for borrowing in 2023-24. The six forecasts that followed attributed revisions to 2023-24 of £11bn, £1bn, £31bn, £19bn, £8bn and £0.3bn to policy, £70bn in all or 2.5 per cent of GDP. Over the same period, the economic outlook improved, which is why the outturn missed the forecast by only 1.4 per cent of GDP in the end. In other words, the method measures how much each plan was undone by later decisions, and differentiates this from how much the economy helped or hurt.

Table 1 shows the results, with the forecasts split into those made between June 2010 and March 2014 and those made from December 2014 onwards (excluding Covid years). In the first period, borrowing came in about 1 per cent of GDP above plan by year 3, and this entirely reflected macro news. Evidently, this was a period where the coalition government held to its plans and the economy fell short. In the second, borrowing has come in fully 2 per cent of GDP above plan by year 3, and three-quarters of that is accounted for by policy decisions taken after the forecast was made. These decisions raised borrowing in the third year of every one of the 24 forecasts since December 2014. So this latter period is not explained away by bad luck.
Notes: Per cent of GDP. Target years 2020-21 to 2022-23 excluded; windows complete to 2026-27, with 2026-27 measured against the October 2026 forecast.

Which decisions explain these slippages? The OBR’s policy measures database records every measure since 2010 by the tax or spending line it affects, so the slippage can be attributed accordingly. Figure 2 does that for the third year of each forecast since December 2014.

The direct cost of the measures announced after each forecast added 1.8 per cent of GDP to year-3 borrowing on average (their indirect effects, mainly the extra receipts that higher spending generates, bring that down to the 1.5 in Table 1). Of the 1.8 per cent, 1.5pp is departmental spending and it is positive in all 15 forecasts. A further 0.2 is the devolved and local authority spending that follows from it via the Barnett formula. Welfare measure net to almost nothing. Fuel duty contributes 0.1, small but present in all 15, because the planned rise is cancelled every time. Tax measures as a whole net to zero at year 3, though by year 5 tax rises outweigh cuts.

The departmental slippage comes in two forms. Spending Reviews give departments budgets for a fixed number of years, currently to 2028-29. Beyond that the forecast rests on a Treasury assumption about total spending growth. Our results say that it is when the next Review replaces that placeholder with settlements that the total comes out higher. In particular, where a forecast’s third year lay beyond the Review period, later departmental decisions added a median 2 per cent of GDP to borrowing, and two-thirds of that arrived at the Review itself. Where the third year already had settled budgets, the additions were smaller and more varied.

So to summarise: of the three explanations we started with, borrowing slippages since 2014 have not in the main been driven by bad macroeconomic news, although there certainly has been plenty of that. They instead reflect departmental spending outstripping forecasts, primarily in the years beyond the planning horizon of the Spending Review. Whether the assumption for those years reflects a planning fallacy of the kind that afflicts most long-range plans, or the incentives the fiscal rules create to pencil in restraint where it costs least, is not settled.

The credible path takes the OBR’s forecast and subtracts from it the typical amount by which later decisions have undone past plans. Concretely, we take the median policy slippage at each horizon from the second panel of Table 1, nothing in the year of the forecast, 0.1 per cent of GDP in year 1, 0.6 in year 2, 1.5 in year 3, 1.6 in year 4 and 1.8 in year 5, and subtract it from the planned primary balance. The band around the result is the interquartile range of the same record. There is no estimation involved—this is just the plan minus what slippage normally occurs.

One point to note before we discuss the results. We focus here solely on slippages from policy decisions, not from macro news. Macro forecasts will also be wrong, and the assumptions underpinning them can be optimistic. For example, the OBR has been criticised for a trend growth path strong than many outside forecasters assume. But the OBR was set up precisely to make those expert, independent judgements, and they are matters on which reasonable people disagree. We are looking instead for the places where a systematic bias is plausible, and Table 1 says that since 2014 that has been in the policy assumptions.

In making these translations we assume that 85 per cent of the slippage lands on the current budget rather than on capital, which is its historical share, and that the extra debt is financed at 4.5 per cent.

To be clear, this is a conditional forecast of how the plan is likely to proceed: it assumes the policy process of the past decade continues, and in particular that next year’s Spending Review raises departmental budgets for 2028-29 to 2030-31 well above the figures the OBR’s forecasts are built on.

That does not seem like a bad assumption. Inflation has run higher than expected since the current settlements were fixed in June 2025, so the OBR now puts the departmental limits at £7bn a year less in real terms than when they were set, and it estimates that unprotected departments would need £11bn more by 2031-32 simply to avoid real cuts from 2028-29. On top of that sits the defence commitment, social care and whatever the Milburn and Timms reviews recommend. None of this is in the credible path above. It rests purely on historical slippage alone.

But the same arithmetic describes a big opportunity. The 2027 Review is the first moment since 2014 at which a government could settle the target year’s budgets at a level in the forecast, and if it did, the gap in the charts above would mostly close. In other words, we would update our priors on the credible path significantly were this to happen.

The prize here would be lower gilt yields. NIESR’s Laubach-style regression results suggest that each percentage point of projected deficit adds 15-20 basis points on the 10-year gilt yield. So a plan that credible delivers 1.5-2 points of primary surplus relative to the credible path could be expected to take 25 to 40 basis points off gilt yields, worth over £10bn each year in debt interest—with wider effects for the whole economy. That would be a credibility dividend worth buying.

articles.title: Budget 2026 special
articles.standfirst:
Afternoon all, While Wednesday’s Budget might have been a more modest affair than we’ve become accustomed to, RF staff were still crunching the numbers late into the night, soundtracked by Treasury officials cheering on the Chancellor for downing a pint getting through his first Budget. Instead of taking Friday a little easier, we’re still here … Continued
The post Budget 2026 special appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: While Wednesday’s Budget might have been a more modest affair than we’ve become accustomed to, RF staff were still crunching the numbers late into the night, soundtracked by Treasury officials cheering on the Chancellor for downing a pint getting through his first Budget. Instead of taking Friday a little easier, we’re still here to bring you bonus content.

Overall, this scattergun Budget did not rise to the scale of the challenges facing Britain. We need more than £100 to the wrong people in the face of another energy price shock, and a forecast for falling living standards over the rest of the Parliament. Read on for five brand new scary charts fit for Halloween: from why things have already got worse, to why it (actually) isn’t all about economic growth.

That said, there were things to welcome this week. A sensible decision on minimum wage, worthwhile reform in closing the gap between tax rates on savings and property income with those on wages, and money to help the PuFiNs fly.
The stage is set for the true reckoning of priorities in 2027 – but first, sleep.

One of the Chancellor’s big choices was to use some of his insurance policy (letting the current budget that he has promised to balance fall from £24bn to £15bn). If things turn out better than expected this will prove a wise move. So far, however, it looks like the Chancellor’s chips are down. The OBR took economic data up to mid-August into account in its forecast. By Budget day, gas prices were far above the OBR’s central forecast and looked dangerously close to its “severe” shock scenario, while oil had climbed two-thirds of the way there. On energy prices, the OBR’s downside scenario is starting to look like the central case (though at our event this week Haskel explained that how long high prices are sustained for will be crucial). In that scenario, inflation tops 5 per cent next year. But the Government does get a sliver of good news. Although the severe scenario does show higher borrowing overall, that’s entirely down to a one percentage point rise in gilt yields that has not yet materialised. So while households are facing something like the severe scenario, the Treasury (for now at least) is not.

One bit of good news the OBR didn’t have time to incorporate was the continued resilience of the UK economy in July and August. And there were 34 pages of the red book dedicated to a plethora of measures aimed to continue to boost economic growth. My favourite was topping up the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank by a combined £20.4 billion (as we’ve been calling for). But at the same time, the Government’s ambitious plans for higher investment have again been chipped away at. Capital departmental spending (CDEL) is now set to fall to 4.1 per cent of GDP in 2029-30, down from 4.3 per cent in the March forecast. The exception is defence investment, thanks to the Defence Investment Plan. Take that out, and we’re actually planning to invest less than we did in 2023-24: CDEL excluding defence has lost over £5 billion since the March forecast. While it has other important aims, defence CDEL is less likely to boost economic growth than other categories like transport or energy, both of which are set to shrink.

Despite there being very little about social security in this Budget, welfare spending dominated the headlines the following day. Two ongoing reviews may prove more memorable than this Budget: Milburn on young people and Timms on disability benefits. For the decade following the pandemic, almost all of the rise in welfare spending is from two sources – benefits for pensioners (£37 billion) and working-age health and disability benefits (another £37 billion). The Prime Minister deserves credit for his boldness on moving away from the triple lock which in the long run will put the first on a more sustainable trajectory; even if on Wednesday the OBR scored the princely sum of zero for savings from it in the first year. The combined response to Milburn and Timms will presumably aim to address the second. The total spend on young people neither earning nor learning runs to around £4 billion, while working-age disability spending in England and Wales stands at nearly £28 billion. Milburn may be more of a headline grabber, but addressing the drivers of higher ill-health and disability across all age-groups remains highly consequential for the public finances as well as living standards.

Families are on track to pay much higher energy bills this year than last. The left panel below shows how unevenly that increase is set to land: up £217 in 2026-27 for the typical household (compared with 2025-26). But there is as much variation between households with the same income as between households of different income. Within every income bracket many households face very large rises, with around one-in-five of the poorest households facing increases of more than £300. This is why help needs to reach those with both low incomes and high energy use.

The Chancellor’s main response, a £100 Household Energy Payment for homes in Council Tax bands A to D, does neither. As the right panel shows, eligibility barely varies across the bottom three quintiles and remains high even at the top, where three-in-five households qualify. A £100 bung to everyone means giving it to many people who don’t need it – either because they are on high incomes, fixed rate tariffs, or have low energy needs. This scatter-gun approach will provide little comfort for many of the one-in-six of the poorest families who already tell us they can’t afford to heat their homes.

The most disappointing thing about this Budget was what it told us about the long-run prospects for living standards. Real household disposable income per person is set to grow by just 0.1 per cent a year on average between 2019 and 2029, compared with 0.9 per cent between 2007 and 2019 and 2.4 per cent in the decade to 2007. TOTC readers will no doubt be familiar with the role economic growth (the blue bars) played in our post financial crisis disappointment. That it’s become relatively more expensive to buy things from the rest of the world (the yellow bars) also matters. But the 2020s squeeze on living standards has a new source (the red bar in the chart below): net taxes and benefits, which added to income growth after the financial crisis, are now a drag on it.

This is not really a story of consolidation – borrowing in 2029-30 is forecast to be little lower than it was before the pandemic. Over this period, taxes are up to pay for higher spending, with health spending, in particular, 1 percentage point higher as a share of the economy. Especially painful is spending an extra 2.4 per cent of GDP on debt interest.

This final chart sums up the dilemma the Chancellor has put off but cannot avoid in 2027. If we cannot afford the public services and defence we want without a bigger red bar – will he choose to disappoint on those or to squeeze household incomes even further?

articles.title: What does the abolition of the gas standing charge mean for households?
articles.standfirst:
While the £100 Household Energy Payment grabbed most of the headlines, another energy bill change announced on Wednesday has got less attention. But John Healey’s request for Ofgem to abolish the standing charge on household gas bills by the end of 2027 will also affect future bills. And because it’s a regulatory change, the Treasury … Continued
The post What does the abolition of the gas standing charge mean for households? appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: While the £100 Household Energy Payment grabbed most of the headlines, another energy bill change announced on Wednesday has got less attention. But John Healey’s request for Ofgem to abolish the standing charge on household gas bills by the end of 2027 will also affect future bills. And because it’s a regulatory change, the Treasury leaves it out of its distributional analysis. So here we’ve tried to fill that gap and understand who will win – and lose – from this switch.

The standing charge, £108 a year for the typical billpayer, is paid by every gas-connected household however little gas it uses. Suppliers will recover it through higher unit rates instead, so the change costs the Exchequer nothing, and efforts to reduce the disparity between gas and electricity costs will – in a small way – help to make the case for more heat pumps in homes.

But it is not free: it moves around £600 million a year from households that use more gas to those that use less, with no regard to their incomes. In effect, it adds to what we at RF have dubbed the “shadow tax and benefit system hidden within energy bills”, with the transfer set by a regulator rather than in a Budget.

Still, upfront, there is a lot to like about it. Standing charges make up a much bigger share of low energy users’ bills than higher users: at today’s prices the charge is an eighth of a typical gas bill, but more for those who use less gas. Prepayment customers who self-disconnect also keep building up standing charges as debt, which abolition would end. The catch is that gas unit rates would rise by around 10 per cent – at a time when they are at record highs with little chance of falling back to earth.

Not all households will benefit. We estimate that 13.3 million (48 per cent) of households in Britain would be better off, by £46 a year on average, and 9.9 million (36 per cent) would be worse off, by £61 – the losses are larger because the same sum falls on fewer households. The other 4.5 million (16 per cent) are not on the gas grid so will be unaffected. But for the typical household the change is small: the median gas-connected household would gain just £13 a year, less than 1 per cent of a typical energy bill in 2026-27.[1]

There are winners and losers in every income group: which side a household lands on depends on how much gas it uses, not on how much it earns. The pattern by income is very mildly progressive (Figure 1). Half (50 per cent) of households in the poorer half of the income distribution would be better off, compared with 46 per cent in the richer half. The picture is similar at the ends of the distribution – 47 per cent of the poorest fifth would gain, against 44 per cent of the richest fifth.
Figure 1: The spread of winners and losers from abolishing the gas standing charge is relatively flat across the income distribution

The bigger divide is by household size, which we show in Figure 2. Larger households use more gas, so would lose out more: 54 per cent of households with two children and 58 per cent of those with three or more would be worse off, paying £20 and £35 a year more on average, respectively. By contrast, nearly two-thirds (65 per cent) of single pensioners would be better off, saving £28 a year on average.
Figure 2: Most households with two or more children would be worse off from abolishing the gas standing charge

The timing of payments changes too. January to March accounts for 43 per cent of a year’s household gas use. Turning a flat daily charge into a higher unit rate pushes more of the bill into winter, by moving a daily charge into one concentrated in times when consumption is high.

For a household using Ofgem’s typical 9,500 kWh a year, payments between October and March would rise by around £20, and those between April and September would fall by around £30. Prepayment customers, who pay as they go, would see more of their bill land in the months when money is tightest – and all would become more exposed to the cost of a cold winter.

The Government has promised “targeted mitigation” for households that lose out but has not said what it will be. Our analysis has shown that it should focus on lower-income families with higher energy use, such as those with children. The difficulty is that the Government still has no tool to find them – even four years into an energy bill squeeze. The benefit system, through which help like the Warm Home Discount is passported, reaches only around a quarter of households and misses most of those in the poorer half of the income distribution.

A social tariff, on the other hand, could shield those for whom higher gas prices pose a welfare risk, allowing the benefits of abolishing the standing charge to be banked while mitigating the risks at the sharp end – as well as helping families struggling with the high cost of energy today. Without it, every reform of this kind – including the overhaul of electricity standing charges promised for next year – will be yet another untargeted transfer between billpayers.
This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.
Jonathan Marshall is a Principal Economist at the Resolution Foundation. You can follow him on Bluesky here.
[1] Based on a typical consumption level of 9,500 kWh of gas per year.

articles.title: New Research Finds That Revenue-Maximizing Top Tax Rate Likely Lower Than Previous Estimates
articles.standfirst: A new paper shows raising top income tax rates on the current tax base may not yield as much revenue as previously estimated, due to opportunities to shift income to different tax bases within the tax code.
paragraphs: Not all taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. hikes bring in more revenue. Setting the rate too high might not yield as much as a lower tax rate would, because tax rates influence how much people work and how much businesses invest—both activities that affect the income tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates.. Economists and policymakers, therefore, are keen on determining the “Goldilocks rate.” A new research paper sheds some light on this question, finding that the income tax rate that maximizes revenue may actually be lower than previously estimated.

An influential policy paper in the “optimal tax theory” literature was published by economists Peter Diamond and Emmanuel Saez in 2011, “The Case for a Progressive Tax.” That paper sought to identify the “peak” of the Laffer curve—the marginal tax rateThe marginal tax rate is the amount of additional tax paid for every additional dollar earned as income. The average tax rate is the total tax paid divided by total income earned. A 10 percent marginal tax rate means that 10 cents of every next dollar earned would be taken as tax. at which tax revenue is maximized.

Building on earlier theoretical work from Saez, the 2011 paper estimated a top revenue-maximizing tax rate of 73 percent in the US. The findings of that paper were frequently misunderstood by policymakers and commentators, including by some who thought that the paper’s findings meant the top tax rate should be set at that rate.

To start, the top revenue-maximizing rate estimated in the paper was inclusive of all taxes at the federal, state, and local levels, including all payroll taxes and sales taxes. That is, the paper did not estimate that revenue would be maximized if the top individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source rate (35 percent at the time) was increased to 73 percent.

A second, and critically overlooked, contributor to the 73 percent figure was the assumption of a tax base that is broader than our system was at the time (and still is). The authors estimated that using the existing, narrower tax base, with numerous deductions and credits, would yield a top revenue-maximizing rate of 54 percent, or 48 percent for just the top federal income tax rate. For context, that rate is not much higher than the combined federal and state income tax rates faced by high-income taxpayers in states such as New York and California.

Diamond and Saez’s 2011 paper was certainly not the last word on this topic. Many papers published since have taken different approaches, producing a range of total government revenue-maximizing tax rates from all sources between 46 percent and 73 percent.

In a new paper building on this work, economists Rachel Moore, Brandon Pecoraro, and David Splinter argue that these papers used tax bases that were either too broad or too narrow, often missing important behavioral adjustments. Given our current tax system, they find that the Laffer curves are flatter than Saez and other authors estimate, implying that the revenue gains from increasing top tax rates are smaller than what those previous estimates suggest.

Policymakers are largely interested in how the change in the top ordinary income tax rate would impact revenue, but a large share of income at the top actually falls outside this tax base. For example, while the ordinary income tax base includes some capital income—such as short-term capital gains and pass-through businessA pass-through business is a sole proprietorship, partnership, or S corporation that is not subject to the corporate income tax; instead, this business reports its income on the individual income tax returns of the owners and is taxed at individual income tax rates. profits—other types of capital income, such as long-term capital gains and qualified dividends, are taxed at lower rates. The ordinary income tax base is reduced further by deductions and credits for various kinds of investment.

The authors improve upon previous studies by constructing different tax bases and using detailed administrative data covering high-income taxpayers to estimate behavioral responses along the Laffer curve. The model allows them to capture different margins of adjustment in response to changes in tax rates. For example, corporations may switch organizational forms to noncorporate structures if tax rates on pass-through business income fall. Similarly, individual income taxpayers may increase tax-deductible activities, such as charitable giving, when their tax rates rise.

Accounting for these additional margins, the authors find that the revenue losses from federal rate increases roughly double compared to previous estimates that use only one tax base. Using a single broad tax base yields a revenue-maximizing federal income tax rate of 55 percent. That revenue-maximizing rate falls to 48 percent when using multiple bases and accounting for all possible behavioral responses (the “true” base), yielding an additional $43 billion in revenue at that rate, or 0.2 percent of GDP.

Taking into consideration all taxes at the federal, state, and local levels, the top federal income tax that maximizes revenue falls even further. The top federal individual income tax rate that would maximize total government revenue from all sources is 39 percent, with an increase to that rate yielding $1 billion in additional total tax revenue. At that rate, the losses to state and local revenue almost fully offset the federal revenue gains. A rate of 39 percent is also very close to the current top federal income tax rate of 37 percent.

Overall, this new paper shows raising top income tax rates on the current tax base may not yield as much revenue as previously estimated, due to opportunities to shift income to different tax bases within the tax code. Policymakers should keep this in mind when thinking about increasing tax rates on high-income taxpayers without making other reforms to the tax code.

Alex Durante is a Senior Economist at the Tax Foundation, working on federal tax policy and model development. Alex worked as a research assistant at the Federal Reserve Board and served as a staff economist on the Council of Economic Advisers.

articles.title: Property Tax Relief on the Ballot: Three Approaches, One Clear Winner
articles.standfirst: This November, states across the country are asking voters to consider changes to their state constitutions to address the burden of rising property taxes.
paragraphs: In November, voters across the country will not only choose who will represent them in elected office, but also whether to approve certain changes to their state constitutions and statutes, including a variety of proposed tax policy changes. Rising property taxes have dominated discussions in many state capitols and among homeowners and business owners. While some states have addressed rising property taxes through legislation, others have turned to the ballot box.

This November, 12 property tax measures are on the ballot across 7 states. The most consequential are proposals to substantially raise homestead exemptions or tighten assessment limits, proposals that would shift property taxA property tax is primarily levied on immovable property like land and buildings, as well as on tangible personal property that is movable, like vehicles and equipment. Property taxes are the single largest source of state and local revenue in the U.S. and help fund schools, roads, police, and other services. burdens in economically distortionary ways. Alternatively, North Carolina voters will consider a levy limit that would limit property tax revenue growth in a structurally sound way.

Assessment limits cap the amount by which a property’s taxable assessed value can increase annually. Oklahoma State Question 847 would tighten the state’s current assessment limit by reducing the annual cap on fair cash value increases for homestead property and agricultural land from 3 percent to 1.75 percent and lower the cap for other property from 5 to 4 percent.

The measure would also modify Oklahoma’s property tax relief provisions for homeowners over the age of 65. Oklahoma’s constitution currently freezes the fair cash value of a homestead for qualifying seniors whose income does not exceed the local median income. State Question 847 would replace this with a tiered, income-based structure, allowing seniors with incomes up to 180 percent of the median to receive a special assessment limit ranging from 0.35 percent to 1.4 percent. Higher-income seniors would receive the standard 1.75 percent limit.

Assessment limits are often created to protect established property owners from rising taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. bills that could price them out of their homes, but they come with numerous unintended consequences.

First, they create a “lock-in” effect, where homeowners may be reluctant to move or improve their property because taxable value resets when a property is sold or substantially improved. This reduces housing mobility and makes it less likely that growing families or older homeowners will relocate to homes that better meet their needs.

Second, assessment limits cause similarly situated properties to have vastly different assessed values based solely on when they were purchased. Because newer property owners are more likely to have taxable values that reflect current market conditions, more of the property tax burden gets shifted onto them.

By widening the gap between market and assessed values—especially for homestead, seniors’, and agricultural properties—Oklahoma State Question 847 would shift more of Oklahoma’s property tax burdens onto non-favored properties, including commercial and industrial properties, rental properties, and second homes.

Homestead exemptions reduce property taxes on primary residences by excluding a portion of the property’s value from taxation. Two states are asking voters to massively expand their existing homestead exemptions.
Florida’s Amendment 3 would substantially increase the state’s homestead exemption for non-school district property taxes.

Under current law, Florida homeowners who qualify are exempt from all property taxes on the first $25,000 of assessed value. A second inflationInflation is when the general price of goods and services increases across the economy, reducing the purchasing power of a currency and the value of certain assets. The same paycheck covers less goods, services, and bills. It is sometimes referred to as a “hidden tax,” as it leaves taxpayers less well-off due to higher costs and “bracket creep,” while increasing the government’s spendin-adjusted exemption of $25,000 applies to assessed value beginning at $50,000 but does not apply to school district property taxes.

Florida Amendment 3 would maintain the existing $25,000 homestead exemption for school district property taxes. For all other property taxes, the amendment would increase the homestead exemption to $150,000 beginning in 2027, and to $250,000 beginning in 2028. Amendment 3 would also direct the legislature to establish a uniform procedure for counties and municipalities to increase the exemption, if they choose, to any higher level, up to the exclusion of all homestead property value.

While Florida Amendment 3 has received significant attention in recent months, Wyoming Initiative 1 should not be overlooked. This measure would add an additional homestead exemption for certain property owners to its two existing homestead exemptions.

In 2024, lawmakers adopted a long-term homeowner exemption, which now stands at 50 percent of the first $3 million in market value on primary residences of owners or spouses 65 or older, who have paid Wyoming residential property taxes for at least 25 years and who live in the home at least eight months per year.

In 2025, lawmakers adopted a 25 percent exemption on the first $1 million in market value (of both land and structures) for owner-occupants of single-family residential housing who reside in the home at least eight months per year. Those claiming the 50 percent long-term homeowner exemption may not simultaneously claim the 25 percent exemption.

Initiative 1 would create a third homestead exemption that would exempt an additional 50 percent of a home’s value (excluding the underlying land), with no value cap, for owners who have been Wyoming residents for at least one year and who lived in the home for at least six months during the preceding year. Eligible homeowners could claim both the 25 percent exemption and the new 50 percent exemption.

While both Florida Amendment 3 and Wyoming Initiative 1 would provide substantial relief to qualifying homeowners, neither would reduce the cost of providing local government services. As a result, the tax burden would ultimately get shifted onto non-favored properties, including commercial and industrial properties. Moreover, because commercial apartment buildings and multi-family dwellings that are not owner-occupied would not qualify for the exemption, the increased tax burden would likely be passed along to many renters. Furthermore, two similarly situated properties could face significantly different tax bills solely due to differences in property classification and the owners’ residency statuses, undermining the principle of tax neutrality.

Conversely, if approved by voters, the North Carolina Property Tax Levy Limit Amendment would require the North Carolina General Assembly to enact a property tax levy limit for local governments. The amendment would supplement North Carolina’s existing statutory property tax rate limit of $1.50 per $100 of assessed value.

Property values have risen significantly in recent years, outpacing inflation. In jurisdictions that have failed to adjust millages downward, property owners have experienced significant increases in their property tax bills. In North Carolina, property values rose substantially faster than inflation-adjusted property tax collections between 2018 and 2023. While some jurisdictions offset valuation increases with lower rates, others chose to capture the revenue windfall generated by higher property values.

North Carolina’s current rate limit constrains tax rates but does not directly limit total property tax collections. Valuation increases can generate significant additional revenue if rates are left unchanged or are reduced only slightly.
Levy limits are the most effective approach for constraining the growth of property tax collections, and they are a reform that each of the states mentioned here could benefit from.

Unlike assessment limits and expanded homestead exemptions, which create significant economic distortions, levy limits constrain property tax collections growth in a neutral, economically efficient manner. They directly control the growth in overall property tax collections by serving as a kind of allowance for government spending. When property values rise such that maintaining a static millage rate would increase property tax collections from existing property beyond a certain level, levy limits require that millage rates be adjusted downward, preventing unlegislated tax increases. Well-designed levy limits permit a reasonable amount of revenue growth, often incorporating adjustments for inflation and new construction.

This approach provides revenue stability for local governments while preserving the relationship between property value and property tax liability. Unlike assessment limits and homestead exemptions, levy limits do not disincentivize moving, improvements to property, or new construction.

In 2026, Iowa lawmakers enacted Senate File 2472, establishing a well-structured 2 percent property tax levy limit for cities and counties, with an allowance for new construction and improvements. Local government officials may adjust millage rates within the overall levy limit, provided they remain within Iowa’s current rate caps. Local governments may exceed the limit with voter approval at a special election.

If voters approve North Carolina’s amendment, lawmakers would have the opportunity in 2027 to follow in Iowa’s footsteps, designing a levy limit that works well for the state. A levy limit would be a structurally sound, long-term reform that preserves the property tax baseThe tax base is the total amount of income, property, assets, consumption, transactions, or other economic activity subject to taxation by a tax authority. A narrow tax base is non-neutral and inefficient. A broad tax base reduces tax administration costs and allows more revenue to be raised at lower rates., provides local governments with a stable and reliable revenue source, and avoids the distortionary policies that shift tax burdens rather than reducing them. Among the property tax relief options appearing on ballots this year, North Carolina’s proposed levy limit stands out as the most effective and economically neutral approach.

Nicole Fox is a Policy Analyst with the Center for State Tax Policy at the Tax Foundation, where she serves as a resource to policymakers in their efforts to modernize and improve the structure of their state tax codes.

articles.title: A “Token Tax” Could Kill the Promise of AI
articles.standfirst: If we want to ensure that AI raises economic growth, we shouldn’t be pursuing tax policies that are stuck in the past and represent some of the worst ideas from the early internet age.
paragraphs: Lawmakers want to taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. artificial intelligence, but the playbook they’re pulling from increasingly resembles a relic of the past.

When it comes to taxing innovation, it’s wise not to reinvent the wheel. But if we want to ensure that AI raises economic growth, we shouldn’t be pursuing tax policies that are stuck in the past and represent some of the worst ideas from the early internet age.

There is no shortage of proposals coming out of Congress to tackle the purported threats AI poses. From Sen. Bernie Sanders’s (I-VT) AI Sovereign Wealth Fund to Sen. Elizabeth Warren’s (D-MA) call for an excise tax on data centers, there is among some policymakers a fear that if AI becomes a dominant part of our economy, the tax code must have a say in its direction.
This is a preview of our full op-ed originally published in City Journal.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Garrett Watson is Vice President of Federal Tax Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. His work has been featured in The Washington Post, The Atlantic, Politico, the Associated Press and other major outlets.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

articles.title: It’s good to be flexible
articles.standfirst:
This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.  Yesterday the Chancellor told us what the minimum wage rates will be from April 2027 (well, strictly speaking he told the Times on Tuesday…). All rates – both adult and youth – will go up by 3.9 per cent. The adult rate goes to £13.21, … Continued
The post It’s good to be flexible appeared first on Resolution Foundation.
paragraphs: This blog was originally published on the Resolution Foundation’s Substack.

Yesterday the Chancellor told us what the minimum wage rates will be from April 2027 (well, strictly speaking he told the Times on Tuesday…). All rates – both adult and youth – will go up by 3.9 per cent. The adult rate goes to £13.21, a 50p increase, worth £1,040 a year for someone working 40 hours a week. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) expects inflation in Q2 next year to be 3.6 per cent; if this comes to pass, then minimum wage earners will see their pay go up slightly in real terms.

There was some chatter online in the form of “oh look, another chunky minimum wage increase”. But in fact, the Low Pay Commission (LPC) was conservative in its recommendations this year, making full use of its new freedom to be flexible in the face of labour market conditions. Some people doubted it would, because it’s not in the LPC’s recent institutional memory to do so: since 2015 the adult minimum wage has been set by following government-set targets for increases, rather than trading off pay gains for workers against employment risks. But it did, and, in my view, came to a sensible decision.

Calling the increases ‘conservative’ might sound peculiar, given that the 3.9 per cent increase in the adult rate is bigger than the 3.7 per cent increase the LPC estimated would be needed back in April for an ‘on-course rate’ (i.e. to stick to the two-thirds of median hourly wages bit of its remit). But it’s true, because new data published last week1 showed median hourly pay growth of 5.9 per cent in the year to April 2026 (see the chart below). Had it stuck doggedly to that part of its remit, this would have led to a 5.7 per cent National Living Wage (NLW) increase. As you can see in the chart, such a figure would have been way ahead of current average earnings growth (3.7 per cent in the three months to August 20262) and even further ahead of where pay growth is expected to be next year (the median forecast for 2027 among external forecasters is 3.3 per cent).

Surely, you might say, the LPC would have been mad to have done that? Maybe. But it’s more or less what happened back in 2025. The 2024 pay data came in stronger than expected (because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) had introduced a new methodology that meant more high earners in its Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings sample), and the LPC’s rigid remit meant this fed straight into the 2025 NLW uprating in a mechanical way. (It was doubly unfortunate that this accidentally big uprating came alongside the hike to employer National Insurance contributions …). The Government learned from that episode and relaxed the LPC’s remit: the ‘two-thirds of median pay’ benchmark for bite of the NLW is now a “key reference point”, not an unbending requirement[MB1] .

There’s a similar story of newfound flexibility on the youth rates. The Government’s policy is that the higher youth rate (which currently applies to 18-20-year-olds) should converge with the adult rate. The LPC had initially interpreted the Government as wanting convergence to happen within the Parliament (i.e. by 2029), which meant closing a 25 per cent gap in five years. This led to bumper increases in the youth rate, seen pretty clearly in the chart below.

If the LPC had done something similar this year – continued closing the gap to the adult rate, with a target of 2029 – then the 18-20-year-old rate would have increased by roughly 10 per cent. But the Government has responded to flashing alarm bells in the youth labour market by relaxing (or clarifying) this part of the LPC’s remit too. The LPC was told explicitly it could choose the pace of the youth-adult convergence (i.e. ‘don’t fixate on 2029’) and that it should prioritise young people’s employment prospects.

I thought this might lead to some convergence, albeit less than in recent years, resulting in a youth uprating just above the adult uprating. But the LPC paused convergence altogether. I think this was a good call. As I set out last week, we can’t say for sure that minimum wage increases are to blame for a deteriorating youth labour market, but we also can’t say that they are not, and it’s not worth taking the risk.

So overall, the LPC and Government have both shown a new flexibility when it comes to minimum wage setting, and that’s to be applauded. If labour market conditions improve, there may be scope for bigger upratings in 2028. At our recent event, Arin Dube said he thought a bite of 70 per cent or higher might be possible. Equally, if the labour market continues to struggle, caution would be the right approach again.
