articles.title: The 2026 Budget buys stability and points in the right direction on growth
articles.standfirst:
The 2026 Budget builds on the back of strong economic growth in the first half of the year. The overall direction of travel is clear and positive, writes Anna Valero, but the challenges of protecting investment and economic growth remain, especially in an environment of continued global economic storms and spending pressures. Enjoying this post? Then … Continued
The post The 2026 Budget buys stability and points in the right direction on growth first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: The 2026 Budget builds on the back of strong economic growth in the first half of the year. The overall direction of travel is clear and positive, writes Anna Valero, but the challenges of protecting investment and economic growth remain, especially in an environment of continued global economic storms and spending pressures.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

The Chancellor’s first Budget had to do three things at once in a challenging and uncertain context: maintain a credible fiscal buffer against future shocks, support households struggling with a prolonged cost of living crisis, and nurture the green shoots of growth that have emerged despite global headwinds (or, more like storms – as the Chancellor put it).

On the first two, the OBR confirmed that the Chancellor is forecast to meet the fiscal rules by 2029-30 with headroom of £15bn against the stability rule (rising to £22bn in 2030-31) which seems reasonable given the context and market expectations; and a package of household support has been set out to provide “breathing space” (though this could have been better targeted). The harder test is the third. Increasing the quantity and quality of public investment, measures to boost business investment, and a successful programme of devolution will be crucial for shaping prosperity.

Growth is what generates the tax receipts to stabilise public finances and raise living standards. The UK economy has shown resilience, with growth ranking top of the G7 in the first half of the year. Recent productivity data restatements imply that our post financial crisis slowdown was less bad than previously thought, but there’s still significant slowdown that must be addressed. The uptick in productivity (per worker) that we have seen since Q3 2024 suggests that this is possible if business investment is encouraged and confidence maintained.
The UK economy has shown resilience, with growth ranking top of the G7 in the first half of the year.

The OBR has upgraded GDP growth projection for this year (from 1.1 per cent to 1.2 per cent). This comes with a downgrade for next year and upgrades later in the forecast period. Business investment is forecast to be 0.5 per cent higher in 2030 than in the March forecast, slightly raising capital deepening and trend productivity. While not mentioned in the speech, the Prime Minister’s recent interest in getting closer to the EU could materially improve the growth outlook – the OBR’s assumption is that Brexit will reduce the level of UK productivity by 4 per cent over 15 years.

The Budget has protected public sector net investment – historically public sector investment has been low and volatile. But quality matters as well as quantity – well designed public investments that catalyse private capital are needed. The (further) £20.4 billion boost to the Public Finance Institutions, enabled by the previous Chancellor’s change to the fiscal rules, is crucial here and will channel more support towards renewable energy, defence, AI and other areas.

The AI package (confirmed at £700 million) which will help the UK to benefit from the opportunities of AI, while managing the risks and shaping adjustment, puts more resource behind the Prime Minister’s ambition to take a lead on these themes during the UK’s G20 presidency. And the Data Centre Covenant is a positive step for ensuring that this type of infrastructure investment benefits communities. On the green transition, the Energy Wealth Fund announced alongside the Jackdaw decision will enable extra tax revenues to be channelled towards clean energy projects, improving energy affordability and resilience and generating sustainable growth.

The main risk is reprioritisation away from areas that were identified as being important for growth and in line with the Modern Industrial Strategy of 2025 (that is already generating positive outcomes), with departments finding savings to be able to fund the Defence Investment Plan.

The absence of new broad-based taxes on business is positive for investment. The anticipated increase to the banks corporation tax surcharge is temporary and smaller than that expected, with these and some other taxes (e.g. on gambling) paying for reliefs. But the more interesting question is whether new targeted reliefs address real market failures that prevent investment in productive, resilient assets. New reliefs for entrepreneurs and to business rates for retail and hospitality businesses are welcome but are not a substitute for deeper reform consistently called for by the IFS and others. Moreover, the key barriers for high-growth firms are at the scale up phase, where pensions reform, catalytic capital and bolder action on procurement and regulation (mentioned by the Chancellor) are likely to matter more. Skills shortages are another barrier consistently highlighted by businesses, and further measures to incentivise investment should be explored.

High energy costs are a problem for UK businesses, particularly energy intensive ones. A key challenge is to ensure that short-term support does not dampen incentives to invest in cheaper, more resilient, clean alternatives. Here, the Chancellor began with an emphasis on longer term energy reforms – including breaking the link between gas prices and the costs of electricity, and pledges to limit policy costs in bills. Such reforms will support electrification as well as reduce costs, and are accompanied by other more immediate support.

The forthcoming 10-year plan, the outcomes of the Milburn and Timms reviews that will inform much-needed welfare reform and associated savings, and next year’s Spending Review will determine whether this direction or travel delivers the desired outcomes.

Non-fiscal measures to reduce the costs of regulation had already been announced before Budget, but the announcement to bring the Better Regulation Executive back was new. This language matters – much regulation exists for a reason, and indeed, new technologies, transitions and risks call for new regulations to shape investment. What matters is that the regulation is designed and implemented effectively, provides certainty and supports innovation.

Large and persistent regional disparities must be addressed, both to improve living standards and to improve national growth performance. In a highly centralised economy, well-designed fiscal devolution can align incentives for growth locally, generate income streams for leaders to borrow against, and give regional leaders – armed with local knowledge – complementary levers that work together for growth. The new fiscal devolution roadmap sets out new steps on business rates retention and a share of income tax assigned to mayors from 2028 (when new powers for visitor levies also come into effect). Building capacity, balancing incentives for growth with equalisation for places losing out, and improving coordination between national and regional policymakers on place-based decision-making will be important for success.

The Budget gives a clear direction of travel: stability and breathing space first, setting up some big decisions ahead. The forthcoming 10-year plan, the outcomes of the Milburn and Timms reviews that will inform much-needed welfare reform and associated savings, and next year’s Spending Review will determine whether this direction delivers the desired outcomes. The last Spending Review involved difficult decisions and prioritisation, and higher inflation erodes the value of settlements. The central challenge will be protecting investment and pro-growth reforms while competing pressures, including defence and any continued global economic storms, mount.

Anna Valero is a Professor in Practice at the LSE’s Centre for Economic Performance and Global School of Sustainability; Director of the CEP’s Growth Programme and Deputy Director of the Programme on Innovation and Diffusion. Her research focuses on the drivers of productivity and innovation in firms and regions, and in particular on informing policies for environmentally sustainable and inclusive growth. Anna was a member of the Council of Economic Advisers to the Chancellor of the Exchequer in 2024-25 advising on growth, and Industrial Strategy Adviser in 2025-2026. She has held a number of other advisory roles for the UK government and policy institutions.

articles.title: Budget 2026 – continuity with Reeves
articles.standfirst:
John Healey’s 2026 Budget follows the fiscal foundations set down by Rachel Reeves, writes John Van Reenen. But while stability has been preserved, many tough decisions including welfare reform and funding increasing healthcare and defence spending have been postponed. Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles. The … Continued
The post Budget 2026 – continuity with Reeves first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: John Healey’s 2026 Budget follows the fiscal foundations set down by Rachel Reeves, writes John Van Reenen. But while stability has been preserved, many tough decisions including welfare reform and funding increasing healthcare and defence spending have been postponed.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

The global backdrop to John Healey’s first Budget was Made in America, crafted by President Trump. Earlier this year, inflation was projected to be heading back to the 2 per cent target, but the Iran War torpedoed that with a huge spike in energy prices. Market jitters over the high and growing US deficit has pushed up bond yields everywhere, and this has added significantly to the cost of servicing UK debt – to the tune of £14bn.

But there is some good news. UK growth has been resilient this year, and productivity growth – the fundamental determinant of living standards in the long term – is looking up. Our research shows that since Labour was elected, output per worker growth has been 1.6 per cent, per annum, compared to 0.3 per cent in the previous decade. Moreover, the ONS now reckons that productivity per hour was twice as fast since the 2008-9 global financial crisis than previously thought. This is still about half of the pre-crisis average, but the UK now looks much less of an outlier.

The Budget has followed the fiscal foundations laid down by Rachel Reeves. The Chancellor kept to the strong framework laid down in 2024. Day-to-day spending has to be balanced in three years, by the end of this parliament. The previous government had targeted five years away, far too distant to be credible.

I believe that there is an unhealthy obsession about the precise “headroom” against this Stability Rule. Nevertheless, the fall from £24bn to £15bn is in line with expectations and uses Reeves’ buffer to do its job of insuring against uncertain times.
The Budget has followed the fiscal foundations laid down by Rachel Reeves.

The Budget has giveaways of 0.25 per cent of GDP 2026/27, most eye-catchingly the £2.6bn in £100 payments to households to help with their energy bills. These giveaways were balanced by tax rises: a temporary 3 per cent increase in the Bank Surcharge (raising £1bn next year) and 2 per cent more on savings and property taxes (£1bn p.a.).

Earlier this month, IMF ​Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva said “The UK is actually one country where action to reduce debt and deficit has been taken decisively.” This fiscal consolidation is possible only through the difficult decision to significantly raise taxes in Labour’s first two budgets. Healey’s tax rises amount to £6.5bn in 2030/31 compared to the £66bn. The past Chancellor took the hit for these politically unpopular decisions.

There has been much glib commentary on the need to radically reduce public spending. But this ignores the fact that the current plans from the 2025 Budget already incorporated tight spending limits over the next three years. This is further sharpened by the increase in inflation because departmental spending plans are set in cash terms, so their real value is eroded when inflation rises. Since the Chancellor has not increased the envelope to compensate for this, it means tough times ahead.
The challenge will be to keep to these plans. The multi-year Spending Review next year that determines the splits between departments will crystallize these trade-offs.

Although the OBR upgraded this year to 1.2 per cent GDP growth, it downgraded next year’s to 1.0 per cent. The better news on UK productivity growth does not (yet) seem reflected in its forecasts, perhaps unsurprisingly as it downgraded long-run productivity growth only last autumn.

Andy Burnham is betting big on decentralisation to boost growth by allowing more local control over taxes such as business rates (20 per cent next year and all by the end of the decade). I welcome this as it will give local leaders more “skin in the game”. But it also requires the government to allow places who use these revenues wisely and do better to pull away from those who do not – even if this generates some regional inequality. And the momentum on national strategic priorities such as the Oxford-Cambridge corridor and Heathrow expansion must not be lost.

Reeves’ net debt rule sensibly made allowance for the assets of public financial institutions, such as the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, as well as liabilities. This has created space for the extra £20bn announced today to help business investments in infrastructure such as energy, AI and defence.
Ending the triple lock is a great move, but we must return to reforming disability benefits.

The Better Regulation Executive is an opportunity to bolster the positive planning reforms and push back against excessively costly ones. Increasing housing supply through existing deregulation (e.g., Planning and Infrastructure Act) is better than the new ‘Your First home Scheme’ which spends £4.7bn on boosting demand.
Perhaps inevitably, this was a “steady as she goes” Budget. It means many crunch decisions have been postponed until next year.

First, welfare needs to be tackled. Ending the triple lock is a great move, but we must return to reforming disability benefits. The Timms and Milburn reviews must be the basis for more radical reform, not reversals and prevarication.

Second, the baroque structure of UK tax needs serious reform. There are too many cliff-edges and regulatory taxes on growth that keep firms small such as the high threshold for VAT registration. Property taxation is a mess.

Third, defence was why Healey ejected Keir Starmer’s. Defence spending increases must be made a growth rich as possible and not come from cuts to other public capital investment. Public R&D, in particular, needs increasing in the military and elsewhere.

Finally, how are we to pay for health over the long-term? Demographics and other forces mean that healthcare costs as a share of GDP will inevitably rise further. The creation of an NHS for social care will add to these costs.

The scale of defence and health spending makes it inevitable that these will require increases in general taxation. It follows that the main parties cannot continue with their refusal to countenance increases in the rates of income tax, VAT or employees’ National Insurance. It is better to face this reality than to be forced to act when the crisis comes.

articles.title: Breathing Space, Not a Strategy
articles.standfirst: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council...
paragraphs: Today’s Budget has seen the Chancellor deliver some ‘breathing space’ to households struggling with cost-of-living pressures via a mild fiscal loosening, most obviously through changes to energy bills and council taxes. Against an already difficult domestic and international macroeconomic backdrop, which has created a strain on the public finances, the net effect of today’s measures has been a reduction in the Chancellor’s buffer against his fiscal rules from £23.6 billion in March to £14.5 billion now. Market reaction to the Budget was subsequently muted. Ten-year gilt yields fell by only a few basis points on Wednesday afternoon, while sterling hardly budged.

Therefore, while today’s Budget appears to have not resulted in a backlash from the markets, maintaining a backloaded path for tax rises and deferring major fiscal decisions on defence and other spending until the 2027 Spending Review to buy time is not a credible fiscal strategy.

The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 100 basis points since February, to around 5.3 per cent. As explained in this blog, some of that rise can be traced to the war in the Middle East and would presumably unwind if there were a resolution. But over half of it likely reflects other factors, including heavy government borrowing worldwide and the AI investment boom, which have pushed up global long-term real interest rates. These are forces that could exert a persistent effect on gilt yields.

The DMO’s financing remit for 2026-27 has been modestly revised up today by £7.4 billion, taking planned gilt issuance to £250.6 billion. This means taking on additional debt at what could prove to be a persistently higher cost of borrowing.
Successive economic shocks this century have ratcheted up the debt-to-GDP ratio. After both the global financial crisis and the pandemic, debt stabilised at a higher level.

But for fiscal policy to act as a shock absorber, the government needs to have adequate capacity to step in and act when the next shock hits the economy. A consistently high debt ratio limits this ability. Therefore, the minimal test of credibility of for today’s budget was whether the Chancellor was willing to stop the debt rising even further.

The OBR forecasts that policies announced in this budget will lead to increased borrowing over the next three years of £12.4 billion, which will then be followed by a reduction of £7 billion on average in the years after. Based on the forecast paths laid out by the OBR today we can see that our minimal test of credibility was not met with Public Sector Net Debt peaking at around 97 per cent of GDP in 2028-29 before falling only slightly to 96 per cent of GDP in 2031-32, higher than the ratio in August this year of 94 per cent.
Today’s Budget comes against a fragile global backdrop as the risk of adverse shocks appears to have increased over the past year. Bond markets are jittery and looking for the next shoe to drop

UK ten-year gilt yields remain the highest in the G7, leaving the public finances exposed to shifts in market sentiment. In our judgement, this strengthens the case for building fiscal buffers. The Chancellor’s decision to reduce headroom by £9 billion therefore leaves the government vulnerable to future shocks.

This is underscored by the path for debt interest now being higher than was set out in March 2026. By the end of the decade UK debt interest is expected to rise to around £150 billion annually – more than the government currently spends on education.

A credible fiscal strategy could help to reduce debt interest. Even modest fiscal restraint could deliver a credibility dividend of 10-20 basis points off gilt rates (worth around £1-2 billion a year by the end of the parliament).

Today’s Budget measures do not attempt to place the debt-to-GDP ratio on a sustained downward path in the medium term. Difficult decisions have, once again, been deferred, leaving the integrity of public finances contingent on good fortune. But hoping for the best is not a credible basis for managing the public finances. This approach leaves the UK government more exposed to renewed market scrutiny in the months ahead.
The longer the Chancellor delays the necessary adjustment, the larger, and more difficult, these adjustments will be.

The intersection of migration policy, public opinions and economic reality has become one of the most pressing challenges for successive UK governments. A challenging labour market and falling net migration have exposed…

articles.title: How Much Does the US Government Lose to Tax Fraud?
articles.standfirst: While the government will never close the tax gap or fully eliminate tax fraud, lawmakers and the IRS can institute several reforms to reduce the gap, including simplifying the tax code, increasing third-party information reporting, and coordinating anti-fraud efforts.
paragraphs: A recent report by the nonpartisan Government Accountability Office (GAO) estimates the federal government loses $116 billion to $304 billion annually to taxA tax is a mandatory payment or charge collected by local, state, and national governments from individuals or businesses to cover the costs of general government services, goods, and activities. fraud. That amounts to between two and six percent of federal taxes owed. It also exceeds the entire budget of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), a leading anti-poverty program.
The report adds to the case for a simpler tax code and better-coordinated fraud enforcement at the IRS.

Tax fraud is one component of the larger tax gapThe tax gap is the difference between taxes legally owed and taxes collected. The gross tax gap in the U.S. accounts for at least $441 billion in lost revenue each year, according to the latest estimate by the IRS (2011 to 2013), suggesting a voluntary taxpayer compliance rate of 83.6 percent. The net tax gap is calculated by subtracting late tax collections from the gross tax gap: from 2011 to 2—the gap between estimated federal taxes owed and actual federal taxes paid on time each year. The GAO study is novel in its attempt to formally measure tax fraud within the tax gap; the IRS does not offer a separate estimate of tax revenue lost due to fraud.

GAO reports that much of the revenue lost due to tax fraud occurs in the so-called “shadow economy.” The shadow economy, which economic literature reviewed by GAO suggests could equal anywhere from two to nine percent of GDP, includes:

The larger tax gap measures taxpayer noncompliance through intentional fraud and unintentional errors, and was about $696 billion as of tax year 2022. That amounts to 15 percent of taxes owed and indicates fraud is about 17 to 44 percent of the tax gap—a substantial share.
After the IRS collected late payments and money recovered through audits (about $90 billion), the remaining gap was $606 billion.

Most of the tax gap, about 77 percent, is from underreporting, with the remainder due to nonfiling and underpayment of tax. Most of the underreporting, about 71 percent, occurs in the individual income taxAn individual income tax (or personal income tax) is levied on the wages, salaries, investments, or other forms of income an individual or household earns. The U.S. imposes a progressive income tax where rates increase with income. The Federal Income Tax was established in 1913 with the ratification of the 16th Amendment. Though barely 100 years old, individual income taxes are the largest source, concentrated in sole proprietorship income, representing $117 billion or 17 percent of the tax gap. The IRS finds that sole proprietorship income and other sources of income with little to no third-party reporting or withholdingWithholding is the income an employer takes out of an employee’s paycheck and remits to the federal, state, and/or local government. It is calculated based on the amount of income earned, the taxpayer’s filing status, the number of allowances claimed, and any additional amount the employee requests. tend to have high rates of noncompliance.

A related issue—and one component of the tax gap—is improper payments associated with refundable tax credits, such as the earned income tax creditA tax credit is a provision that reduces a taxpayer’s final tax bill, dollar-for-dollar. A tax credit differs from deductions and exemptions, which reduce taxable income rather than the taxpayer’s tax bill directly. (EITC) and the child tax credit (CTC). Improper payments are either overpayments or underpayments that the government should not have made or could not verify were made to the correct person in the correct amount. According to the latest estimates by the Treasury Department and the IRS, improper payments in fiscal year 2025 totaled $28.1 billion for four major refundable tax credits.

As with the overall tax gap, not all improper payments of refundable credits are due to intentional fraud. The complex rules and confusing structure of the EITC, CTC, and PTC can lead to unintentional errors—and ultimately overpayments or underpayments—which are all labeled improper payments in government data.
It is not possible to eliminate fraud completely, which GAO recognizes, nor is it possible to eliminate the tax gap. However, improvements could be made to reduce fraud and the tax gap.

And what of the bulk of the tax gap that is not due to fraud? Based on IRS analysis of the tax gap as well as our understanding of the problems associated with tax complexity in the US and other countries, we recommend the following:

Tax complexity is a serious problem. It leads to taxpayer confusion and errors and imposes a significant compliance cost, about $544 billion this year—nearly the size of the tax gap. Much of the tax code’s complexity and compliance cost falls on businesses.

The complexity of the business tax code reflects the challenge of defining business income, including rules that differ by business form (C corporations, S corporations, partnerships, sole proprietorships, etc.), and a multitude of information reporting requirements (such as 1099 forms) that generally serve to bolster compliance across the broader federal tax system. In that sense, it is challenging to streamline the tax code in a way that boosts compliance.

One option is fundamental reform that replaces complicated corporate and other business income taxes with a tax on distributed profits, combined with a simplified individual income tax at the same rate. This approach has been successful in Estonia and other countries, resulting in low compliance costs, a low corporate tax gap, and a competitive tax code with revenues on par with other developed countries. A more piecemeal approach would eliminate unnecessarily complicated deductions, credits, minimum taxes, and other special provisions from the tax code.

Congress can also reduce improper payments of refundable credits by simplifying the tax code and streamlining definitions. For example, the EITC currently differs by filing status and number of children, and parents and guardians must go through a complex set of steps to determine if their child is eligible. The qualifying child rules also differ between the EITC and CTC, adding to taxpayer confusion.

The EITC and CTC could be simplified by consolidating the child benefit in one credit—a reformed child credit—and limiting the EITC to a per-worker incentive regardless of family dimensions. This was proposed by former Sen. Mitt Romney (R-UT), for example.

Another way to reduce improper payments is to expand Treasury’s Do Not Pay system. As noted by Romina Boccia, Treasury has recently bolstered the system and found some success in preventing payments to deceased recipients. However, Treasury lacks statutory authority to expand the system to effectively check improper payments related to employment status, income, and identity.

The federal government loses hundreds of billions of dollars per year to tax fraud, and hundreds of billions more to unintentional noncompliance. While it is impossible for the federal government to eliminate tax fraud or fully close the tax gap, Congress can make improvements to the tax code—and the IRS to tax administration—that reduce the gap and close openings for fraudsters. At the top of the list should be simplifying a Byzantine tax code that contributes to the gap between taxes owed and taxes paid.
Subscribe to our free newsletter to get the latest tax data, news and analysis.

Dr. William McBride is the Chief Economist & Stephen J. Entin Fellow in Economics at the Tax Foundation, where he oversees major research projects primarily related to reforming the federal tax code, advancing sound tax policy, and improving the federal government’s fiscal outlook.

Andrew Lautz is Senior Director of Federal Policy with Tax Foundation’s Center for Federal Tax Policy. Before joining Tax Foundation, he was Director of Tax Policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center and Director of Federal Policy at the National Taxpayers Union. Andrew’s research and perspectives on federal tax policy have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, and other major publications.

The post The Budget should not price young people out of work first appeared on LSE British Politics.
paragraphs: As part of the Budget the Chancellor usually announces any changes to the minimum wage. As AI is eating into entry level jobs, Grace Lordan makes the case for why the Government should refrain from further increasing the youth minimum wage relative to the adult rate.
Enjoying this post? Then sign up to our newsletter and receive a weekly roundup of all our articles.

John Healey is about to deliver his first Budget, and the first fiscal event of Andy Burnham’s premiership. The figures from the Office for National Statistics, put vacancies at 691,000, below pre-pandemic levels, with payrolled employment still falling. Youth unemployment is 15.6 per cent, with 54,000 more young people out of work than a year ago. In the three months to July the rate reached 16.4 per cent, the highest since 2014. Around a million young people are not in education, employment or training, and the Learning and Work Institute counts 5.3 people out of work and wanting a job for every vacancy.

The Government is already trying to help, paying firms to take on young people, through a £3,000 Youth Jobs Grant and a Jobs Guarantee that funds six months of part-time wages for the long-term unemployed. Healey has also added £100 million for mayor-run apprenticeship services.

Yet within weeks of the Budget, the Low Pay Commission will recommend the minimum wage rates for April 2027, and its remit still says the Government remains committed to aligning the 18-20 rate with the National Living Wage. That rate rose already by 8.5 per cent in April, to £10.85, against a 4.1 per cent raise for adults. One arm of the Government pays firms to hire young people. Another makes them more expensive. In a time when AI is eating away at entry-level jobs and the country has one million NEETs, the Government should stop raising the youth minimum wage faster than the adult rate.

For most of the minimum wage’s life, the evidence supported raising youth rates. Employers absorbed the cost, trimmed hours or raised prices, and jobs did not vanish. The Low Pay Commission still finds no robust evidence linking the youth rate to youth unemployment, and the Resolution Foundation concludes that minimum wage policy has not been a key driver of the rise in the NEET rate since 2019, and the IFS finds no clear evidence that it has been.
Once a worker and a machine are close substitutes, the price of the worker decides which one gets hired.

That held while the tasks a younger worker did had no substitute. That is no longer the case. Generative AI now drafts, summarises, codes, answers tickets and reconciles data. This is the routine work that was the first rung of a professional career. Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab finds that in the US since generative AI spread, employment of 22 to 25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations has fallen 13 per cent relative to other workers, concentrated where AI automates rather than augments. Britain’s figures point in the same direction. Fifteen months after graduating, 72 per cent of employed graduates were in professional-level jobs, down from 75 per cent a year earlier.

My work with Cecily Josten found that the jobs safest from automation are those needing non-linear abstract thinking, or people skills combined with brains, with codifiable routine jobs going first. Entry-level work is codifiable by design. Once a worker and a machine are close substitutes, the price of the worker decides which one gets hired.

But most minimum wage jobs are not knowledge work; they are in cafés, supermarkets and warehouses. What reaches them is then the second-round effect. When graduates cannot find professional work they move down the ladder. This is not just theory: one in ten employed graduates are in retail, catering, waiting or bar work fifteen months after graduating. Beaudry, Green and Sand found the same cascade in the United States after 2000, as high-skilled workers took less skilled jobs and pushed lower-skilled workers further down the ladder, some out of work altogether.

With David Neumark I studied US data from 1980 to 2015 on jobs that are easy to automate. Raising the minimum wage cut the share of those jobs held by low-skilled workers, who became more likely to end up out of work or in worse jobs. The effects were largest for older workers in manufacturing, and we found some evidence that opportunities improved for the higher-skilled workers who tend the machines.

I then repeated the exercise for Britain in a report commissioned by the Low Pay Commission. Using data from 1994 to 2017, a £1 rise in the minimum wage cut the share of automatable low-skilled employment by 0.24 percentage points, and by 0.58 in manufacturing. The effects were very modest, implying substitution had so far been limited. In the main estimates, workers under 25 were not the group affected. The machines of that era were robotic arms, replacing older men on assembly lines. But the report warned that the set of automatable jobs was evolving, and that the past was no guide to who would be replaced next.
the 18 to 20 minimum wage rate has risen 45 per cent in three years, from £7.49 to £10.85, taking it from 72 to 85 per cent of the adult rate.

If you raise the price of a worker whose tasks a machine can do, some of that work can move to the machine. In 2017 it was older factory workers. In 2026 it is younger professional workers, and also possibly school leavers on tills and counters that self-service machines can replace. In fact, the Bank of England’s agents report warehouse operators looking to automate after recent labour cost inflation, and retail and hospitality have shed 117,000 employees in a year, more than all other industries combined. Out-of-work benefit claims have risen most among 18 to 20-year-olds, from 7.2 to 9.4 per cent between 2022 and 2025. Meanwhile the 18 to 20 minimum wage rate has risen 45 per cent in three years, from £7.49 to £10.85, taking it from 72 to 85 per cent of the adult rate. A price rise of that size, for workers who have just become substitutable, lies outside anything in the Commission’s known evidence base.

Picture a café manager choosing between a graduate who cannot find professional work, a school leaver with few qualifications, and a kiosk. The school leaver costs £10.85 an hour, the graduate £12.71. Convergence would close that gap, removing the one thing the school leaver can compete on, so the job goes to credentials or to the machine. After minimum wage rises in the US, employers became more likely to demand a high school diploma for low-wage jobs, and more-skilled teenagers left school for work, pushing less-skilled teenagers into neither work nor study. The Bank of England’s agents report British firms favouring “experienced, immediately productive hires”.

That is why this is so dangerous. Those pushed out have the fewest alternatives. 84 per cent of NEETs aged 18 to 24 carry at least one disadvantage, and unemployment in youth raises the risk of unemployment well into adulthood, at least for men. The gains, meanwhile, flow up. At a large US retailer, the extra teenagers employed after a minimum wage rise were disproportionately the more affluent. In Britain, full-time students make up more than a quarter of young people in low hourly pay, and university students are disproportionately from better-off homes. A policy meant for the low paid might end up favouring the student with a bedroom at home over the school leaver whose only income is the job.

The Resolution Foundation estimates that holding the youth rate at its 2023 share of the adult rate would have put 15,000 more 16 to 20-year-olds in work in 2025-26, at no cost to the Exchequer. It is not a free lunch. The 230,000 young people already paid the current rates would be worse off. But a pay rise is worth nothing to someone who is not hired, and the Foundation itself now recommends pausing convergence and dropping the commitment to it.

The Government has expressed concern over the future of NEETs, so one thing the Chancellor could do is announce that the 18 to 20 rate will not move further towards the adult rate while youth unemployment is rising, and the Commission’s remit should be amended to match.

The Commission should measuring the substitutability of young workers directly. Its evidence base was built on robotic arms, not language models or self-service kiosks. For each job where the youth rate bites, it should ask how close the machine substitute is and how many over-qualified applicants are queuing for it, and let the answers steer the rate.
The test for 28 October is simple. Taken together with the rates for April 2027, does the Budget make a young person cheaper or dearer relative to the machine that can now do their first job?
Nine years ago my report for the Commission concluded that substitution had so far been limited, and asked policymakers to monitor the trend. The trend has arrived. The “so far” has run out.

Grace Lordan is Associate Professor in Behavioural Science at London School of Economics and Founding Director of The Inclusion Initiative. She served as an expert advisor to the UK government on their skills and productivity board and currently leads the £2 million ESRC-funded Diversity and Productivity from Education to Work (DAPEW) project. Her book Think Big: Take Small Steps and Build the Future You Want is published by Penguin.

articles.title: Proposing heating efficiency standards for Europe
paragraphs: More than half of the European Union’s natural gas imports are burned to keep buildings warm, with the heating and cooling of buildings using fossil fuels responsible for 12 percent of the bloc’s greenhouse gas emissions in 20241. Both the gas import bill and emissions could be reduced if the installation of heat pumps in EU buildings were ramped up. Europe has a strong manufacturing capacity and innovation base for producing heat pumps, which are beneficial for the climate, energy security, affordability and European jobs.

However, heat pumps cost more to buy and install than gas boilers: up to five times more, depending on the country (Toleikyte et al, 2024). Because a heat pump is about three times as efficient as a boiler, it is cheaper to run only if electricity costs less than about three times as much as gas. In 2025, this cost ratio was 1.9 in France but 3.2 in Germany2, meaning the extra cost of a heat pump is recouped in about three years in France but 13 years in Germany (LCP Delta, 2025).

In July 2026, the European Commission published an Electrification Action Plan (European Commission, 2026), with a goal of making electricity cheaper relative to gas, including through tax reform. In relation to heat pumps, the Commission said it would explore a “clean heat market mechanism” to narrow “the upfront cost difference for heat pumps”. At the time of writing, no further details have been offered on how such a system might work.

In this analysis, we propose basic principles for such a scheme. We draw inspiration from the EU’s carbon dioxide emission standards for new cars, which have spurred sales of electric vehicles3. We also look at lessons from what we regard as an unsuccessful attempt by the United Kingdom to introduce a heating market mechanism and draw on a comprehensive analysis of options by Agora Energiewende (2025). We begin with a brief overview of the market for heat pumps in the EU, then discuss how to design a scheme based on the efficiency of heating appliances as a useful benchmark. Finally, we set out three arguments on the benefits of such a system.

Despite their relatively higher cost, EU sales of heat pumps have grown since 2019, reaching 28 percent of sales of water-based heating systems in 2025 (Figure 1). Sales jumped in 2022 and 2023 during the European energy crisis and have since fallen back slightly. Heat pumps make up 97 percent of heating sales in Sweden and 70 percent in Denmark. In Germany, heat pumps outsold gas boilers for the first time in 2025, comprising 48 percent of all sales4.

About half (53 percent) of Europeans heat their homes with self-contained systems, 27 percent use central heating shared by their building and 13 percent are connected to district heating networks5 (Eurostat, 2026). Across this building stock, approximately 68 million gas and 18 million oil boilers are installed, compared to around 11 million hydronic heat pumps6. Thus, about one in ten heating systems are heat pumps, many of which serve several households (in apartment blocks, for example).

Rather than generating heat – like a boiler does by burning fuel – a heat pump extracts heat from outside air and transfers it indoors for space and water heating7. This makes heat pumps remarkably efficient. One unit of electricity delivers around three units of heat. By comparison, an efficient gas or oil boiler typically delivers around 0.9 units of heat per unit of energy consumed. The heat-pump efficiency gain could cut heating bills by up to 60 percent (European Commission, 2026).

The scheme’s aim would be for the share of heat pumps in overall heating sales to increase steadily from about 30 percent today (see Figure 1). This could be achieved by setting heat pump sales quotas that tighten each year for the companies that manufacture and sell heating systems. Companies that fail to meet their quotas would be fined proportionately to how far from the target they are. Companies that sell more heat pumps than required, including companies that manufacture only heat pumps, would generate credits that can be sold to lagging firms.

In April 2025, the UK launched a Clean Heat Market Mechanism, which requires manufacturers to sell specified numbers of heat pumps relative to gas boilers, with a £500 fine for each unit below the target8. Early evidence suggests that manufacturers that sell both technologies have responded by discounting heat pumps to meet the target, rather than by purchasing credits from other manufacturers (Agora Energiewende, 2025). This suggests that an EU scheme must set ambitious targets and sufficiently high fines. If the target is not ambitious enough, demand does not increase, and the result is to shift sales away from heat-pump-only manufacturers to those that also sell boilers.

A second lesson from the UK scheme is how to define what counts towards the target. Heat pumps come in different shapes and sizes, with varying efficiencies. The UK scheme covers only hydronic heat pumps, excluding air-to-air units9. Instead of listing technologies in scope, an EU scheme should be based on appliance energy efficiency.

Heating appliances sold in the EU are already rated for energy efficiency10. These ratings could provide the basis for manufacturer-wide efficiency standards, tightened annually. More-efficient heat pumps would contribute more towards the quota than less-efficient units, while hybrid units would contribute less. Manufacturers exceeding their quotas would generate credits that can be sold to those falling short. The approach would be similar to EU vehicle emissions standards, under which annual fleet-wide carbon dioxide emissions targets are applied to carmakers11.

A complication is that heating appliances differ in their capacities and uses. While hydronic heat pumps typically provide enough heat for a whole home, air-to-air units often serve individual rooms, and multiple units can be installed in single homes. Air-to-air units are also used for cooling; excluding them, as the UK scheme does, is not appropriate. However, counting them in full would be disproportionate. A fractional credit could be applied based on rated heating capacity and estimated potential to displace fossil-fuel heating.

Boosting heat pump sales is uncontroversial as a way to cut emissions and gas imports. Heat pumps are the most cost-effective technology to decarbonise heating at scale (Rosenow, 2022). Heating efficiency standards, as proposed above, should offer three main benefits.

Most households face borrowing or spending constraints. Upfront rather than lifecycle costs weigh substantially more on decision-making when purchasing energy technologies such as solar panels or heat pumps (De Groote and Verboven, 2019; ICF, 2024).

EU policy on heat pumps focuses currently on reducing their running costs. The European Commission’s Electrification Action Plan asks countries to bring household electricity prices to no more than 2.5 times the price of gas by 2030, mainly by cutting taxes and levies on electricity (European Commission, 2026). In addition, from 2028, a carbon price will be put on fuels used for heating in the EU12. This will improve the investment case for heat pumps, though the carbon price would need to be very high in certain markets. In Germany, a carbon price of around €350 per tonne of CO2 would be needed to repay a heat pump’s extra cost within ten years13. That is more than twice the roughly €150 per tonne analysts expect by 203014.

A heating efficiency standard would complement these policies by creating a direct financial incentive for manufacturers to compete aggressively to make heat pumps more affordable. Each additional heat pump sold would help manufacturers meet their obligations and avoid fines or the cost of purchasing credits. Manufacturers could also pass some of the cost of compliance onto gas boiler sales. Over time, a larger and more predictable heat pump market should also reduce costs by providing investment certainty for production, distribution and financing models.

Household decisions on what kind of heating unit to adopt depend heavily on advice from installers. Gas boilers have been the incumbent option for decades. Shifting to heat pumps requires overcoming path dependence.

One in four heating systems in the EU is replaced only following a breakdown (Energy Systems Catapult, 2026). Heat pumps are then often not a practical alternative, not least because there is a relative shortage of specialists trained in heat pump installation (LCP Delta, 2025; HPA UK, 2024).

Boiler manufacturers incentivise installers, much as carmakers set sales targets and bonuses for their dealers. Most installers are trained and certified in academies primarily funded by boiler manufacturers (Toleikyte et al, 2024). Manufacturer loyalty schemes pay installers for each boiler fitted; Ideal Heating, for example, pays £20 to £55 per boiler registered15.

A heating efficiency standard would push manufacturers to invest in commercial loyalty schemes for efficient installations, giving installers an incentive to recommend heat pumps. Following the introduction of the UK Clean Heat Market Mechanism, manufacturer Worcester Bosch began paying installers £500 for each heat pump fitted, matching the £500 fine per missing heat pump16.

EU factories have a manufacturing capacity of 7.7 million heat pumps per year, but sold only two million units in 2024 (Volt et al, 2025). The sector employed about 80,000 people in the EU in 2023, and Europe accounts for almost half of global heat pump patent families (inventions patented in one or more countries) filed since 2000 (Bruegel, 2026). Steady demand would help European producers fill idle capacity and reduce costs.

National subsidies in Europe have boosted heat-pump take-up, but have also been stop-start. Sales of air-to-water heat pumps fell by 35 percent in Italy in 2024 when a tax credit covering up to 110 percent of renovation costs ended. Austria saw a sales dip of 17 percent in 2025 after federal grants for replacing fossil heating systems expired (EHPA, 2025a; EHPA, 2026). A clear annual trajectory would provide manufacturers with more certainty about demand.

articles.title: The Minimal Credibility Test For The Autumn 2026 Budget
articles.standfirst: The ground has been prepared for a quiet Budget, albeit one in which the Chancellor’s buffer against the fiscal rules comes in perhaps £10 billion lower than the £23 billion...
paragraphs: The ground has been prepared for a quiet Budget, albeit one in which the Chancellor’s buffer against the fiscal rules comes in perhaps £10 billion lower than the £23 billion the OBR found in March. This so-called “headroom” is nothing more than the margin by which the OBR expects the current budget to be in surplus three years out, the point at which the fiscal rules are now tested. Running it down means a higher expected level of borrowing three years from now than previously planned (and nothing about the years in between).

In this week’s blog, Ben Caswell and I consider whether that is the right call from a macroeconomic standpoint. Our answer is no, for three reasons. First, the economy does not need a fiscal stimulus. Second, the rise in borrowing costs this year looks mostly persistent, so the argument for borrowing through a temporary shock does not apply. Third, markets are jittery and looking for the next shoe to drop. This is the environment to strengthen our fiscal position, not weaken it, and the case is stronger still if one believes the risk outlook has deteriorated.

Assuming we do end up with extra borrowing at the Budget, the minimal test of credibility is whether the higher borrowing through year three of the forecast is accompanied with correspondingly lower borrowing in the years after it: whether, in the language of control theory, the framework delivers “integral control”, so that overshoots in the stock of debt are made up later rather than forgiven. It is the minimal test because the government’s planned consolidation path is already time-inconsistent: back-loaded towards the last possible date for the next general election, when governments are not traditionally incentivised to deliver fiscal restraint. Our recent survey with Ipsos suggests that the public are ahead of the politicians in understanding the scale of fiscal retrenchment needed to bring the public finances into good shape.

Growth has proved far more resilient than almost anyone expected in March. GDP has grown by 1.8 per cent so far this year, with four months still to go. That is remarkable, and it exceeds anyone’s estimate of trend; our own is 1.3 per cent. The labour market tells the same story. Unemployment has fallen since the start of the year and is now half a percentage point below the OBR’s March forecast.

Inflation, meanwhile, is above target and rising. CPI inflation was 3.5 per cent in September, up for three months running, and with energy prices higher again since the summer most of the shock has still to reach consumer prices. We expect inflation above 4 per cent in the first quarter of next year. Some of the direct effect of the energy shock of course. But pay growth is running close to 4 per cent, against the 3 per cent or so the Bank of England regards as consistent with the target, and the main round of pay settlements falls early in the new year, when inflation will be above 4 per cent. The risk of second-round persistence has grown.

If we take the OIS curve literally, markets already price 100 basis points or more of increases in Bank Rate over the next twelve months. A Budget that adds to demand would push that path higher still; the looser the fiscal stance, the more of the work falls to the Bank of England. The policy mix the economy needs is tighter fiscal policy and, in time, easier monetary policy, not the reverse.

The case for dipping into the buffer rests on a respectable piece of economics: borrowing should be used to absorb temporary shocks, while taxes and spending should adjust to permanent ones (Barro, 1979). Borrowing through a permanent shock, however, postpones the adjustment and makes it bigger. So the judgement call for the Chancellor is whether the shock he would be borrowing through will pass.

Our assessment is that part of shock to global yields will dissipate if there is a resolution to the conflict in the middle east. The ten-year gilt yield has risen by around 110 basis points since the conflict began in February, to about 5.4 per cent, its highest since 2007, and the rise has been global. Roughly a third of the UK move reflects higher inflation compensation and the policy rates expected to deal with it.

The rest is likely to prove persistent. The real rate the market prices for 2031 to 2036 has risen by 75 basis points in the UK and by almost 100 in the US. That is harder to square with a temporary energy shock story. It is easier to rationalise as a global shift in the real interest rate, driven by the AI investment boom and the scale of government borrowing everywhere, with a term premium on gilts that has been rising since July on top. Around two-thirds of the rise in borrowing costs, on this reckoning, is here to stay.

The interest rate on new government borrowing is now above the growth rate of the economy, which turns the debt arithmetic from a tailwind into a headwind: the primary surplus needed simply to hold the debt ratio steady has risen, and every pound borrowed at today’s rates adds to that bill. With interest rates at 5 per cent, say, and a primary deficit of -1.5 per cent of GDP, the economy would need to grow in cash terms by 6.5 per cent annually to keep debt stable.

None of this is certain of course. But standard frameworks for decision-making under uncertainty point to fiscal conservatism. A Bayesian would treat most of the move as persistent, because changes in real rates historically are. A robust control approach asks which mistake is worse: tightening now and finding that rates fall back is a reversible error. Borrowing more and finding that they stay high may be harder to reverse.

The environment in which the Budget will be delivered next week is not a forgiving one. Global bond markets are looking for the next weak link. Attention is on France today, but the UK has been there twice in four years, in autumn 2022 and January 2025, and its 10-year yield is already the highest in the G7. It is not hard to imagine how the UK could come under the bond market’s spotlights in the months ahead. The risk outlook has, in our judgement, deteriorated: adverse shocks are more likely than they were a year ago. These are circumstances in which to build fiscal buffers, not run them down.

The public share the concern. In our survey with Ipsos, 52 per cent think a severe loss of market confidence in the UK’s ability to repay its debt is likely within five years, and 16 per cent of which think it very likely. Those are sobering numbers.

There is also an opportunity here, and an asymmetry. A Budget that markets judged credible could take 10 to 20 basis points off gilt yields through a lower term premium, worth £1 to 2 billion a year by the end of the Parliament. A Budget that they did not could cost several times that: on the OBR’s own reckoner, a 50-basis point repricing adds around £6 billion a year to debt interest by the end of the decade. The downside is larger than the upside, and the buffer is the one thing in this the Chancellor controls.

Suppose the Chancellor does borrow more. The minimal test of credibility is whether higher borrowing through the third year of the forecast is matched by correspondingly lower borrowing in the years after it, so that the stock of debt (relative to GDP) returns to the path planned in March rather than settling on a higher one. Engineers call this approach “integral control”—monetary economists will recognise it as the difference between a price-level target, which claws back an overshoot, and an inflation target, under which bygones are bygones.

The figure below illustrates this strategic choice facing the Chancellor. Both borrowing paths meet the fiscal rules (which do not require integral control), but only one delivers the same debt reduction path planned in March.1

It is a minimal test because the plan it would be applied to is already back-loaded and already hard to believe. The March forecast requires the primary balance to improve by around £100 billion a year by the end of the decade, a swing from the current primary deficit of 1.5 per cent of GDP to a primary surplus of the same magnitude. Almost all of it comes after 2027, with the largest single step in 2029-30, the year of the latest possible general election. If borrowing costs remain elevated, the debt interest bill could be £11-17 billion higher by 2030-31, raising the surpluses required further still. And at today’s borrowing costs, this would do no more than hold the debt ratio at 95 per cent.

The record on delivering surpluses of that kind is shown below. With the exception of the forecasts made at the height of the pandemic, every OBR forecast since 2010 has shown a primary surplus within its horizon. None of them has arrived; the UJ has not run one since 2001.

There is a further risk to the plan. The March forecast and the Spending Review settlements were set before the conflict pushed up inflation. On unchanged plans, the same cash buys 2.1 per cent less by 2030 than departments were promised. The flip side is that higher inflation flatters the near-term public finances precisely because cash spending plans stand still while cash receipts rise, and the OBR’s Budget forecast is likely to show that gain. It is only real if the squeeze is delivered. The record suggests it will not be, and the pressure points are already visible: pay review bodies reporting against inflation above 4 per cent, and the calls to raise real spending on the NHS and defence.

Pulling this together, the case for higher borrowing at this Budget is thin. It rests on a gamble that that the Bank of England won’t respond to the fiscal stimulus by raising Bank Rate; that market yields will fall back to pre-conflict levels; that there are no further adverse shocks; and that the government will deliver a 2 per cent annual real spending squeeze on departmental budgets relative to what it promised a year ago.

It also seems blind to the scale of debt reduction the country needs to deliver over the medium term. On this, the public appear to have a better appreciation of the problem than is evident in political discourse. In our survey with Ipsos, 58 per cent expect further significant steps to reduce debt within five years, beyond what is already planned, and four in ten of those expect them only after the next election. Two-thirds expect higher taxes at this Budget. When half the sample was shown the facts on debt and debt interest, neither expectation moved, because people already knew. Voters are divided on how the adjustment should fall, between taxes and spending and between high earners, business and waste, which is why the conversation to have now is about its size and timing rather than how. The public, it seems, are ready for that conversation.

1 The current fiscal rules are analogous to inflation targets. The stability rule tests whether the current budget is in balance in the third year of the forecast; the investment rule tests whether the debt ratio is falling in that same year. Both are tests of a single year, and neither asks where the debt ratio is relative to where it was meant to be.
